items.title: A cellular view of seed development and germination.
items.abstract: Seeds are fundamental to global food security, yet their encapsulated structure, dense storage compounds, and spatial heterogeneity have created a "hidden box" problem, often restricting research to bulk and tissue approaches that mask cell type-specific regulatory programs. Advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics now enable systematic dissection of seed biology at cellular resolution. This review provides a cellular view spanning the developmental continuum from fertilization to seedling establishment by synthesizing single-cell and spatial transcriptomic studies in Arabidopsis thaliana and major crops (Oryza sativa-rice, Zea mays-maize, Hordeum vulgare-barley, Glycine max-soybean, Triticum aestivum-wheat). These technologies reveal previously undetected cellular complexity and heterogeneity: distinct transcriptional subpopulations within morphologically uniform tissues, specialized endosperm microdomains mediating nutrient transfer and metabolic polarity, cell type-specific genomic imprinting patterns, and spatially segregated hormone signaling hubs controlling dormancy and germination. Integration of transcriptional profiling with chromatin accessibility and transcription factor binding data has enabled construction of cell type-specific gene regulatory networks for seeds, advancing from correlation to causal inference and identifying master regulators of developmental transitions. These approaches illuminate how early embryonic patterning establishes transcriptional identities, how metabolic zonation coordinates storage compound accumulation and mobilization, how chromatin states maintain dormancy and license germination competence, and how spatiotemporal coordination integrates hormone signaling with energy metabolism across tissues. Single-cell and spatial approaches are establishing seeds not as opaque structures but as assemblies of coordinated cellular programs amenable to systematic analysis and targeted manipulation for crop improvement.
items.authors: He C, Auroux L, Lewsey M, Whelan J.

items.title: Comparison of whole-tree water transport and storage coordination in four tree species of contrasting hydraulic strategies.
items.abstract: Our knowledge about coordination of water transport at the whole-tree scale has been limited in its consideration of water storage and release from different tissues (i.e., sapwood and heartwood) along the xylem pathway. Here, we measured water transport and storage at spatially and temporally intensive scales in four tree species of contrasting hydraulic strategies (loblolly pine (Pinus taeda), southern red oak (Quercus falcata), Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), and trembling aspen (Populus tremuloides)) over the growing season in North Carolina (mesic) and Idaho (semi-arid), USA. We quantified the coordination of sap flow and volumetric water content at different heights along the main tree trunk and xylem tissue depths. Further, we investigated seasonal patterns of daily water storage and use in the different systems. Coordinated lags in sap flow between upper and lower heights along the trunk were present in all study species except oak. Whole-tree coordination of water transport and storage was more evident in the mesic system than in the semi-arid system. The angiosperm species displayed greater water storage use than the gymnosperm species in both systems, with water storage use patterns related to rain events in the mesic system and related to soil-moisture dry down in the semi-arid system. Our findings emphasize the importance of understanding water transport and storage at species- and ecosystem-specific levels inferred from spatially and temporally intensive tree measurements.
items.authors: Tucker LM, Reinhardt K, Johnson DM, Emanuel RE, Minick KJ, Bahramian J, Love DM, Rojas J.

items.title: Genome-wide characterization of DUB genes in Betula platyphylla and BpUBP3 function in pollen tube growth.
items.abstract: The ubiquitination/deubiquitination system is a key regulatory mechanism for maintaining proteome homeostasis in eukaryotic cells. Deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs), which remove ubiquitin from substrate proteins, regulate plant development, stress responses, and other physiological processes. Although DUBs have emerged as important regulators of plant growth and stress responses, their systematic genomic characterization in white birch (Betula platyphylla) remains limited, restricting our understanding of their potential roles in the reproduction of woody plants. In this study, 56 BpDUB genes were identified in white birch (Betula platyphylla) and classified into six conserved subfamilies (UBP, OTU, UCH, MJD, JAMM, and MINDY). Comparative and synteny analyses revealed that DUB genes are evolutionarily conserved while exhibiting lineage-specific divergence across angiosperms. Promoter analysis showed that BpDUBs harbor diverse cis-acting elements associated with growth and development, stress responses, hormone signaling, and transcription factor binding. Treatment with the broad-spectrum DUB inhibitor PR-619 markedly impaired both pollen germination and pollen tube elongation, supporting the involvement of DUB activity in pollen development. RNA-seq analysis showed that BpUBP3 exhibited stage-specific induction during pollen germination, and AS-ODN-mediated downregulation of BpUBP3 reduced pollen germination and pollen tube growth. These findings provide preliminary evidence supporting a role for BpUBP3 in pollen germination and pollen tube growth and provide a basis for further investigation of DUB functions in reproductive development in white birch.
items.authors: Wang X, Zhao C, Shi J, Mei Z, Jiang Y, Shi J, Lan X.

items.title: Characterization of the sexual reproductive process in the perennial tree Robinia pseudoacacia.
items.abstract: Sexual reproduction in perennial plants, especially woody species, remains poorly understood, and most studies have focused on annuals such as Arabidopsis thaliana. This gap hinders understanding of perennial reproductive processes and limits tree breeding. Here we characterized the sexual reproductive process of Robinia pseudoacacia, a perennial leguminous tree, and established standardized methods for studying its reproduction. We optimized cytological assays for pollen viability, in vitro germination, and pollen tube dynamics, achieving over 90% pollen viability and germination efficiency within 8 h. R. pseudoacacia pollen exhibited reproductive thermotolerance and maintained over 20% germination at 37 °C, a temperature lethal to A. thaliana pollen. This thermotolerance was associated with maintenance of stable plasma membrane integrity and an organized F-actin cytoskeleton. R. pseudoacacia pollen also germinated on A. thaliana stigmas, penetrated the styles, and targeted 3.6% of A. thaliana ovules, although post-zygotic incompatibility prevented seed formation. The ANX-RALF signaling module is conserved in R. pseudoacacia, and antisense oligodeoxynucleotide-mediated suppression of RpANX2 disrupted pollen tube growth. Moreover, aberrant pollen tube guidance was linked to its low seed set. These findings provide a systematic characterization of sexual reproduction in a perennial tree and establish methodological foundations for reproductive studies in woody perennials, with implications for tree breeding.
items.authors: Lin H, Wang XJ, Sun K, Yan CL, Guan KX, Feng T, Yang J, Luo K, Xu C, Meng JG.

items.title: Nodulation Signaling Pathway 2: A Proposed Multifunctional Signaling Hub for Coordinating Plant Architecture, Rhizosphere Chemistry, and Symbiotic Associations Under Nutrient Stress.
items.abstract: Under nutrient stress, plants adjust shoot branching, root remodeling, and symbiotic associations to optimize survival and growth. The GRAS-type transcription factor NODULATION SIGNALING PATHWAY 2 (NSP2) participates in these responses through context-dependent interactions with partners: NSP1, MYB40, and SLR1, and is indirectly repressed by SMAX1 via NSP1 and SLR1. NSP2 functions differ among species: it directly binds DNA in rice (Oryza sativa) strigolactone (SL) biosynthesis, whereas in M. truncatula it acts as a co-regulator in nodulation and flavonoid regulation, with NSP1 or MYB40 providing DNA-binding activity; the NSP2-MYB module also appears conserved in barley (Hordeum vulgare). Through these partnerships, NSP2 is proposed to coordinate three interconnected modules influencing plant architecture, rhizosphere chemistry, and symbiotic associations. The NSP1-NSP2 heterodimer activates SL biosynthesis under phosphate deficiency, remodeling root/shoot architecture and balancing N/P uptake in rice. The NSP1-NSP2-SLR1-SMAX1 quaternary module integrates phosphate, gibberellin, and karrikin signals to orchestrate arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis in rice. Under nitrogen limitation and rhizobial infection, the NSP2-MYB40 module enhances flavonoid biosynthesis to promote rhizobial nodulation in Medicago truncatula. These findings suggest that the NSP2-centered network could be targeted to improve nutrient-use efficiency, although further field validation is required.
items.authors: Wang Y, Zhao Y, Liu R, Wang S, Li Y.

items.title: Woody root and shoot xylem anatomy reveal patterns of whole-plant axial variation and suggest structure-function tradeoffs.
items.abstract: Plants must balance multiple functions across their large woody bodies, including water transport, biomechanical support, and storage. While vessel diameters within woody shoots have been intensively studied, woody roots compose a substantial portion of the plant body and remain comparatively understudied. Moreover, little is known about axial variation in xylem fibers and parenchyma. We excavated root systems of six Populus balsamifera L. spp. trichocarpa trees and examined xylem traits at 1-m increments from root tip to shoot tip. At each sampled location we measured several anatomical and functional traits. Anatomical traits included the percentage area of vessels, fibers, secondary wall area, and parenchyma; fiber diameter and wall thickness; vessel element diameter, wall thickness, and length; and inter-vessel pit area and density. Hydraulic functional traits included hydraulic conductivity and embolism resistance. Vessel diameter increased from organ apices toward the root-shoot junction in both roots and shoots, reaching maximum values in older root tissues. Model comparison strongly favored piecewise regressions over a single power-law relationship reflecting the inability of a single global scaling relationship to capture the pronounced structural transitions between root and shoot tissues. Axial trends for other traits differed between roots and shoots, resulting in unique combinations of vessel and non-vessel traits at each position along the tree axis. Across the plant axis, roots exhibited higher vessel and parenchyma fractions and lower fiber fractions than shoots, whereas shoots showed greater secondary wall investment. Structural and functional traits were highly correlated with one another, with roots generally showing higher hydraulic conductivity and greater embolism vulnerability relative to shoots. Together, these results show that whole-plant xylem structure is highly coordinated yet strongly divergent across different regions of the large woody plant body. Whole-plant xylem structure and function, especially that of woody roots, is essential to our understanding of whole-plant structure and function.
items.authors: Jacobsen AL, Rodriguez-Zaccaro FD, Percolla MI, Fickle JC, Robles C, Bear A, Valdovinos-Ayala J, Pratt RB.

items.title: β-Carbonic anhydrase SlβCA4 is required for normal growth, carbon assimilation and stomatal plasticity in tomato
items.abstract: β-Carbonic anhydrases (βCAs) catalyze the reversible interconversion of CO 2 and bicarbonate and contribute to plant carbon metabolism and environmental responses. However, the physiological functions of individual βCA isoforms in crops remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated two chloroplast-localized βCAs, SlβCA1 and SlβCA4, in tomato ( Solanum lycopersicum ). We combined subcellular localization, CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis, grafting, leaf gas-exchange measurements, and controlled environmental treatments to examine their roles in growth, photosynthesis, and stomatal developmental plasticity. Both proteins localized to chloroplasts but their disruption resulted in markedly different phenotypes. While SlβCA1 mutants showed largely normal growth and photosynthesis, SlβCA4 mutants exhibited severe root and shoot growth defects. Grafting mutant shoots onto wild-type rootstocks partially restored vegetative growth, indicating that impaired root function contributes to the growth defects. SlβCA4 mutants also showed reduced CO 2 assimilation and stomatal conductance, while electron transport remained largely unaffected. Elevated CO 2 partially improved leaflet growth but did not restore plant height or root elongation. Furthermore, unlike wild-type plants, SlβCA4 mutants failed to increase stomatal index in response to elevated temperature. These findings reveal distinct physiological roles for chloroplast-localized βCAs in tomato and identify SlβCA4 as an important contributor to plant growth, photosynthesis, and temperature-dependent stomatal developmental plasticity.
items.authors: Meyers, O., Stern Tal, M., Singh, J., Nagar, Y., Biton, I., Yarran, A., Kutsher, Y., Zait, Y., Nir, I.

items.title: Roles and mechanisms of halophilic/salt-tolerant microorganisms in mitigating plant salt stress and promoting growth.
items.abstract: Soil salinization is a major constraint on global agricultural productivity and food security, largely because excess salts disrupt osmotic balance, nutrient acquisition, ion homeostasis, and redox stability in plants. Halophilic and salt-tolerant microorganisms, including plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, endophytes, and fungi, have emerged as promising biological tools for improving crop performance in saline environments. This review synthesizes current evidence on how these microorganisms mitigate salt stress and promote plant growth across diverse crop systems. The major mechanisms include modulation of phytohormone homeostasis, especially through auxin production and ACC deaminase activity; enhanced nutrient acquisition via nitrogen fixation, phosphate solubilization, and siderophore production; maintenance of ionic balance through reduced Na+ toxicity and improved K+/Na+ homeostasis; reinforcement of antioxidant defense systems; stimulation of osmolyte accumulation; and effective rhizosphere colonization through exopolysaccharide secretion and biofilm formation. Representative studies in rice, wheat, maize, tomato, soybean, cucumber, chickpea, common bean, quinoa, and banana consistently show improvements in germination, biomass, physiological resilience, and, in some cases, yield under salinity stress. However, important challenges remain, including strain specificity, inconsistent field performance, limited mechanistic resolution, ecological safety concerns, and the difficulty of translating laboratory strains into stable commercial products. Future progress will depend on multi-omics-guided mechanism dissection, precision microbiome engineering, improved formulation and delivery systems, and rigorous long-term field validation. Overall, halophilic/salt-tolerant microorganisms represent a promising strategy for saline agriculture and sustainable crop production.
items.authors: Cheng Z, Rong P.

items.title: The genome sequence of Net-leaved Willow, Salix reticulata L. (Malpighiales: Salicaceae)
items.abstract: We present a genome assembly of Salix reticulata (Net-leaved Willow; Streptophyta; Magnoliopsida; Malpighiales; Salicaceae). The assembly consists of two haplotypes with total lengths of 396.19 megabases and 393.95 megabases. Most of the haplotype 1 assembly (89.89%) was scaffolded into 19 chromosomal pseudomolecules. Haplotype 2 was assembled to scaffold level. The mitochondrial genome assembly has a length of 643.14 kilobases and the plastid genome assembly has a length of 155.5 kilobases. This assembly was generated as part of the Darwin Tree of Life project, which produces reference genomes for eukaryotic species found in Britain and Ireland.

items.title: Specialized Metabolites in Cereal Crops Under Abiotic Stress: Regulatory Mechanisms, Functional Validation, and Breeding Implications.
items.abstract: Cereal crops increasingly encounter drought, salinity and alkalinity, heat, waterlogging, potentially toxic elements, and compound stresses that constrain productivity and grain quality. Secondary metabolites, also referred to as specialized metabolites in the recent literature, represent a dynamic component of cereal stress adaptation rather than a passive catalogue of stress markers. This review aims to synthesize current evidence on how specialized-metabolite pathways contribute to abiotic stress responses in cereals, with particular emphasis on regulatory mechanisms, evidence strength, chemical form, subcellular localization, recovery, and translational relevance. We critically assess evidence from transcriptomics, metabolomics, genetic perturbation, biochemical assays, multi-omics integration, and physiological studies across major cereal crops and evaluate evidence according to causal, associative, and in vitro categories. The evidence reveals that perturbations at the plasma membrane, cell wall, chloroplast, mitochondrion, and endomembrane system levels generate reactive oxygen species, Ca2+ signatures, phospholipid signals, and hormone changes that are decoded by CDPK/CPK, CBL-CIPK, SnRK2, and MAPK cascades. These signaling networks converge on MYB-bHLH-WD40, WRKY, NAC, ERF/AP2, HSF, and bZIP regulators and redirect carbon and reducing power through phenylpropanoid, flavonoid, lignin, carotenoid, terpenoid, benzoxazinoid, cyanogenic, and related pathways. Comparative analysis across rice (Oryza sativa L.), wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), maize (Zea mays L.), barley (Hordeum vulgare L.), oat (Avena sativa L.), sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L.), and millets shows conserved regulatory features but substantial crop-, genotype-, tissue-, developmental-stage-, and dose-dependent variation. Functional evidence further indicates that enzyme activity, chemical modification, transport, and subcellular compartmentation can determine whether metabolites contribute to ROS buffering, photosynthetic and membrane protection, cell-wall reinforcement, osmotic or ionic homeostasis, toxic-ion sequestration, or signaling. The review also identifies important limitations in current research, including overreliance on associative omics evidence, insufficient consideration of combined stresses and rehydration, growth-defence trade-offs, and limited field and reproductive-stage validation. To distinguish growth dilution from genuine biosynthetic increases, absolute metabolite content per grain or organ should be measured alongside concentration per unit dry weight. We conclude that improving cereal resilience requires context-dependent and experimentally validated coordination of regulators, biosynthetic enzymes, chemical modification, transport, and compartmentation rather than indiscriminate elevation of total specialized-metabolite concentration.
items.authors: Shah MA, Azeem I, Ullah R, Ahmad H, Liaqat W, Jan MF.

items.title: Cross-species transcriptomic plasticity and root architectural adaptations in Brachypodium (Brachypodium distachyon) and barley (Hordeum vulgare) genotypes under different ammonium and nitrate availability.
items.abstract: Nitrogen (N) form and availability shape the root phenotype by altering the root transcriptome and modulating root system architecture. However, it remains unclear whether these N-responsive architectural traits and their underlying regulatory networks are conserved or divergent between closely related grass species. Here, we compared root architectural and transcriptomic responses to nitrate and ammonium supply in Brachypodium distachyon and eight barley (Hordeum vulgare) genotypes under N starvation, optimal N supply, and high-N conditions. High-resolution root phenotyping revealed contrasting species-specific responses to N form. Barley generally showed enhanced lateral root elongation under nitrate but reduced total root length and limited lateral root proliferation under ammonium, indicating ammonium sensitivity. In contrast, B. distachyon maintained greater root architectural plasticity under ammonium, producing a highly branched and thinner root system. Cross-species module preservation and gene regulatory network analyses identified conserved hub genes, including FERONIA, peroxidase-like genes, CuAO-like genes, aspartyl proteases, and PEPC1-associated modules, as potential integrators of N signaling and root architectural remodeling in barley and B. distachyon. Taken together, our findings indicate that the two Pooideae species share conserved regulatory components but deploy them within distinct network contexts, leading to divergent root strategies in response to nitrate and ammonium. Ultimately, these results provide candidate genes and regulatory modules for improving root plasticity and N use efficiency in cereals.
items.authors: Rouina H, Singh D, Arlt C, Marshall-Colon A, Stich B.

items.title: Light modulates organ-specific gibberellin-abscisic acid crosstalk during drought response in Arabidopsis thaliana.
items.abstract: Main conclusionContinuous blue light enhances drought tolerance in Arabidopsis by modulating ABA and GA pathways, whilst controlled GA catabolism, especially via GA2ox7/8, is important for stomatal regulation and drought adaptation. In response to drought, plants undergo physiological and developmental adjustments to reduce water loss and survive the stress, including reduced shoot growth, altered root architecture, and stomatal closure. These processes are regulated by phytohormones, including gibberellins (GAs), which mediate growth adjustments, and abscisic acid (ABA), which promotes stomatal closure. In addition, light signalling plays a crucial role in plant adaptation to drought. Here, we investigated how progressive water restriction affects hormone levels, gene expression, and leaf temperature in Arabidopsis thaliana shoots and roots under two contrasting light regimes: white light under short-day and continuous low-intensity blue light, with a focus on GA and ABA signalling pathways. The hormonal contribution to the drought response was investigated by analysis of ABA and GA mutants. Plants grown under continuous blue light experienced less-drought stress compared with white light as reflected in growth performance and differential gene expression. Drought increased ABA levels in leaves and roots, with stronger accumulation in roots under both light conditions. By contrast, GA production was decreased in leaves and increased in roots under drought in white light, but with little change in blue light. The change in GA status in leaves was associated with down-regulation of GA-biosynthetic 20-OXIDASE genes and up-regulation of GA-catabolic 2-OXIDASE genes (AtGA2ox6, AtGA2ox9). ABA- and GA-deficient mutants were unaffected by water restriction, whilst GA-overproducers lacking GA2ox genes or overexpressing AtGA20ox1 were hypersensitive to drought, with the C20-GA2ox genes GA2ox7 and GA2ox8 proving particularly critical with compromised stomatal regulation.
items.authors: Miksteinová T, Szecówka M, Petřík I, Urbanová T, Trávníčková T, Špundová M, Fellner M, Hedden P.

items.title: Mulberry-soybean intercropping reshapes rhizosphere metabolites and microbiota alongside enhanced soybean nodulation.
items.abstract: Woody perennial-legume intercropping may improve nitrogen-use efficiency, but the belowground links among root-zone configuration, soybean nodulation, rhizosphere chemistry, microbial assembly and nitrogen movement remain unclear. We conducted a greenhouse pot experiment with soybean monoculture (Mono-S), mulberry monoculture (Mono-M), full-contact mulberry-soybean intercropping (Int), and root-separated intercropping with a 30 μm nylon-mesh barrier (Int + B). Physiological and N-related traits were assessed with six pot-level biological replicates, whereas untargeted rhizosphere metabolomics, bacterial full-length 16S rRNA profiling and fungal full-length ITS profiling used three pot-level replicates per treatment-plant component. Relative to Mono-S, Int increased soybean total nodule number by 12.3%, nitrogenase activity by 21.6%, whole-plant N accumulation by 9.1% and shoot dry weight by 26.5%. GmNIN and GmENOD40 transcript abundance was 2.60- and 2.22-fold higher, respectively, in Int-S than in Mono-S. Metabolomics revealed broad, host-specific treatment-associated shifts across multiple chemical classes, while selected putatively annotated soybean isoflavonoids and mulberry flavonoids showed contrasting response patterns. Host-specific PERMANOVA revealed significant differences in bacterial and fungal community composition. 15N label applied to soybean-side soil was recovered in mulberry roots, stems and leaves under both intercropping configurations, indicating recovery of soil-applied 15N label in mulberry. Mean land equivalent ratios exceeded 1 in both treatments and differed significantly. Cross-omics associations were largely treatment-structured, highlighting the need for targeted validation of specific metabolite-microbe relationships. Overall, full root-zone continuity was associated with the strongest coordinated soybean symbiotic and growth responses, while both intercropping configurations produced distinct rhizosphere restructuring. These findings provide a framework for understanding rhizosphere-mediated interactions in woody perennial-legume intercropping systems.
items.authors: Liu C, Li J, Zhu K, Liu G, Liu J, Zou J, Huang G.

items.title: The point of disconnection: early-drought fine root shrinkage is driven by plant water use in Pinus radiata.
items.abstract: Understanding the root-soil interface is essential for determining when plants become hydraulically isolated from their soil environment during drought. Emerging evidence suggests roots shrink substantially during dehydration, but the drivers and water-flow implications remain elusive, with few data linking shrinkage across soil and plant water status. Using Pinus radiata, a widespread isohydric conifer, we use synchrotron-based Micro-CT to scan intact roots < 2.5 mm in soil during mild plant drying (prior to embolism) to isolate relationships between shrinkage, soil (Ψsoil) and xylem (Ψplant) water potential. Fine roots in situ began shrinking during the earliest stages of Ψplant drying (-0.2 MPa to -0.88 MPa), losing 14.8 ± 10.3% initial transverse-sectional area (62% of observed shrinkage) prior to incipient soil drying (0-72 kPa Ψsoil). Ψplant was a significantly better predictor of shrinkage than Ψsoil, showing a linear shrinkage-Ψplant relationship across this early drying gradient when normalised to shrinkage at -1 MPa, accounting for variable initial Ψplant. Ψplant decline was linearly coordinated with cortical lacunae formation. This Ψplant-driven pattern identifies root shrinkage as an essential component of plant hydraulic function during commonly experienced water potential gradients, occurring long prior to stomatal closure and xylem embolism. This reveals water use from cortical tissues as a key physiological process defining plant-soil disconnection during water deficit.
items.authors: Harrison Day BL, Zhou Y, Tonet V, Huang R, Midson A, Choat B.

items.title: Short-Rotation Coppice Pellets as Biofuels in a Modern Boiler with an Electrostatic Precipitator: Particulate Matter and Carbon Monoxide Emissions.
items.abstract: Alternative pellet feedstocks must be evaluated for energy performance and air pollutant emissions. This study assessed particulate matter (PM) and carbon monoxide (CO) emissions from short-rotation coppice (SRC) pellets combusted in a pellet boiler equipped with an electrostatic precipitator (ESP). Pine and birch pellets served as references. Emissions were measured with and without the ESP and expressed per flue gas volume, fuel energy, and fuel mass. Pellet species significantly affected PM and CO, whereas the ESP significantly reduced PM but did not significantly affect CO. The ESP reduced mean PM concentrations by 52.5%, from 53.81 to 25.54 mg m-3. The highest PM concentration occurred for willow without the ESP (90.96 mg m-3), and the lowest for pine with the ESP (17.51 mg m-3); the highest value was 419.5% greater. Poplar produced relatively low PM but the highest CO emissions. Among SRC fuels, black locust provided the most balanced profile, combining relatively low PM and CO with the highest combustion efficiency (93.20%). Pine and birch, particularly with the ESP, produced the lowest emissions. These findings indicate that SRC pellets showed emission suitability for use in the tested boiler based on PM and CO emission levels.
items.authors: Warmiński K, Dudziec P, Nocoń A, Stolarski MJ.

items.title: The genome sequence of the Dwarf Willow, Salix herbacea L. (Malpighiales: Salicaceae).
items.abstract: We present a genome assembly of Salix herbacea (Dwarf Willow; Streptophyta; Magnoliopsida; Malpighiales; Salicaceae). The primary assembly has a total length of 421.43 megabases. Most of the primary assembly (92.79%) is scaffolded into 19 chromosomal pseudomolecules. The mitochondrial genome assembly has a length of 692.62 kilobases and the plastid genome assembly has a length of 155.63 kilobases. This assembly was generated as part of the Darwin Tree of Life project, which produces reference genomes for eukaryotic species found in Britain and Ireland.
items.authors: Ruhsam M, Hollingsworth PM, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh Genome Acquisition Lab, Plant Genome Sizing Collective, Darwin Tree of Life Barcoding collective, Wellcome Sanger Institute Tree of Life Management, Samples and Laboratory team, Wellcome Sanger Institute Scientific Operations: Sequencing Operations, Wellcome Sanger Institute Tree of Life Core Informatics team, Tree of Life Core Informatics collective, Darwin Tree of Life Consortium.

items.title: Mammalian phosphodiesterase inhibitors reveal a role for cAMP in plant cell reprogramming toward embryogenesis in crop and forest species.
items.abstract: Somatic embryogenesis is an example of plant cell totipotency and an essential tool for plant breeding and biotechnology, yet its low efficiency remains a major limitation in many species. Although 3', 5'-cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) is increasingly recognized as a signaling molecule in plants, its role in developmental cell reprogramming is unknown. Here, we investigated whether pharmacological modulation of cAMP homeostasis using small-molecule inhibitors of mammalian phosphodiesterases (PDEs) could increase the rate of cell reprogramming towards embryogenesis in plants. Four structurally diverse PDE inhibitors were evaluated in three embryogenesis systems: microspore embryogenesis of Brassica napus and Hordeum vulgare, and somatic embryogenesis of Quercus suber. PDE inhibitors quantitatively enhanced cell reprogramming and initiation of embryogenesis in all three species, whereas structurally-related inactive analogues did not. Biochemical analyses demonstrated that treatment with the representative PDE7 inhibitor TC2.43 significantly increased cAMP levels, providing functional evidence that PDE inhibition modulates cAMP homeostasis in plant embryogenic cultures. Increased cAMP level was accompanied by increased expression of key embryogenesis regulators (FUS3, LEC2 and SERK1-like) and auxin biosynthesis and signaling genes (TAA1/TAR2 and ARF5), suggesting that cAMP signaling would be integrated into the molecular network controlling embryogenic competence acquisition. These findings on three evolutionarily distant angiosperms, two crops and a forest tree, suggest that the embryogenesis-promoting effects of PDE inhibition would be conserved across diverse taxa. Moreover, they identify changes in cAMP levels as a new player in embryogenic induction and suggest mammalian PDE inhibitors as promising chemical additives for improving in vitro plant regeneration.
items.authors: Pérez-Pérez Y, Carneros E, Rueda-Varela C, García-Rubia A, Martínez A, Gil C, Testillano PS.

items.title: Conspecific density enhances sound seed production during high-seed years in European beech
items.abstract: Climate change is reducing the supply of sound seeds available for forest regeneration, creating a need to identify management strategies that can counteract these losses. Managing local tree density offers one potential approach, as neighbouring trees can enhance pollination but also increase losses to seed predators. In masting species, which produce highly variable but synchronised seed crops, the balance between these benefits and costs may depend on annual reproductive effort. Here, using seeds collected beneath 314 European beech (Fagus sylvatica) trees across three stands in Poland and the United Kingdom over three years, we examined how conspecific density within 5–50 m buffers influenced pollination efficiency, pre-dispersal seed predation, sound seed production, and seed mass. During the high-seed year, predicted sound seed production increased almost 2-fold from low to high conspecific density, coinciding with a tendency for seed predation to decline with increasing density. In contrast, during low-seed years, seed predation increased with density, while pollination efficiency increased with density in one of two years. Mean seed mass decreased by approximately 9% with density in a high-seed year. These findings suggest that dense neighbourhoods can increase the number of sound seeds available for regeneration when their predation costs are weakened by high seed production. Future studies should determine whether greater seed supply outweighs reduced seed mass in its effects on seedling establishment and survival. Maintaining higher local densities of reproductive trees may therefore help sustain sound seed supply during mast events and partly buffer the consequences of masting breakdown for European beech regeneration.
items.authors: Kondrat K, Szymkowiak J, Barczyk M, Eichert U, Jerzyńska P, Bogdańska M, Foest J, Ryczkowski P, Hacket-Pain A, Bogdziewicz M.

items.title: Manipulation of the PtWOX11-PagKNAT2/6b Module Bidirectionally Regulates Petiole Traits in Populus.
items.abstract: Canopy architecture is a critical determinant of productivity in crops and trees, with leaf positioning being a key factor. Petiole length and angle govern leaf positioning and light interception in many flowering plants, yet the molecular mechanisms that coordinately regulate these two traits in woody plants remain largely unexplored. Here, we show that a transcriptional module in poplar enables bidirectional control over petiole length and angle. Petiole morphogenesis entails a developmental transition from a meristematic state to a differentiation state, a process blocked by the class I KNOX transcription factor PagKNAT2/6b. Using yeast one-hybrid, electrophoretic mobility shift assays, chromatin affinity purification and transient expression assays in tobacco leaves, we provide evidence that WUSCHEL-RELATED HOMEOBOX 11 (PtWOX11) binds the PagKNAT2/6b promoter in vitro and transactivates it in heterologous systems. Transcriptomic and qPCR analyses reveal that PtWOX11 maintains a meristematic transcriptional program and suppresses differentiation genes, including those for cell expansion and wall thickening. Accordingly, overexpression of PtWOX11 produces compact petioles with upright leaf angles, whereas its dominant repression yields hyperelongated petioles with reduced leaf angles. Together, these findings suggest a mechanistic framework for manipulating petiole traits and offer a potential strategy for modifying canopy architecture in bioenergy poplar.
items.authors: Liu B, Li J, Yan X, Zhang J, Xin G, Zhang L, Lu MZ, He D, Zhang D, Zhao Y, Wang X.

items.title: Genome-wide identification of the TIFY gene family in Sorghum bicolor and functional characterization of SbTIFY9 in salt stress tolerance.
items.abstract: The TIFY gene family is a plant-specific group of transcriptional regulators characterized by a conserved TIFY domain (TIF[F/Y]XG), participating in plant development, phytohormone signaling and abiotic stress responses. In this study, 21 SbTIFY genes were genome-widely identified in sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L.). According to phylogeny and protein structures, SbTIFY proteins were grouped into JAZ and ZML subfamilies, and the JAZ subfamily was further divided into five clades. These proteins contain 101-429 amino acids and are unevenly distributed across six chromosomes. Genes from the same subgroup possess similar exon-intron structures and conserved motifs. Promoter analysis uncovered abundant cis-elements associated with hormone signaling, stress responses and developmental processes. Synteny analysis detected seven orthologous pairs between sorghum and Arabidopsis, and 25 pairs between sorghum and rice (Oryza sativa). Expression profiling revealed that multiple SbTIFY members exhibited differential expression across developmental organs and under stresses including anthracnose infection, cold, heat, flooding, and salt. SbTIFY9 displayed strong induction under multiple stresses: its transcript level increased approximately 10-fold at 12 h and approximately 31-fold at 24 h of salt treatment, implying its vital function in salt response. Subcellular localization confirmed SbTIFY9 resides mainly in the nucleus. Heterologous overexpression of SbTIFY9 in Arabidopsis improved true leaf expansion, fresh weight at germination, and root growth and biomass at seedling stage under 125 and 150 mM NaCl, demonstrating its positive role in salt tolerance. This work provides insights into the evolution and stress functions of sorghum TIFY family.
items.authors: Chen Z, Chen S, Ding Y, Yang W, Lu J, An Y, Li C, Xu J, Li K, Ren M.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Ex Vitro Genetic Transformation and Regeneration of Populus.
items.abstract: Genetic transformation is a powerful tool in the realm of plant sciences, enabling the study of endogenous and heterologous genes and conferring novel traits to transformed plant species, notably in crop species of agricultural importance. The ability to genetically transform plants has historically been contingent upon the development of tissue culture methods for the species of interest, a significant technical limitation due to the recalcitrance of many plant species in tissue culture. Recent advances in molecular techniques and biotechnological resources have facilitated the development of methods that enable the genetic transformation of plants without the need for tissue culture. In this study, we have developed a method to transform the model tree system Populus using Agrobacterium rhizogenes carrying the RUBY visual marker gene as well as methods to regenerate whole transgenic plants, all with a tissue culture-free protocol. This method greatly simplifies the genetic transformation procedure for the poplar model system and could potentially be applied to other tree species that lack developed tissue culture protocols.
items.authors: Carlson E, Newhouse A.

items.title: [Identification of SPS family genes and regulation of photosynthetic pigment stability by PthSPS1/2/3 in Populus cv.741].
items.abstract: Solanesyl diphosphate synthases (SPSs), are key enzymes in the isoprenoid metabolic pathway, catalyze the biosynthesis of solanesyl diphosphate (SPP). In plants, the SPS family includes geranyl diphosphate synthase (GPS), farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FPS), geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase (GGPPS), and SPS, catalyzing the stepwise condensation to form SPP. SPP is involved in the biosynthesis of solanesol and plastoquinone (PQ), both of which play important roles in plant growth, development, and the regulation of photosynthesis. Here, to elucidate the functions of the SPS subfamily in woody plants, we took 'Poplar 741' [Populus. alba×(Populus. davidiana+Populus. simonii)×Populus. tomentosa] as the experimental material. A total of 29 family members distributed across four subfamilies-PthSPS/PthFPS/PthGPS/PthGGPPS-related to the isoprenoid pathway were identified at the genome-wide level, located on 8 chromosome groups. Among them, 24 members were localized to chloroplasts and 5 to the cytoplasm. Three highly homologous PthSPSs were predicted as unstable hydrophilic proteins in chloroplasts. Subsequently, PthSPS1/2/3-edited mutant regenerated plants of 'Poplar 741' were generated via the CRISPR/Cas9 system. Phenotypic observation revealed three phenotypes: albino, green, and chimeric. PCR identification and sequencing analysis confirmed insertions and deletions (indels) at the target sites of PthSPS1/2/3. Physiological and biochemical analyses showed that the content of SPP, chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, and carotenoids were significantly lower in the albino mutants (pthsps1/2/3) than in the wild type, indicating that PthSPS1/2/3 regulated the stability of photosynthetic pigments. These results provide a new direction for further dissecting the roles of the isoprenoid metabolic pathway in photosynthesis, growth, and development of woody plants.
items.authors: Xu Z, Wang Z, Xu Y, Zhang X, Tang Y, Jiang H, Wu J.
items.journal: Sheng wu gong cheng xue bao = Chinese journal of biotechnology

items.title: Condition Monitoring of Standing Trees Based on Dendro-Acoustic Emissions
items.abstract: In the areas of road safety, fruit growing and forestry, there is an increased need for assessing the vitality of standing trees. Various dendro-acoustic emissions (DAEs) potentially allow conclusions to be drawn about the vitality of the trees and various diseases and pest infestations. All types of DAE events produce structure-borne sound inside the tree and can be automatically measured and evaluated by a piezoelectric sensor node attached to the tree trunk. The events are characterized by short, broadband cracking signals. Depending on the type of event, these differ in their number, strength and acoustic center frequency and can be separated from various types of background noise such as traffic, wind, rain, etc. In the frame of a German collaborative research project (TreeMon), an autonomous sensor prototype for long- and short-term monitoring using LoRaWAN technology was developed and successfully tested in the field. We present selected results of various test and field measurements at different trees, including several hardwood species like beech, birch and fruit trees. We compare temporal DAE profiles of single trees with simultaneously recorded weather, dendrometer and sap flow data and demonstrate first interesting correlations between them.
items.authors: Schubert F, Duckhorn F, Reinhold M, Kühmstedt M, Zange C, Hennig C, Hopfner M, Wilhelms A, Scharff C, Walther S, Scharff W, Binder M, Georgi R.

items.title: Phloem-Limited Disease Impacts Citrus Carbohydrate Dynamics Distinctly from Source-Sink Manipulation
items.abstract: Source-sink dynamics are defined by the interdependence of source and sink tissues and are key determinants of plant growth and productivity. This dynamic can, be altered by disease. One example is huanglongbing (HLB), a phloem-limited disease that impacts several economically important tree species by disrupting carbon partitioning and altering source-sink relationships. Though HLB is widespread in citrus, the specific mechanism in which phloem disruption impacts the co-regulation of carbon dynamics from source to sink has not been fully described. To address this, we took advantage of a natural study under field conditions, in which infected and uninfected trees were growing in the same field. After identifying trees that were uninfected, infected with symptoms, or infected without symptoms, we manipulated source:sink ratio by girdling branches and defoliating at 0%, 50%, and 75% of the original leaf area per fruit, while leaving a control treatment with no defoliation or girdling and used fruits as the sink of interest. We measured gas exchange, biomass, and non-structural carbohydrates in leaves, stems and fruits in response to these treatments. Our results show that leaf photosynthetic responses to HLB were primarily driven by stomatal regulation rather than biochemical limitations. HLB increased leaf dark respiration without altering the relationship between respiration and leaf soluble sugars. Among the plant organs, stem starch reserves were the most responsive to source-sink manipulation and were strongly correlated with multiple carbon pools and biomass in both fruits and leaves. Although HLB altered fruit carbon dynamics, it did not change fruit responses to source-sink manipulation. Overall, HLB affects source and sink tissues independently of the experimental source-sink manipulation. The stem serves as a transient carbon reserve and is sensitive to both HLB and source-sink manipulation. These findings raise further questions regarding total carbon fluxes and the importance of feedback inhibition of photosynthesis.
items.authors: Alade, D. O., Gersony, J., Levy, A., Vincent, C.

items.title: ABA and Stomatal Biology: From Transcriptional and Biosynthesis to Multicellular Coordination Across Cell Types.
items.abstract: Abscisic acid (ABA) was first identified in plants over six decades ago and is now recognized as one of the central phytohormones in plants, regulating growth, development, and physiological adaptation to environmental changes. In this Centennial Update, we use two influential ABA-related articles published in Plant Physiology in the early 2000s and discuss complementary advances in stress-responsive transcription and ABA biosynthetic regulation. We extend the Update from ABA-relevant gene discovery to recent advances in multicellular coordination of stomatal control. Growing evidence supports the view that ABA-regulated stomatal movement and gas exchange are coordinated across multiple cell types, including guard cells, mesophyll cells, bundle sheath cells, and vascular tissues in roots and leaves. We also highlight emerging tools to dissect this ABA-mediated multicellular network by using emerging technologies in single-cell and spatial omics, plant optogenetics, and artificial intelligence (AI). These advances will shape ABA research from single cell models toward multicellular collaborative networks for understanding plant-environment interactions. Together, this article links the history of ABA research with emerging single-cell resolution datasets and AI-assisted computational approaches, proposing a framework for moving ABA biology from well-established guard-cell signaling models toward a broader understanding of multicellular ABA coordination.
items.authors: Xu B, Chen ZH.

items.title: Genetic architecture and genomic prediction of stem forking across two generations of loblolly pine (Pinus taeda L.)
items.abstract: Abstract Stem forking, assessed as a binary trait, is an important defect in Pinus taeda (loblolly pine) that reduces timber quality and product value. We investigated its genetic architecture and prediction accuracy using data from a two-generation breeding population evaluated in multi-environment trials. Genetic parameters were estimated using animal and family models with conditional penalized quasi-likelihood (PQL) and marginal PQL. We conducted genome-wide association and family-based linkage mapping to identify QTL. Individual-tree heritability on the latent scale was low (0.09–0.13), whereas family-mean heritability was high (0.93), indicating significant additive genetic control at the family mean level, but substantial environmental effect at the tree level. The probit PQL models produced slightly higher heritability estimates, whereas logistic and marginal models produced similar estimates. Association and linkage analyses identified a significant lineage-specific QTL on linkage group 3 but fitting it as a fixed covariate did not improve prediction accuracy. Across-generation family-level predictive ability was moderate (0.40). Forking had modest additive genetic correlations with tree height (0.36) and stem diameter (0.24). These results indicated that the underlying (unobserved) inheritance of stem forking in P. taeda is polygenic, while its expression among individual trees is strongly influenced by environmental and developmental factors. Response to genomic selection at the family level will be effective in reducing stem forking, while prediction of outcome for individual trees remains challenging.
items.authors: Guner P, Shalizi MN, Walker TD, Isik F.

items.title: Definition of RING gene family in sugar beet (Beta vulgaris L.) and functional characterization of BvRING-HCa-9 in plant salt stress tolerance.
items.abstract: BackgroundRING-type E3 ligases are key enzymes in protein ubiquitination modification and crucial regulators in plant growth and development. However, their roles in sugar beet (Beta vulgaris L.) remain unclear. To determine the types and distribution of RING-type proteins in sugar beet, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the RING family genes. By analyzing RING gene expression profiles under salt stress, a candidate gene (BvRING-HCa-9) associated with salt stress was identified. The goal is to characterize the functions of the sugar beet RING gene family in plant salt stress tolerance.ResultsA total of 446 RING-type proteins in the sugar beet genome were identified. The coding genes are distributed across all nine chromosomes, with varying expression patterns among subtypes. Collinearity and Ka/Ks analyses suggest that the RING family in sugar beet has undergone limited duplication events and is under strong purifying selection, indicating evolutionary conservation. Many BvRING genes are transcriptionally responsive to salt stress. Among them, BvRING-HCa-9 possesses ubiquitin E3 ligase activity and is localized in the nucleus and plasma membrane. Overexpression of BvRING-HCa-9 in transgenic Arabidopsis enhanced salt tolerance.ConclusionThe 446 RING-domain genes in sugar beet are evolutionarily conserved, and majority of the genes are transcriptionally responsive to salt stress. Among them, BvRING-HCa-9 was characterized to encode a E3 ligase and it plays an important role in plant salt tolerance. These findings provide a valuable resource for functional studies of other RING family genes in plant stress resilience.
items.authors: Jiang X, Wang S, Bing Y, Ma C, Chen S, Wang Y, Li H.

items.title: The genome sequence of the Silver Birch, Betula pendula Roth (Fagales: Betulaceae).
items.abstract: We present a genome assembly of Betula pendula (Silver Birch; Streptophyta; Magnoliopsida; Fagales; Betulaceae). The assembly consists of two haplotypes with total lengths of 403.47 megabases and 411.74 megabases. Most of the haplotype 1 assembly (99.95%) was scaffolded into 14 chromosomal pseudomolecules. Haplotype 2 was assembled to scaffold level. The mitochondrial genome assembly has a length of 743.77 kilobases and the plastid genome assembly has a length of 160.61 kilobases. Gene annotation of the haplotype 1 assembly by Ensembl identified 29,794 protein-coding genes. This assembly was generated as part of the Darwin Tree of Life project, which produces reference genomes for eukaryotic species found in Britain and Ireland.
items.authors: Christenhusz MJM, Royal Botanic Gardens Kew Genome Acquisition Lab, Plant Genome Sizing Collective, Darwin Tree of Life Barcoding collective, Wellcome Sanger Institute Tree of Life Management, Samples and Laboratory team, Wellcome Sanger Institute Scientific Operations: Sequencing Operations, Wellcome Sanger Institute Tree of Life Core Informatics team, Tree of Life Core Informatics collective, Darwin Tree of Life Consortium.

items.title: Leaf-to-root ROS signaling recruits rhizosphere Bacillus: a synbiotic mechanism for rice adaptability under foliar Cd stress.
items.abstract: In paddy fields near mining sites or transport corridors, elevated foliar cadmium (Cd) exposure is an emerging threat to rice (Oryza sativa) production. While rice recruits beneficial rhizosphere microbes against environmental stress, how this recruitment is coordinated under foliar Cd stress remains elusive. We assessed physiological responses to foliar Cd exposure in 26 rice cultivars and characterized rhizosphere bacterial communities and root exudates in six representative cultivars. Foliar Cd reduced leaf biomass by 6-29% and induced pronounced oxidative stress. In parallel, this foliar stress reshaped the rhizosphere microbiota, with consistent enrichment of Bacillus. This microbial shift was accompanied by increased root exudation of L-valine and L-leucine, which was associated with reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling and increased root membrane permeability. Crucially, these amino acids promoted chemotaxis and root colonization by the representative Bacillus strains SRS50 and SRS107, selected from 11 candidates among 241 rhizosphere isolates, whereas colonization was reduced in ROS-deficient mutants. Functionally, application of a 'synbiotic' (amino acid-Bacillus combination) reduced grain Cd concentrations by 40.5-43.3%, associated with Bacillus-induced leaf lignification. These findings highlight a plant-microbe feedback loop that contributes to rice adaptation to foliar Cd stress.
items.authors: Liu J, Yang X, Gao Y, Chen W, Chen Y, Moreno-Jiménez E, Williams PN, Yan M, Ren S, Zhao X, Bi Q, Wang C, Li B, Li T, Tao Q, Dai Z.

items.title: Dynamic transcriptomic profiling of Salix triandra under freezing stress identifies StWRKY31 as a positive regulator of cold tolerance.
items.abstract: Salix triandra is a fast-growing shrub willow native to temperate and cold regions, possessing remarkable freezing tolerance. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying this natural cold hardiness remain largely unexplored. In this study, we performed a time-course transcriptomic analysis of S. triandra seedlings subjected to freezing stress at -4 °C. A total of 11,287 differentially expressed genes were identified and clustered into six distinct co-expression modules with dynamic temporal patterns, revealing a multi-phasic transcriptional response involving early stress perception, metabolic adjustment, and sustained cellular protection. Among the differentially expressed transcription factors, a WRKY family member designated StWRKY31 (EVM0008367) was identified as a cold-induced candidate gene, belonging to a mid-to-late adaptation module peaking at 24 h. Subcellular localization analysis showed that StWRKY31 localizes to the nucleus. Heterologous overexpression of StWRKY31 in Arabidopsis significantly enhanced freezing tolerance, as evidenced by improved survival rates under both non-acclimated and cold-acclimated freezing assays. In the StWRKY31-overexpressing Arabidopsis lines, reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation was reduced, superoxide dismutase (SOD) and peroxidase (POD) activities were increased, proline content was elevated, and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels were decreased. Moreover, StWRKY31 upregulated the expression of cold-responsive marker genes (AtGSTF8, AtZAT10, and AtHY5) in a time-dependent manner, with elevated basal expression prior to cold exposure, suggesting a potential defense priming state. These findings suggest that StWRKY31 functions as a positive regulator of freezing tolerance. This study contributes to understanding the regulatory dynamics of cold adaptation in woody plants and provides a valuable candidate gene for breeding cold-tolerant varieties.
items.authors: Jia C, Chen Y, Yin T.

items.title: Membrane environment-dependent relocation of phloem-loading sucrose transporters.
items.abstract: Plasma membrane transporters play an essential role in plant development and all physiological processes. Their activity is tightly controlled by a variety of mechanisms, including the rate of transporter endocytosis. There is evidence that the local membrane environment, in particular the sterol content, influences transporter endocytosis. Here, we analyzed the sucrose transporters StSUT1 (potato) and AtSUC2 (Arabidopsis) transiently expressed in Nicotiana benthamiana epidermal cells. Using live-cell imaging of fluorescent protein fusions combined with extracellular quenching by Trypan Blue, we quantitatively distinguished plasma membrane-localized from internal transporter pools. Pharmacological perturbation of sterols and sphingolipids with methyl-β-cyclodextrin, fenpropimorph and myriocin reduced sucrose transporter abundance at the plasma membrane and decreased uptake of the fluorescent sucrose analogue esculin. In Arabidopsis leaves, methyl-β-cyclodextrin treatment reduced endogenous AtSUC2 protein levels, confirming sterol-dependent regulation in planta. Single-molecule localization microscopy of AtSUC2-reporter constructs revealed its enrichment in ∼50 nm plasma membrane domains, with the localization becoming more homogeneous upon sterol depletion. Together, our results demonstrate that plasma membrane lipid composition modulates sucrose transporter localization and abundance, with likely relevance for the regulation of phloem loading and other membrane proteins.
items.authors: Yin S, Zhang X, Burt P, Kühn C, Liesche J.

items.title: Identification of bromodomain family genes across the cotton genome and the enhancement of plant growth and development by GhBRD34
items.abstract: Abstract Background Bromodomain (BRD)-containing proteins are important regulators of plant growth, development, and responses to environmental stress. However, the understanding of their specific biological functions and molecular mechanisms in cotton is limited. Results Here, we performed a genome‑wide survey and identified 69 GhBRD family members, which are located on 24 chromosomes of the upland cotton genome. Analysis of the promoter regions revealed several conserved cis-acting elements that play roles in light signaling, abiotic stress responses, and phytohormone signaling. Available transcriptome datasets revealed that four of these genes ( GhBRD1 , GhBRD33 , GhBRD34 , and GhBRD68 ) exhibited consistently high expression across different tissues, suggesting that these genes participate in various aspects of plant growth and development. When GhBRD34 was silenced through virus‑induced gene silencing in upland cotton, plant growth and development were markedly suppressed, resulting in reduced plant height and a relatively small leaf area. Conversely, GhBRD34 overexpression in Arabidopsis not only promoted growth and development but also rendered the plants more sensitive to drought conditions. Conclusions Our findings lay a solid foundation for future studies aimed at dissecting the molecular pathways through which GhBRD34 influences growth, development, and drought responsiveness in upland cotton.
items.authors: Wu H, Liu X, Li Y, Yan Q, Wei Y, Li C, Liu H, Xie L, Wang X, Ma K.

items.title: DELLA proteins modulate responsive and buffered transcriptional programs in Arabidopsis and rice roots under water limitation
items.abstract: Water limitation constrains plant growth and productivity, yet the molecular mechanisms regulating root responses remain incompletely understood. The DELLA repressors of gibberellin signaling are key growth regulators under stress, but their role in shaping transcriptional responses to water limitation, and its conservation, remain unclear. Here, we investigated DELLA function in roots of Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa under reduced water availability simulated by polyethylene glycol (PEG). Loss of DELLA function reduced the sensitivity of root growth to water limitation, affecting primary root elongation in A. thaliana and crown root formation in O. sativa. Transcriptomic profiling revealed extensive DELLA-dependent regulation, partitioned into two modes: (i) genes requiring DELLAs for appropriate responses to water limitation ('WT-responsive'), and (ii) genes whose responsiveness is detected predominantly in the absence of DELLAs ('buffered', an operational label for an expression pattern, not a demonstrated mechanism). These patterns suggest that DELLAs both enable specific responses and apparently constrain broader transcriptional responsiveness under osmotic stress. Although the requirement for DELLA function is conserved, the developmental outputs and downstream transcriptional programs are largely species-specific. Together, our results identify DELLAs as key modulators of root responses to water limitation, with a proposed dual role in shaping and limiting transcriptional dynamics.
items.authors: Wong, C., Alabadi, D., Blazquez, M. A., Catarino, B.

items.title: The transcription factor PdePHR1 increases phosphorus accumulation in poplar shoot and promotes root growth.
items.abstract: BackgroundTrees are major primary producers and long-term carbon sink by yielding a substantial amount of woody biomass, which relies on sufficient acquisition of mineral nutrient from soil by roots. Phosphate (Pi) is an essential, but often limited in soils, macronutrient. To sustain growth during Pi starvation, plants trigger an array of adaptive responses that are mainly controlled by the transcription factor of the PHOSPHATE RESPONSE 1 (PHR1) family. However, how the PHR1 functional homolog might influence the performance of forest trees remains unknown.ResultsIn this work, we identified PdePHR1from Populus deltoides x P. euramericana as a MYB-CC type transcription factor. Furthermore, overexpression of PdePHR1 in P. davidiana x P.bolleana triggers the expression of the Pi starvation response genes in replete Pi conditions, including genes mediating Pi uptake, remobilization, and signaling. Moreover, plants with overexpression of PdePHR1 exhibit enhanced Pi acquisition and translocation, leading to higher phosphorus accumulation in shoots under optimal conditions. Additionally, PdePHR1 overexpressing lines display substantially longer adventitious roots and more biomass accumulation independent of external Pi availability. Furthermore, overexpression of PdePHR1 sufficiently improves poplar performance under both Pi-replete and long-term depleted conditions.ConclusionsOur data support that PdePHR1 acts as a central positive regulator of Pi starvation response and root growth. PdePHR1 overexpression is sufficient to enable not only increased phosphorus accumulation in shoot but also greatly enhanced root growth and overall woody biomass accumulation regardless of Pi availability. These findings provide a potential tool for increasing tree productivity and sustainable carbon sequestration under various environmental conditions.
items.authors: Wang Q, Chen L, Jia D, Wang F, Pu T, Li W.

items.title: Coordinated Changes in Water Relations, Antioxidant Defense, and Metabolic Enzyme Activities in Maize Seedlings Under Salt Stress
items.abstract: Salinity is a major abiotic stressor that restricts plant growth and development and impairs physiological and biochemical processes. This study aimed to investigate the effects of salt stress on the morphophysiological traits, oxidative status, antioxidant defense system, and associated metabolic processes of maize (Zea mays L.) seedlings. The results showed that increasing salinity exacerbated oxidative stress, impaired water status and photosynthetic activity, and markedly reduced growth in maize seedlings. Increasing NaCl concentrations progressively inhibited plant growth and leaf development, with the most pronounced effects observed at 250 mM NaCl. Salt stress enhanced antioxidant enzyme activity and induced substantial changes in the non-enzymatic antioxidant system. Glutathione (GSH) content declined progressively with increasing stress intensity, whereas ascorbic acid (AsA) content increased under moderate stress but decreased sharply at high salinity. Isoenzyme analyses revealed changes in the band intensities of BPO, GPO, APX, and CAT isoforms in response to increasing NaCl concentrations. Strong positive correlations were observed among the NAD(P)-dependent metabolic enzymes NAD-MDH, NADP-MDH, and NADP-ME. Taken together, morphophysiological traits, antioxidant and metabolic enzyme activities, and non-enzymatic antioxidant levels may serve as useful indicators for assessing salt stress tolerance in maize.
items.authors: Aliyeva N, Aliyeva D, Gurbanova U, Babayev H, Amrahov N, Mammadov Z, Huseynova N, Aliyev S, Huseynova I.

items.title: VvSLR1-VvGAD1 mediated regulation of VvGA20ox4 contributes to GA homeostasis and seed development in grapevine.
items.abstract: Gibberellins (GAs) are widely used in grape cultivation to promote berry enlargement and induce seedlessness, but their effects on seed development and the regulatory mechanism remain poorly understood. In this study, exogenous GA3 significantly reduced seed weight in grapevine, indicating impaired seed development. To investigate the underlying mechanism, we characterized the grape DELLA protein SLENDER RICE 1 (VvSLR1). Overexpression of VvSLR1 in tomato caused a dwarf and compact phenotype but had limited effects on fruit and seed development under normal conditions. However, GA3 treatment caused a stronger reduction in seed formation in VvSLR1-overexpressing plants, whereas paclobutrazol (PAC), an inhibitor of GA biosynthesis, allowed relatively normal seed formation, indicating that the effect of VvSLR1 on reproductive development is GA-dependent. In grape calli, VvSLR1 overexpression altered GA metabolism and the expression of several VvGA20ox and VvGA3ox genes, suggesting a role for VvSLR1 in GA homeostasis. We further identified GAMETOPHYTE DEFECTIVE 1 (VvGAD1), whose Arabidopsis homolog is involved in gametophyte development, as a nuclear-localized VvSLR1-interacting protein. VvGAD1 associated with the promoter of GA 20-oxidase 4 (VvGA20ox4), and co-expression of VvGAD1 and VvSLR1 significantly enhanced VvGA20ox4 promoter activity. Moreover, heterologous expression of VvGA20ox4 in Arabidopsis increased silique length and seed number, while exogenous GA3 suppressed VvGA20ox4 promoter activity. Together, these findings suggest that VvSLR1 acts as a regulatory node linking GA signaling and homeostasis, with the VvSLR1-VvGAD1-VvGA20ox4 relationship representing a potential regulatory branch involved in GA-dependent seed development.
items.authors: Zhang S, Zhang F, Zhang C, Wang L, Yadav V, Zhou X, Wu X, Wang X, Zhong H.

items.title: Canopy traits reveal climate-associated genetic differentiation in a California oak common garden
items.abstract: Background and Aims: Phenotypic variation in plant populations reflecting historical climate adaptation may affect performance under future climates. In long-lived trees, height and stem diameter are commonly used to assess growth, but these measures may not fully capture complementary structural and functional dimensions of performance, such as canopy development and vigor. We investigated whether canopy traits reveal climate-associated genetic differentiation in Quercus lobata. Methods. Using drone-based remote sensing of 1,395 12-year-old Quercus lobata trees from 601 families in a common garden, we quantified canopy volume and greenness, using the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI). Previous analyses indicated that trees originating from warmer climates grew more in common gardens than those from cooler climates. To assess whether canopy traits showed similar patterns, we tested for family-level variation in each trait and associations with climate of origin. Key Results. Canopy volume and greenness showed significant genetic variation among families and significant associations with climate of origin. Trees from hotter climates had greater canopy volume and greenness than trees from cooler climates. Conclusions. These covarying traits provide novel evidence of climate-associated genetic differentiation in tree performance, consistent with historical climate selection. Trees originating from climates with hot summers, moderate winters, and low precipitation performed best in the garden, suggesting that they will perform better than trees adapted to cool, wet conditions under future climate change.
items.authors: Goetz, A. R. B., Young, D. J., Sanghera, K. K., Wright, J., Sork, V. L.

items.title: Interspecific difference in seasonal change of stomatal O3 uptake and annual cumulative stomatal O3 uptake estimated by species-specific Jarvis-type models for 10 Japanese urban greening tree species.
items.abstract: Tropospheric ozone (O3) is a detrimental gaseous air pollutant for human health. Urban greening trees can reduce the atmospheric O3 concentration in urban areas by absorbing it through the stomata into the leaves, but the most effective species for this purpose remain unclear. This study addresses this gap by developing new species-specific Jarvis-type stomatal conductance (gs) models for 10 typical Japanese urban tree species. Using these models, we examined the seasonal changes in stomatal O3 uptake, the annual cumulative stomatal O3 uptake (COU), and their determining factors in the 10 species. Firstly, developing species-specific gs models is imperative for accurately quantifying O3 uptake, because the optimal gs models for all the species incorporated limiting functions due to photosynthetic photon flux density (flight) and leaf phenology (fphen), while other environmental functions were not necessarily included. Secondly, evergreen trees generally showed greater annual O3 uptake due to longer leaf duration, whereas deciduous trees had potential for greater O3 removal in early spring, when atmospheric O3 concentrations peak. Thirdly, within the five evergreen broad-leaved tree species, Osmanthus fragrans exhibited relatively high physiological activity over a prolonged period, resulting in the highest COU. Within the five deciduous tree species, Styrax japonicus exhibited the highest COU, due to the highest gmax and tolerance to relatively high air temperature and vapor pressure deficit, some of which differ from previously reported findings. These insights provide a scientific basis for optimizing urban tree selection to improve air quality.
items.authors: Yagita A, Oi N, Endo W, Waragai T, Ohta A, Takahashi K, Watanabe M, Izuta T.

items.title: An AGC kinase cascade regulates ROP signaling for the correct timing of pollen germination.
items.abstract: In flowering plants, the timing of pollen germination is crucial for successful fertilization and an important trait for seed and fruit crops. Environmental factors tightly regulate pollen germination, with germination-suppressing conditions on the pollen-producing anther and germination-promoting conditions on the receiving stigma. Using genetic, biochemical, and cell biological methods, we show that this environmental sensitivity of pollen germination in Arabidopsis thaliana is regulated by a 3-PHOSPHOINOSITIDE-DEPENDENT KINASE 1 (PDK1)-AGC1.5/AGC1.7 kinase cascade. We show that PDK1 hyperphosphorylates downstream AGC1.5/7 kinases to enhance their activity. Pollen-specific phosphoproteomics identified multiple proteins involved in pollen growth whose phosphorylation is controlled by AGC1.5/7. Two germination-promoting RHO OF PLANTS GUANINE NUCLEOTIDE EXCHANGE FACTORS (ROPGEFs) are phosphorylated by AGC1.5/7 at a novel site, reducing ROPGEF plasma membrane polarization. Loss of PDK1-AGC kinase signaling resulted in precocious pollen germination on the anther, which was rescued by high AGC1.5 kinase activity. Conversely, AGC1.5/7 overexpression or a phosphomimic ROPGEF version inhibited precocious pollen germination. Distinct subcellular localization of PDK1 and AGC1 kinases upon pollen germination is likely to alleviate their inhibitory effect. Our data indicate that the correct timing of pollen germination requires the fine-tuned activity of a PDK1-AGC1 kinase cascade inhibiting ROPGEFs on the anther, preventing precocious pollen germination.
items.authors: Zhao T, Lepper A, Anzenberger F, Brajkovic S, König K, Shikata H, Xiao Y, Küster B, Schwechheimer C, Offringa R, Denninger P.

items.title: High Light Intensity Potentiates Bacillus amyloliquefaciens PMB05-Associated Plant Immunity and Bacterial Soft Rot Control in Arabidopsis thaliana.
items.abstract: Bacterial soft rot, caused by Pectobacterium carotovorum subsp. carotovorum, affects numerous vegetable crops. Beneficial microbes like Bacillus amyloliquefaciens PMB05 offer a sustainable alternative to traditional copper- or antibiotic-based controls, which risks the development of pathogen resistance. Bacillus amyloliquefaciens PMB05 enhances disease resistance to soft rot by intensifying PAMP-triggered immunity (PTI). Although our previous research showed that PMB05-intensified PTI correlates with a reduced photosynthetic electron transport rate under high light conditions, it remains unclear whether increasing light intensity can strengthen PMB05-mediated immune signaling to further enhance disease resistance in plant leaves. In this study, Arabidopsis plants were grown under varying light intensities to address this question. Furthermore, expression of the type III elicitor, HrpN protein, was applied to evaluate the impact of PMB05 treatment on immune activation. HrpN acts as a PAMP that can trigger plant defense responses. The results revealed that higher growth light intensity was associated with PMB05-intensified PTI response by increasing reactive oxygen species generation but suppresses callose deposition. In addition, PMB05-facilitated PTI-mediated stomatal closure occurred more rapidly and tightly under high light, thereby restricting pathogen invasion into leaf tissues. Disease assays further confirmed that higher light intensity significantly reduced soft rot severity in A. thaliana, while the combination of high light and PMB05 treatment achieved superior control efficacy. Furthermore, PMB05-associated disease protection under high growth light was not detected in sid2, npr1, and nahG plants, indicating that intact SA-associated functions are required for the detectable protective phenotype under the conditions tested. These findings demonstrate that environmental light management can strategically potentiate immunity-intensifying microbes, establishing a novel paradigm for sustainable disease control through the coordinated manipulation of light conditions and microbial application.
items.authors: Li AT, Tsai YC, Tsai YC, Blanco SD, Chung HY, Huang TP, Lin YH.

items.title: Substrate-mediated facilitation of softwood and hardwood deconstruction by sequential white-rot and brown-rot fungal treatment.
items.abstract: Translating natural, successional wood decomposition into an engineered two-stage fungal pretreatment offers a promising strategy for biomass deconstruction, yet how pioneer white-rot fungal modifications facilitate subsequent brown-rot decay remains unclear. Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) was pretreated with Trametes versicolor (Tv) and Phanerochaete chrysosporium (Pc) and subsequently exposed to Gloeophyllum trabeum (Gt). After 15-day BRF incubation, second-stage mass loss increased by 40.9% and 126.2% in the Tv- and Pc-pretreated groups, respectively, relative to the control without WRF pretreatment. FTIR, chemical-composition and qualitative HSQC-NMR analyses collectively indicated that this accelerated degradation of Scots pine was associated with the WRF-induced modification of the lignin-carbohydrate matrix. Furthermore, this substrate-mediated facilitative effect was also observed in red oak (Quercus rubra L.), for which second-stage mass loss reached 13.1% and 14.7% after P. chrysosporium and T. versicolor pretreatment, respectively, compared with 6.7% in the control. Under the fungal combinations and laboratory conditions tested, these results show that WRF-induced substrate modification can facilitate subsequent brown-rot deconstruction and provide a basis for further exploring sequential fungal treatments in woody biomass.
items.authors: Wu D, Li Y, Huang C, Chen X, Li X, Zhu Y, Li X.

items.title: AtDJB3, a J-domain protein, regulates seed amyloid accumulation and ABA-mediated early developmental transition in Arabidopsis thaliana.
items.abstract: Main conclusionOur study shows that AtDJB3 modulates seed amyloid-like protein assemblies to regulate ABA sensitivity, thereby coordinating germination and early seedling development, and shaping adaptive responses during early plant growth. Molecular chaperones are highly abundant in seeds, yet their roles during the transition from seed to seedling remain poorly defined. In this study, we identify AtDJB3, an aggregate-remodeling J-domain protein (JDP), as a regulator of abscisic acid (ABA)-mediated responses during early developmental transitions in Arabidopsis thaliana. AtDJB3 expression is induced by ABA and depends on the transcription factors ABI3 and ABI5 during germination. A T-DNA insertion mutant of AtDJB3 (atdjb3-1) exhibited enhanced germination but impaired post-germinative growth in the presence of ABA compared to wild-type plants, indicating a role for AtDJB3 in fine-tuning ABA responses across distinct developmental phases. Consistently, atdjb3-1 seeds showed improved radicle emergence and cotyledon opening under osmotic stress, often associated with ABA-mediated growth inhibition. Notably, dry atdjb3-1 seeds accumulated elevated levels of amyloid-like protein assemblies, linking altered aggregate remodeling to the observed changes in ABA-regulated seed-to-seedling progression. Together, these findings implicate AtDJB3 as an important component of the ABA signaling network that coordinates developmental timing and stress adaptation in A. thaliana.
items.authors: Satheesh G, Biswal AK, Babu KA, Sahi C.

items.title: IRON DEFICIENCY RESHAPES THE POPLAR ROOT AND EXUDATE METABOLITE PROFILES AND DRIVES EXUDATE-MEDIATED IRON MOBILIZATION
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Iron (Fe) deficiency under alkaline conditions limits Fe bioavailability and reshapes plant metabolism. We asked how Fe deficiency at pH 7.5 alters the metabolite profiles of roots and root exudates of Populus × canescens , and whether exudates mobilize Fe at high pH. Hydroponically grown plants were deprived of Fe for 20 and 27 days. Roots and exudates, collected in nutrient solution and in distilled water, were profiled by UHPLC–QTOF MS, and metabolites were annotated using MS/MS molecular networking (MetGem) and public spectral libraries. Fe deficiency caused significant global shifts in both root and exudate metabolomes. In roots, phenylpropanoids increased at 27 days (proanthocyanidins, neochlorogenic acid, naringenin), whereas the salicylate glycoside salicortin decreased, suggesting a redirection of phenylpropanoid flux. In nutrient-solution exudates, eight flavonoids, including quercitrin, accumulated strongly at 27 days, and catecholic coumarins such as fraxetin were detected in roots and exudates. Exudates from Fe-deficient plants increased Fe mobilization from Fe(III) oxides at pH 7.5, and quercitrin solubilized Fe as efficiently as fraxetin. Alkaline Fe deficiency thus reconfigures poplar root and exudate metabolomes, and exuded flavonoids, not only coumarins, may contribute to Fe mobilization at high pH.
