HIGHLIGHT Iron deficiency at alkaline pH reshapes poplar root and exudate metabolomes; exuded flavonoids such as quercitrin, alongside coumarins, contribute to iron mobilization from insoluble iron oxides.
items.authors: Cieschi, M. T., BOUZARI, N., Citerne, S., Alvarez-Fernandez, A., Touboul, D., Thomine, S.

items.title: Native AMF from wild Paeonia ostii enhance root development via PoCCD4-mediated hormone homeostasis and reshape rhizosphere microbiome assembly and function.
items.abstract: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) play vital roles in plant growth and rhizosphere microbiome assembly. Tree peony (Paeonia sect. Moutan DC.) is an economically valuable perennial crop, yet the symbiotic mechanisms between it and native AMF remain poorly understood. In this study, we surveyed the rhizosphere AMF community of wild P. ostii from its native habitat, and isolated two dominant species: Funneliformis mosseae and Claroideoglomus etunicatum. Inoculation with these AMF significantly improved root development and leaf photosynthetic efficiency. Furthermore, the promotion involved a novel pathway whereby carotenoid cleavage dioxygenase 4 (PoCCD4) mediated strigolactone and abscisic acid homeostasis in P. ostii roots. Beyond direct effects on host plant growth, AMF inoculation fine-tuned rhizosphere microbiota composition, reinforcing host-driven assembly and favoring beneficial consortia without altering overall diversity. Correlation analyses revealed that the AMF-shaped microenvironment established a disease-suppressive network linked to soil nutrient dynamics and phytohormone profiles. This study elucidates the interaction mechanisms between native AMF and P. ostii, uncovers their co-adaptive relationships, and offers a scientific basis for developing AMF inoculants for sustainable tree peony cultivation.
items.authors: Shao Y, Wen Z, Ye C, Yang M, Fuzzati N, Zhang B, Cavellec C, Jiang W, Li L, Hao Q, Shu Q, Li Y.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: A heat-assisted tt Lb Cas12a workflow incorporating crRNA 3′-tailing enables efficient multiplex biallelic genome editing in hybrid poplar
items.abstract: In forest trees, high genome-editing efficiency in primary transformants is particularly important for functional genomics and trait improvement, as long generation times severely limit the use of subsequent generations to recover fully edited genotypes. This challenge is further compounded in hybrid poplar, where paralogous gene copies and allelic variation make efficient multiplex editing particularly difficult. We optimized Lb Cas12a-mediated editing in Populus × canescens ( Populus tremula × Populus alba ), clone INRA 717-1B4, by targeting four paralogous PtaABA8ox4 loci using temperature-tolerant tt Lb Cas12a, a two-stage heat treatment, and crRNA 3′-tailing. The heat-treatment regime preserved transgenic recovery, while ttLbCas12a -based constructs and heat treatment substantially increased biallelic editing. All seven lines in the highest-performing group, combining tt Lb Cas12a, 3′-tailed crRNAs, and heat treatment, were biallelically edited at all four targets. crRNA 3′-tailing altered predicted secondary structures and showed a consistent numerical tendency toward improved editing, but its independent effect was not statistically resolved. Mutations were dominated by small deletions, and biallelic out-of-frame recovery increased in ttLbCas12a -based contexts without scaling proportionally with biallelic editing. Thus, heat-assisted tt Lb Cas12a-mediated approaches enable efficient multiplex editing in hybrid poplar, whereas genotype quality remains dependent on repair outcome and somatic uniformity.
items.authors: Zahn, V., Fendel, A., Fladung, M., Bruegmann, T.

items.title: Picea pan-transcriptomes reveal signatures of complex phylogenetic conflict and adaptation.
items.abstract: Coniferous forests are among the ecosystems most exposed to rapid climate warming, and a well-resolved phylogeny of Picea is essential for understanding the evolutionary processes that have shaped diversification and regional differentiation across the genus. Here, we analysed pan-transcriptomes spanning 37 Picea species from across Northern Hemisphere forests. Our analyses reveal a bipartite pan-transcriptomic architecture in which core genes (9.4%) are associated primarily with fundamental cellular functions, whereas dispensable and private components (90.6% combined) are more strongly associated with ecological differentiation. Species trees inferred from low-copy orthologues resolve four major clades, and approximately 275 loci are sufficient to recover a stable backbone topology. Coalescent analyses indicate pervasive genealogical discordance, with incomplete lineage sorting (ILS) showing the greatest relative importance (27.75%) and gene-flow signals contributing less (7.27%). The most variable gene families (7.4%) further delimit three biogeographically structured regional groups: Qinghai-Tibet Plateau lineages are characterized by genes involved in environmental stress, signalling and low-oxygen responses; East Asian lineages show greater representation of protein metabolism and ubiquitin-mediated regulation; and Holarctic lineages are characterized by photosynthesis, chloroplast function, cell-wall processes and secondary metabolism. Together, these findings link regional gene-family differentiation with the persistence of ancestral polymorphism and provide a phylogenomic framework for understanding spruce diversification and for developing hypotheses relevant to climate-resilient forest conservation.
items.authors: Fan Z, Liu L, Ma L, Lai Q, Weng C, Lu S, Zhu H, Chen J, Sun Y, Ru D.
items.journal: Cladistics : the international journal of the Willi Hennig Society

items.title: Forest succession and demographic groups interact to influence insect herbivory on woody seedlings.
items.abstract: Most tropical forests are subject to human disturbances, creating successional communities of varying forest ages. Changes in abiotic conditions and dominant plant species over succession may drive shifts in insect herbivory with forest age, influencing patterns of forest recovery. We quantified leaf insect herbivory (incidence and percentage standing damage) on 4774 seedlings of 185 woody species within 10 1-ha forest plots spanning a successional gradient from 9 to 129 years since disturbance in lowland tropical moist forest in Panama. We classified species as lianas vs. trees and further divided trees into five demographic groups according to their position along the growth-survival and stature-recruitment trade-off axes (slow, fast, long-lived pioneer, short-lived breeder, intermediate). We measured understory light availability to determine whether differences in herbivory were related to decreasing light availability during succession. At the forest plot level, herbivory incidence, but not damage, on woody seedlings increased with forest age. Herbivory incidence increased similarly with forest age for seedlings of trees and lianas. However, the relationships between forest age and herbivory incidence varied among tree demographic groups. Specifically, fast and short-lived breeders had a significantly greater increase in herbivory incidence with forest age compared to slow species. Understory light availability decreased on average with forest age but did not explain variation in herbivory. Our findings improve understanding of how past human disturbance influences natural enemy pressure on seedlings and suggest that decreased herbivory in early-successional forests may contribute to forest recovery while increased herbivory in late-successional forests may maintain seedling diversity.
items.authors: Cinoğlu D, Weissflog A, Dent DH, Farrior CE, Comita LS.

items.title: Rhizosphere triangular warfare: mechanistic insights for plant- beneficial microbe- pathogen interactions.
items.abstract: The rhizosphere is a living physical space that is constantly evolving and is characterized by a complex interplay between beneficial microbes, pathogens, and plants, mediated by molecular and ecological interactions. These three-way relationships constitute a rhizosphere "triangular warfare system," which controls plant health, nutrient uptake, disease resistance, and plant resilience. This review provides a mechanistic overview of the molecular, metabolic and ecological processes underlying these tripartite interactions. We discuss how plants integrate pattern-triggered immunity (PTI), effector-triggered immunity (ETI), microbiome exudation, and hormone signaling to select beneficial microbes to exclude pathogen entry. Beneficial microbes deploy volatile organic compounds, induction of systemic resistance (ISR), secretion systems, phytotoxins, siderophores, lytic enzymes, and microbiome-disrupting strategies to enhance plant fitness, whereas pathogens use virulence effectors, lytic enzymes, secretion systems, phytotoxins, siderophores, and microbiome-disrupting strategies to overcome host defenses and restructure rhizosphere communities. Recent advances in multi-omics have revealed the intricate signaling networks, metabolic interactions, and microbial competition shaping these relationships under various environmental conditions. We further explore emerging opportunities in microbiome engineering, synthetic microbial consortia and disease-suppressive soil management for sustainable crop protection. This review synthesizes existing mechanistic knowledge and introduces the concept of 'rhizosphere triangular warfare' as a stepping stone toward the next generation of microbiome-based agriculture and precision rhizosphere engineering under environmental changes.
items.authors: Singh P, Singh RK, Guo DJ, Singh MP, Zhang BQ, Song XP, Upadhyay SK, Li YR.

items.title: Predation risk alters prey caching behavior and resultant tree establishment patterns.
items.abstract: The drivers of plant dispersal and distribution are poorly understood. For nut-bearing trees, interactions between seeds and caching granivores can have a strong influence on population dynamics as unrecovered caches often recruit new trees. Granivore-seed interactions may be constrained by predators as fear alters caching and foraging behavior. We investigated how predation risk affects caching and foraging behavior in fox squirrels (Sciurus niger) and subsequent recruitment patterns of American turkey oak (Quercus laevis) acorns. We marked and tracked acorns to locate fox squirrel cache and consumption points where we assessed fox squirrel perceived predation risk, measured how caching influenced acorn survival and dispersal, and surveyed juvenile oak distributions. Fox squirrels perceived greater risk at caches than consumption points, suggesting predation risk influences caching decisions and cache distribution. Buried acorns survived at higher rates and only buried acorns germinated, though survival did not vary with dispersal distance. Juvenile oaks and cache locations showed similar hump-shaped patterns of establishment away from nearest potential source trees. We conclude that predation risk indirectly shapes plant establishment by altering granivore behavior.
items.authors: Potash AD, McCleery RA.

items.title: Thioredoxins as hormone-responsive redox regulators in wheat: transcriptomic and structural insights.
items.abstract: Thioredoxins (TRXs) are small central redox proteins involved in stress responses and plant development, but their hormone-dependent regulation remains poorly characterized. In this study, a genome-wide identification of the TRX family in Triticum aestivum (Ta) was performed using Arabidopsis thaliana TRXs as orthologs. Phylogenetic analysis allowed the identification of a total of 48 TRXs, including 22 typical TRXs, 22 atypical TRXs, and four thioredoxin reductases (TRs). The identified classes in wheat were conserved compared with the Arabidopsis genome; however, no extra classes were identified. To assess the regulation of the wheat TRX genes under hormonal treatments, including abscisic acid (ABA), ethylene (ET), indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), and methyl jasmonate (MeJA), an in silico analysis was performed using the GEO dataset. The transcriptomic analysis and the quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) validation revealed that the atypical TRXs were more responsive to hormones than the typical TRXs and TRs. Among these atypical TRX members, atypical cysteine/histidine rich thioredoxin (ACHT), chloroplast drought stress protein of 32 kDa (CDSP32), nucleoredoxin (NRX), and TRX-L3 groups were the most hormone-responsive. ABA strongly upregulated the TaACHT4.2 gene, whereas TaNRX1.1 responded to IAA and ET. On the other hand, ABA, IAA, ET, and MeJA downregulated TaCDSP32.1, TaNRX1.2, TaNRX1.3, and ACHT members. The molecular docking analysis suggested a potential interaction between the selected atypical TRXs and ABA, IAA, and MeJA. The multidomain TRXs, such as TaCDSP32.1 and TaNRX1.1, showed a high affinity for ABA and IAA, whereas TaTRX-L3.1.3 showed a high affinity for MeJA. This study highlights the importance and potential functions of poorly characterized atypical TRXs as hormone-responsive redox regulatory nodes in wheat and provides a basis for future functional validation under hormonal and stress conditions, as well as during plant development.
items.authors: Bouzenita MH, Tahir RA, Fan M, Estanbooli AS, Chibani K.

items.title: Species-specific divergence in Phytophthora infestans resistance between Nicotiana benthamiana and potato mediated by 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid pretreatment.
items.abstract: BackgroundLate blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, is a devastating oomycete disease threatening global potato (Solanum tuberosum) production. 1-Aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid (ACC), has also been proposed to act as a bioactive signal in plant stress responses, but its contribution to plant immunity remains elusive.ResultsHere, we show that ACC pretreatment exerts opposite effects on P. infestans resistance in Nicotiana benthamiana and the potato cultivar 'Favorita', revealing strong species-specific transcriptional reprogramming. In N. benthamiana, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are enriched in defense-related pathways, including plant-pathogen interactions, hormone signaling, and secondary metabolism. In potato, DEGs mainly involve primary metabolism, cell wall remodeling, and photosynthesis regulation. The jasmonic acid (JA) biosynthesis and signaling pathway emerge as a central hub underlying this divergence. ACC markedly induces JA-related genes in N. benthamiana but fails to activate them in potato. Exogenous MeJA enhances resistance, whereas the JA biosynthesis inhibitor DIECA weakens the ACC-associated resistant phenotype in N. benthamiana and aggravates disease in potato. Antioxidant-enzyme assays and DAB staining support distinct ROS-associated responses between the two species. Transient expression assays of JA- and protease inhibitor-related candidate genes further support their roles as downstream contributors to disease resistance.ConclusionsCollectively, our findings suggest that ACC pretreatment produces species-specific defense outcomes against P. infestans through differential recruitment of a JA-associated regulatory network and downstream defense layers, including protease inhibitors and ROS-associated responses. These results refine our understanding of ACC/ethylene-associated immune regulation and provide candidate targets for sustainable late blight management and resistance breeding.
items.authors: Zhang Y, Li Y, Shi Y, Zhao C, Fu J, Wang Q.

items.title: SDG26 integrates ABA-dependent and ABA-independent pathways to regulate cold stress responses in Arabidopsis via chromatin modification.
items.abstract: Plants constantly face adverse environmental conditions, with temperature drops posing major threats to growth and productivity. To adapt, plants have evolved complex mechanisms of transcriptional reprogramming. While various cold-responsive pathways have been described, the contribution of chromatin-level regulation, particularly histone modifications, remains poorly understood. Here, we identify the histone methyltransferase SET DOMAIN GROUP 26 (SDG26) as a positive regulator of cold stress responses in Arabidopsis thaliana. We show that SDG26 is transcriptionally induced and posttranscriptionally stabilized by cold, and that its loss of function compromises several abscisic acid (ABA)-related phenotypes. At the molecular level, SDG26 promotes the expression of cold-responsive genes, including members of the CBF-COR regulon, through direct chromatin binding and deposition of histone H3 lysine 36 trimethylation (H3K36me3). Additionally, SDG26 modulates ABA biosynthesis, catabolism, and transport, thereby promoting ABA accumulation, stomatal closure, and drought tolerance. Collectively, our results reveal that SDG26 integrates ABA-dependent and ABA-independent pathways to fine-tune Arabidopsis responses to abiotic stresses. We further establish SDG26 as a chromatin modifier contributing to stress-responsive H3K36me3 enrichment at specific loci. Together, our findings position SDG26 as a chromatin-based hub that coordinates cold acclimation and water conservation to enhance plant resilience.
items.authors: Zhang X, Lapierre J, Zumsteg J, Erhardt M, Shen WH, Berr A.
items.journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology

items.title: Sample preparation of some plant tissues for transmission electron microscopy using high pressure freezing and freeze substitution.
items.abstract: For sample preparation of biological block sectioning, high pressure freezing and freeze substitution (HPF-FS) is a better choice than chemical fixation. Freezing fixation can retain the original structures and preserve the soluble materials, and avoid the disadvantage of chemical fixation. Using high-pressure freezing, plant tissues are more difficult to freeze successfully than animal tissues and microbes because they have cell walls and varying degrees of vacuolation. For plant tissues, including the roots of Arabidopsis thaliana, 1-hexadecene is an ideal cryoprotectant/filler. The ability of highly vacuolated plant tissues (such as mature leaves and petals) to effectively remove intercellular air is crucial for successful high pressure freezing. Using the anthers of Arabidopsis thaliana, the leaves of Brachypodium distachyon, Axonopus compressus and Plantago asiatica, and the petals of Phalaenopsis bellina as examples, we found an effective method to remove air from the intercellular spaces: plant tissue in 1-hexadecene is placed in a vacuum desiccator, and then the air is removed using a vacuum pump, resulting in the release of numerous air bubbles. Plant tissue samples taken at different degassing times are then subjected to high pressure freezing and the subsequent required procedures of sample preparation. Based on the presentation of fine structures, the optimal time for different plant tissues can be determined and shows a positive correction with sample thickness. Good HPF-FS results show that the lipid bilayer within each organelle of the plant cells is clearly visible.
items.authors: Hsu CM, Chou YC, Yen HJ, Jane WN.

items.title: Elucidation and reconstitution of the poplar salicortin biosynthetic pathway.
items.abstract: Salicinoids are specialized benzenoid (C6-C1) metabolites characteristic of the Salicaceae family. Although salicinoids have long been recognized as effective defense compounds and pharmacologically active constituents in willows and poplars, the biosynthetic pathway underlying their formation remains largely unresolved. Through integrated metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses of black cottonwood (Populus trichocarpa) roots, we identified candidate genes involved in salicinoid biosynthesis belonging to the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase family 92 (CYP92) and the progesterone 5β-reductase/iridoid synthase-like enzyme (PRISE) family of short-chain dehydrogenases/reductases. Co-expression of all identified candidate genes, together with the previously characterized glycosyltransferase gene PtUGT71L1, acyltransferase gene PtACT47, and cinnamic acid-CoA ligase gene PtCNL5, in Nicotiana benthamiana resulted in the production of salicortin, the most abundant salicinoid in poplar. Further characterization of the P450 candidates revealed that two enzymes catalyze ortho-hydroxylation of both aromatic rings of the proposed salicortin precursor, benzyl benzoate, while two other P450s catalyze the subsequent oxidative dearomatization of the benzoic acid-derived ring of benzyl benzoate. The resulting dieneone intermediate is converted by PRISE enzymes via a 1,4-reduction to form the characteristic 1-hydroxy-6-oxocyclohex-2-en-1-carboxylic ester moiety of salicortin. Functional redundancy among the identified CYP92 and PRISE enzymes may reflect the central role of these compounds in plant defense.
items.authors: Lackus ND, Ma D, Nakamura Y, Luck K, Gordon H, Reichelt M, Alam RM, Paetz C, Constabel CP, Gershenzon J, Köllner TG.

items.title: Conifer Needle Epidermal Imprints for Stomatal Size and Density Measurements.
items.abstract: Stomata play a central role in regulating plant water loss and gas exchange, making functional trait data on stomatal density and size increasingly relevant in the context of climate change. Expanding comparative datasets for these traits requires simple, low-cost methods that can be applied consistently across species and environments. However, while simple stomatal imprint techniques using nail varnish and adhesive tape are widely established for angiosperms, their application to conifer needles is challenging. Stomata in conifers are typically sunken within epistomatal chambers and occluded by densely meshed wax tubules, which can prevent accurate replication of stomatal complexes in epidermal imprints and thereby limit reliable measurement of stomatal size. In addition, stomata are often heterogeneously distributed across needle surfaces and may occur on multiple surfaces depending on species, requiring tailored sampling approaches for accurate density estimation. Consequently, reliable measurement of stomatal traits in conifers would require chemical processing and advanced microscopy, making these methods time-intensive, expensive and less suitable for large-scale comparative studies. Therefore, we lack an approach for conifers that generates high-quality trait data while remaining fast, simple, and comparable to established angiosperm methods. Here, we present a straightforward protocol for preparing stomatal imprints in conifer needles based on standard methods for angiosperm species but including simple preprocessing steps to improve imprint consistency and quality. We further provide guidance for identifying, imaging, and quantifying stomata while accounting for their species-specific spatial distribution on needle surfaces. The protocol enables reliable measurements of stomatal size and density using basic laboratory equipment and standard light microscopy. We demonstrate its applicability across 12 northern hemisphere conifer species, highlighting its suitability for comparative trait-based studies. © 2026 The Author(s). Current Protocols published by Wiley Periodicals LLC. Support Protocol 1: Sampling conifer needles for stomatal traits Basic Protocol 1: Epidermal imprints using nail varnish Basic Protocol 2: Measurement of stomatal density and size.
items.authors: Sachsenmaier L, Franz S, Kahl A, Kretz L, Wirth C.

items.title: Growth-defense trade-offs in Quercus variabilis and Quercus mongolica seedlings under drought stress.
items.abstract: IntroductionIntensified drought induced by climate change is threatening the natural regeneration of forests, yet coexisting tree species can maintain their survival and regeneration by adopting divergent carbon allocation strategies. This study compared leaf-scale drought responses of Quercus variabilis and Q. mongolica seedlings originating from the ecotone of the Zhongtiao Mountains.MethodsMultiple indicators were measured under four water regimes: control (CK), light drought (LD), moderate drought (MD), and severe drought (SD), including leaf morphology, photosynthetic and gas exchange parameters, hydraulic traits, carbon storage traits, stress defense traits, and nutrient stoichiometry. Principal component analysis (PCA) and structural equation modeling (SEM) were used to evaluate interspecific differences in drought adaptation strategies.ResultsDrought suppressed leaf growth and gas exchange, lowered leaf water potential and relative water content, aggravated damage to hydraulic function, and boosted biochemical responses associated with stress defense in both species. For Q. variabilis, leaf non-structural carbohydrate (NSC) concentrations were tightly correlated with growth-related traits, indicating that NSCs play a vital role in sustaining growth and accumulating carbon after growth limitation, reflecting a growth-prioritized resource allocation strategy. In contrast, leaf NSCs of Q. mongolica seedlings exhibited stronger coordinated covariation with stomatal behavior and antioxidant defenses, suggesting that this species prioritizes defense maintenance and physiological stability under drought stress, representing a defense-prioritized resource allocation strategy.DiscussionSeedlings of Q. variabilis and Q. mongolica adopt growth-prioritized and defense-prioritized adaptation strategies under drought, respectively. Such physiological divergence serves as a physiological foundation for niche differentiation, divergent regeneration patterns, and coexistence of seedlings of the two Quercus species within the ecotone.
items.authors: Xue Z, Yin S, Guo Y, Cui K, Wu L, He X, Wu H, Gao R, Bai J.

items.title: WLG coordinates multi-stress tolerance in rice by regulating DST-dependent H2O2 homeostasis and stomatal aperture.
items.abstract: Abiotic stresses reduce rice growth and yield, yet the mechanisms underlying multiple stress tolerance are unknown. Here, we show that the E3 ubiquitin ligase WIDTH OF LEAF AND GRAIN (WLG) enhances drought, salt, and heat tolerance by ubiquitinating and degrading DROUGHT AND SALT TOLERANCE (DST). This degradation represses PEROXIDASE 24 PRECURSOR (Prx24) expression, increasing guard-cell H2O2 accumulation, reducing stomatal conductance and transpiration rate, thereby improving water retention and limiting sodium uptake under abiotic stress conditions. Elevated H2O2 also induces the expression of heat shock proteins, contributing to enhanced tolerance to heat stress. DST, in turn, transcriptionally represses WLG, establishing a negative feedback loop that fine-tunes H2O2 homeostasis and stress responses. Moreover, WLGhap.B promotes stronger DST degradation than WLGhap.A. Our findings elucidated the WLG-DST-Prx24 module as a central regulatory mechanism governing H2O2 dynamics under multiple abiotic stresses, highlighting the potential of WLGhap.B for developing multiple stress-resistant rice varieties in a changing climate.
items.authors: Wang Z, Wang S, Yue Z, Feng X, Chen Y, Yuan Y, Liang D, Xiong L, Hu H.

items.title: Shoot to root transport of the HY5 transcription factor drives root developmental plasticity under neighbour shade
items.abstract: Plants perceive competitors through the reflection of Far-Red light from neighbouring leaves. A decrease in the Red: Far-red light ratio (R:FR) is perceived by phytochrome photoreceptors and triggers elongation responses aboveground, allowing plants to anticipate future competition for light; their primary energy source. However, low R:FR perception by the shoot also prompts an alteration of root development, possibly to conserve resources. An important regulator of this response is the bZIP transcription factor ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL 5 (HY5), which can be transported from the shoot to the root, where it suppresses auxin signaling and lateral root outgrowth. However, it remains unknown whether HY5 transport is the direct link between shoot-perceived low R:FR and a decrease in lateral root outgrowth. We therefore sought to uncover the mechanics and speed of HY5 transport. To this end, we constructed shoot-specific inducible lines to perform live-imaging of HY5 transport using a vertical confocal microscope. This allowed us to follow the transport and unloading of HY5 from the phloem into the protophloem pericycle, where it becomes nuclearly localized, in real time over a 24-hour period. To mimic plant competition, we applied supplemental FR light and observed that this increased the HY5 protein levels in the shoot and subsequent HY5 protein transport from shoot-to-root. Finally, we were able to show that shoot-expressed HY5 is necessary and sufficient to induce the root response to shoot perceived Far-Red light. This work showcases in detail how a small general transcription factor functions as a long-distance signal between shoot and root and integrates environmental signalling over long distances in the plant.
items.authors: van der Velde, K., Ali, A., Hoogers, V., Stamm, F., Patnaik, A., Heliel, O., Rietveld, D., Akyuz, T., Retzer, K., Petrasek, J., Pierik, R., van Gelderen, K.

items.title: Low concentration silver ion decreases endogenous indole-3-acetic acid concentration in Arabidopsis root and increases root mass
items.abstract: Abstract Chemical biology research using chemicals has elucidated several mechanisms underlying the endogenous biosynthesis of indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) in plants. However, there has been little chemical biology research focused on the regulation of endogenous IAA concentrations in plant tissues, and only a few studies using silver ion (Ag + ) as a chemical have been reported to investigate how IAA concentrations in plant tissues change when this metal is applied to plant cultivation media. Previous studies have predominantly utilized Ag + concentrations in the range of several mg/L (tens of µM), the levels known to affect plant physiology. In this study, we conducted cultivation experiments with Arabidopsis thaliana to investigate how the presence of Ag + at low concentrations of bellow 2 µM, which do not induce silver-ion toxicity for usual plants, affects endogenous IAA concentrations in plant tissues and, consequently, root growth. Our experimental data showed that Ag + at low concentrations of 0.46–1.85 µM reduced excess IAA concentration in roots, thereby promoting root growth in A. thaliana .
items.authors: Matsuyama E, Ikeda-Ohtsubo W, Endo G.

items.title: Contrasting resistance and recovery of co-occurring conifers to larch caterpillar defoliation in a Northeast China temperate forest.
items.abstract: Climate change has been linked to the intensification of forest pest outbreaks, posing a serious threat to non-coevolved tree species because of their potentially weak defensive capabilities. However, unlike broad-scale climatic disturbances such as drought and heatwaves, insect outbreaks are highly heterogeneous in space and among host species, and the response of occurring conifers to such outbreaks remains poorly understood. The core area of the Changbai Mountain Nature Reserve in northeastern China was severely defoliated in 2019 by larch caterpillars (Dendrolimus superans Butler)-a conifer-feeding defoliator that prefers larch but also attacks other conifers. In this region, a vegetation transition zone between the broadleaf-Korean pine and spruce-fir forests hosts multiple conifer species co-existing within short distances under similar defoliation intensities. We monitored 1,837 trees in 2019 (pre-disturbance), 2021 and 2024, and sampled needles of healthy individuals of each species in 2024 to obtain species-level proxies of intrinsic foliar traits. Results revealed that: (i) mortality of attacked Korean pine peaked within 2 years, with little subsequent increase, resulting in a cumulative mortality rate of 31.3%; in contrast, mortality of spruce and fir continued to increase until the fifth year, reaching a combined cumulative rate of 78.6%, while larch exhibited nearly 100% survival. (ii) a deciduous habit, low needle biomass allocation and low carbohydrate concentrations enhanced survival by reducing canopy regeneration costs. (iii) regarding radial growth responses, spruce showed stronger compensatory growth but weaker recovery ability than fir and Korean pine, likely due to its limited carbon and nutrient reserves. Considering these findings, prioritizing the protection of non-coevolved conifers is recommended to minimize biomass loss during pest outbreaks. This study also provides important insights for temperate and boreal conifer forest conservation, highlighting the high vulnerability of spruce-fir forests to larch caterpillar outbreaks.
items.authors: Wang X, Jia X, Yan X, Lu D, Liu Y, Bai S, Jin S, Yu D.

items.title: Host genotype, resistance status and seasonal temperature shape the Norway spruce phyllosphere mycobiome.
items.abstract: The influence of the phyllosphere microbiome on plant health and disease development is well established. However, the roles of host resistance phenotype, seasonal variations, and accumulated temperature in shaping the phyllosphere mycobiome of Norway spruce (Picea abies) remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated (i) the phyllosphere mycobiome assembly of a subset of Heterobasidion partially resistant and susceptible Norway spruce genotypes, (ii) how fungal community composition in these genotypes changes across seasons and with temperature, and (iii) the extent to which the phyllosphere mycobiome shared taxa with the seed-associated fungal communities of the same genotypes. Needle samples were collected from Heterobasidion partially resistant and susceptible Norway spruce seedlings growing in an open field in May, July and September 2022. Fungal communities were characterized using internal transcribed spacer (ITS) amplicon sequencing. Alpha diversity metrics (richness, diversity and evenness) of the phyllosphere fungal community were significantly different between susceptible and partially resistant Norway spruce genotypes. Although the distributions showed substantial overlap between resistance classes, all three alpha-diversity metrics differed significantly between the groups (p < 0.05). Community composition was associated with both host resistance phenotype and temperature-related variables, with average and accumulated temperature explaining a greater proportion of variation than host resistance phenotype. Less than 1% of phyllosphere fungal taxa overlapped with the seed-associated fungal communities. Network analyses further revealed seasonal differences in fungal association patterns between partially resistant and susceptible seedlings.
items.authors: Ren W, Wen Z, Wang K, Azeez AA, Asiegbu FO.

items.title: Transcriptional Analysis Reveals Different Fertilizer Treatments Improve the Yield and Quality of Tomato Fruits by Postponing Age-Triggered Senescence.
items.abstract: Inappropriate fertilization has led to adverse environmental effects and food-safety issues. Biostimulants have been widely used to improve the growth, yield, and quality of crops. However, the effects of biostimulants on age-triggered senescence in plants, which affect the later yield and quality, have scarcely been reported. In this study, the fertilization formulas that were modified according to the requirements of plants in different growth stages, and adding yeast extract agents or microorganisms were respectively used in soilless tomato culture as three fertilization treatments. The Yamazaki formula was set as the control. As results, leaf senescence was delayed by the three fertilization treatments, and the yield and quality of the tomatoes were improved. RNA-seq analysis was used to identify the underlying regulatory mechanisms. The results showed that the genes expression levels remained unchanged in leaves in response to the three fertilization treatments. However, the "MAPK signaling pathway-plant" and "Plant-hormone signal transduction" processes between the roots and leaves were significantly affected, including auxin, gibberellin, ethylene, jasmonic acid, cytokinin, brassinosteroid, and the salicylic acid regulatory pathways. In addition, senescence-related transcription factors were significantly differentially expressed between roots and leaves, including WRKY, MYB, and AP2-EREBP. Our results confirm that using three fertilization formulas can improve the tomato yield and quality, and indicate that a close association exists between root and leaf senescence.
items.authors: Yang X, Sun S, Huang L, Xu J, Xie K, Zhou B, Yang F, Li J.

items.title: MYB156 promotes root sucker formation by repressing IDD14 and CKX1 to elevate cytokinin levels in Populus.
items.abstract: Root suckers enable clonal propagation of rooting-recalcitrant poplars, conferring rejuvenated traits such as enhanced survival and accelerated growth. Despite widespread clonal propagation and ecological restoration, the essential genes controlling sucker development remain unidentified. MYB156 is a positive regulator of root sucker formation in white poplar (Populus davidiana × P. bolleana). MYB156 is predominantly expressed in proliferation-competent root cells, including vascular cambium and phellogen. Gain- and loss-of-function analyses demonstrated that MYB156 overexpression enhanced root suckering and secondary growth, whereas myb156 mutants were severely compromised in both. Meanwhile, cytokinin levels increased two- to fivefold in roots with MYB156 overexpression but were significantly reduced in myb156 mutant roots. MYB156 directly represses IDD14 and CKX1, reducing cytokinin catabolism and alleviating IDD14-mediated suppression of cytokinin accumulation; IDD14 RNAi lines similarly showed elevated cytokinin and enhanced suckering. Cytokinin response elements in the MYB156 promoter and MYB156 autoactivation establish a cytokinin-MYB156 positive feedback loop amplifying cytokinin signaling in meristematic zones. Live imaging with the cytokinin response reporter TCSn:RFP demonstrated that suckering in MYB156-overexpressing plants shifted from the phellogen to the vascular cambium. These findings establish a MYB156-CKX1/IDD14-cytokinin module that creates a permissive context for suckering, providing a transcriptional blueprint for clonal propagation.
items.authors: Pang H, Li B, Chen Y, Ding L, Lyu W, Wang X, Wang H, Wei J, Zheng L.

items.title: Transcription Factor TabZIP12 Orchestrates the ABA Signaling Pathway to Regulate Drought Tolerance in Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.).
items.abstract: Drought-induced osmotic stress severely compromises crop yield productivity and threatens global food security. This study reports TabZIP12, a wheat bZIP transcription factor, in regulating osmotic stress tolerance. Under drought and abscisic acid (ABA) treatment, TabZIP12 expression was significantly upregulated with a dose- and time-dependent manner. Y-2H, BiFC, Co-IP, and In vitro pull-down assays confirmed a physical interaction between TabZIP12 and the kinase TaSnRK2.6. This kinase further interacted with the phosphatase TaPP2C50, which in turn interacted with the ABA receptor TaPYL1. These interactions suggest the TabZIP12-involved constitution of a synergistic signaling module (TaPYL1-TaPP2C50-TaSnRK2.6-TabZIP12). Transgene analyses revealed the essential functions of the signaling module members. Of which, TaPYL1, TaSnRK2.6, and TabZIP12 positively while TaPP2C50 negatively regulated drought tolerance, due to their roles in modulating key physiological processes associated with stomatal movement, osmolyte biosynthesis, root morphology, ABA biosynthesis, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging. TabZIP12 possessed an ability in binding with the promoters of critical stress-responsive genes, namely SLAC1 gene TaSLAC1-4, P5CS gene TaP5CS1, PIN-FORMed gene TaPIN3, NCED gene TaNCED3, and APX gene TaAPX6 and activated their activation. Transgenic validation confirmed these genes in positively modulating drought adaptation. Notably, in a wheat variety panel sharing contrasting drought response, the transcripts of TabZIP12 and its target genes correlated significantly with plant dry matter and yield under drought conditions. Haplotype analysis identified TabZIP12-Hap1 as a favorable allele associated with enhanced drought tolerance. Our findings elucidate novel mechanisms underlying the bZIP-mediated drought response and provide valuable genetic resources for breeding drought-resistant wheat varieties.
items.authors: Hou X, Wang Z, Zhang J, Shi X, Liu J, Wang J, Fu X, Zhang H, Wang H, Guo C, Xiao K.

items.title: Advances in the Functions and Molecular Mechanisms of SPL Transcription Factors in Plant Flower Development.
items.abstract: SQUAMOSA PROMOTER BINDING PROTEIN-LIKE (SPL) transcription factors constitute a plant-specific family defined by a conserved SBP DNA-binding domain. They recognize cis-elements containing the core GTAC motif and cooperate with various co-regulators to govern downstream gene expression, thereby participating in leaf morphogenesis, phase transition, fruit development, anthocyanin accumulation and abiotic stress adaptation. Notably, the abbreviation SPL is also used for the unrelated SPOROCYTELESS/NOZZLE (SPL/NZZ) protein, which belongs to a separate family lacking the SBP-box domain; these two families should not be confused. Flower development, a central reproductive program in angiosperms, encompasses the acquisition of flowering competence, the vegetative-to-reproductive transition, floral meristem specification, organ patterning, and gametophyte formation. This review summarizes structural characteristics and classification of SPL proteins, distinguishes miR156/miR157-targeted paralogs from non-targeted ones, and synthesizes current understanding of their molecular functions across successive floral stages. Acting as signaling hubs, SPLs integrate photoperiod, gibberellin-DELLA, age-dependent miR156/miR157, temperature, sugar and cytokinin signals to fine-tune flowering time. They drive the reproductive transition via direct activation of LFY, FUL and AP1, and later remodel inflorescence architecture and floral organ size by balancing cell proliferation and expansion. In addition, they maintain fertility by modulating gametogenesis. Based largely on findings from Arabidopsis thaliana, we construct an updated regulatory framework for SPL-dependent floral development, compare conserved and lineage-divergent functions across herbaceous and woody species, identify unresolved questions, and discuss potential applications for crop improvement.
items.authors: Wu Q, Pan X, Zhou L.

items.title: Genome-wide analysis of cork oak NLRs reveals RNL-associated duplications and immune receptor candidates associated with biotic and abiotic stress response.
items.abstract: The Nucleotide-Binding Domain Leucine-Rich Repeat (NLR) gene family is a central component of plant immune systems, yet its diversity and evolutionary dynamics remain poorly characterized in long-lived tree species. Here, we performed a genome-wide analysis of the NLR gene repertoire in Quercus suber (cork oak) using a newly developed annotation tool-InterNLR-which identifies and classifies NLRs as canonical and non-canonical. We identified a total of 374 canonical NLRs, and 544 non-canonical NLRs-which may represent pseudogenes, gene fragments or evolutionary intermediates. Phylogenetic analyses based on the NB-ARC domain highlighted the distinct evolutionary trajectory of RNL proteins, which function as "helper" NLRs and show evidence of clade-specific gene duplication. Transcriptomic analyses revealed significant differences in gene-level expression among NLR classes in cork oak stem tissues, mainly driven by contrasts involving the non-canonical N class. Seven cork oak NLR genes, sharing putative orthology with abiotic stress-responsive NLRs found in other species, were also differentially expressed in stems under drought conditions. From these, four candidate NLRs arise as candidate components of shared or convergent responses to drought and P. cinnamomi infection. Population-genetic analyses of RNA-seq-derived variants from expressed NLR loci in two Iberian populations further revealed heterogeneous patterns among expressed NLR loci, with a predominance of positive Tajima's D values. Together, these results provide new insights into the evolution, expression, and functional diversification of NLRs in cork oak. This work advances our understanding of immune gene architecture in an ecologically and economically important forest tree species.
items.authors: Gonçalves LM, Oliveira MM, Barros PM.

items.title: Rhizosphere dynamics and microbial mechanisms for improving plant resilience to soil salinity.
items.abstract: The rhizosphere is a critical interface where salinity-induced ionic, osmotic, and oxidative stresses are shaped by reciprocal interactions between plant roots, soil properties, and microorganisms. The paper discusses how microbial traits governing ion transport, antioxidant capacity, hormonal signaling, and nutrient mobilization contribute to plant resilience to soil salinity and examines the physiological, molecular, and ecological basis of these interactions. Under saline conditions, changes in root architecture and exudation profiles influence the recruitment and activity of microbial communities, including halotolerant and plant-beneficial taxa capable of producing exopolysaccharides, 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate (ACC) deaminase, siderophores, and other functional metabolites. These interactions create reciprocal feedbacks that connect microbial community assembly with root physiology, nutrient mobilization, and stress signaling. Beneficial microorganisms alleviate ionic and osmotic stress through biofilm formation, improved rhizosphere water retention, regulation of sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+) transport, and modulation of key ion transport systems involved in plant K+/Na+ homeostasis. They also influence phytohormonal networks involving indole-3-acetic acid, abscisic acid, and jasmonate, while enhancing antioxidant defenses and redox homeostasis. By integrating these interconnected processes, the review highlights the rhizosphere as a dynamic functional system in which microbial activities can reinforce plant physiological adaptation to salinity. This framework provides a basis for understanding how rhizosphere processes can be harnessed to improve plant salinity resilience and develop more effective microbiome-informed strategies for sustainable crop production in salt-affected soils.
items.authors: Kaya C, Ashraf M, Shabala S.

items.title: Trait-specific benefits of association-based marker preselection for genomic prediction in slash pine
items.abstract: Abstract Slash pine ( Pinus elliottii Engelm. var. elliottii ) is a leading resin-producing conifer and multipurpose industrial tree species, valued as a renewable source of rosin and turpentine for the naval-stores and bio-based chemical industries, and of timber and pulp; yet simultaneous improvement of growth, wood quality, oleoresin yield, and resin chemistry is constrained by long generation intervals and late-expressed traits. Using 240 open-pollinated trees genotyped with 53,229 transcriptome-derived SNPs, we characterized marker associations for 12 traits and evaluated genomic selection (GS) with GWAS, SNP ranking, QTN discovery, and model fitting restricted to training folds. Training-fold GWAS showed differences in association patterns among trait classes: growth traits showed the strongest, most recurrent associations, wood-quality traits moderate signals, and oleoresin traits weaker, less stable associations. Annotation of significant, large-effect, and recurrent QTN-tagged transcripts converged on nucleotide and RNA processing, respiratory energy and cell-wall precursor supply, and lipid-terpenoid metabolism, providing hypotheses for growth, wood formation, and resin physiology. Using fold-contained GWAS outputs as marker priors, model-averaged predictive ability increased by 11.9% for growth, more than five-fold the 2.2% gain for wood quality, but did not improve oleoresin traits. The selected configurations for diameter at breast height and height yielded PA values of 0.493 and 0.365, respectively, no single GS model dominated across traits, and fixed large-effect or recurrent QTN covariates rarely surpassed optimized genomic baselines without fixed QTN effects, suggesting limited additional predictive value of these covariates under the tested configurations. GS-selected elite sets retained 80.3–95.1% of the same-cycle phenotype-BLUP benchmark gain; assuming 15-year conventional and 7-year GS cycles yielded a projected 1.7-2.0-fold annualized benchmark advantage. These results support further evaluation of trait-specific, GWAS-informed prediction in slash pine. Model selection reused the cross-validation results, and independent family, site, and generation validation is needed; realized breeding gains were not measured.
items.authors: Ding X, Zhang Y, Luan Q, Fan H, Tan Z, Jiang J.

items.title: Maize STEM BENDING1 controls plant architecture through cell wall and auxin pathways.
items.abstract: Crop yield is largely determined by plant architecture. Identifying the key genes responsible for maize architecture can help optimize plant architecture for high-density planting. Here, we characterized a dominant stem bending mutant (Stb1) in maize, which exhibited bent stems and curved leaves leading to a slanted architecture. Genetic mapping delimited Stb1 to a 3.7 Mb interval on chromosome 1. Transcriptome analysis suggested that Stb1 mutation impaired the molecular pathways related to cell wall components and environmental stimuli. Consistently, lignin and hemicellulose contents were altered between the convex side and concave side of Stb1 stems. In addition, the shoot gravitropism regulator LAZY1 transcripts and endogenous auxin levels were differentially accumulated between the two sides of Stb1 stems. Our study reveals that STB1 plays a role in maintaining upright stems through cell wall and auxin-related pathways, providing a new target for optimizing maize shoot architecture.
items.authors: Zhao S, Farid B, Liu X, Dong L, Yang F.

items.title: Stomatal Dynamics Multilevel Regulation and Physiological Response of Prunus mira Koehne under Extreme CO2 Toxicity Stress.
items.abstract: Rising atmospheric CO2 levels not only drive global warming but also exert toxic effects on plant photosynthesis and physiology under extreme exposure, however the adaptive responses of stress tolerant species such as Prunus mira Koehne remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the physiological and stomatal response mechanisms of P. mira under 5% CO2 conditions. The results of our physiological and biochemical analyses revealed that 5% CO2 concentrations reduced chlorophyll content and impaired photosynthetic efficiency. Concurrently, high CO2 stimulated alternative respiration, disrupted membrane integrity, elevated ROS (reactive oxygen species) levels, and increased antioxidant enzyme activities. In guard cells, high CO2 triggered accumulations of ROS and NO (nitric oxide), leading to stomatal closure, reduced stomatal conductance, while transpiration rates fluctuated during the treatment period. Moreover, pharmacological analyses suggested the involvement of Ca2+ in regulating ROS and NO accumulation, while ASA (ascorbic acid) promoted scavenging of excess H2O2. Our results suggest that ROS accumulation and Ca2⁺ signaling are involved in stomatal regulation under extreme CO2 toxicity stress. In summary, these findings provide mechanistic insights into plant responses under acute extreme CO2 toxicity and lay a foundation for understanding stress signaling robustness in woody species.
items.authors: Li J, Li M, Qi X, Wang M, Liu J, Meng F.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Iron Oxide Nanoparticles Alleviate Cold Stress in Rice by Reducing Oxidative Damage and Enhancing Antioxidant Defense Systems, and Transcriptional Networks.
items.abstract: Cold stress significantly impairs the rice (Oryza sativa L.) growth and yield, particularly in temperate regions where abrupt temperature fluctuations often occur during the early growth stages. Given the need for novel strategies to improve crop cold tolerance, we evaluated the efficacy of iron oxide nanoparticles (Fe2O3) in enhancing rice cold stress resilience. The reported mechanisms involve promoting plant growth and development, alleviating oxidative stress and inducing defense responses. Using RNA-seq, we analyzed the physiological and transcriptomic responses of rice to cold stress and Fe2O3 treatment. Under cold stress, the NPs elicited a strong antioxidant response-elevating superoxide dismutase (SOD), peroxidase (POD), and catalase (CAT) activities, which led to a marked reduction in oxidative damage, as shown by decreased ROS and MDA levels. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed that NP treatment modulated key pathways related to carbohydrate metabolism, photosynthesis, hormone signaling, and antioxidant metabolism. Collectively, our findings establish that Fe2O3 nanoparticles ameliorate cold stress by preserving chloroplast structure, stomatal architecture, reduce oxidative stress marker, enhancing antioxidant defense system and stabilize photosystem and providing a promising nanozyme-based approach for rice protection against cold induce damage.
items.authors: Ullah S, Ateeq M, Xiong D, Khan A, Sui L, Khan EH, Waqas M, Yang N, Jianliang H.

items.title: The heat stress transcription factors HsfA3a/b enhance heat stress resistance by regulating HSP26.5-1/-2 in Sorbus pohuashanensis.
items.abstract: Heat stress impacts the growth and value of ornamental plants such as Sorbus pohuashanensis. Heat stress transcription factors (Hsfs) and heat shock proteins (HSPs) are critical in the response of plants to heat stress. However, the roles of HsfA3a/b and HSP26.5-1/-2 in the heat tolerance mechanisms of woody plants remain elusive. Here, we report the isolation of SpHsfA3a/b and SpHSP26.5-1/-2 from S. pohuashanensis and their molecular characterization. SpHsfA3a/b and SpHSP26.5-1/-2 were expressed at higher levels in leaves and fruits. Furthermore, their expression levels increased dramatically under heat stress. Overexpression of SpHsfA3a/b and SpHSP26.5-1/-2, as well as complementation of hsfa3 mutants with SpHsfA3a/b in Arabidopsis thaliana, significantly increased plant survival under heat stress. This enhanced survival was accompanied by reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) content, increased proline and soluble sugars, and elevated antioxidant enzyme activities. The positive regulatory genes related to the heat stress responses were upregulated, while the negative regulatory gene was downregulated in the transgenic SpHsfA3a/b-overexpressing Arabidopsis lines and the complemented hsfa3 mutant lines under high temperature stress. Yeast one-hybrid and dual-luciferase reporter assays showed that SpHsfA3a/b directly bound to and activated the promoters of SpHSP26.5-1/-2. In summary, SpHsfA3a/b directly regulate the expression of SpHSP26.5-1/-2 and play crucial, synergistic roles in enhancing thermotolerance. This study elucidates a key transcriptional regulatory module, SpHsfA3a/b-SpHSP26.5-1/-2, in the heat stress response of S. pohuashanensis and provides candidate genes for improving the heat resistance of forest trees.
items.authors: Wu Q, Qi X, Di Z, Zhang Y, Zhang R, Jin Y, Lu Y, Han Y, Zheng J.

items.title: Live spatial validation of plant-microbe interactions in the rhizosphere with light-sheet fluorescence microscopy.
items.abstract: Plant-microbe interactions in the rhizosphere are spatial events, yet mechanisms are often inferred from bulk samples, endpoint images, or community profiles averaged across heterogeneous root zones. Rather than surveying LSFM hardware or rhizosphere imaging broadly, this review evaluates light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) as a platform for claim-level live spatial validation. Evidence is separated into four levels: A, direct LSFM evidence; B, an LSFM-compatible sample or device demonstrated with another modality; C, a correlative or validation modality; and D, a proposed future application. Within the verified full-text evidence set, direct evidence is concentrated in whole-rhizosphere tracking of Bacillus populations, plant reporter responses during early root-fungus interactions, and rhizobial attachment and infection of root hairs. Many arbuscular mycorrhizal and biocontrol applications remain prospective. We compare instrument and sample choices across field of view, numerical aperture, voxel sampling, time interval, spectral channels, and matrix realism; define root-centric metrics for arrival, residence, occupancy, growth, and persistence; and distinguish simultaneous, sequential in situ, and destructive endpoint validation. LSFM can identify where and when a candidate interaction occurs, but identity, activity, perturbation, and functional assays are still required before mechanism is assigned. A minimum reporting checklist is proposed to connect optical settings, environmental context, hierarchical sampling, registration error, and open analysis. The strongest role of LSFM in rhizosphere research is therefore targeted and evidence-bounded: resolving a live spatial prediction and directing independent tests of what the interaction does and why.
items.authors: Dong X, Cheng Q, Ma J, Wang F, Lin H.

items.title: Fruit growth rate influences cortical xylem transport, calcium delivery, and bitter pit incidence of apple.
items.abstract: Bitter pit of apple is commonly ascribed to calcium dilution because symptoms are positively associated with fruit mass. A dilution effect implies that calcium transport or supply cannot keep pace with fruit growth but does not identify the mechanism. Disparate sink:source ratios or transient photosynthetic inhibition were used to alter 'Honeycrisp' fruit growth rate (FGR) to study fruit xylem transport kinetics and peel calcium concentration. FGR and xylem dysfunction increased with decreasing sink:source ratio. Xylem transport declined to 50% of maximum 1.7 weeks earlier under Low than High sink:source ratios and peel calcium decreased concomitantly with xylem transport. Treatment effects on bitter pit incidence were explained by integrating time-dependent xylem transport curves into an empirical 'cumulative xylem' function. Regressing this function on FGR conflated treatment differences. When photosynthetic light reactions were inhibited by episodic limb shading, FGR was reduced and xylem transport increased; shade removal caused transient surges in FGR and concomitant reduction in xylem transport. Changes in calcium concentration were less responsive to shade due to stomatal limits to water transport. Combined, the results support that FGR compromises xylem transport, effectively limiting calcium supply and exacerbating bitter pit, the magnitude of which depends on the onset of xylem dysfunction.
items.authors: Griffith C, Einhorn TC.

items.title: A Gnotobiotic Rice Pathosystem Reveals How the Microbiome Suppresses Rice Blast Disease
items.abstract: Rice blast disease caused by the hemibiotrophic fungal pathogen Magnaporthe oryzae poses a major threat to global rice production, creating an urgent need for sustainable disease management strategies. Because plant-associated microbiomes can contribute to pathogen suppression and host defense, their role in rice blast resistance is of considerable interest. However, interactions among M. oryzae , rice, and the rice microbiome remain poorly understood. Using a gnotobiotic rice pathosystem, we investigated how microbiome colonization influences host responses to infection and how bacterial community structure changes following pathogen challenge. Microbiome colonization significantly reduced blast disease severity, while differential abundance analyses identified infection-associated shifts in bacterial community composition, including enrichment of Brevibacillus -associated taxa. Functional characterization of cultured endophytes revealed plant growth-promoting traits and antagonistic activity against M. oryzae . Two synthetic communities assembled from healthy- and infected-derived isolates significantly reduced disease severity, demonstrating that disease suppression can be recapitulated using simplified microbial communities. Interestingly, axenically grown plants exhibited elevated basal expression of multiple defense-associated genes but greater disease severity and reduced chitin-induced ROS production compared with holoxenic plants. In contrast, microbiome-colonized plants displayed enhanced ROS responsiveness and reduced disease, suggesting that the rice microbiome promotes a more effective and regulated immune state rather than simply increasing defense activation. Together, these findings advance our understanding of rice-microbiome- M. oryzae interactions and establish a tractable experimental platform for mechanistic studies of microbiome-mediated disease suppression.
items.authors: Johnson, T. R., Kemmerer, L. E., Payne, N., VanWeelden, M., Roesch, L. F., Fernandez, J.

items.title: Integrated transcriptome and hormone dynamics uncover biphasic defense responses in sugar beet infected by Cercospora beticola.
items.abstract: BackgroundCercospora leaf spot (CLS), caused by the hemibiotrophic fungus Cercospora beticola, is a destructive foliar disease that threatens sugar beet production worldwide. Despite its economic significance, the molecular interaction between sugar beet and C. beticola is poorly understood.ResultsWe report integrated time-resolved transcriptomics and hormone profiling of CLS infection spanning the asymptomatic and symptomatic phases. Our data revealed broad transcriptional changes, with defense and hormone-related processes being most altered. We detected transcriptional signatures consistent with activation of pathogen-associated molecular pattern- and effector-triggered immunity, along with differential expression of genes encoding putative receptor-like kinases and receptor-like proteins as well as nucleotide-binding (NB) leucine‑rich repeat (LRR) receptors (NLRs). Defense activation was evident as early as 3 days post-inoculation (dpi), including upregulation of pathogenesis-related proteins, genes related to systemic acquired resistance, and the hypersensitive response (HR). At 7 dpi, several biological processes, including defense response, showed overall downregulation, suggesting a pathogen-mediated suppression of transcriptional responses. During the symptomatic phase, defense-related genes-particularly those associated with HR and numerous putative NLRs-were induced again, illustrating a bi-phasic regulation pattern. Cis-element enrichment analysis showed significant overrepresentation of defense-related WRKY and AT-hook motif nuclear-localized protein binding motifs within the protomers of genes upregulated from 11 to 25 dpi. Parallel quantification of major phytohormones demonstrated stage-dependent modulation of infection-related hormone groups across the infection cycle.ConclusionOur analysis revealed that a susceptible sugar beet genotype mounts an early and transient defense response against C. beticola, which appears to be pathogen-suppressed but later reactivated during symptom development. By integrating time-resolved transcriptome analysis and hormone profiling, our study links major defense transcriptional programs and phytohormone dynamics, providing a comprehensive view of sugar beet responses to CLS that complements and extends previous genotype-focused work.
items.authors: Ebinezer LB, Natwick M, Rangel LI, Jaswal R, Branch E, Secor G, Bolton MD, Wyatt NA.

items.title: ERF Transcription Factor PagERF135A Negatively Regulates Drought Tolerance in Poplar by Modulating Sucrose Metabolism and Brassinosteroid Biosynthesis.
items.abstract: Drought is one of the primary environmental constraints limiting poplar growth. Identifying key drought-resistance genes and their regulatory mechanisms is crucial for genetic improvement of drought tolerance in poplar. Time-course transcriptome analysis of 84K poplar (Populus alba × P. glandulosa) under drought stress revealed that the ERF family is among the most responsive transcription factor families, and PagERF135A exhibited the most significant upregulation, suggesting a key regulatory role. Genome-wide identification of the ERF family in 84K poplar identified 276 members, with expansion primarily through segmental duplication, and purifying selection dominated their evolution. PagERF135A is a nuclear-localized transcription factor with transcriptional activation activity. Overexpression of PagERF135A reduced drought tolerance in transgenic poplars, manifested by aggravated oxidative damage, diminished osmotic adjustments, and impaired PSII and PSI activities. Integrated transcriptomic and WGCNA analyses showed that PagERF135A overexpression suppressed drought-induced expression of soluble sugar synthesis genes in starch-sucrose metabolism, down-regulated brassinosteroid biosynthesis and signaling genes, and promoted catabolic genes. Thus, PagERF135A negatively regulates drought tolerance by disrupting carbon metabolic flow and brassinosteroid signaling homeostasis. Our findings provide new insights into ERF-mediated drought response mechanisms in poplar.
items.authors: Qi S, Yang M, Zhang R, Chang Y, Bi C, Yao T, Liu H, Zhang Y, Dai S, Ding C, Wang Z, Zhang H.

items.title: AcCHI, a Chitinase from Atriplex canescens, Confers Enhanced Tolerance to Osmotic and Salt Stress in Glycine max by Reinforcing Antioxidant and Osmotic Responses.
items.abstract: Soybean is the most crucial oilseed and plant-protein crop worldwide, yet its yield is frequently threatened by salinity and drought stress. In this study, the chitinase gene AcCHI was cloned from the highly stress-tolerant plant Atriplex canescens and heterologously overexpressed in soybean to generate stable T3 homozygous transgenic lines. Wild-type and transgenic plants were subjected to water-withholding drought treatment, 20% PEG6000-induced osmotic stress, and 150 mM NaCl salt stress. After drought treatment, the survival rate of transgenic lines reached 2.66-2.69 times relative to wild-type plants. Under osmotic and salt stress conditions, AcCHI-overexpressing lines exhibited better-maintained photosynthetic performance, higher proline accumulation, and lower malondialdehyde (MDA) levels compared with wild-type controls. Enhanced antioxidant enzyme activities and weakened histochemical ROS staining were also observed in transgenic leaves. Stress-responsive genes associated with DREB, RD22, and SOS pathways showed stronger stress-inducible expression in transgenic plants. Our results show that heterologous AcCHI expression is associated with improved osmotic- and salt-stress tolerance in soybean seedlings under laboratory conditions. This study provides new observational insights into chitinase-linked abiotic-stress responses and offers candidate genetic resources for breeding stress-tolerant soybean varieties.
items.authors: Sun J, Luo S, Zhang J, Li J, Zhou Y, Li B, Zhao M, Lyu Q.

items.title: Heavy metal stress mitigation in plants by metal-resistant fungi: molecular and biotechnological insights.
items.abstract: Heavy Metals (HMs) are persistent, non-biodegradable metallic elements that accumulate into soils due to weathering processes and anthropogenic activities, such as mining, smelting and industrial discharges. They can be classified as essential (Cu, Zn, Ni, Fe, Mn), which are toxic in excessive amounts, and non-essential (Cd, Pb, As, Hg), which are dangerous even in small amounts. HMs affect plant metabolism causing production of Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS), growth inhibition and nutrient deficiency, Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings germination was lowered to 55% and 21% at concentrations of 50 and 100 mg L⁻1 CdCl₂. Phytochelatins, metallothioneins and vacuole sequestration protect plants, but become ineffective at high concentrations of HMs. Metal-resistant fungi help to cope with stress conditions using mechanisms of biosorption, bioaccumulation, biomineralization, bioleaching and biotransformation, adapted Aspergillus niger managed to leach 78.5% Ni and 82.3% Mo during 30 days, while Penicillium chrysogenum eliminated 63% Cd in soil. Partners of fungi, such as Trichoderma and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, regulate production of ROS, activation of MAPKs and ABA/JA/SA/ethylene/auxin signaling pathway and expression of MT, PCS, GST, ABC, NRAMP and HMA genes under control of WRKY, MYB, NAC and bZIP transcription factors.
items.authors: Choudhary S, Singh K, Sharma A, Mehta A, Gupta S, Juneja G.

items.title: Root-applied taurine reduces grain cadmium and improves rice yield by decreasing Cd transport and increasing Cd retention in roots.
items.abstract: Taurine (TAU) can improve plant stress tolerance, but its effect on cadmium (Cd) accumulation in rice remains poorly understood. Here, we compared seed soaking, root application, and foliar spraying of TAU using hydroponic and full-season pot experiments with rice (Oryza sativa L. cv. Kitaake). The results showed that root application of TAU was the optimal approach, which can significantly promote rice growth and reduce Cd accumulation. In the hydroponic experiment, 10 mg L-1 TAU increased shoot and root dry weights by 37.3% and 63.3%, respectively, and decreased shoot Cd concentration by 29.0%. In the pot experiment, root-applied TAU decreased brown-rice Cd concentration by 23.3% and increased grain yield by 14.7%. Root application of TAU reduced expression of OsNRAMP1, OsNRAMP5, OsIRT1, and OsIRT2 genes associated with Cd uptake and the OsHMA2 gene in charge of xylem loading by 29.7%, 11.4%, 48.8%, 11.1%, and 22.0%, respectively, whereas increased expression of the OsHMA3 gene involved in Cd vacuolar sequestration by 27.5%. Integrated transcriptomic, metabolomic, and physiological analyses showed that TAU activated the jasmonic acid signaling and phenylpropanoid pathway and promoted root cell-wall lignification, thereby increasing Cd retention in the cell wall by 20.2%. These results suggest that root-applied TAU decreases Cd accumulation in rice grain through coordinated changes in Cd uptake, translocation, and root retention while increasing grain production, offering a potential strategy for the safe utilization of Cd-contaminated paddy fields.
items.authors: Tao Q, Zheng H, Chen Y, Liu J, Reng S, Yan M, Yang X, Li B, Wang C.

items.title: Overexpression of a Malus baccata NAC Transcription Factor Gene MbNAC40 Increases Cold Tolerance in Arabidopsis.
items.abstract: As a primary apple rootstock extensively cultivated across Northeast China, Malus baccata (L.) Borkh. constantly suffers from low temperature, drought and salt damage throughout its growth cycle. NAC transcription factors take critical parts in coordinating plant adaptation to various adverse environments, yet relevant functional research on this woody rootstock species remains limited. In this work, a NAC family gene designated MbNAC40 was cloned from M. baccata, and its biological function was explored via heterologous transformation in Arabidopsis thaliana. Sequence analysis revealed that the open reading frame of MbNAC40 spans 1467 bp and encodes a 488-amino-acid protein targeted to the cell nucleus. After 24 h cold acclimation at 4 °C, plants were subjected to -4 °C freezing stress for 12 h, then recovered at 25 °C for 3 d. Transgenic Arabidopsis lines overexpressing MbNAC40 exhibited much stronger cold tolerance relative to wild-type plants. Transgenic materials retained more chlorophyll and synthesized more osmoprotective proline, accompanied by enhanced activity of three antioxidant enzymes (SOD, POD and CAT). Meanwhile, multiple stress-marker genes (AtCAT1, AtCSD1, AtAPX6, and AtP5CS1) associated with ROS and osmotic adjustment were significantly activated in overexpression lines. Taken together, these results confirm that MbNAC40 acts as a positive modulator of cold resistance in Arabidopsis, which provides a valuable gene resource for molecular breeding of cold-resistant M. baccata rootstock varieties.
items.authors: Jiao K, Li Y, Song P, Li W, Zhang Z, Wang T, Li X, Han D.

items.title: Genome-Wide Characterization of the Wheat Pum Gene Family and Heterologous Functional Analysis of TaPum-III-5b in Arabidopsis Under Salt Stress.
items.abstract: Pumilio (Pum)-family proteins are evolutionarily conserved RNA-binding proteins that regulate post-transcriptional processes; however, their specific functions in staple crops, for example, wheat (Triticum aestivum), remain poorly understood. We identified 56 TaPum genes and classified them into three phylogenetic subgroups (I-III). The larger TaPum family size in allohexaploid wheat was associated with retention of A-, B-, and D-subgenome homoeologs, segmental duplication, and tandem duplication. After separating homoeologous pairs, 17 segmental duplication pairs and five tandem duplication pairs were identified, and ratios of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitutions (Ka/Ks) below 1 were consistent with purifying selection. Subgroup-specific motifs and the uneven distribution of cis-acting elements, particularly abscisic acid (ABA)- and methyl jasmonate (MeJA)-responsive elements, suggested potential divergence in promoter regulatory architecture. Transcriptomic profiling and independent quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction analysis showed more consistent response of TaPum genes to salt stress than to cold or drought stress. Salt stress strongly promoted TaPum-III-5b expression, and its encoded protein exhibited nuclear and cytoplasmic localization. Heterologous overexpression of TaPum-III-5b in Arabidopsis thaliana increased salt tolerance, as indicated by enhanced survival; augmented peroxidase, superoxide dismutase, and catalase activities; and diminished accumulation of reactive oxygen species and malondialdehyde. Electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) demonstrated sequence-specific binding of TaDREB2B to a dehydration-responsive element (DRE)-containing sequence in the TaPum-III-5b promoter, whereas dual-luciferase (Dual-LUC) analysis showed activation of the wild-type promoter. Together, these results support a proposed regulatory framework in which TaPum-III-5b may contribute to salt-stress responses through as-yet-unidentified downstream RNA targets. This study characterizes the Pum gene family in wheat and identifies the TaDREB2B-TaPum-III-5b module as a candidate regulatory pathway associated with salt-stress responses. Its potential application in wheat improvement requires further validation in wheat.
items.authors: Zheng W, Cui Z, Li P, Wang M, Huang C, Li W, Sun X, Liu Y, Sun M, Yan B.

items.title: Integrative molecular mechanisms of lodging resistance in rice (Oryza sativa L.) culms: from DELLA-OsGSK2-BZR1 signaling to cell wall engineering and QTL-based breeding.
items.abstract: Rice lodging, permanent culm displacement from the vertical position, reduces grain yield and quality, potentially causing up to ~80% yield loss. Lodging resistance is a multifactorial trait shaped by stem morphology, internal anatomy, and cell wall chemistry. A central unresolved question in the field concerns the relative contribution of lignin versus cellulose to culm mechanical strength, a debate that has significant implications for targeted breeding and cell wall engineering. This review offers a comprehensive integration of two key questions: (1) What are the current molecular regulatory mechanisms underlying lodging resistance-associated culm traits in rice? (2) How can these mechanisms be translated into effective breeding strategies?. How can these mechanisms be translated into effective breeding strategies? Unlike earlier reviews that focused on individual mechanisms, this synthesis integrates hormonal crosstalk, hierarchical NAC-MYB cascades, emerging evidence for epigenetic regulation, and QTL-based breeding into a unified conceptual framework centered on the DELLA-OsGSK2-BZR1 module. Our synthesis reveals that plant architecture is governed by extensive phytohormone crosstalk centered on the proposed DELLA-OsGSK2-BZR1 module, where gibberellin and brassinosteroid synergistically modulate elongation and thickening, whereas auxin, strigolactone, ethylene, and jasmonic acid fine-tune plant height and tillering. Major-effect loci, such as SCM2/APO1 and SCM3/OsTB1, enable the concurrent improvement of strength and yield, with QTL pyramiding reported to increase culm diameter by up to ~39% in specific genetic backgrounds. Vascular bundle development and cell wall biosynthesis (lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose) are coordinated by hierarchical NAC-MYB transcriptional cascades, with recent advances suggesting epigenetic regulation through DNA methylation, histone modification, and DELLA-mediated chromatin silencing in rice. We further discuss how these mechanistic insights may guide modern breeding through marker-assisted selection, genome selection, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated precision engineering, and ideotype design, providing a roadmap for developing next-generation lodging-resistant rice varieties.
items.authors: Sherif A, Tang C, Dong C, A X, Sun Y, Yang Y, Ge N, Nie R, Hassan AA, Zhang F, Yang Y.

items.title: Loss of ALN Function in Arabidopsis thaliana Induces Allantoin Accumulation and Enhances Antioxidant Enzyme Responses to Copper Toxicity.
items.abstract: Environmental contamination with heavy metals severely impairs crop productivity, primarily by inhibiting growth and triggering oxidative damage. To counteract these adverse effects, plants undergo complex metabolic reprogramming. Among these adaptations, the accumulation of purine-derived ureides-particularly allantoin-has been proposed as a protective mechanism, though its role under copper (Cu) stress remains unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that wild-type (Arabidopsis thaliana, WT) plants accumulate allantoate-the product of allantoin hydrolysis catalyzed by allantoinase (ALN, EC 3.5.2.5)-rather than allantoin when exposed to Cu toxicity. However, blocking this downstream catabolic step via loss of ALN function results in allantoin accumulation and is associated with enhanced Cu tolerance. Under Cu stress, aln-1 and aln-4 loss-of-function mutants maintained higher biomass and accumulated lower levels of malondialdehyde, superoxide anions, and hydrogen peroxide compared to WT. Furthermore, aln lines exhibited a stronger Cu-induced activation of key antioxidant enzymes (SOD, CAT, POD, APX) alongside higher expression of genes encoding specific isoforms targeted to multiple cellular compartments: cytosolic (CSD1), chloroplastic (CSD2, tAPX), peroxisomal (APX3, CAT3), and apoplastic (Prx51, Prx47). These results reveal that the loss of ALN function promotes a multi-compartmental antioxidant response under Cu toxicity, highlighting the pivotal role of purine catabolism in plant redox homeostasis and pointing to ureide metabolism as a potential avenue for enhancing crop stress tolerance.
items.authors: Bylińska K, Michniewska B, Rusin W, Sagi M, Zdunek-Zastocka E.
