items.title: Physicochemical Assessment of Plant-Derived Residues as Potential Components of Substrates for Pleurotus ostreatus Cultivation.
items.abstract: Plant-derived residues may provide locally available components for mushroom cultivation substrates, but their variable composition requires preliminary physicochemical characterization. The aim of this study was to evaluate the physicochemical parameters of selected plant-derived residues in terms of their suitability as substrate components for the cultivation of Pleurotus ostreatus. The primary raw materials used were: oak sawdust, birch sawdust, wheat straw, triticale straw, rapeseed straw, and hemp shives. In addition, spent coffee grounds and apple pomace were applied as supplements enriching the substrate. The tested materials were subjected to physicochemical analyses including the determination of pH value, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, calcium, sodium, organic carbon, and heavy metal content. The lignocellulosic materials showed high C:N ratios (80-257), indicating the potential need for nitrogen supplementation. Spent coffee grounds had the highest nitrogen content (21.61 g·kg-1 DM) and the lowest C:N ratio (25.96), while apple pomace showed the lowest pH (3.85). Wheat and triticale straw supplemented with spent coffee grounds were identified as promising candidates for further cultivation trials, supporting the valorization of plant-derived residues in line with circular economy principles. As the study was limited to preliminary physicochemical screening, lignocellulosic-fraction analysis, physical characterization, and cultivation trials are required before the technological suitability of the proposed mixtures can be confirmed.
items.authors: Koziak K, Piekut J, Krasowska M, Zgłobicka I, Zapora E.

items.title: Grapevine rust fungus Neophysopella tropicalis deploys protein effectors with plant immunity-suppressing activity during sequential stages of pathogenesis.
items.abstract: Germination of urediniospores marks the onset of infection by Neophysopella tropicalis, the causal agent of Asian grapevine leaf rust, yet the molecular mechanisms enabling this obligate biotrophic fungus to establish infection remain largely unknown. We combined transcriptomics, histological analyses, and functional assays to identify and characterize candidate effector proteins deployed during the earliest stages of pathogenesis. RNA sequencing of in vitro-germinated urediniospores identified 303 genes encoding predicted secreted proteins bearing hallmarks of fungal effectors, grouped into 142 sequence families and revealing a remarkably diverse repertoire of effector candidates. Fifteen highly expressed N. tropicalis effector candidate (NtEC) genes, representing thirteen distinct sequence families, were selected for expression profiling by reverse transcription quantitative PCR across infection stages. Chitin-targeted fluorescence microscopy provided a developmental framework for interpreting expression across germination, penetration, and early colonization. Although identified during germination, seven NtECs accumulated transcripts predominantly during host penetration and early biotrophic colonization, suggesting specialized roles in infection establishment. Using the Type III Secretion System of Pseudomonas fluorescens EtHAn, we demonstrated that three NtECs (NtEC-05, NtEC-09, and NtEC-10) strongly suppressed AvrB-triggered hypersensitive cell death in Nicotiana benthamiana, while three others (NtEC-11, NtEC-12, and NtEC-13) exhibited moderate immune-suppressing activity. Together, these findings provide the first comprehensive characterization of the N. tropicalis effector repertoire, demonstrating that early infection involves coordinated, sequential deployment of evolutionarily diverse effectors associated with plant immune suppression. This work establishes an integrated framework for discovery and functional prioritization of rust fungus effectors and provides a valuable molecular resource for future studies on grapevine-rust interactions.
items.authors: Maia T, Ferro JV, Husein G, Bombardelli RGH, Monteiro-Vitorello CB.

items.title: Modeling diseased xylem networks.
items.abstract: Vascular wilt pathogens induce xylem blockages that disrupt plant water transport, posing critical threats to agricultural productivity and food security. Key processes including xylem transport, vessel blockage, and pathogen spread within the xylem remain poorly understood, largely due to our limited ability to internally monitor infected tissues. This review explores how complementary mathematical modeling alongside laboratory studies can elucidate features governing these critical processes. I first provide a brief history of xylem imaging and quantification, highlighting technological advances, and persistent limitations. I then review modeling approaches to describe xylem water transport and pathogen dynamics, emphasizing that different pathogens require fundamentally different modeling frameworks. Existing xylem flow models may provide suitable hydraulic conductivity estimates for healthy stems under idealized conditions; however, they lack explicit representation of pit membranes and lumen-occluding structures, limiting their applicability to diseased stems where these features are actively modified during infection. Previously described biofilm models can replicate bacterial colony growth in controlled experimental settings but are often too complex for integration with flow simulations and rely on parameters that are difficult to quantify experimentally. Finally, I highlight directions and challenges for modeling occlusion and spread at the local scale and discuss how these models might be scaled to network-level architecture. While these types of models remain computationally challenging, advances in multiscale imaging technologies and scaling approaches promise significant progress in the coming decades. Insights from such models stand to advance both our understanding of disease progression and the development of resilient crops for an uncertain climate future.
items.authors: Walker NC.

items.title: Generation and characterization of a barley strigolactone mutant collection: from plant architecture to drought stress response.
items.abstract: Strigolactones (SLs) are known to regulate shoot architecture and to be involved in plant responses to environmental stress, whereas their specific contributions to drought adaptation in barley remain incompletely defined. In this study, we analysed transcriptional, hormonal, and physiological responses to water deficit in barley SL mutants affected in early biosynthesis (Hvd10 and Hvd17), late biosynthesis (Hvmax1a), or signalling (Hvd14). The Hvd10, Hvd17, and Hvd14 mutants exhibited the typical high-tillering phenotype of SL deficiency, whereas Hvmax1a displayed characteristics similar to the wild type (WT), indicating functional differences within the SL biosynthetic pathway. Transcriptome analysis showed a clear overlap in gene expression among the high-tillering SL mutants under both control and drought conditions. We also used computational methods to identify potential transcription factors that might regulate SL-dependent gene expression. A drought experiment showed that SL mutants exhibited reduced biomass, relative water content, and photosynthetic efficiency, with the most pronounced effects observed in the high-tillering lines. Drought also activated the abscisic acid (ABA) pathway in all genotypes, with particularly high accumulation of ABA metabolites in the high-tillering SL mutants. Notably, Hvmax1a resembled the mutant-like metabolic profile, despite maintaining a wild-type-like architecture. Taken together, these results provide new insights into the roles of SL pathway components in drought responses and highlight functional differences among individual genes influencing both plant architecture and stress-related transcriptional programmes. Furthermore, the mutants generated in this study using Cas9-mediated genome editing represent a valuable genetic collection for future research into SL-mediated development and stress responses in barley.
items.authors: Fontana IM, Buchcik W, Kumlehn J, Melzer M, Hensel G, Daszkowska-Golec A, Marzec M.

items.title: Root gene regulatory network analysis reveals roles for defense hormones and secondary metabolites in establishment of disease-suppressive soil
items.abstract: Plants recruit beneficial microbiota in their rhizosphere to alleviate stresses. In Arabidopsis thaliana, foliar infection by Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (Hpa) has been shown to establish a disease-suppressive microbiome that promotes protection against Hpa infection of the subsequent plant generation grown in this conditioned soil - a phenomenon known as soil-borne legacy (SBL). The root responses involved in SBL establishment have remained largely unclear. In this study, time-series RNA-seq of roots from Hpa-infected plants grown in natural soil was conducted over seven days post-inoculation. A gene regulatory network of the responding roots was constructed. The role of predicted key components was verified in follow-up assays. Root transcriptional reprogramming started within one day after foliar infection. Genes associated with salicylic acid (SA)-mediated defense were upregulated, while those linked to secondary metabolism and jasmonic acid (JA) responsiveness were downregulated. SA accumulation increased at 1 dpi, and JA decreased by 3 dpi. Transcriptional regulation occurred primarily in the tips of the roots. Mutant analyses confirmed that SA, JA, indole glucosinolates, camalexin, and flavonoids contribute to SBL establishment. Our findings reveal rapid systemic transcriptional reprogramming in roots upon foliar pathogen attack, uncovering novel roles of hormone signaling and secondary metabolism in shaping a disease-suppressive soil beyond their known defense functions.
items.authors: Qi, R., Glavincheska, I., Spooren, J., Liu, X., Van Laatum, M., Verstappen, F., Kappers, I. F., Berendsen, R. L., Pieterse, C. M., Van Wees, S.

items.title: Calcium silicate effects on wheat phosphorus nutrition depend on phosphorus-source chemistry
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose Silicon (Si) amendments can improve crop phosphorus (P) nutrition, but the effect is inconsistent. We tested whether wheat’s response to a calcium-silicate amendment depends on the chemical form of P supplied, in a factorial sand-culture experiment. Methods Wheat ( Triticum aestivum cv. Omer) was grown in sand culture with soluble KH 2 PO 4 , hydroxyapatite (HA), FePO 4 or no added P (NoP), each with or without CaSiO 3 . CaCl 2 balanced calcium in the NoSi treatments. Shoot and root biomass, the shoot ionome, root architecture and soluble phosphate in an abiotic sand-mineral assay were measured. Results CaSiO 3 effects depended strongly on P source, and the response mode differed among sources. On hydroxyapatite, the limiting source, CaSiO 3 drove growth and P uptake, increasing shoot biomass by 85%, root biomass by 86% and estimated shoot P content by 56%, with a larger, coarser root system. On soluble KH 2 PO 4 it drove growth, increasing shoot biomass by 65%. On FePO 4 , already high-biomass, CaSiO 3 produced only a weak, non-significant trend but raised shoot Fe and Mn by 49 and 119%. With no added P it had little effect. An abiotic assay showed CaSiO 3 raised pH and conductivity but decreased soluble PO 4 -P by 79 to 98%. Conclusion A single calcium-silicate amendment produced several P-source-dependent response modes rather than one generic effect. The abiotic assay showed that CaSiO 3 locked up rather than released phosphate, so the hydroxyapatite response points to plant- and rhizosphere-mediated acquisition rather than bulk phosphate release.
items.authors: Karwa S, Halpern M.

items.title: Navigating Guaiacyl and Syringyl Lignin Structural Complexity in Intact Plant Cell Walls Through 13C Chemical Shift Mapping by Two-Dimensional Solid-State NMR.
items.abstract: Lignin is a structurally complex and heterogeneous biopolymer whose in situ architecture remains difficult to resolve because of extensive spectral overlap and structural perturbations introduced during isolation and dissolution. These challenges have limited direct interrogation of native lignin within intact plant cell walls and underscore the need for analytical approaches capable of resolving lignin structure in its native context. Here, we present a framework that assists systematic 13C solid-state NMR identification of guaiacyl- and syringyl-based lignin motifs, including their associated monolignol units and interunit linkages with reduced level of ambiguity directly in native lignocellulosic materials. This approach is applicable to solid-state NMR analysis of 13C-enriched plant systems or dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) analysis of unlabeled plant samples. By compiling and organizing diagnostic chemical shift patterns for syringyl and guaiacyl units across selected major linkage types, we delineate regions of uniqueness and overlap in 2D 13C correlation spectra. The scope is restricted to G/S-based lignin mapping, with applications to Arabidopsis, hardwoods, and softwoods. Application to Arabidopsis wild-type and lignin mutants, as well as to the hardwood species poplar and eucalyptus and the softwood spruce, reveals species-, genotype-, and developmental stage-dependent structural variations. The analysis further highlights the uncertainty arising from the structural complexity of the lignin network and demonstrates the need for higher dimensional correlation approaches for assignment of lignin structure. This work establishes a reference for the continued development of solid-state NMR-based G/S lignin analysis and advances the ability to interrogate native lignin architecture in intact plant cell walls.
items.authors: Xiao P, Sahu P, Debnath D, Dingwell DA, Dickwella Widanage MC, Cunningham CH, Pu Y, Wang T.

items.title: Burlap-ribbon traps are effective for detecting Agrilus (Coleoptera: Buprestidae) eggs and associated parasitoids.
items.abstract: Agrilus species (Coleoptera: Buprestidae) often oviposit in bark cracks and crevices to protect their eggs from natural enemies and unfavorable conditions, making field detection of eggs and associated parasitism challenging. Burlap-ribbon traps, which mimic tree bark texture, have been shown to induce emerald ash borer (EAB), Agrilus planipennis Fairmaire, to lay eggs on covered ash (Fraxinus sp.) surfaces. We evaluated these traps for detecting eggs of EAB and its congener bronze birch borer (Agrilus anxius Gory), as well as associated egg parasitism, using ash trees exhibiting different amounts of canopy decline and on girdled Fraxinus pennsylvanica and Betula papyrifera. Of 55 traps deployed on ash trees, 42 traps remained undisturbed, with EAB eggs recovered from 76% of those traps. Parasitized EAB eggs were detected on 21% of the undisturbed traps, with an average parasitism rate of 21%. On girdled trees, EAB eggs were recovered from traps installed on all F. pennsylvanica trees, and A. anxius eggs from traps on 3 of 5 B. papyrifera trees. Significantly more total eggs and parasitized eggs were recovered from B. papyrifera than EAB eggs from F. pennsylvanica, and parasitism rates were higher for A. anxius. These findings show that burlap-ribbon traps reliably detect Agrilus eggs and parasitoids across host species, canopy conditions, and girdling treatments, and could be a useful tool for biological control monitoring programs.
items.authors: Petrice TR, Duan JJ, Schmude JM.

items.title: Deciphering the genomic and functional basis of virulence and immune modulation in Pantoea stewartii.
items.abstract: Pantoea stewartii subsp. indologenes is an emerging cereal phytopathogen with unclear virulence mechanisms. We sequenced a rice seed-borne strain, HR3-48, and classified it as P. stewartii subsp. indologenes (Pnsi) through phylogeny of 92 housekeeping genes, ANI (> 99%), and dDDH (> 96%) comparisons. HR3-48 harbors a conserved plant-pathogenic PSI-1 type III secretion system (T3SS) and a single flagellar locus (flag-1) with multiple fliC genes. The tandem fliC456 cassette is functionally redundant for motility and flagellum assembly but contributes significantly to eliciting plant immune responses in Nicotiana benthamiana. The T3SS structural gene hrcQ-U determines hypersensitive response (HR) induction. HR3-48 causes necrosis in maize and rice, a phenotype primarily reliant on T3SS. The flagellin-derived epitope flg22PanM, a key polymorphism of L19M, triggered robust reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and inhibited Pst DC3000-induced HR in N. benthamiana, whereas flg22PanE (L19E) showed weak or no activity in these early immune assays, indicating that the 19th residue dictates the specificity of plant immune recognition. Both peptides suppress Arabidopsis seedling growth. Collectively, our data indicate that PSI-1 T3SS in Pnsi HR3-48 is a major virulence determinant in cereal hosts, whereas polymorphic flagellins modulate MTI (MAMP-triggered immunity) outputs and motility of HR3-48, with the 19th residue of flg22 contributing to differential immune perception. It remains unclear how immune suppression is mediated by effectors.
items.authors: Liu J, Peng N, Zhang X, Wei HL.

items.title: PyMYB106-PyLAC12 Modulates Callus Browning Through Phenylpropanoid-Flavonoid Metabolism in Pinus yunnanensis.
items.abstract: Callus browning is the main obstacle in the process of in vitro culture of woody plants, which is more serious in conifers. Here, multi-omics integration and transgenic approaches are employed to dissect the regulatory network of callus browning in Pinus yunnanensis. Browning callus showed marked reductions in total phenolics, flavonoids, and flavanols, with a concurrent increase in total quinone content. Non-browning callus maintained low endogenous hormone homeostasis while sustaining elevated salicylic acid (SA) and 6-benzylaminopurine (6-BA) levels to enhance reactive oxygen species scavenging capacity. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and two-way orthogonal partial least squares (O2PLS) identified PyLAC12 as the central driver of browning. Overexpression of PyLAC12 substantially reduced phenolic acid and flavonoid contents and exacerbated browning, whereas PyLAC12 knockout produced the opposite effect. The upstream transcription factor PyMYB106 was further identified to directly bind the CAACCA motif and positively regulate PyLAC12. Collectively, this study elucidates the molecular mechanism by which the PyMYB106-PyLAC12 module drives callus browning through reprogramming flavonoid-phenylpropanoid metabolic network.
items.authors: Zhang T, Li J, Sun X, Zhang S, Cui K.

items.title: Water use strategies of Populus euphratica across age classes along groundwater depth gradients in the lower Tarim River.
items.abstract: How water source use and intrinsic water-use efficiency (iWUE) are linked across tree age classes under contrasting groundwater conditions remains unclear in desert riparian forests. We assessed water use strategies of young, middle-aged, and mature Populus euphratica in the lower Tarim River during ecological water conveyance (EWC) and non-EWC periods by combining hydrogen and oxygen stable isotopes of xylem and potential source waters with a Bayesian mixing model and leaf δ13C-derived iWUE. Across the five monitoring sections, mean groundwater depth was significantly lower during EWC than during non-EWC periods, averaging 4.7 and 4.9 m, respectively. At the Kunasite (DW) and Yingsu (F) sections, MixSIAR posterior mean contributions during EWC were 16.0-23.1% for groundwater, 14.4-17.6% for river water, and 6.6-19.0% for individual 40-cm soil layers. During non-EWC periods, posterior mean contributions from individual soil layers ranged from 10.9 to 20.3%, with relatively greater contributions from deeper layers. Associations between water source contributions and iWUE varied among age classes during EWC but were nonsignificant during non-EWC periods. Across sampling periods, mean iWUE was 58.29, 53.08, and 51.37 μmol mol-1 in young, middle-aged, and mature trees, respectively. The relationship between iWUE and groundwater depth also varied among sampling periods, with no consistent directional pattern. Based primarily on changes in the contributions of shallow and deep soil water along the groundwater depth gradient, we identified 4.5-6.0 m as a preliminary groundwater depth range associated with shifts in water source use by P. euphratica. These results show that water source use and iWUE in P. euphratica vary with hydrological conditions and tree age, providing empirical evidence for assessing its responses to EWC and groundwater variation in desert riparian forests.
items.authors: Li G, Hao S, Ye M, Jiang X, Feng Z, He D.

items.title: The redox-phytohormone nexus, illustrated by the jasmonate paradigm.
items.abstract: Redox-sensitive protein switches and transcriptional networks are integral to phytohormone signaling networks. The jasmonate (JA) signaling pathway, which incorporates the coronatine insensitive 1 (COI1)-Jasmonate ZIM-domain (JAZ) co-receptor and the MYC2 transcription factor, is a relatively recent evolutionary innovation that has emerged only in land plants. Earlier JA signaling systems relied on electrophilic oxylipins, such as 12-oxo-phytodienoic acid (OPDA) and dinor-12-oxo-10,15(Z)-phytodienoic acid (dn-OPDA), and reactive oxygen species (ROS), particularly H2O2. All plant 14-3-3 proteins, such as General regulatory factor 8 (GRF8), contain a conserved redox-sensitive cysteine. Sulfenylation of GRF8 relieves inhibition of MYC2, thereby facilitating JA signaling in arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana). This mechanism may represent a primordial oxylipin signaling system, overlain by the more recent COI1-JAZ system, revealing hormone signaling plasticity that can be targeted for engineering stress-resilient crops.
items.authors: Song RF, Foyer CH, Liu WC.

items.title: Proteomic and Molecular Biological Analyses of Response Mechanism in Rice (Oryza sativa L. cv. Koshihikari) Under Drought Stress.
items.abstract: Drought stress severely limits rice growth, while roots play a key role in sensing water deficits and triggering adaptive responses. To investigate time-dependent molecular responses in rice (Oryza sativa L. cv. Koshihikari) under drought stress induced by polyethylene glycol (PEG), seedlings were exposed to 10 and 20% PEG for 4 and 8 days, followed by morphological, proteomic, immunoblot, polymerase chain reaction, and ATP content analyses. Primary root length and total root fresh weight were significantly decreased with 20% PEG for 8 days compared with untreated. Proteomic analysis revealed changes in the abundance of rice root proteins under 20% PEG treatment between 4 and 8 days, with differentially abundant proteins enriched in Gene Ontology categories related to nuclear components, protein phosphorylation, and ATP binding. Selected proteins related to protein protection, redox-associated processes, and cytoskeletal responses were examined using immunoblot and polymerase chain reaction analyses. Glutathione S-transferase decreased and heat shock protein 70 increased with PEG for 8 days. The expression of NADPH-dependent codeinone reductase was upregulated and heat shock protein 17.9 was downregulated by PEG for 8 days. ATP content per unit fresh weight decreased in roots after PEG treatment. These results suggest that prolonged PEG-induced osmotic stress inhibits rice root growth through alterations in cellular energy status, the abundance of proteins involved in protein protection and glutathione S-transferase-mediated detoxification, and the expression of genes associated with reactive carbonyl species metabolism.
items.authors: Shohag S, Yamaguchi H, Hitachi K, Tsuchida K, Komatsu S.

items.title: Genome-wide characterization of Ferritin gene family reveals BnaFER1.1 as a key regulator of salt stress tolerance in rapeseed (Brassica napus).
items.abstract: Ferritins (FERs) are essential iron-storage proteins that maintain iron homeostasis, yet their contributions to growth and salt tolerance in Brassica napus remain poorly understood. In this study, a genome-wide analysis identified 9 BnaFER genes in the rapeseed genome. These genes were unevenly distributed across eight chromosomes and exhibited conserved gene structures and protein domains, indicating evolutionary conservation. Promoter analysis revealed numerous cis-acting elements associated with hormone, light, and stress responses. Expression profiling revealed that most BnaFER genes responded to salt stress, with both induction and repression patterns under NaCl treatment. BnaFER1.1, a chloroplast-localized member, was selected for functional characterization due to its strong stress responsiveness. Heterologous expression in Arabidopsis enhanced plant growth, increased silique length, silique number, and seed area and significantly improved salt tolerance. Physiological analyses revealed increased activities of catalase (CAT) and peroxidase (POD) and reduced accumulation of hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) and malondialdehyde (MDA). Moreover, AtNHX1 and AtRD29A were significantly upregulated under salt stress in transgenic plants, indicating potential for improved ion homeostasis and osmotic adjustment. Collectively, BnaFER1.1 enhances salt tolerance through coordinated regulation of ROS detoxification and stress-responsive pathways. Our findings provide an important genetic foundation for the functional elucidation of BnaFER1.1 genes and a novel gene resource for improving salt tolerance in rapeseed.
items.authors: Jia Z, Qi D, Xue Z, Wang M, Li D, Liu Y, Zhang H, Sun N, Wang L.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: A planthopper-secreted miRNA facilitates viral infection by disrupting plant growth-defense balance in rice.
items.abstract: Insect vectors can enhance the pathogenicity of plant arboviruses, yet the molecular mechanisms driving this cross-kingdom manipulation remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that white-backed planthoppers secrete a specific microRNA, miR-133, into rice to facilitate southern rice black-streaked dwarf virus (SRBSDV) infection. Mechanistically, insect-derived miR-133 functions via cross-kingdom RNA interference to directly repress the GOLDEN2-LIKE transcription factor 31 (OsGLK31). OsGLK31 acts as a dual regulator that promotes growth via OsYUCCA-mediated auxin biosynthesis and confers antiviral immunity through OsLOX11-mediated jasmonic acid (JA) biosynthesis. In the absence of infection, the plant repressor OsJAZ10 binds to OsGLK31 to specifically inhibit its immune function, thereby prioritizing growth. However, insect infestation disrupts this balance: insect-secreted miR-133 represses OsGLK31 expression, while OsJAZ10 blocks the transcriptional activity of residual OsGLK31 protein on OsLOX11. This coordinated blockade suppresses both auxin and JA biosynthesis, causing severe dwarfism and dampened viral resistance. Our findings reveal miR-133 as a cross-kingdom effector that disrupts the host plant growth-defense balance to pave the way for viral invasion, offering potential targets for antiviral crop improvement.
items.authors: Zhang B, Jia S, Zhu Y, Gao Q, Ding W, He H, Gao H, Jing D, Li Y, Qiu L.

items.title: Temporal turnover and fire severity shape postfire beetle (Coleoptera) diversity at a forest range edge.
items.abstract: In recent decades, wildfires have increased in frequency and severity, reshaping forest structure and biodiversity. Yet it remains unclear whether postfire insect assemblages are driven primarily by fire severity, vegetation structure, or broader temporal community turnover, particularly in fragmented range-edge forests. We investigated flight-active beetle (Coleoptera) assemblages 2 years after a 2022 wildfire in the Lost Pines region of Texas, an isolated loblolly pine (Pinus taeda L.) forest at the species' western range margin. Using historical data from 2011, we evaluated temporal turnover and compared diversity and assemblage composition between contemporary burned and unburned sites. We also quantified fire severity and vegetation structure to analyze their effects on richness and abundance. Contemporary and burned sites supported higher richness and abundance than historical and unburned sites, although evenness declined as opportunistic species became dominant. Beetle assemblage differed significantly between sampling periods and burn status, indicating substantial temporal turnover amplified by wildfire. Fire severity showed strong positive associations with richness and abundance, whereas vegetation structure played a secondary but important role. Richness and abundance increased with woody plant richness, tree diversity, tree size, live tree density, and shrub richness. In contrast, dead tree variables were generally weak or negative predictors, suggesting that the influence of fire-generated deadwood may be transient and strongest shortly after disturbance. Together, these findings indicate that postfire flight-active beetle assemblages in the Lost Pines are shaped by the interaction of long-term temporal turnover and fire-driven successional dynamics, with fire severity acting as the dominant driver of community change.
items.authors: Yáñez BE, Strobel JE, Gabbard VL, Corbeil KA, Plowes RM, Gilbert LE, Wray KP, Gibson S, Meisenhelder K, Wild A, Maguiña-Conde R.

items.title: Identification of LsSLR1 gene in Leymus secalinus and validation of its function in Arabidopsis thaliana.
items.abstract: Leymus secalinus is a rhizomatous perennial high-quality gramineous forage that expands its habitat and adjusts its ecological niche through underground rhizome differentiation. Rhizomes are its strategy to adapt to drought, salinity and other adversities, and have important ecological and breeding value. Although tillering regulation has been well studied in gramineous crops, the molecular mechanisms underlying rhizome differentiation in forage grasses remain largely unexplored, hindering molecular breeding for stress tolerance. This study cloned a growth-related gene LsSLR1 (SLENDER RICE1) from L. secalinus and characterized its biological function. LsSLR1 encodes a DELLA subfamily protein of the GRAS (GIBBERELLIC ACID INSENSITIVE/REPRESSOR OF GA1-3/SCARECROW) transcription factor family, and shows the closest sequence homology to PhSLR1. LsSLR1 showed nuclear-cytoplasmic dual localization and high expression in leaves, as well as in upward and horizontal rhizome apical buds, suggesting a potential association with rhizome development. Overexpression of LsSLR1 in Arabidopsis altered GA feedback gene expression, promoted lateral root formation and branching, and shortened the growth cycle. Overexpression of LsSLR1 also enhanced the tolerance of transgenic lines to salt stress, drought stress and abscisic acid (ABA) stress. This study preliminarily characterized the potential roles of LsSLR1 in plant growth and provided preliminary evidence for its stress-related functions via multiple experimental approaches. These findings provide a theoretical basis for understanding rhizome tillering regulation in L. secalinus and offer new insights into the evolution of tillering traits in gramineous plants, with implications for forage molecular breeding.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s12298-026-01821-4.
items.authors: Li J, Zhang X, Miao Y, Zhao D, Feng X, Li H, He W.
items.journal: Physiology and molecular biology of plants : an international journal of functional plant biology

items.title: Oak gall wasps lack conserved microbial symbionts
items.abstract: Herbivorous insects frequently rely on microbial partners to exploit their host plants, yet for gall-inducing insect taxa, there were few attempts to comprehensively resolve their microbial associations. To address this gap, we characterised microbial abundance, composition and specificity in three Polish populations of cherry oak gall wasps (Cynips quercusfolii), a highly specialized phytophagous lineage. Using quantitative sequencing of bacterial and fungal marker region amplicons, we tested whether these insects harbour conserved microbiota likely associated with gall induction or host specialisation. Cynips quercusfolii and their associated parasitoid Torymus auratus harboured notably low bacterial loads, with a median of ca. 2.28 × 10⁴ 16S rRNA gene copies per insect. Their bacterial communities, primarily comprising genera with broad environmental distributions, were highly inconsistent among individuals and populations, and no bacterial lineage was consistently abundant or broadly conserved across the sampled gall wasps. In turn, fungal communities showed a stronger population-specific pattern. These results indicate oak gall wasps do not maintain abundant, conserved microbial symbionts despite their specialised herbivorous lifestyle. Instead, their bacterial communities appear sparse, variable, and dominated by environmental or transient taxa. This contrasts with symbiont-dependent lifestyles in many herbivores and suggests gall induction is unlikely to rely on stable bacterial mutualisms.
items.authors: Naeem S, Rojas-Guerrero D, Łukasik P.

items.title: WAK This Way: The Roles of Wall-Associated Kinases in Plant Disease Resistance.
items.abstract: Plant wall-associated kinases (WAKs) and WAK-like kinases (WAKLs) are closely related subfamilies of receptor-like kinases (RLKs) that bridge the plant cell wall and cytoplasm and mediate essential signaling functions. Beyond their developmental roles, accumulating evidence highlights their important contributions to plant immunity. Initially identified in Arabidopsis thaliana, these proteins have emerged as important regulators of plant responses to biotic stresses. This review focuses on the disease-resistance functions of this protein family and their associated signaling pathways across diverse plant species. Notably, recent genetic evidence has challenged the long-held view that Arabidopsis WAKs serve as bona fide receptors for oligogalacturonides (OGs), highlighting unresolved questions about how WAKs and WAKLs perceive pathogen invasion. Based on current knowledge, we propose a working model for pathogen recognition by WAKs and WAKLs and outline potential shared immune signaling pathways mediated by this receptor family.
items.authors: Zhong T, Ojiambo PS, Rellán-Álvarez R, Balint-Kurti P.

items.title: Contrasting physiological-biochemical responses and elemental homeostasis in Pinus sylvestris families exposed to As, Cd and Pb.
items.abstract: Contamination with As, Cd and Pb can limit tree establishment on degraded substrates, but family-level variation in Scots pine responses remains poorly resolved. This study evaluated three open-pollinated maternal half-sib families of Pinus sylvestris L. under controlled hydroponic exposure to As, Cd and Pb. Growth, photosynthetic pigments, soluble sugars, phenolic and flavonoid contents, malondialdehyde, antioxidant enzyme activities, elemental composition and metal(loid) accumulation indices were analysed, with PCA and Random Forest used as exploratory integrative tools. Significant family and treatment interactions were observed for all measured physiological and biochemical traits, indicating non-uniform responses among families. Cd produced the clearest toxicity profile, characterized by strong chlorophyll (up to -56.0%) and carotenoid (up to -52.6%) losses, increased lipid peroxidation (up to +70.9%) and marked Fe, Mn and Zn disruption. Pb was retained predominantly in roots (up to 12.96 ± 0.45 g/kg DW), with very low translocation to shoots, but high Pb exposure strongly inhibited root elongation (up to -70.5%). As caused comparatively moderate pigment effects but was associated with increased S (up to +147.4%) and changes in secondary-metabolite and antioxidant traits. No family showed consistently superior performance across all metal(loid)s, although response strategies differed. These results identify integrated physiological and elemental screening of Scots pine reproductive material for phytostabilization-oriented restoration as potentially relevant, while field validation under realistic contaminated-substrate conditions before practical application remains necessary.
items.authors: Šilanskienė M, Striganavičiūtė-Oržekauskienė G, Sirgedaitė-Polikaitienė V, Vaškevičienė I, Praspaliauskas M, Kniuipytė I, Lemanas E, Vaitiekūnaitė D.

items.title: OsVIPP1 Supports Rice Leaf Chloroplast Development and Is Associated with Seed Metabolic Changes and Yield-Related Traits.
items.abstract: Plastid membrane integrity is essential for plant growth, development, and metabolism, yet the functions of vesicle-inducing protein in plastids 1 (VIPP1) throughout the crop life cycle remain unclear. Here, we characterized OsVIPP1 in rice using CRISPR/Cas9 knockout, overexpression, and RNA-interference lines, together with ultrastructural, transcriptomic, metabolomic, and targeted biochemical analyses. osvipp1 knockout seedlings exhibited an albino-lethal phenotype, disorganized thylakoid membranes, disrupted intermembrane connections, and altered expression of chloroplast-encoded genes, supporting an essential role for OsVIPP1 in plastid membrane development. Both overexpression and RNA interference delayed seed germination, reduced plant height, and impaired yield-related traits. Integrated transcriptomic and untargeted metabolomic analyses associated altered OsVIPP1 expression with lipid, carbon, and phytohormone-related pathways. In overexpression seeds, abscisic acid content increased to 1.95 times the wild-type level, accompanied by the accumulation of several fatty acids and soluble sugars, whereas abscisic acid and most fatty acids decreased in RNA-interference seeds. These findings indicate that OsVIPP1 supports thylakoid spatial organization in leaves, whereas altered OsVIPP1 expression is associated with metabolic changes in mature seeds and yield-related phenotypes.
items.authors: Zhu Y, Zhang J, Li H, Zhou Z, Lin Y, Zhou F.

items.title: Nitric Oxide Signaling in Photosynthetic Resilience: Linking Photoprotection and Carbon Gain in Tropical Crops.
items.abstract: Tropical crops are increasingly exposed to climate-driven, recurrent combinations of heat, excessive irradiance, high vapor pressure deficit (VPD), drought, flooding, salinity, and pathogen pressure that collectively impair photosynthesis and reduce crop productivity. Unlike individual stress events, these interacting stresses simultaneously disrupt photoprotection, electron transport, carbon assimilation, stomatal regulation, and chloroplast redox homeostasis, ultimately limiting whole-plant carbon gain under fluctuating environments. Nitric oxide (NO) has emerged as a central signaling molecule coordinating these adaptive responses, yet its roles in photosynthetic regulation remain dispersed across molecular, physiological, and crop-specific studies. This review presents an integrated framework linking chloroplast-level NO signaling with whole-plant photosynthetic performance in major tropical crops, including maize, sugarcane, banana, cassava, and oil palm. We propose that NO regulates photosynthetic resilience through three interconnected axes: (i) reversible protein S-nitrosylation that modulates photosynthetic complexes and Calvin-Benson cycle enzymes; (ii) maintenance of chloroplast redox homeostasis through coordinated reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) signaling, antioxidant networks, and S-nitrosothiol metabolism; and (iii) ABA-mediated stomatal regulation that optimizes the trade-off between carbon assimilation, stomatal conductance, and water-use efficiency under environmental stress. We further discuss the emerging roles of S-nitrosothiols (SNOs) and S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO) as central regulators of NO homeostasis and potential biochemical indicators linking chloroplast signaling with whole-plant carbon performance. By synthesizing current evidence across climate-relevant stress combinations, including heat + high light, drought + high VPD, flooding + hypoxia, salinity + pathogen interactions, this review provides a conceptual framework for understanding NO-mediated photosynthetic resilience and identifies key research priorities for developing NO-based strategies to enhance productivity and climate resilience in tropical cropping systems.
items.authors: Islam MS, Methela NJ, Cho YB, Lee MS, Mun BG.

items.title: Comparison of synthetic and post-synthetic molecular genetic methods of reducing xylan glucuronidation in hybrid aspen for biorefinery applications.
items.abstract: BackgroundThe pattern of xylan backbone substitution by 4-O-methylglucuronic acid (mGlcA) and O-acetyl groups generated during biosynthesis in the Golgi apparatus plays a key role in molecular interactions between secondary cell wall polymers in hardwoods, thus regulating biorefinery properties of woody biomass. This study aims at comparing the effects of two different approaches to reduce xylan glucuronidation, targeting either xylan biosynthesis by RNAi suppression of GLUCURONIC SUBSTITUTION OF XYLAN1 genes (denoted Gux1RNAi) or by xylan post-synthetic modification in the secondary cell wall by apoplastic wood-specific expression of a fungal α-glucuronidase from family GH67 (denoted WP:GH67) in hybrid aspen (Populus tremula L. x tremuloides Michx.). The effects of reducing xylan glucuronidation by these two approaches on xylan acetylation and solubility, and recalcitrance of wood to enzymatic hydrolysis were compared.ResultsBoth approaches reduced mGlcA/xylose (Xyl) ratio by approx. 30% without altering Xyl content in alkali extracts, while xylan acetyl content in subcritical water extracts was increased only in Gux1RNAi lines. The Gux1RNAi lines showed reduced glucuronidation in the major xylan domain containing evenly-spaced mGlcA, whereas the WP:GH67 lines were affected in both odd and even glucuronidation patterns. Interestingly, the arrays containing mGlcA every second xylosyl unit were not affected by any modification, whereas an increase in xylo-oligosaccharides containing O-2,3 diacetylated Xyl was found in Gux1RNAi lines only. Neither modification consistently affected glucose or Xyl yields in saccharification without or with acid pretreatment, whereas xylan extractability in subcritical water was increased in Gux1RNAi, but not in WP:GH67 lines.ConclusionOur study supports the hypothesis that acetylation competes with glucuronidation by GUX1 during biosynthesis, and increased acetylation caused by GUX1 suppression rather than reduced xylan glucuronidation per se improves xylan extractability. The 30% reduction in glucuronidation did not affect enzymatic saccharification, supporting the concept that cell wall structure and recalcitrance in transgenic lines are maintained by xylan domains which were not affected by either transgenic modification.
items.authors: Sivan P, Urbancsok J, Gandla ML, Donev EN, Derba-Maceluch M, Roach M, Jönsson LJ, Vilaplana F, Mellerowicz EJ.

items.title: Foundational characterization of tomato fruit RALF peptides reveals structural and functional specialization within the SlRALF family.
items.abstract: Rapid Alkalinization Factor (RALF) peptides regulate plant growth and cell wall signaling, but their roles in fruit development remain unclear. Here, we characterized tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) fruit-associated RALF peptides and their interactions with leucine-rich repeat extensins (LRXs). Expression analyses identified SlRALF5, SlRALF7, and SlRALF10 as the main fruit-expressed RALFs. SlRALF10 was associated with early fruit development, whereas SlRALF5 and SlRALF7 remained expressed during ripening. Sequence analyses showed that SlRALF5/7 retain conserved motifs of canonical RALFs, while SlRALF10 displays divergent structural features and altered charge distribution. Synthetic SlRALF5 and SlRALF7 inhibited root growth and induced extracellular alkalinization, whereas SlRALF10 lacked both activities. Co-immunoprecipitation assays showed that all three peptides interact with the fruit-expressed proteins SlLRX2 and SlLRX5. Structural modeling predicted distinct electrostatic properties for the SlLRX5/SlRALF10 complex compared with SlRALF5. These results reveal structural and functional specialization among tomato fruit RALF peptides and suggest that distinct SlRALFs may differentially respond to cell wall remodeling during fruit development and ripening.
items.authors: Montano JA, Carrera M, Wang X, Mesa-Rojas P, Luna AM, Schaller A, Morilla I, Doblas VG.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Biopriming of Durum Wheat Seeds with Diazotrophic Bacteria Improved Physiological and Biochemical Pathways Under Salt Stress.
items.abstract: A significant strategy for sustainable management, by decreasing the use of chemical fertilizers, can consist of technology based on suitable levels of plant growth promoting bacteria (PGPB) seed biopriming. The main goal of this work was to demonstrate the positive effect of PGPB as seed biopriming factor on the growth of durum wheat plantlets under stress. plantlets physiological and biochemical pathways modifications were assessed in controlled growth chamber under salt stress. Seeds bioprimed with bacterial strains, in particular, Bacillus pumilus (MA9), Virgibacillus halodenitrificans (MA14), Bacillus subtilis (MA17), and Bacillus pumilus (MA19), demonstrated the best development of durum wheat seedlings under salt stress. The total length and total dry weight were altogether higher in bioprimed than in unbioprimed plants. The PGPB-bioprimed plants were very sound and hydrated, and the unbioprimed plant leaves were parched within 120 mM NaCl. In contrast to explants without PGPB, all the biochemical variables, for example, auxin, proline, soluble sugars, amino acids, and protein, were essentially improved in bioprimed explants. Biopriming with MA17 fundamentally diminished the reactive oxygen species (ROS) rate, particularly without salt stress. In any case, this impact of the hindrance of "ROS" was more pronounced under stressful conditions. The explant antioxidant prevention agent pathways catalase (CAT) and ascorbate peroxidase (APX) and the chlorophyll content were improved after seed biopriming with PGPB when explants with unbioprimed seeds had low cell reinforcement pathways under the two treatments, particularly under pressure. The bioprimed plants additionally had higher K+/Na+ proportions and expanded intracellular K+ ion activity. Hence, it can be anticipated that seed biopriming with PGPB is a novel technology that can improve healthy plant development under saline conditions. This study shows that PGPB has a significant effect in initiating resistance under stressful conditions in plants and can be utilized to develop new bioinoculants to reduce the use of chemical fertilizers.
items.authors: Hadj Brahim A, Said Z, Frikha E, Jlidi M, Ben Ali M, Ben Ali M.

items.title: The effect of Rhizobium-field pea symbiosis on host plant quality and subsequent herbivory by the pea leaf weevil, Sitona lineatus (Coleoptera: Curculionidae)
items.abstract: Abstract Legumes develop symbiotic relationships with rhizobia bacteria, enabling biological nitrogen fixation and providing nitrogen for plant growth and development. This nitrogen availability influences plant nutrition and chemical defense that affect herbivores. The pea leaf weevil (PLW), Sitona lineatus L. is an herbivore of legumes that depends on nutritious foliage and root nodules for food in different parts of its lifecycle. Adult PLW overwinter and emerge in spring to seek hosts and mates. Following host colonization, reproductively active weevils mate and oviposit in the soil. Larval development occurs in root nodules followed by pupation in the soil. Adults that emerge in the fall prepare to overwinter in a reproductively inactive state. We tested the hypothesis that Rhizobium -field pea interactions influence plant traits and subsequent herbivory by adult PLW in different physiological states. Field pea plants were inoculated with different Rhizobium leguminosarum strains that either fix nitrogen (wild-type; nif+ ) or do not fix nitrogen (mutant-type; nif- ) and were compared to nitrogen and water-treated plants as positive and negative controls. The nif+ positively affected field pea height, nitrogen and chlorophyll content compared to the nif- inoculated plants. Rhizobium -mediated plant traits only affected adult PLW in the fall when weevils were preparing to overwinter. The fall weevils preferred the nif+ over the nif- , nitrogen or water-treated plants. Fall weevil preference for nif+ treated plants suggests that host nutritional quality, rather than plant defense, drives weevil feeding behaviour before winter. Understanding the effect of rhizobia-mediated plant-herbivore interactions will help develop sustainable management strategies for pests of legumes.
items.authors: Fatukasi OI, Thilakarathna MS, Evenden ML.

items.title: RNA N6-methyladenosine modifications in plants: molecular mechanisms and biological roles.
items.abstract: RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications dynamically modulate RNA stability, splicing, and translation in plants, influencing developmental and stress response processes. In this review, we provide an overview of the key protein complexes involved in RNA m6A modification, including methyltransferases, demethylases, and m6A-binding proteins. We then demonstrate that m6A modulates vegetative growth, reproductive processes, responses to stresses, and hormone signaling. In agronomically important crops, RNA m6A modifications affect stress resilience, developmental timing, and quality traits, such as drought tolerance, salt resistance, male fertility, pollen viability, and fruit maturation. Furthermore, we elucidate the molecular mechanisms of RNA m6A. Finally, we explore advancements in m6A detection technologies, highlighting emerging trends and future directions. These strategies provide a conceptual framework for moving plant m6A research from descriptive epitranscriptomics toward trait-oriented crop and forest tree improvement.
items.authors: Yang M, Wu D, Hu Z, Lin J, Li Y, Li R.

items.title: Pathogenesis versus symbiosis: a dual perspective on plant-microbe interactions.
items.abstract: Plants function as integral components of soil ecosystems, embedded within diverse microbial consortia that engage in continuous chemical and informational exchange. This molecular dialog governs how plants distinguish harmful, neutral, and beneficial microbes, transforming the rhizosphere into a dynamic signaling interface. Microbial interactions operate along a chemical continuum in which metabolites, volatiles, peptides, and other small molecules act across aqueous, lipidic, and chemically heterogeneous microenvironments to shape recognition and response. The physicochemical organization of rhizosphere metabolites may influence their diffusion, stability, and accessibility, although direct evidence for these effects remains limited. Within this framework, plant recognition is reinterpreted as a fluid, context-dependent communication process rather than a binary separation of immunity and symbiosis. This review synthesizes recent advances in the molecular architecture of this continuum, from receptor-mediated signaling to metabolite-driven ecological filtering, and examines how these overlapping systems determine host specificity, community stability, and adaptive resilience. Special attention is given to the regulatory roles of reactive oxygen species (ROS), phytohormones, and redox metabolites as both stress indicators and inter-organismal communicators. By integrating biochemical, ecological, and systems perspectives, this review highlights implications for developing microbiome-based, climate-smart, and sustainable agricultural practices.
items.authors: Dong Y, Shamsy R, Ahammed GJ.

items.title: PPR9 mediates mitochondrial nad transcript maturation required for complex I biogenesis and early plant development in Arabidopsis.
items.abstract: The biogenesis and function of plant mitochondria relies on the expression of the organellar genome, which involves extensive post-transcriptional processing of organellar transcripts in order to generate mature functional RNAs. This includes the removal of introns from many essential organellar transcripts through splicing, a process mediated by diverse nuclear-encoded RNA-processing factors, including numerous members of the pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) protein family. Here, we report the analysis of PPR9 (At1g03560), a mitochondrial P-class PPR protein originally identified in genetic screens for essential protein cofactors. Loss of PPR9 function results in embryonic arrest at early stages of seed development. In vitro rescued homozygous ppr9 mutant plants could be recovered and maintained using a modified in vitro embryo-rescue method. The mutants display delayed growth and development which are associated with altered mitochondrial functions. Molecular analyses reveal that PPR9 functions in the splicing of several mitochondrial transcripts encoding respiratory complex I (CI) subunits, including nad2 intron 3 and nad7 introns 1 and 2. Accordingly, CI assembly is disrupted in ppr9 plants, resulting in altered OXPHOS activity and broad physiological defects. Together, these findings identify PPR9 as a key regulator of mt-RNA maturation in Arabidopsis, enabling CI biogenesis and optimal respiratory functions, and further highlight the roles of nuclear-encoded factors in coordinating mitochondria functions and (early) plant growth and development.
items.authors: Kobaivanov E, Maltz T, Kittel M, Matan R, Mizrahi R, Carmi N, Ostersetzer-Biran O.

items.title: Spatiotemporal co-transcriptomics uncovers coordinated rhizobia-legume stress programs supporting nitrogen fixation in Medicago.
items.abstract: Rhizobial nitrogen fixation in legume nodules requires precise spatial and temporal coordination between host and bacterial gene expression. Here, we applied spatial enhanced resolution omics sequencing (Stereo-seq) to profile Medicago nodules across five developmental stages, generating a co-transcriptomic atlas of nodule development. Using a mixed-probe capture strategy, we simultaneously detected host and rhizobial transcripts within the same tissue sections, enabling analysis of host-microbe transcriptional coordination during symbiosis. We identified dynamic changes in host cell composition and developmental trajectories and uncovered two transcription factors, MtERF82 and MtDOF53, required for maintenance of the indeterminate nodule meristem. Rhizobial and host genes exhibited stage- and zone-specific expression patterns along the nodule apex-to-base axis. Notably, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-associated stress responses in both host cells and rhizobia were linked to symbiotic nitrogen fixation. Functional analyses further showed that MtERF71 and MtCBF1 promote nitrogen fixation by regulating ROS homeostasis and activating key symbiotic genes, highlighting stress signaling as an integral component of mutualistic symbiosis.
items.authors: Shao W, Shi X, Guo X, Xiang S, Xiao Y, Guang X, Fang D, Lian X, Luo L, Sun Y, Xu P, Zhuang Y, Chen L, Chen X, Wen J, Yan M, Wang Y, Xie P, Mao Y, Tang C, Wu J, Tian C, Wang Y, Zhong L, Zhao C, Zhao Y, Zhang X, Wei T, Gu Y, Yang J, Liu H, Xu X, Wang E.

items.title: Foliar carbon dots improve drought tolerance in soybean through genotype-dependent hydraulic and metabolic pathways.
items.abstract: Although foliar application of carbon dots (CDs) has emerged as a promising strategy to alleviate drought, whether CDs act through hydraulic or biochemical pathways, and whether their effects are genotype-dependent, remains unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of foliar CDs application (50 mg L-1 CDs) at the podding and seed-filling stages on photosynthetic performance, hydraulic property, abscisic acid (ABA) and indole-3-acetic acid contents, oxidative stress, antioxidant defense, and osmotic adjustment substances in wild (Y15) and cultivated (Zhonghuang 13) soybeans under full (75%-95% field capacity, FC) and deficit (55%-65% FC) irrigation. The results showed that leaf net photosynthetic rate (An) and stomatal conductance (gs) were reduced by 10.6%-54.1% and 34.5%-75.9%, while intrinsic water use efficiency was increased by 31.5%-124.7% during the podding and seed-filling stages under deficit irrigation. Leaf hydraulic conductance (Kleaf) was decreased by 21.8% at the podding stage, and bulk modulus of elasticity (ε) was increased by 31.0% at the seed-filling stage under deficit irrigation. Wild soybean exhibited greater Kleaf and catalase activity, whereas cultivated soybean showed superior photosynthetic capacity and growth potential. Foliar CDs application primarily enhanced predawn leaf water potential by 27.9%, and ɛ by 49.6% at the seed-filling stage, and Kleaf by 35.4% at the podding stage, while concurrently down-regulating the stress-induced over-accumulation of CAT, proline, and soluble sugars (SS). Crucially, in wild soybean, CDs improved An by increasing Kleaf, which promoted stomatal opening and carbon assimilation. ABA played only a secondary role by negatively regulating Kleaf. In cultivated soybean, CDs promoted SS accumulation and then osmotic adjustment substances thereby enhancing gs and An, while ABA and hydraulic pathways were not significant. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that foliar CDs alleviate drought in soybean through genotype dependent mechanisms of hydraulic facilitation in wild soybean versus metabolic reprogramming in cultivated soybean. This study provides a physiological basis for the genotype-sensitive application of CDs as a drought-resilience strategy in soybean production.
items.authors: Su X, Li H, Zhang Y, Mo Y, Gao Z, Cheng G, Zhang H, Wang X, Zhang B.

items.title: Valorization of Agri-Food Industry Waste as a Source of Phytohormones and Evaluation of Its Biostimulatory Potential in Oat (Avena sativa L.) Cultivation.
items.abstract: The valorization of agri-food industry waste is an important approach to obtaining value-added materials for agricultural applications while supporting the principles of a circular economy. Such waste may contain valuable nutrients and biologically active compounds, including plant hormones. This study aimed to evaluate the phytohormone content of post-production residues from the agri-food industry and to assess the biostimulatory potential of the material with the highest total phytohormone concentration that was also available in sufficient quantities as a post-production residue in oat (Avena sativa L.) cultivation. Phytohormones were determined in 37 samples using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis. A total of 35 compounds representing six groups of plant hormones were identified: auxins, cytokinins, gibberellins, brassinosteroids, abscisic acid, and salicylic acid. Five samples-apple pomace, senna leaves, sage leaves, chicory roots, and tobacco stalks-contained all 35 compounds, whereas coffee grounds contained only eight. Brassinosteroids and auxins were the predominant hormone groups. Lemon balm leaves exhibited the highest total phytohormone concentration (511.26 ng·g-1 dry weight), while coffee grounds had the lowest (0.05 ng·g-1 dry weight). Dried and ground lemon balm leaves were therefore selected for a pot experiment conducted under controlled phytotron conditions. High proportions of lemon balm leaf waste reduced shoot growth, biomass accumulation, relative chlorophyll content, and nitrogen balance index (NBI), while increasing flavonoid and anthocyanin accumulation. In contrast, lower amendment promoted biomass production and maintained physiological and photosynthetic performance at levels comparable to or higher than those of the control plants. Most chlorophyll a fluorescence parameters remained relatively stable, although PIABS decreased at the highest amendment proportions. These findings indicate that lemon balm tea-processing waste may represent a potential source of biologically active compounds for agricultural applications. Its use at appropriate proportions may contribute to the valorization of plant-derived waste while supporting sustainable crop production and the principles of a circular economy.
items.authors: Sienkiewicz A, Kowczyk-Sadowy M, Obidziński S, Cwalina P, Piotrowska-Niczyporuk A, Bajguz A, Adamczuk A, Ciereszko I, Kulus I.

items.title: A single amino-acid switch reprograms ROP6 signaling to drive functional evolution in plants.
items.abstract: Rho-related GTPases of plants (ROPs) are evolutionarily conserved molecular switches that typically maintain PIN-formed proteins at the plasma membrane (PM), yet their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we reveal that a single amino-acid substitution at residue 194 acts as a core determinant, driving the evolutionary split between Brassicaceae and Malvaceae ROP6 orthologs: glycine enforces PM stabilization, whereas alanine licenses endocytic function. In cotton, the Malvaceae-predominant alanine mutated GhROP6 displays an auxin-independent manner. The distinct activity is attributed to the recruitment of three GhRIC effectors that directly bind the actin cytoskeleton and promote F-actin assembly and bundling. The resulting actin reorganization facilitates GhPIN3a internalization and proteolysis, consequently enhancing cotton fiber elongation. Our findings demonstrate that a single amino-acid change can reprogram ROP signaling and uncover a molecular switch underlying the functional evolution of ROP6 in regulating plant development.
items.authors: Zhang L, An Y, Lan T, Cui J, Du X, Mu L, Liu L, Xu M, Li Q, Cheng L, Zeng J, Hou L, Pei Y, Zhang M.

items.title: Small but big player: the important role of microRNAs in rice.
items.abstract: Rice is a staple food for more than half of the global population. Research on rice crop establishment and tolerance to biotic and abiotic stresses helps enhance rice productivity and safeguard food security. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate diverse biological processes in rice, including growth, development, and stress resilience by modulating different target genes. They coordinate rice growth and development primarily through phytohormone signaling (abscisic acid, auxin, and gibberellin) and metabolic pathways (cell proliferation and fatty acid metabolism). Furthermore, they regulate rice stress tolerance by modulating hormone signaling pathways and metabolic pathways such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging. Understanding these regulatory networks is crucial for optimizing rice yield and enhancing stress tolerance. This review synthesizes current understanding of the pivotal roles of miRNAs in regulating rice development and adaptive responses to environmental stimuli. It further discusses the emerging prospects of miRNA applications in rice breeding, laying a conceptual foundation for harnessing miRNA pathways to improve rice productivity and stress resilience, thereby contributing to global food security and agricultural sustainability.
items.authors: Zhou S, Wu T, Wang S, Liu X, Huang K, Hu B.

items.title: Threatened Conifers Need Targeted and Integrated Conservation: A Case Study of Pinus dabeshanensis.
items.abstract: Due to global warming, over-exploitation, habitat degradation, environmental pollution, and alien species invasion, around 28% of assessed global species are threatened, with conifers being especially endangered. China has attached great importance to biodiversity conservation, and implemented a series of targeted initiatives over the past two decades to protect and conserve the endangered species in China. Pinus dabeshanensis W.C.Cheng et Y.W.Law is a conifer species with an extremely small population and is listed as Grade I in the national key protected wild plants in China. Despite conservation efforts, the effectiveness of these measures remains unknown. In this study, we have assessed the conservation effectiveness of this critically endangered conifer species, and identified conservation gaps to achieve a new conservation plan for the species. This paper should also be helpful for planning conservation of other endangered conifers. We conducted a systematic assessment of the current state of P. dabeshanensis, and the effectiveness of in situ and ex-situ conservation, artificial propagation, and reintroduction based on field investigations and a comprehensive review of the published literature, and thereby identified the conservation gaps. The results suggest that the natural population of P. dabeshanensis is extremely small, being composed of only 320 recorded individuals sporadically distributed in Henan, Hubei, and Anhui. Although populations in Yingshan of Hubei, Shangcheng in Henan, and Jinzhai of Anhui are protected in national nature reserves, the largest known wild population in Dawanggou of Yuexi in Anhui is not protected by any nature reserve. Ex-situ conservation is still at a preliminary stage, with very small numbers planted in botanical gardens and lacking the full range of the species' genetic diversity. We also found that the species suffers from reproductive failure including low pollination success and poor seed set. While reintroduction practices have been conducted at several localities, seedling survival rates vary greatly due to a lack of subsequent management/protection. The lack of standardized reintroduction protocols and management guidelines hinders a consistent and effective implementation of these practices. Although many Chinese institutions including universities, nature reserves, and botanical gardens have been involved in the conservation of P. dabeshanensis, the overall effectiveness has been limited due to inadequate coordination and fragmented efforts. To substantially advance conservation effectiveness, there needs to be a targeted species conservation plan. Within this framework, it will be necessary to combine different approaches in order to ensure the effective protection of this endangered pine. The present study has involved a comprehensive investigation into the conservation effectiveness of P. dabeshanensis, identified critical conservation gaps, and proposed an integrated conservation strategy. Our findings and suggestions will also be valuable for the conservation of other endangered gymnosperm species.
items.authors: Xu Y, Tan C, Ferguson DK, Yang Y.

items.title: Chicken-manure digestate contains phytohormones with potential biostimulant activity in lettuce.
items.abstract: Liquid digestate from anaerobic digestion is a potential liquid fertilizer, but its high water content complicates storage, transport, and application. Beyond basic nutrients, its profile of biostimulants, particularly phytohormones, remains insufficiently characterized. This study used widely targeted metabolomics and targeted UPLC-MS/MS to compare chicken-manure digestate collected before membrane pretreatment (BK) with the final concentrate produced by an industrial U-NRO system (MC). BK and MC represented one composite industrial sample pair, with three independently prepared analytical replicates per matrix rather than independent process replicates. In total, 1465 metabolites were annotated and 49 phytohormone-related analytes were quantified. MC contained higher measured concentrations of several auxin-, salicylic acid-, jasmonic acid-, gibberellin-, cytokinin-, and melatonin-related compounds, whereas the summed abscisic acid-related pool decreased markedly. Pathway annotation based on the detected metabolites suggested several possible metabolic routes associated with the occurrence of phytohormone-related compounds in the digestate. The co-detection of tryptophan and several indole-related metabolites was consistent with possible tryptophan-associated transformations, while phenylalanine- and salicylic-acid-related metabolites suggested a possible association with phenylalanine- and phenylpropanoid-related pathways. In germination assays, 0.33% MC increased seedling length without reducing germination speed, whereas 3.3% MC was phytotoxic. In the pot experiment, no harvest-stage phenotypic trait differed significantly between the full-fertilizer control and the selected 70% fertilizer plus MC. Overall, the study establishes a molecular inventory of an industrial digestate concentrate and defines a preliminary concentration-dependent plant-response range.
items.authors: Qiong Y, Kaijun W, Kuo F, Mingyue Z, Quanyuan W, Yanchen L.

items.title: Physiological and Molecular Mechanisms of Tree Responses to Combined Drought and Low-Nitrogen Stress: A Review.
items.abstract: Drought and low nitrogen often co-occur in forests, yet their combined effects cannot be inferred reliably from single-stress studies. This review synthesizes physiological and molecular evidence for tree responses to combined drought and low nitrogen at four levels, namely stress perception, signal transduction, metabolic reprogramming, and adaptive phenotypes. It compares single-stress baselines and evaluates reported interactions in photosynthesis, water-use efficiency, root traits, and carbon-nitrogen allocation. The review distinguishes direct tree evidence from mechanistic context derived from crops and model plants. Abscisic acid-nitrogen signaling crosstalk is considered alongside reactive oxygen species, energy, hydraulics, and transcriptional regulation as candidate integration routes. Candidate genes are classified by species context and experimental evidence; responsiveness to the two single stresses is not interpreted as proof of a combined-stress function. The review also assesses the opportunities and current limitations of multi-omics and genome editing for trees. It identifies priorities for factorial experiments, multi-year validation, and molecular breeding for climate-resilient forestry.
items.authors: Xu Y, Yang Z, Yu L, Wang X, Li C, Wei M.

items.title: Mediator CKM and MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 reinforce auxin responsiveness to sustain MUTE expression during stomatal lineage differentiation.
items.abstract: MUTE functions as a pivotal transcription factor that governs the transition from self-renewal to differentiation in meristemoids during stomatal development. This transition requires MUTE expression to reach a critical threshold, yet the mechanisms that maintain its expression homeostasis remain unclear. Here, we show that the Mediator CDK8 kinase module (CKM) acts as a transcriptional coactivator of the MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 complex to regulate meristemoid fate. Specifically, CKM cooperates with MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 to promote the transcription of the auxin-responsive genes, such as SAUR52 and SAUR53, thereby enhancing local auxin response in meristemoids. AUXIN RESPONSE FACTORs (ARFs), including ARF6, ARF7, and ARF19, then bind to MUTE promoter and contribute to its transcription, establishing a positive feedback loop. Disruption of CKM or MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 components reduces SAUR52/53 expression and auxin responses, leading to decreased MUTE transcription, excessive meristemoid self-renewal divisions and arrested differentiation. These defects can be partially rescued by exogenous auxin application or by overexpression of SAUR53 in the mutants. Together, our results uncover a self-reinforcing transcriptional-auxin circuit in which CKM-assisted MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 amplifies auxin response, and auxin reciprocally sustains MUTE expression. This feedback mechanism ensures that MUTE reaches the threshold required to terminate meristemoid self-renewal and initiate differentiation, revealing how transcriptional regulation and hormone signaling are integrated to control stem cell-like behaviors during tissue patterning.
items.authors: Li S, Zuo C, Zhu L, Yan M, Wang L, Zhang C, Yang K, Le J.

items.title: Extremophilic and conventional PGPR consortia enhance wheat tolerance to microplastic-osmotic co-stress.
items.abstract: Microplastic contamination and water limitation increasingly co-occur in agricultural systems, creating complex constraints on plant growth that may be alleviated through microbial biostimulation. This study evaluated the ability of a conventional plant growth-promoting rhizobacterium, B. subtilisubtilis RC72, and an extremophilic P. poaeoae strain, applied individually or in combination, to improve wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) performance under polypropylene microplastic and polyethylene glycol-induced osmotic stress. A controlled glasshouse experiment comprising 16 treatment combinations was used to assess plant growth, biomass allocation, root architecture, water relations, photosynthetic pigments, oxidative damage, osmolyte accumulation and antioxidant responses. Microplastic and osmotic stress reduced plant growth, biomass and physiological performance while altering root traits and increasing oxidative stress. Bacterial inoculation improved several stress-responsive traits, including biomass, pigment accumulation and root development, although oxidative responses were strongly treatment dependent; notably, the Mp + Peg + Pp + Ba treatment exhibited the highest MDA accumulation. Multivariate analyses further showed that microbial treatments associated with improved growth and pigment traits were separated from treatments characterized by stronger oxidative responses. Overall, B. subtilis and P. poae modulated wheat responses in a trait- and treatment-dependent manner, and the data did not demonstrate consistent superiority of the extremophilic strain across the measured parameters. The effectiveness of stress-adapted PGPR therefore appears to depend on bacterial identity and the specific environmental stress combination rather than on extremophilic origin alone. These findings indicate that PGPR responses under combined microplastic and osmotic stress are strongly dependent on bacterial identity and stress context, and that selection of microbial inoculants should therefore be based on treatment-specific performance rather than an assumption of universally beneficial consortium or extremophile effects.
items.authors: Kahraman ND, Anas M, Kucukmaras SD, Khan Z, Eken N, Hakki EE.

items.title: Interaction between FmRAV4 (a RAV transcription factor) and FmMYB1 (a MYB transcription factor) confers drought tolerance via ROS scavenging in Fraxinus mandshurica.
items.abstract: Drought stress severely restricts plant growth and development. Although AP2/ERF family transcription factors (TFs) participate extensively in abiotic stress responses, they remain largely unexplored in Fraxinus mandshurica. In this study, we identified and functionally characterized FmRAV4, a TF from the RAV subfamily. FmRAV4 is localized in the nucleus, lacks transcriptional activation activity, and is significantly upregulated in leaves under drought stress. Functional analyses using transient overexpression, gene silencing in F. mandshurica, and stable transformation in Arabidopsis thaliana demonstrated that FmRAV4 enhances drought tolerance by increasing SOD and POD activities, scavenging excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), and alleviating membrane lipid peroxidation. Mechanistically, yeast one-hybrid, EMSA, and ChIP-qPCR assays revealed that FmRAV4 directly binds to conserved CAACA motifs in the promoters of FmSOD2, FmPOD1, FmPOD2, and FmPOD4 to activate their transcription. Importantly, yeast two-hybrid, luciferase complementation imaging, and pull-down assays confirmed that FmRAV4 physically interacts with FmMYB1 both in vivo and in vitro, and that FmMYB1 upregulation improves drought tolerance in F. mandshurica. Co-overexpression of these two genes synergistically activates antioxidant genes in a concentration-dependent manner, thereby enhancing ROS scavenging and conferring stronger drought tolerance than single-gene overexpression. Collectively, these findings reveal that the FmRAV4-FmMYB1 interaction forms a synergistic regulatory module mediating drought tolerance, providing valuable genetic resources for the molecular breeding of drought-tolerant woody plants.
items.authors: Nie X, Nie X, Xu X, Wu Y, Bai T, Ma X, Zhao Z, Zheng A, Cui X, Xie J, Ji X.

items.title: WHIRLY1 Interactome Profiling Reveals the Chloroplast Fate Correlation with Stromule-like Morphologies in Arabidopsis Leaves Under Dark and DBMIB Stress Conditions.
items.abstract: The WHIRLY family comprises DNA/RNA-binding proteins localized to multiple subcellular compartments, including organelles and the nucleus. However, the subcellular distribution and functional roles of WHIRLY protein complexes are not fully characterized. In this study, a WHIRLY1 protein pulldown coupled with mass spectrometry analysis was used to profile the interacting proteome in an Arabidopsis thaliana plant overexpressing WHIRLY1-GFP. This analysis identified over 770 interacting proteins, with RNA-binding proteins representing the most enriched functional category. Subcellular compartmental mapping revealed distinct spatial organization: oxidation-related, cytoskeleton-associated, and chloroplast/mitochondrion-targeted RNA-binding proteins were significantly enriched at the chloroplast periphery. Conversely, a subset of nuclear envelope-associated proteins, including NOT3, TUBB3, and histone H4, were connected with the formation of tubular stromule-like structures under growth light conditions as opposed to extended dark conditions. Under DBMIB-induced stress, however, reconfiguration of the WHIRLY1 interactome occurred: plastid ribosomal structural components declined, while the transcription factor GRF6 accumulated in the nucleus, concomitant with the formation of vesicular stromule-like structures. Biomolecular fluorescence complementation and yeast two-hybrid assays confirmed direct interactions between WHIRLY1 and stromule-localized proteins, several RNA-binding proteins, and nuclear proteins. Collectively, these findings suggest that the dynamic assembly of the WHIRLY1 interactome in conjunction with stromule biogenesis acts as a regulatory nexus coordinating chloroplast functions under stressful conditions.
items.authors: Li M, Huang D, Yu Y, Zhang K, Yang P, Qiu Y, Zheng X, Lin W, Ren Y, Wu B, Miao Y.

items.title: Allelopathic Effects of Aqueous Leaf and Bark Extracts of Myrica esculenta on Germination and Seedling Growth of Traditional Agricultural Crops under Laboratory and Nursery Conditions
items.abstract: Abstract Agroforestry systems are widely recognized for enhancing agricultural productivity and ecosystem sustainability in the Himalayan region; however, successful tree–crop integration depends on the compatibility between component species. This study evaluated the allelopathic effects of aqueous leaf and bark extracts of Myrica esculenta Buch.-Ham. ex D. Don on seed germination, seedling growth, and biomass production of five traditional Himalayan crops ( Eleusine coracana , Setaria italica , Amaranthus caudatus , Vigna umbellata , and Panicum miliaceum ) under laboratory and nursery conditions. A completely randomized design with four treatments (control, 5%, 7%, and 9% aqueous extracts) and five replications was adopted.
