Germination, growth, and biomass parameters were analysed using one-way ANOVA followed by Duncan's Multiple Range Test (P ≤ 0.05), while Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Hierarchical Cluster Analysis (HCA) were employed to evaluate multivariate treatment responses. The results revealed significant concentration-dependent allelopathic effects, with leaf extracts exhibiting greater phytotoxicity than bark extracts. Under laboratory conditions, leaf extracts reduced germination by 32.91% in E. coracana , 18.34% in S. italica , and 11.18% in A. caudatus , whereas bark extracts caused maximum inhibition in A. caudatus (21.52%). In nursery experiments, E. coracana was the most susceptible species, showing mean germination inhibition of 19.87% and 38.68% under leaf and bark extracts, respectively. Radicle growth was generally more sensitive than plumule growth, while low extract concentrations occasionally stimulated seedling growth, indicating hormetic responses. PCA showed that the first two principal components explained 72.9% of the total variation (PC1 = 46.9%; PC2 = 26.0%), and HCA clearly distinguished control from extract-treated groups. Overall, M. esculenta exhibits significant allelopathic potential, particularly through its leaves, with crop responses varying among species. The findings provide valuable insights into tree–crop compatibility and support the selection of suitable crop combinations for sustainable agroforestry systems in the Garhwal Himalaya.
items.authors: Granthi D, Bali RS, Bijalwan A, Butola BS, Dhanai CS, Singh N, Mehra TS.

items.title: Methyl jasmonate reduces the damage caused by low temperature combined with low light: By regulating photosynthetic capacity and hormone levels of pepper seedlings (Capsicum annuum L.).
items.abstract: Low temperature combined with low light (LL) stress is a major issue restricting the yield and economic benefits of protected vegetables. As a typical thermophilic vegetable, the growth and yield of Peppers (Capsicum annuum L.) are easily limited by LL conditions. Methyl jasmonate (MJ), a signal molecule, plays a vital role in plant stress responses. Therefore, this study investigated the regulatory mechanisms of Methyl jasmonate-induced cold tolerance in peppers. The results indicated that the 200 μmol L-1 MJ pretreatment significantly increased the leaf area of pepper seedlings under LL stress (10 °C/5 °C, 100 μmol m-2 s-1/0 μmol m-2 s-1, 12 h/12 h), and the net photosynthetic rate and stomatal conductance increased by 284.61% and 62.77%, respectively. MJ pretreatment induced stomatal opening of pepper leaves under LL stress, reduced Y (NPQ) and Y (NO), increased RC/CS, and up-regulated the expression of the CaPsb S gene encoding a chloroplast protein, thereby significantly increasing the net photosynthetic rate. Meanwhile, MJ significantly increased the contents of K, Ca, Mg, Fe, and Mn in pepper plants under LL stress, the contents of endogenous IAA, ZT, GA3, and JA in pepper leaves, induced the up-regulated expression of CaJMT and CaMJE genes, enhanced the activities of JMT and MJE enzymes, promoted the synthesis of JA, and then improved the stress resistance of pepper plants. The results showed that MJ could significantly affect chlorophyll content under low-temperature, low-light conditions, regulate hormone levels, induce the expression of jasmonic acid synthesis genes, and optimize the photosynthetic index, thereby improving the low-temperature, low-light tolerance of pepper seedlings. Using multi-index synergistic analysis, we assessed the synergistic effects among hormones, elements, and photosynthetic indices. This study is expected to improve pepper yield and quality in facility cultivation and provide insights for pepper resistance breeding.
items.authors: Pu K, Rui W, Gao Y, Zhang M, Sun W, Zhang L, Liang Z, Huo J, Zhang J, Ma Y, Li J, Xie J.

items.title: Metagenomic profiling reveals that divergent fire-adaptive strategies drive distinct fungal succession in pine litter decomposition.
items.abstract: Decomposing litter is a critical driver of fuel bed formation and forest fire regimes, yet how divergent plant fire-adaptive strategies influence litter chemistry and subsequent fungal decomposition dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we conducted a 6-month reciprocal litterbag experiment by incubating litter from two contrasting pine species-the fire-tolerant Pinus taiwanensis and the fire-avoiding P. morrisonicola-in both their own native habitat and that of the other species, coupled with genome-resolved metagenomics to track fungal succession and lignocellulolytic functional profiles. We found that the fire-avoiding P. morrisonicola exhibited significantly accelerated decomposition, driven by inherently lower initial C:N ratio and less recalcitrant litter, whereas the fire-tolerant P. taiwanensis exhibited slower decomposition rates. Metagenomic profiling revealed a distinct functional succession underlying this process. Early decomposition was dominated by Ascomycota (e.g., Leotiomycetes), which rapidly colonized the litter to initiate biopolymer breakdown. As easily decomposable substrates depleted, a functional shift occurred. Specifically, the highly recalcitrant P. taiwanensis litter selectively recruited Basidiomycota (e.g., Agaricales and Trechisporales) equipped with diverse lignin-modifying enzymes, reflected by a late-stage temporal surge in ligninolytic gene abundances. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that plant fire-adaptive strategies act as a strong filter, shaping litter chemistry to drive specific taxonomic and functional fungal succession. This study provides a mechanistic understanding of the eco-evolutionary linkage between plant traits, microbiome assembly, and ecosystem-level fire dynamics.
items.authors: Fang YH, Liu HN, Chen YJ, Hsu TW, Chiu CA, Chiang PN, Huang CL.

items.title: Exogenous riboflavin activates stress-responsive gene networks in Arabidopsis.
items.abstract: Riboflavin is the precursor of flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), vital coenzymes for a wide array of plant metabolic processes, supporting photosynthesis, mitochondrial electron transport and fatty acid oxidation. While exogenous riboflavin application has been reported to improve plant responses to a range of abiotic and biotic stresses, the molecular responses associated with these protective effects remain largely unknown. Here, we present a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis of riboflavin-treated Arabidopsis seedlings, revealing significant changes in gene expression related to stress responses, signal transduction and secondary metabolism. Riboflavin treatment altered the expression of genes within specific cellular functional categories, suggesting a broad reprogramming of plant metabolism. Exogenous riboflavin caused pronounced changes in the expression of stress-responsive transcriptional regulators, including DREB19 and DREB2C, which are involved in stress-responsive signalling pathways. The transcriptional changes were consistent with a shift from growth-associated to stress-responsive functions, including repression of photosynthesis-related genes and activation of pathways associated with oxidative stress responses. These transcriptomic findings were accompanied by changes in cellular redox status, as riboflavin-treated seedlings exhibited reduced ROS accumulation, lower malondialdehyde levels, indicative of diminished lipid peroxidation and temporally regulated activities of CAT, SOD and APX. Furthermore, exogenous riboflavin altered the expression of genes involved in flavin metabolism, including FMN/FHY, which encodes a key bifunctional enzyme catalyzing the interconversion of riboflavin and FMN in the cytosol. Collectively, these results indicate that an acute increase in riboflavin availability triggers coordinated transcriptional and redox responses associated with stress-related pathways and flavin metabolism, highlighting the importance of tightly regulated riboflavin homeostasis in plants.
items.authors: Tsitsekian D, Kamargiakis E, Mylona P, Livanos P, Avgeri F, Bailes CL, Roje S, Rigas S, Daras G.

items.title: Symbiosis with Penicillium sp. D7 rewires molecular modules to boost plant growth and As(III) stress tolerance.
items.abstract: Arsenic (As) contamination severely compromises plant growth and agricultural productivity, particularly in environments affected by mining or industrial activities. Microbial symbionts adapted to metalliferous soils represent a promising yet underexploited resource for enhancing plant tolerance to As toxicity. In this study, we isolated root-associated fungal endophytes from three plant species thriving on As-rich tailings of the Mónica mine (Bustaviejo, Spain) and identified Penicillium sp. strain D7 as a highly As-tolerant symbiont with pronounced plant growth-promoting effects. When co-cultivated with Arabidopsis thaliana, D7 significantly enhanced shoot biomass under As(III) stress by five-fold and mitigated characteristic toxicity symptoms. Transcriptome profiling revealed that D7 reprograms host hormone signalling in a tissue-specific manner: the fungus suppresses abscisic acid (ABA) biosynthesis and ABA-responsive stress pathways in roots, while simultaneously inducing auxin biosynthesis and signalling in shoots, consistent with improved growth performance. Furthermore, D7 elicited the coordinated induction of key components of the plant's intrinsic As detoxification machinery, including ARQ1, PCS1|CAD1, and the vacuolar transporters ABCC1 and ABCC2. Functional analyses using the cad1-3 mutant and the abcc1 abcc2 double mutant demonstrated that vacuolar sequestration of As(III) in roots is essential for D7-mediated stress tolerance, indicating that fungal colonization enhances the host's capacity for intracellular detoxification rather than reducing As uptake. Together, these results demonstrate that Penicillium sp. D7 reinforces plant resilience to As(III) by simultaneously attenuating stress perception, promoting growth-related hormonal programs, and stimulating vacuolar sequestration of As. This study highlights D7 as a promising microbial tool for supporting vegetation establishment and phytostabilization efforts in As-contaminated environments.
items.authors: Rodríguez-Dobreva E, Patel MK, El Wahabi O, Taboada-Ramírez M, Martínez-Fenoll S, Benito B, Vicente-Carbajosa J, Pollmann S.

items.title: Comparative transcriptomic and rhizosphere microbiome profiling and cross-omics association analysis of wild and cultivated Panax japonicus var. major.
items.abstract: IntroductionPanax japonicus var. major is an important medicinal plant endemic to China and is rich in terpenoid saponins with diverse pharmacological activities. Excessive harvesting of wild resources has accelerated the transition toward cultivation, raising questions about differences between wild and cultivated populations.MethodsTranscriptomic and rhizosphere microbiome analyses were conducted in sampled wild and cultivated populations, followed by an exploratory cross-omics association analysis.ResultsTranscriptome comparisons identified 10,416, 8,782, and 5,441 differentially expressed unigenes in roots, rhizomes, and leaves, respectively. Functional enrichment analyses showed differences in plant hormone signal transduction, MAPK signaling, plant-pathogen interaction, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, and terpenoid biosynthesis pathways. Several terpenoid biosynthesis-related genes, including AACT, HMGS, HMGR, DXS, and TPS, had higher transcript levels in wild plants. Rhizosphere microbiome analyses showed differences in bacterial and fungal community composition among the sampled groups. Exploratory cross-omics analysis identified candidate associations between several microbial taxa and terpenoid biosynthesis-related genes.DiscussionThese taxonomic assignments do not establish the functional roles of the detected microorganisms. Because terpenoid and saponin concentrations were not measured, the transcriptomic differences do not demonstrate greater metabolite accumulation or improved medicinal quality. Moreover, because the populations were sampled from different sites and the microbiome data lacked independent biological replication within each sampling group, the observed patterns do not establish effects of cultivation status or habitat, nor do they demonstrate causal plant-microbe interactions. The results provide hypotheses for future controlled studies of P. japonicus var. major.
items.authors: Xiang Q, Yang Y, Gao X, Zhang H, Gui R, Li K, Li Y.

items.title: Genome-wide identification of UDP-glycosyltransferase gene family in Dendrobium huoshanense and functional characterization of DhUGT44 mediating flavonoid 7-O-glycosylation and cold tolerance.
items.abstract: UDP-glycosyltransferases (UGTs) play essential roles in glycosylating plant specialized metabolites, thereby modulating their stability, solubility, and bioactivity to regulate growth, development, and environmental adaptation. Dendrobium huoshanense, a rare and endangered medicinal orchid endemic to China, is renowned for its rich bioactive glycosides, including polysaccharides, flavonoids, and alkaloids, which underpin its high medicinal value. However, systematic genome-wide identification and evolutionary analysis of the UGT gene family in Dendrobium remain limited, hindering their application in stress tolerance and quality improvement. In this study, we performed the first comprehensive genome-wide identification and functional characterization of the UGT family in D. huoshanense by integrating bioinformatics analyses with molecular experiments. A total of 71 DhUGT genes were identified and phylogenetically classified into 12 subfamilies. These genes are unevenly distributed across chromosomes, with tandem duplications as the primary driver of family expansion. Cis-regulatory element analysis showed that most DhUGT promoters are enriched with phytohormone- and abiotic stress-responsive motifs. By integrating multi-omics transcriptomic data, we identified DhUGT44 (subfamily L) as a high priority candidate, exhibiting consistently high expression across tissues, cultivation conditions, and growth stages. Its promoter contains cold-responsive elements, and RT-qPCR confirmed significant induction under low temperature stress in leaves. Subcellular localization assays demonstrated dual localization of DhUGT44 to the plasma membrane and chloroplasts. In vitro enzymatic assays and transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana revealed that DhUGT44 specifically catalyzes 7-O-glycosylation of flavonoid substrates. Furthermore, heterologous overexpression of DhUGT44 in Arabidopsis thaliana significantly enhanced primary root growth under cold stress compared to wild-type plants, indicating its positive role in cold tolerance. This study provides the first systematic insight into the evolutionary dynamics and transcriptional regulation of the UGT family in D. huoshanense, while elucidating the flavonoid glycosylation function and cold tolerance regulatory role of DhUGT44. These findings offer valuable genetic resources and a theoretical basis for molecular breeding and metabolic engineering of stress tolerance and bioactive compounds in Dendrobium.
items.authors: Liu S, Ren J, Liu M, Yin Y, Xu T, Lai E, Guo L, Han B, Yi S.

items.title: clf mutation affects cold stress response and development in Arabidopsis thaliana
items.abstract: Abstract Background Plants acquire freezing tolerance through cold acclimation, a period at low, non-freezing temperature during which gene expression is reprogrammed. This response is driven by the C-repeat binding factors (CBFs) but unfolds on chromatin shaped by the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), which silences genes through the histone mark H3K27me3. Several Polycomb components converge on the CBF loci; what the histone methyltransferase CURLY LEAF (CLF) alone contributes to the cold response is not known. Results To ask whether CLF controls the cold response, we compared the transcriptomes of wild type and clf-29 plants before cold, after three hours of cold, after four days of acclimation and after a further drop towards freezing temperature. The canonical pathway does not depend on CLF: the CBF genes and their COR targets were induced normally in the mutant. To see what the loss of CLF does instead, we compared the two genotypes within each condition. We found a broad misregulation that builds up with age at control temperature, from about one thousand to several thousand genes, and that acclimation almost abolishes, leaving fewer than two hundred. To establish whether any part of the cold response depends on CLF, directly or not, we tested the genotype-by-treatment interaction and scored the genes for H3K27me3. We found such a dependence almost only at acclimation, on genes that are depleted of H3K27me3 and relate to growth; the genes responding to short-term cold only in the mutant are enriched for H3K27me3 but not for the telobox motif that recruits PRC2. Finally, we measured survival to freezing: clf-29 survived better than the WT, most clearly after acclimation. Conclusions CLF is not required for the canonical cold pathway, consistent with redundant Polycomb control of the CBF loci. Its loss mainly affects a developmental programme whose deregulation builds up during growth at control temperature and is strongly attenuated by cold. Cold acclimation thus emerges as a condition in which the H3K27me3-dependent effects of CLF can be separated from secondary, growth-related ones, and the improved survival of the mutant suggests that CLF restrains, rather than supports, the acquisition of freezing tolerance.
items.authors: Longo C, Fiorella GF, Lepri A, D'Orso F, Possenti M, Proietti G, Tartaglia GG, Ioio RD, Colantoni A, Vittorioso P.

items.title: Single-nucleus transcriptomic profiling reveals cell type-specific responses of the soybean root tip to aluminum stress.
items.abstract: Aluminum (Al) toxicity resulting from soil acidification poses a major constraint on crop productivity. Although the root apex serves as the primary site for Al perception and adaptive remodeling, cell type-resolved responses to prolonged Al exposure remain poorly characterized. Here, we employed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) to generate a cell type-resolved transcriptomic atlas of the soybean (Glycine max) root tip under Al stress. We profiled a total of 79,201 high-quality nuclei and identified nine major root cell types. Our results reveal that Al stress elicits shared transcriptional responses across cell types while reshaping root cell type composition. Notably, the proportion of nuclei increased in the epidermal cell layer (from 34.16% to 70.41%). In contrast, a significant reduction in nuclear number was detected within the cortical cells (from 40.70% to 8.53%). Interestingly, microscopic examination further indicated a pronounced expansion of regions exhibiting patterns inconsistent with the decrease in cortical nuclei. Cell type-specific analyses identified a total of 20,544 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and showed that epidermal cells primarily responded to Al stress by activating transcriptional programs associated with transport, cell wall reinforcement, and defense, accompanied by enhanced fatty acid biosynthesis and cuticle-related pathways. In contrast, cortical cells exhibited repression of cell cycle-related transcriptional programs, consistent with their reduced cell abundance and indicating that limitations in cell division are closely associated with cortical cell loss. Furthermore, untargeted metabolomic profiling supported an important role of lipid metabolism in the response to Al stress. Collectively, our study reveals cell type-specific response patterns of the soybean root tip to long-term Al stress at single-nucleus resolution and provides new insights into the cellular mechanisms underlying aluminum tolerance in crop roots.
items.authors: Liu Q, Wang S, Yan R, Xu K, Zhang Y, Wei Y.

items.title: Growth responses of precious tree species with different plant characteristics to three lithological soil types and their interaction effects.
items.abstract: Based on specific nutrient requirements, precise tree species-site matching is the cornerstone of effective silviculture. To explore plant-soil interactions, this study investigated the nutrient utilization strategies of three tree species with distinct traits (Ormosia hosiei Hemsl. et Wils, Ormosia henryi Prain, and Phoebe bournei (Hemsl.) Yen C. Yang) cultivated in soils derived from slate, sandstone, and coal-bearing sandy shale. We further analyzed the interactive effects between plant characteristics and lithological substrates. Results indicated that cultivation significantly altered soil physicochemical properties. Notably, O. hosiei significantly increased soil organic matter in slate and sandstone (p < 0.05) while minimizing AN consumption in these two soil types. Lithological soils significantly influenced seedling growth, nutrient utilization, and biomass accumulation. Although all species performed optimally in coal-bearing sandy shale, their driving soil factors varied. Redundancy and correlation analyses revealed that soil AK and BD drove O. hosiei growth by regulating leaf-root resource allocation and nutrient uptake. For O. henryi, growth was co-limited by AK, BD, and AP. It adapted to the soil environment by optimizing an "aboveground nitrogen (SNR) and underground phosphorus (RPR)" allocation pattern to achieve trait differentiation. In contrast, the growth of P. bournei was primarily driven by soil pH. It regulated inter-organ phosphorus partitioning and whole-plant NUE, and PUE via pH-mediated nutrient availability, thereby maintaining growth homeostasis across different environments. This study systematically elucidates the adaptive strategies and nutrient allocation mechanisms of different species across varied lithological soils. These findings provide a robust theoretical framework for precise species-site matching and efficient plantation management during the structural adjustment of degraded coniferous forests in southern China.
items.authors: Zhou X, Wei X, Su S, Wang X.

items.title: DendroClim: A Free Interactive Web Application for Interpreting Climate–Growth Relationships in Tree Rings
items.abstract: Climate directly influences tree-ring width, making tree-ring records a key indicator of environmental variability. This study aimed to develop DendroClim, a free interactive web application that transforms numerical predictions from climate reconstruction models into real-time geometric representations of tree-stem cross-sections, thereby facilitating the visual interpretation of the relationship between climate and radial growth. The platform was developed using HTML5, CSS, and JavaScript. For model parameterization, samples from 36 Pseudotsuga menziesii (Mirb.) Franco trees were collected in the Sierra de Arteaga, Coahuila, Mexico, and analyzed using dendrochronological techniques. Meteorological records of precipitation (P) and temperature (T) were correlated with the ring-width index (RWI), and regression equations were derived to estimate RWI and geometrically represent it as a stem cross-section. The results showed that RWI was positively associated with winter precipitation and negatively associated with spring maximum temperature explaining 55.6% of the variance in radial growth in the multiple regression model and 24.5% in the precipitation model. DendroClim incorporates four modes for generating tree-stem cross-sections (Random, Widths, Climate, and Model), enabling the geometric reconstruction of up to 1,500 rings. A dedicated module for constructing skeleton plots was also integrated to facilitate the understanding of their construction, interpretation, and cross-dating. Evaluation of DendroClim using 3,360 unit tests across 33 functions demonstrated high reliability: 30 functions (90.9%) achieved a 100% success rate, two achieved 50%, and one achieved 0%. DendroClim provides a dynamic, interactive, intuitive, gamified, and freely accessible platform for understanding tree-growth responses to precipitation, temperature, or their combined effects. In conclusion, DendroClim represents a scientifically rigorous tool for paleoclimatic simulation and environmental education without compromising the integrity of forest resources.
items.authors: Méndez-González J, Sosa-Díaz L, Nájera-Luna JA, Cerano-Paredes J, Villanueva-Díaz J, Flores A, Montoya-Jiménez JC, García-Montiel E.

items.title: Molecular Mechanism of AtCAX3-Induced BPA Tolerance in Plants.
items.abstract: Cation/H+ Exchangers (CAXs) are involved in the sequestration of cations such as Ca2+, Mn2+, Li+, Zn2+, and Cd2+ from the cytosol into the vacuole using proton gradients. Our previous studies demonstrated the involvement of AtCAX3 in Cd2+ tolerance. In this study, we investigated whether AtCAX3 is also involved in tolerance to the endocrine disruptor Bisphenol A (BPA). Furthermore, to examine the role of the autoinhibitory domain of AtCAX3 in BPA tolerance, the empty vector (pYES5), AtCAX3, Δ36-AtCAX3 (deletion of the N-terminal regulatory region; NRR), and Δ90-AtCAX3 (deletion of both the NRR and regulatory-dependent region; RDR) were overexpressed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and the atcax3 knockout mutant of Arabidopsis thaliana. In Arabidopsis, BPA tolerance, Ca2+ levels, and antioxidant enzyme activities were highest in Δ90-AtCAX3-overexpressing plants, followed by Δ36-AtCAX3, AtCAX3, Col-0, and atcax3. Conversely, ROS levels followed the opposite pattern. Interestingly, the expression levels of Ca2+ importer genes (AtCNGC10 and AtMCA1) were increased, whereas those of Ca2+ exporter genes (AtACA10) were decreased in the order of Δ90-AtCAX3 > Δ36-AtCAX3 > AtCAX3 > Col-0 > atcax3. These results suggest that elevated Ca2+ levels may contribute to ROS reduction. Taken together, deletion of the autoinhibitory domain of AtCAX3 enhances BPA tolerance by reducing BPA-induced ROS accumulation through increased Ca2+ accumulation and activation of antioxidant defense systems. Furthermore, enhanced Ca2+ homeostasis may interfere with the positive feedback loop between BPA-induced ROS generation and Ca2+ spikes. These findings can be applied to develop BPA phytoremediators and BPA-resilient crops.
items.authors: Shin H, Kim D, Lee J, Kee KH, Yoo HH, Hwang S.

items.title: Trichoderma harzianum M2 Induces Systemic Resistance to Fusarium Crown Rot and Remodels Root Architecture to Promote Phosphorus Uptake in Wheat.
items.abstract: Wheat production is severely constrained by Fusarium crown rot (FCR) caused by Fusarium pseudograminearum and low soil nutrient use efficiency, making biocontrol an important strategy for sustainable agriculture. This study characterized a newly isolated Trichoderma harzianum strain, M2, and explored its bioprotective and growth-promoting mechanisms in wheat. Identified via morphological and phylogenetic analyses, strain M2 exhibited 91.24% in vitro inhibition against pathogenic F. pseudograminearum. Its 105 cfu/mL spore suspension remodeled root architecture and increased seedling biomass in hydroponic and pot experiments. Greenhouse and field assays recorded FCR control efficacies of 90.12% and 71.70%, respectively; field application of M2 reduced the disease index from 82% to 28%. RNA-seq and qRT-PCR indicated that M2 confers FCR resistance by triggering induced systemic resistance. Microscopy demonstrated that M2 penetrates root epidermal cells, forms biofilm-like structures and stably colonizes root xylem tissues. Furthermore, M2 enhanced soil phosphorus uptake and phosphorus accumulation in wheat. Collectively, endophytic root colonization and multi-hormone regulatory pathways enable T. harzianum M2 to improve wheat defense and performance, representing a promising agent for eco-friendly wheat production.
items.authors: Li J, Jin Y, Wang Y, Chen Y, Wang T, Yang X.

items.title: The potassium homeostasis-stress adaptation continuum: An integrative signaling platform for plant survival.
items.abstract: Potassium (K+) is the predominant cation in plants and has traditionally been viewed as essential for nutrition and osmotic regulation. Studies over the past decade have demonstrated that it is also key to plant response coordination under conditions such as drought, salinity, temperature extremes, and pathogen attack. This review discusses the literature on K+ homeostasis-stress adaptation that highlights K+ transmembrane flux as an integrative signaling platform connecting Ca2+ signaling, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, hormonal regulation, and immune responses. The K+ pathway from rhizosphere perception to shoot function is assessed, and the CBL (calcineurin B-like protein)-CIPK (CBL-interacting protein kinase) signaling module is highlighted as a context-dependent regulator of K+ transport. We identify the absence of a dedicated K+ sensor as an evolutionary puzzle and propose that plants may rely on distributed sensing-membrane potential, Ca2+ signatures, and transporter-kinase complexes-rather than a single receptor. We define the K+ homeostasis-stress adaptation continuum as the temporal, spatial, and functional integration of K+ perception, transport and signaling during stress adaptation. The review suggests future opportunities for crop improvement, including the use of natural allelic variation in Clade IV high-affinity K+ transporters to engineer the CBL-CIPK-TORC (target of rapamycin complex) regulatory network that can improve potassium use efficiency and tolerance to multiple stresses. By presenting K+ homeostasis as an integral part of plant stress adaptation, this review provides a scientific basis for future breeding and biotechnological approaches.
items.authors: Hu B, Ma S, Chen N, Peng X, Yang C, Li T.

items.title: Plant embryogenesis from zygotic genome activation to seed maturation: Comparative mechanisms and engineering opportunities.
items.abstract: Plant embryogenesis converts a zygote into a patterned, maturation-competent embryo. Since the major syntheses published in 2019 and 2021, allele-resolved transcriptomics, single-cell and spatial profiling, and three-dimensional imaging have revealed substantial variation in zygotic genome activation and cleavage geometry across angiosperms, challenging models derived solely from Arabidopsis. Here, we organize recent advances along a comparative zygote-to-seed trajectory and ask how conserved regulatory modules are redeployed across lineages, how early patterning is coupled to seed maturation, and which developmental transitions can be engineered in crops. We first compare the maternal-to-zygotic transition and associated chromatin-state changes, explicitly distinguishing observations from hypotheses about their evolutionary drivers. We then examine how PIN-FORMED (PIN)-dependent auxin transport, local auxin biosynthesis, membrane and peptide signaling, and WUSCHEL-RELATED HOMEOBOX (WOX)-family transcription factors establish embryonic axes and meristems. Next, we connect these early programs to source-sink relations, nutrient partitioning, proteostasis, and hormone-redox control during seed maturation, while separating maturation from dormancy release and germination. Finally, we assess how spatial multi-omics, live imaging, CRISPR activation, and synthetic apomixis can interrogate or engineer these transitions. This framework identifies conserved modules, lineage-specific solutions, and major evidence gaps that must be resolved before embryogenesis can be predictably manipulated for crop improvement.
items.authors: Zhou W, Li Y, Zhao T, Azhar R, Wu J, Hussain I, Liu K, Li W, Yu X.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Melatonin and auxin act synergistically to restore photosynthetic efficiency and redox homeostasis in copper-stressed Brassica juncea.
items.abstract: Copper (Cu) is an essential micronutrient involved in mitochondrial respiration, photosynthesis, and oxidative stress regulation, however, at supra-optimal concentrations it displays toxicity and inhibit plant growth and productivity. Melatonin (MT), an indoleamine with potent antioxidant activity, while as, indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), a key growth and photosynthesis promoter, both hold strong potential to mitigate abiotic stress. Considering their potential, we hypothesized that whether the antioxidant action of MT and the growth-promoting action of IAA would act synergistically or antagonistically. Results demonstrated that Cu stress enhanced the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), superoxide (O2-) malondialdehyde (MDA), and electrolyte leakage (EL) levels, thereby damaging chloroplast organization and structure, decreasing photosynthetic efficiency, CO2 assimilation, and ultimately hinder plant growth. However, the follow-up application of IAA and/or MT proved effective in alleviating Cu-stress in plants by improving all the physio-biochemical traits via maintaining the redox homeostasis and reducing oxidative stress biomarkers. Moreover, both these indolamines proved effective to repairs the anatomical damage induced by Cu. The prominent results were obtained by combined application of both IAA and MT. The findings highlight the interplay between PGR's, antioxidant defence mechanisms and nutrient homeostasis, providing insights to develop new strategies for improving crop resilience and addressing environmental concerns associated with heavy metal accumulation in agricultural ecosystems.
items.authors: Mir AR, Arif Y, Bi MH, Zhang YH, Yang D, Cai L, Hayat S, Fang XW.

items.title: Strategies for the Use and Conservation of Trichoderma spp. for the Growth of Forest Trees in Nurseries.
items.abstract: Deforestation and the degradation of forest ecosystems are critical problems affecting biodiversity and the sustainability of rural communities, especially in Latin America. Ecological restoration seeks to restore these ecosystems by using forest nurseries to produce native plants. However, diseases such as the damping-off complex, caused by fungi like Rhizoctonia sp., Pythium sp., and Fusarium sp., are common and affect seedlings in these nurseries. The use of biological agents, such as the fungus Trichoderma, has proven effective in controlling these pathogens and promoting plant growth. Trichoderma works through mechanisms such as nutrient competition, mycoparasitism, and the production of antimicrobial metabolites, thereby promoting plant health by activating their natural defenses. Strains such as T. harzianum and T. viride have been extensively studied and have shown good results in disease control. However, their use in forest nurseries has been limited by their high cost and limited knowledge of their efficacy. In Mexico, research has shown that inoculating seedlings with Trichoderma improves germination, growth, and disease resistance. Conserving Trichoderma through methods such as cryopreservation and freeze-drying is crucial to ensuring its long-term availability. Future research is expected to optimize commercial formulations and explore the use of native strains adapted to local conditions, contributing to the sustainability of forest ecosystems.
items.authors: Barrera-Ramírez R, Gómez-Godínez LJ, Muñoz-Flores HJ, Ruíz-Rivas M, Aguirre-Noyola JL.

items.title: Embryonal degreening and seed longevity require plastid LEA proteins.
items.abstract: Seeds enable plant embryos to endure extended periods and environmental extremes. Orthodox seeds acquire desiccation tolerance during maturation, before metabolic quiescence. Coordinated thylakoid disassembly and Chl degradation lead to embryo degreening, a hallmark of orthodox seed maturation. While degreening is hormonally controlled, our understanding of the molecular players involved and its physiological significance remains incomplete. By serendipity, we observed a stay-green seed phenotype in an Arabidopsis thaliana mutant lacking two LATE EMBRYOGENESIS ABUNDANT (LEA) proteins, LEA42 and LEA48, which we identified as the most abundant LEA proteins in seed mitochondria and plastids. Using lea48xlea42 as a model for impaired LEA function in seed mitochondria and plastids, proteomic, transcriptomic and transmission electron microscopy analyses indicate incomplete thylakoid degradation. Freshly harvested lea48xlea42 seeds were unaffected in germination but were impaired in germination after high-temperature/high-humidity ageing. Genetic complementation with specifically targeted LEA expression in either mitochondria or chloroplasts revealed that seed longevity support is associated with plastidial, but not mitochondrial, LEA. Light exposure of mature seeds ('light storage') reduced longevity, providing a physiological framework for embryo degreening. Our data identify a role for LEA proteins in remodelling seed plastids before maturation drying and highlight LEA-dependent embryo degreening as a decisive contributor to seed longevity.
items.authors: Brandt D, Vilchez AC, Eirich J, Heinkow P, Hembach L, Zheng K, Barreto P, Niemeier JO, Lebok L, Feussner I, Buchert F, Amunts A, Kühn K, Macherel D, Ischebeck T, Melzer M, Finkemeier I, Schwarzländer M.

items.title: The Core Circadian Clock Gene PiLUX, a MYB-Family Transcription Factor, Enhances Cold Tolerance in Plumbago indica L.
items.abstract: Low-temperature stress is a key environmental factor limiting the introduction and cultivation of plants native to tropical and subtropical regions; however, the molecular mechanisms governing their cold tolerance are not fully understood. In this study, we identified a core circadian rhythm gene-PiLUX-in the ornamental and medicinal plant Plumbago indica L. (P. indica) and systematically analyzed its role in the plant's response to low temperatures. Transcriptomic analysis and physiological measurements indicated that PiLUX is significantly upregulated following cold induction; furthermore, its transcriptional levels show positive correlations with cold-tolerance-related physiological indicators such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging capacity, osmoregulatory substance accumulation, and membrane lipid peroxidation. In transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana (A. thaliana), heterologous overexpression of PiLUX enhances cold tolerance but also delays flowering, suggesting that reproductive development is sacrificed to conserve nutrients for cold tolerance. VIGS experiments confirmed that PiLUX knockdown exacerbates oxidative damage in P. indica under cold stress and reduces its recovery ability. The experimental results and transcriptomic data suggest that PiLUX may participate in the low-temperature response downstream of, or in parallel with, the CBF pathway; however, direct regulatory evidence is still required. This study provides insights into the adaptation strategies of thermophilic plants under low-temperature stress and offers a theoretical basis and genetic resources for cold-tolerance breeding in P. indica.
items.authors: Zhao ZA, Li YR, Li DH, Liao HJ, Gan TJ.

items.title: Combustion Kinetics of Natural Polymers in Lemon-Tree Pruning Wood at High Heating Rates: Criado Master Plots and Šesták-Berggren Modelling.
items.abstract: Lemon-tree pruning wood is a lignocellulosic natural-polymer solid whose cell wall is built from cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin. This study evaluates the use of this polymer matrix as a solid biofuel by combining physicochemical characterization with non-isothermal oxidative conversion at 20-80 K min-1. Lemon-tree branch (LTB) from orchards in Nubaria, Egypt, was analyzed for proximate and ultimate composition, Van Soest fiber fractions, HHV, FTIR, XRD and SEM-EDX. Thermogravimetric combustion was carried out in air at 20, 40, 60 and 80 K min-1. Apparent activation energies were obtained by five isoconversional methods (FR, FWO, KAS, STK, VY) and by Kissinger analysis of the two dry-fuel DTG peaks. Reaction models were screened by Criado master plots, a single-event Šesták-Berggren fit and Coats-Redfern. LTB is a moderately crystalline xylem (cellulose 52.11 wt%, CrI 52.6%, lignin 17.11 wt%) with moisture 7.10 wt%, volatile matter 77.80 wt%, fixed carbon 19.90 wt%, ash 2.30 wt% and HHV 18.50 MJ kg-1. Nitrogen and sulfur are 0.55 and 0.18 wt%. Combustion proceeds in three stages: Stage 1 moisture release, Stage 2 holocellulose-dominated oxidative devolatilization (65-68 wt% loss, Tp1 ≈ 600-640 K) and Stage 3 char oxidation (≈25 wt% loss, Tp2 ≈ 710-730 K). Mean isoconversional Ea on α = 0.1-0.7 is 98-115 kJ mol-1 and rises to ~212 kJ mol-1 at α = 0.8. Criado plots follow F2/F3/D3 up to α ≈ 0.5; a Šesták-Berggren function with m = 0.174 and n = 2.3 describes the Stage 2 window (R2 = 0.890) as an empirical fit only. Coats-Redfern selects F2 for Stage 2. ΔH tracks Ea, ΔG is positive, and ΔS is negative on Stage 2. LTB is a low-ash woody pruning fuel suitable for pellets or co-firing if Stage 3 is completed above ~750 K.
items.authors: Ismail MA, Dubdub I, Mousa S, Al-Yaari M.

items.title: Integrating niches of the pathogen, multiple host and vector species highlights abiotic constraints and host-vector interactions shaping pine wilt disease risk in China.
items.abstract: BackgroundPine wilt disease (PWD), caused by Bursaphelenchus xylophilus (PWN), is a major threat to forest health and pest management in China. Because PWD results from interactions among the pathogen, vector insects, and host plants, single-component analyses may misrepresent disease risk and overlook species-specific contributions. We integrated the environmental niches of the pathogen, hosts, and vectors to characterize abiotic constraints and biotic influences on PWD risk, quantify species-specific contributions and interactions, and inform surveillance priorities.ResultsEnsemble ecological niche models were developed for PWN, 17 susceptible hosts, and 10 potential cerambycid vectors across China and integrated with GeoDetector analysis. Although suitability patterns were broadly consistent, PWN had a much narrower suitable range than hosts and vectors, and this concordance declined under future climate scenarios. Bioclimatic variables were the primary determinants of habitat suitability for most species, whereas PWN showed narrower optimal ranges for key environmental drivers than most hosts and vectors. GeoDetector revealed substantial interspecific variation in explanatory power for PWN suitability, with Pinus massoniana, P. thunbergii, and Monochamus alternatus showing the highest q-values (0.78, 0.77, and 0.79, respectively). All host-vector combinations explained PWN suitability better than either species alone.ConclusionPWD risk in China cannot be inferred from host or vector availability alone, but is shaped by stronger abiotic constraints on PWN and host-vector interactions. Climatically marginal regions with suitable hosts and vectors should be prioritized for surveillance, and species with high q-values warrant further investigation. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
items.authors: Wang W, Du T, Ye J, Huang X, Li Y, Zhang Z, Shi L.

items.title: Melatonin-mediated metabolic reprogramming and stress adaptation in plants.
items.abstract: Key messageMelatonin acts as a multifunctional regulator of plant stress adaptation by reprogramming primary and secondary metabolism and coordinating ROS, nitric oxide, and phytohormone signalling. Integrating metabolomics with transcriptomics and proteomics provides new insights into these mechanisms and highlights melatonin as a promising strategy for enhancing crop resilience and productivity under diverse environmental stresses. Plants, being sessile, are continuously exposed to diverse environmental challenges, which disrupt cellular homeostasis and reduce crop productivity. To survive under such conditions, plants have evolved complex defence mechanisms involving metabolic reprogramming and coordinated molecular signalling networks. Among the regulatory molecules involved in stress adaptation, melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) has emerged as a multifunctional signalling compound that plays a pivotal role in plant growth, development, and stress tolerance. Acting as a potent antioxidant and signalling regulator, melatonin modulates multiple metabolic pathways associated with energy metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, carbohydrate metabolism, and secondary metabolite production. These metabolic adjustments enhance the accumulation of osmoprotectants, antioxidants, and defence-related metabolites, thereby improving plant resilience under stress. Recent advances in metabolomics, together with transcriptomics and proteomics, have provided deeper insights into melatonin-mediated metabolic regulation in plants. High-throughput analytical platforms such as liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS), gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) enable comprehensive profiling of stress-responsive metabolites and reveal how melatonin orchestrates metabolic network reprogramming. Emerging evidence indicates that melatonin interacts with reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, and multiple phytohormones to regulate gene expression, protein abundance, and metabolite accumulation, thereby integrating stress perception with physiological adaptation. This review summarises current knowledge on melatonin biosynthesis, signalling pathways, cross-talk and its role in regulating primary and secondary metabolism under diverse stresses. Emphasis has been laid on metabolomics-driven insights and multi-omics integration to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying melatonin-mediated stress tolerance and to support strategies to improve crop resilience and productivity.
items.authors: Hussain B, Colgecen H, Karahan H, Fariduddin Q.

items.title: Effects of short-term salt stress on photosynthetic characteristics, physiological metabolism, and ion homeostasis in soybean seedlings.
items.abstract: BackgroundSalt stress is a major abiotic stress limiting soybean production, with the seedling stage being the most salt-sensitive period. Elucidating the growth, photosynthetic, and physiological response mechanisms of soybean seedlings to salt stress holds significant theoretical value for breeding salt-tolerant cultivars.MethodsIn this study, we systematically investigated the effects of varying NaCl stress intensities (0-160 mmol⋅kg⁻¹) on plant growth, photosynthetic gas exchange, chlorophyll fluorescence, antioxidant physiology, and ion homeostasis using a salt-tolerant cultivar (Zhonglongdou 136, ZLD136) and a salt-sensitive cultivar (Henong 85, HN85).ResultsThe results demonstrated that increasing salt concentrations significantly inhibited plant growth and photosynthetic carbon assimilation. However, ZLD136 exhibited superior phenotypic stability and photoprotective mechanisms, evidenced by a significant increase in non-photochemical quenching (NPQt). Salt stress triggered a substantial rise in malondialdehyde (MDA) content and relative electrical conductivity (REC); notably, ZLD136 effectively mitigated membrane lipid peroxidation by maintaining higher antioxidant enzyme (superoxide dismutase SOD, peroxidase POD, and catalase CAT) activities and accumulating more osmolytes, including proline (Pro) and soluble sugars (SS). Furthermore, the salt-tolerant cultivar more efficiently coordinated the mitochondrial respiratory electron transport chain (cytochrome c oxidase COX and alternative oxidase AOX pathways) to dissipate excess reducing power and maintain cellular energy homeostasis. ZLD136 also possessed a stronger capacity for ion regulation, significantly outperforming HN85 in maintaining higher leaf K⁺/Na⁺ and Ca²⁺/Na⁺ ratios.ConclusionsSalt tolerance in soybean seedlings involves a comprehensive synergistic network, and the salt tolerance advantage of ZLD136 primarily stems from its superior ability to maintain ion balance, highly efficient photoprotective mechanisms, and a robust antioxidant defense system. Comprehensive analysis revealed that with intensifying salt stress, the physiological responses of soybean gradually transitioned from relying on the antioxidant enzyme system to the synthesis of osmolytes. Moreover, maintaining ion homeostasis (particularly a high leaf K⁺/Na⁺ ratio) is the core prerequisite for alleviating physiological and metabolic disorders, safeguarding photosynthetic functions, and ensuring short-term plant growth.
items.authors: Zhou X, Zhen J, Wang X, Qu Z, Ma Y, Zhao W, Wei X, Dong S, Li X.

items.title: Synaptotagmin-mediated plasma membrane homeostasis is required to recruit the endocytic machinery during cold stress
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Endocytosis depends on plasma membrane (PM) lipid composition, yet how plants sustain endocytic machinery recruitment during stress remains unclear. We investigated whether synaptotagmins SYT1 and SYT3 function in membrane homeostasis and endocytosis in Arabidopsis thaliana. In this work, we revealed that cold stress reversibly blocked FM4-64 internalization in syt1syt3 double mutants by displacing peripheral and core TPC subunits from the PM. Loss of SYT1 reduced brassinosteroid receptor internalization during cold stress, while double mutants showed enhanced brassinosteroid signaling. SYTs and VAP27 genes showed a condition-dependent genetic interaction in endocytosis: the syt1/vap27-1/vap27-3 triple mutant resembles vap27-1/vap27-3 under control conditions and syt1 during cold stress, suggesting overlapping contributions to endocytic regulation. Using molecular dynamics simulations of protein-membrane interactions, phosphoinositide depletion combined with increased diacylglycerol weakened TPC core membrane association. Our findings identify SYT1 and SYT3 as essential components for sustaining endocytosis during abiotic stress and support a model in which lipid homeostasis at endoplasmic reticulum-PM contact sites preserves the membrane composition required for TPC-dependent endocytosis.
items.authors: Aznar-Moreno, J. A., Del Espino, A., Moya-Cuevas, J., Perez-Sancho, J., Wilbrink, G., Neubergerova, M., De Meyer, A., Vanneste, S., Grones, P., Rubio, L., Pleskot, R., Van Damme, D., Amorim-Silva, V., Botella, M. A.

items.title: Shoot and Root Metabolomes of the Xeric Plant Ajania tenuifolia React Differently to Arid Conditions in a Hot-Dry Valley.
items.abstract: Drylands cover almost half of the earth and are highly vulnerable to projected climate change. Understanding how domestic plants react to these harsh conditions is critical for vegetation management. We investigated the leaf and root metabolomes of the xeric shrub Ajania tenuifolia, as well as its responses to hot and dry conditions. Although the leaf water content of plants in dry and hot habitat decreased significantly compared to plants grown at the more humid site, the levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), total carbon (C), nitrogen (N), δ13C, as well as the C and N fractions, were largely conserved. These findings suggest that A. tenuifolia has maintained its oxidative homeostasis and carbon-water balance in the face of adverse conditions. Plants grown in the drier and hotter habitat exhibited an increased tendency to accumulate sugar, particularly trisaccharides in their leaves. This was accompanied by a reduction in the investment directed towards phenolic compounds in their roots. Under hot and dry conditions, N metabolism was stimulated as indicated by the synchronous increases of δ15N in both leaves and roots. Leaves accumulated photorespiratory and osmoprotective amino acids, while roots exhibited elevated levels of antioxidants and N-containing compounds. The present study demonstrated that A. tenuifolia employs a whole-plant resilience strategy involving stomatal regulation, ROS scavenging, and osmotic protection to cope with stressful conditions. Our results also underscore the significance of N metabolism in stress resilience in hot and dry conditions, and offer valuable insights for vegetation management in arid and semi-arid areas under changing climate.
items.authors: Yuan Z, Yang F, Zhu L, Liu L, Liao Z, Du B.

items.title: Transcriptome, metabolite profiling and functional genomics provide molecular insights into sweetpotato sprouting.
items.abstract: Short dormancy period of sweetpotato (Ipomoea batatas) storage roots causes significant economic losses. To unravel the molecular mechanism of sweetpotato sprouting, a comparative transcriptome was performed using storage roots incubated under non-sprout (15 °C) and sprout favouring conditions (25 °C). Our analysis revealed that 7404 genes were differentially expressed between non-sprouting and sprouted storage roots incubated at 25 °C. Further, we observed that gibberellin (GA) biosynthesis gene IbGA3OXIDASE and abscisic acid (ABA) catabolism gene ABA 8'-HYDROXYLASE were upregulated by > 10-fold and > 40-fold, respectively, at the onset of sprouting. Metabolite profiling showed increased GA and cytokinin levels, but reduced ABA content in the sprout initials. Based on conserved expression patterns of phytohormone-related genes during sprouting in potato tubers and sweetpotato storage roots, two genes that were downregulated during sweetpotato sprouting - IbPYL4 (ABA receptor) and IbGA2OXIDASE (GA catabolic enzyme) - were independently overexpressed in potato. Transgenic potato plants overexpressing IbPYL4 or IbGA2OXIDASE exhibited low percentages of tuber sprouting and reduced sprout length. Furthermore, knockdown of the ABA 8'-HYDROXYLASE gene (ABA catabolism) significantly reduced sprout length in sweetpotato storage roots compared to wild-type plants. Overall, our study suggests that selective candidate genes (ABA 8'-HYDROXYLASE, IbPYL4, IbGA3OXIDASE, and IbGA2OXIDASE) could be targeted for developing sweetpotato genotypes with enhanced shelf-life.
items.authors: Patil AB, Vyawahare AB, Barvkar VT, Gawade NS, Barbole RS, Joshi RS, Kadoo NY, Kondhare KR.

items.title: Genome-Wide Identification and Expression Profiling of the GATA Gene Family Reveals Candidate Genes Associated with GA3-Induced Shoot Elongation in Citrus grandis 'Wanbai'.
items.abstract: Plant GATA transcription factors are zinc-finger proteins involved in signal transduction, growth and development. However, their potential involvement in plant height and gibberellin-associated shoot growth in pummelo insufficiently characterised. In this study, members of the CgGATA gene family were identified genome-wide and characterised through analyses of physicochemical properties, chromosomal distribution, phylogenetic relationships, gene structures, conserved motifs, collinearity and predicted cis-acting elements in putative upstream regulatory regions. RT-qPCR was used to examine expression profiles across sampled tissues, and expression changes associated with prolonged gibberellin (GA3) treatment in 'Wanbai Pummelo' shoot tips, and expression patterns in tall and dwarf pummelo genotypes. A total of 23 CgGATA genes were identified and classified into four phylogenetic subfamilies. Members of the same subfamily generally shared similar gene structures and conserved-motif compositions. Comparative collinearity analysis identified more syntenic GATA gene pairs between pummelo and sweet orange than between pummelo and Arabidopsis thaliana. The putative upstream regulatory regions contained predicted elements associated with light, phytohormone, growth and stress responses. The genes exhibited distinct expression profiles across the sampled tissues, with many showing relatively high within-gene values in stems and leaves. Prolonged GA3 treatment promoted seedling shoot elongation and was associated with changes in the transcript abundance of several CgGATA genes at 28 d. Integration of these expression profiles, the tall dwarf comparison and predicted gibberellin-responsive elements prioritised CgGATA11 and CgGATA18 as candidates for investigating plant height variation and shoot elongation in pummelo. These findings provide a basis for functional studies but do not establish that either gene directly regulates gibberellin signalling or plant height.
items.authors: Ma C, Xu Y, Han J, Kong Y, Yang L, Feng D, Fu H, Hussain SB, Chen P, Guo L.

items.title: Meloidogyne enterolobii effector transthyretin-like protein 1 targets plant heat shock protein 90 to manipulate host immunity and promote nematode parasitism.
items.abstract: Meloidogyne enterolobii has a wide host range and high pathogenicity, making it one of the most economically damaging root-knot nematode species. Effectors secreted by M. enterolobii are key players in the cross-talk between nematode and its host. Here, we functionally characterize a transthyretin-like effector protein (MeTTL1) from M. enterolobii. In situ hybridization revealed that MeTTL1 was expressed specifically in the dorsal esophageal gland of M. enterolobii, with the peaked transcript levels during the early parasitic stage. Immunolocalization confirmed the in planta secretion of MeTTL1 throughout nematode migration and its accumulation inside the giant cells. Host-induced gene silencing of MeTTL1 decreased nematode parasitism, reducing gall numbers by 43.6% and nematode counts by 64.1%, whereas Arabidopsis plants overexpressing MeTTL1 exhibited increased susceptibility to M. enterolobii, with gall numbers increasing by 117.1% and nematode counts by 77.7%. Furthermore, MeTTL1 actively suppresses plant immunity by attenuating flg22-induced callose deposition, inhibiting Gpa2/Rbp1-triggered cell death, and downregulating defense-related genes. Luciferase complementation and co-immunoprecipitation assays demonstrated that MeTTL1 interacts with members of the plant Hsp90 family, which are known to be involved in plant immune responses. Moreover, we confirmed that the MeTTL1 C-terminal is critical for the interaction. Notably, Arabidopsis hsp90.3 mutants exhibited increased susceptibility to M. enterolobii, supporting the biological significance of the MeTTL1-Hsp90.3 association in parasitism. In conclusion, our study demonstrates that MeTTL1 one of the key virulence factors secreted by M. enterolobii, promoting nematode parasitism by targeting plant Hsp90 family proteins to suppress host immunity.
items.authors: Zhang X, Shen H, Sun W, Jian H, Liu Q.

items.title: Phosphate rock drives greater arsenic accumulation in Pteris vittata than calcium carbonate by enhancing arsenic metabolism and reshaping rhizosphere microbiome.
items.abstract: Poorly-soluble phosphate rock (PR) and CaCO3 can enhance arsenic accumulation in calcicolous As-hyperaccumulator Pteris vittata, but their mechanisms under soil conditions remain unclear. P. vittata was grown for two months in As-contaminated soil (100 mg kg-1) receiving 2.0 g kg-1 Ca as PR, CaCO3, or soluble CaCl2. Plant nutrients, rhizosphere chemistry and bacterial communities, and As-metabolism genes were examined. Compared with CaCO3, PR increased frond As and P by 35% and 28% to 3128 and 3158 mg kg-1, while CaCO3 produced slightly greater biomass and 10-15% higher rhizosphere available As and P. PR upregulated P-transporter PvPht1;3, arsenate reductase PvHAC2, and arsenite antiporters PvACR3 and PvACR3;3 by 2.0-2.3 fold, whereas CaCO3 induced PvPht1;3, PvPTB1;2, and PvACR3;1/3;2 by 1.7-3.3 fold relative to the soil control. PR retained a more diverse bacterial community (Shannon: 4.20) containing taxa associated with P cycling and As tolerance, whereas CaCO3 showed lower diversity (3.76) under elevated pH. These findings link superior As accumulation under PR to P acquisition, distinct As-metabolism transcriptional responses, and rhizosphere restructuring, providing a mechanistic basis for selecting PR to enhance As accumulation during phytoremediation of As-contaminated soils.
items.authors: Jin R, Zhou Q, Deng S, Hu C, Zhou Q, Ma L.

items.title: Delineating plant responses to the 3',5'- and 2',3'-cAMP isomers.
items.abstract: Much like in animals, both the 3',5'- and the 2,'3'-cAMP isomers are present in plants. The former is the enzymatic product of adenylate cyclases (ACs), the latter is an RNA degradation product. While there is increasing evidence that both isomers can elicit or modulate a broad range of physiological responses, the question of the specificity of responses to isomers has remained, at least partially, unresolved. To delineate isomer-specific responses in Arabidopsis thaliana, we applied a comparative proteomics approach. Our results demonstrate that exposure to 200 nM of either isomer can elicit similar changes in the proteome, supporting the existence of isomer-insensitive targets predominantly involved in RNA processing and metabolism. The 3',5'-specific proteins are enriched in categories such as protein transport and the establishment of protein localization, consistent with the recognised roles of ACs and 3',5'-cAMP in the cytosolic microenvironment. Several RNA-processing components are selectively regulated by the 2',3'-isomer, including proteins that play a critical role in spliceosome stability. At the physiological level, both isomers equally mitigate H2O2-induced net K+ efflux and Ca2+ influx in roots. However, when examining isomer specificity in well-characterized downstream targets, the Cyclic Nucleotide-Gated Channels 2 and 18 (CNGC2 and CNGC18), we noted strict selectivity for 3',5'-cAMP and this would imply that in vivo gating requires catalytically active of ACs.
items.authors: Davide E, Domingo G, Di Iacovo A, Marsoni M, Yun P, Bossi E, Shabala S, Gehring C, Bracale M, Vannini C.

items.title: The MdVQ22-MdWRKY33d complex regulates MdPER55 and MdDREB1D expression to modulate apple salt tolerance by reactive oxygen species scavenging.
items.abstract: Apple is a globally significant fruit tree with considerable economic value. However, it is severely affected by soil salinization, which leads to a reduction in both yield and quality. Since salt tolerance in grafted apple trees largely depends on the rootstock, this study compared transcriptomic responses between salt-tolerant (R5-5) and salt-sensitive (M9T337) rootstocks under salt stress. A key salt-responsive gene, MdWRKY33d, was identified. Overexpressing MdWRKY33d in apple improved salt tolerance, while silencing it had the opposite effect. Additionally, under salt stress, compared with the control, chlorophyll fluorescence values, superoxide dismutase (SOD), peroxidase (POD), and catalase (CAT) levels were elevated in MdWRKY33d transgenic apple and poplar materials. Functional analyses demonstrated that MdWRKY33d directly activates the expression of Peroxidase55 (MdPER55) and Dehydration-Responsive Element-Binding protein1D (MdDREB1D), thereby enhancing reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging and salt tolerance in transgenic plants. Yeast two-hybrid screening identified MdVQ22 as an interacting partner of MdWRKY33d, which was confirmed by pull-down, bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), and luciferase complementation imaging (LCI) assays. MdVQ22 negatively regulated apple salt tolerance by suppressing MdWRKY33d-mediated transcriptional activation of MdPER55 and MdDREB1D. Collectively, this study explores a putative regulatory module MdVQ22-MdWRKY33d-MdPER55/MdDREB1D to coordinate the responses to apple salt stress and provides potential targets for engineering salt-tolerant varieties.
items.authors: Hou H, Li S, Zhang Q, Chen G, Wu W, Liu X, Jiang S, Xu J, Liang X, Meng D, Khusniddinugli AT, Ilkhomovich FM, Zhang Y.

items.title: Antibacterial mechanism of hypocrellin against Ralstonia solanacearum in tobacco and its modulation of the endophytic microbiome.
items.abstract: The photosensitive compound hypocrellin, derived from the traditional Chinese medicinal fungus Shiraia bambusicola Henn., shows potential as a novel pesticide. To evaluate its efficacy against bacterial wilt disease caused by Ralstonia solanacearum in tobacco, this study examined its antibacterial mechanisms through in vitro experiments and analyzed their impact on tobacco endophytic microbiota. An optimized hypocrellin offering a promising sustainable formulation-with a 2:3 ratio of hypocrellin A to hypocrellin B-was developed for enhanced antibacterial activity, and its interaction with bacterial DNA, intracellular components, and membrane integrity was systematically investigated. Hypocrellins exhibited strong antibacterial effects by disrupting the cell wall and membrane integrity of R. solanacearum, increasing membrane permeability, and inducing the leakage of intracellular K+, soluble proteins, and reducing sugars. Dual DNA-binding mechanisms were suggested: electrostatic adsorption to phosphate groups, followed by groove insertion, and intercalation between base pairs. In tobacco plants, hypocrellin treatment significantly altered the endophytic microbial community, increasing microbial richness and diversity, increasing the proportion of Bacillota and Pseudomonadota, and significantly reducing pathogen abundance. Predictive functional analysis based on PICRUSt2 suggested that hypocrellin may have influenced metabolic pathways associated with microbial basal metabolic activity and proliferation potential. Hypocrellins mitigate R. solanacearum infection through multi-target mechanisms: physical disruption of bacterial membranes and DNA, restoration of beneficial endophytic microbiota, and activation of metabolic pathways critical for plant defense.IMPORTANCEThis study highlights the multi-target antibacterial mechanisms and microbiome-modulating effects of hypocrellin, offering a promising candidate for a sustainable strategy for controlling soil-borne diseases. Unlike conventional chemical pesticides, hypocrellin acts through physical disruption of bacterial membranes and DNA interaction, while simultaneously restoring beneficial endophytic microbiota and activating metabolic pathways critical for plant defense in tobacco. Its ability to suppress Ralstonia solanacearum and enhance microbial ecological balance positions hypocrellin as both an effective antibacterial agent and a microbiome regulator. These findings provide a scientific basis for developing hypocrellin-based bio-pesticides and support further research into its application in eco-friendly agricultural practices.
items.authors: Du W, Sun C, Wang J, Liu J, Wang Y, Huang W, Liu G, Li J, Wang R, Su Z, Zhao W, Wang C.

items.title: Comparative Study on Photoinhibition Characteristics and Adaptation Mechanisms of New Current-Year Needles of Pinus densiflora var. zhangwuensis and Pinus sylvestris var. mongolica in Sandy Land Environments.
items.abstract: Whether photoinhibition occurs in tall trees of Pinus densiflora var. zhangwuensis and P. sylvestris var. mongolica in summer and their response mechanisms to strong midday light in sandy land are not yet clear. Therefore, three standard trees were selected for each species as biological replicates by randomly setting up standard plots. Daily changes in the chlorophyll a fluorescence parameter of current-year needles (CYNs) and one-year needles (OYNs) in different parts of the standard tree crowns (in sun branches and shade branches) of the two species were comparatively studied, and the potential hydraulic transport capacities of the sample branches were also evaluated. The results are as follows: (1) The daily changes in the maximal photochemical efficiency of PSII (Fv/Fm) in the sun CYNs of P. sylvestris var. mongolica obviously presented a descending-ascending trend, and its lowest value was observed at noon. The maximum non-photochemical quenching (NPQ) of the sun CYNs in this species was observed at noon, and an NPQ of greater than 1 lasted for 4-5 h. (2) The midday Fv/Fm of the sun CYNs in P. densiflora var. zhangwuensis was close to the morning and shade CYN levels. Compared with P. sylvestris var. mongolica, the NPQ of the sun CYNs of P. densiflora var. zhangwuensis remained low under the condition of high light at noon, but the number of active reaction centers per unit cross-sectional area (RC/CSm) and the electron transfer efficiency (Fm/Fo) were higher. Further analysis of the variation in the light energy absorbed by each reaction center (ABS/RC) showed that the variation in the NPQ in the sun CYNs of the two species was very similar to that of ABS/RC, and the two indices had a very significant positive correlation (the correlation coefficients of P. sylvestris var. mongolica and P. densiflora var. zhangwuensis were 0.7535 and 0.7193, respectively, p P. densiflora var. zhangwuensis were 1.26 and 1.28 times those of the pit of P. sylvestris var. mongolica, respectively, and the theoretical hydraulic conductance (Kt) in the sun branches of the former was 6.32 times that of the latter. The above results suggested that photoinhibition might also be involved in the tall trees of P. sylvestris var. mongolica, while P. densiflora var. zhangwuensis had a more effective mechanism to avoid photoinhibition.
items.authors: Meng P, Zhang M, Wang X, Liu J.

items.title: Functional analysis of mango MiFCA2 gene involved in the regulation of flowering and stress response in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: Abstract FLOWERING CONTROL LOCUS A ( FCA ), as a core component of the autonomous flowering time pathway, can also regulate flowering time in response to environmental temperature. However, the function of FCA in Mangifera indica (mango) remains unclear. Elucidating the regulatory pathways of FCA genes under temperature and abiotic stress could improve mango flowering and resilience under unfavourable environmental conditions. In this study, two FCA2 genes were isolated from two mango varieties with different flowering habits and named MiFCA2-SJ and MiFCA2-JH . Both proteins contain two RRM domains and one WW domain, along with a relatively long glycine-rich region. The expression of MiFCA2-SJ peaked during early flowering, whereas that of MiFCA2-JH peaked towards the end of flowering. Both genes were expressed primarily in leaves. In transgenic Arabidopsis, MiFCA2-SJ plants exhibited early flowering at 13°C/31°C but no significant phenotypic change at 22°C, whereas MiFCA2-JH plants flowered earlier at all three temperatures. Furthermore, MiFCA2-SJ/JH participated in the ABA signalling pathway and responded differently to drought and salt stress. MiFCA2-SJ/JH were localized to the nucleus. Protein interaction assays demonstrated that MiFCA2-SJ interacts with MiFY, the stress-related proteins MiPP2C25B and MiZFP4. In summary, MiFCA2 may play a key role in the temperature-regulated flowering and stress adaptation of mango.
items.authors: He S, Meng Y, Shu M, He Z, Mo X, Chen S, Mo W, Zhang Y, Luo C, He X.

items.title: Mechanosensation of rice root border cells activates serotonin-mediated pre-invasion behaviors in Meloidogyne graminicola via DEG/ENaC channels.
items.abstract: BackgroundPlant-parasitic nematodes (PPNs) locate host roots primarily through chemosensation, yet the sensory events that convert root contact into the stylet thrusts required for host penetration remain obscure. Root border cells (RBCs), terminally differentiated cells shed from the root cap, constitute the first point of physical contact between the root and invading nematodes, but whether and how RBCs trigger pre-invasion behaviors is unknown.ResultsHere we showed that rice (Oryza sativa) RBCs induce preparasitic second-stage juveniles (pre-J2) of the rice root-knot nematode Meloidogyne graminicola to exhibit stylet thrusting, feeding behaviors, and marked up‑regulation of the serotonin biosynthesis gene Mg‑tph‑1 in a density‑dependent manner. Among RBC components, the insoluble polysaccharide cellulose is the predominant inducer. We identified two Degenerin/Epithelial Sodium Channel (DEG/ENaC) mechanosensory genes, Mg‑del‑1 and Mg‑unc‑105, both highly expressed in infective J2. RNA interference targeting either gene reduced nematode motility and abolished RBC‑ or cellulose‑induced stylet thrusting and feeding. Furthermore, silencing Mg‑del‑1 or Mg‑unc‑105 downregulated the serotonergic pathway genes Mg‑unc‑43 and Mg‑tph‑1, and markedly reduced 5‑HT immunoreactivity in J2 responding to mechanical stimulation.ConclusionsWe propose that specific DEG/ENaC channels mediate the mechanosensing of RBCs or root cellulose by root‑knot nematodes, activating a downstream serotonergic circuit that drives stylet thrusting. This work uncovers a previously uncharacterized mechanosensory pathway in plant‑nematode interactions and identifies nematode DEG/ENaC channels as promising targets for disrupting parasitism, offering a new mechanosensory‑based strategy for nematode control.
items.authors: Long X, Xiao W, Shi X, Ye S, Peng D, Ding Z, Yang Z.

items.title: Identification of heat-tolerant germplasm and elucidation of heat tolerance mechanisms in polyploid rice.
items.abstract: Heat stress has become one of the major abiotic stresses limiting rice growth and development. Polyploid rice represents an important approach in rice breeding and may contribute to heat tolerance improvement; however, the processes by which polyploid rice responds to heat stress remain mainly ambiguous. In this study, we evaluated the heat tolerance of 40 neo-tetraploid rice lines at the seedling stage. Among them, six lines displayed high heat tolerance (HD441-HD446), and 16 lines showed low heat tolerance (HD465-HD480). Cytological observations of the two lines, HD441 and HD477, which exhibited marked differences in survival rate, indicated that HD441 maintained a more stable root structure. Physiological investigations indicated that HD441 exhibited more stable antioxidant enzyme activities and accumulated less reactive oxygen species (ROS) under heat stress. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that the expression levels of heat shock protein genes (e.g., OsHSP18.2 and OsHSP60-3B) under both physiological and heat stress conditions differed significantly between the two lines. Temporal differential expression analysis further demonstrated that the expression levels of photosynthesis-related genes (e.g., OsRBCS2 and OsRBCS5) were significantly upregulated in HD441 under heat stress, and that the chloroplast structure of HD441 remained more stable than that of HD477. Integrated metabolo-transcriptomic analysis revealed that flavonoid biosynthesis was a key pathway in the heat stress response of HD441. These findings collectively offer significant insights into the regulatory processes governing high-temperature responses in polyploid rice.
items.authors: Cao L, Sun L, Yin J, Guo H, Wu J, Lu Z, Chen Z, Wang L, Shahid MQ, Liu X.

items.title: A novel Phytophthora-specific putative lipid-binding protein triggers plant immunity.
items.abstract: Plants recognize conserved pathogen-derived molecules to activate pattern-triggered immunity (PTI), yet many secreted proteins from oomycete pathogens remain functionally uncharacterized. Here, we identified PcCF16, a previously uncharacterized secreted protein from Phytophthora capsici, through activity-guided fractionation of the pathogen secretome. PcCF16 induced cell death and PTI-associated gene expression in Nicotiana benthamiana, and purified recombinant PcCF16 triggered reactive oxygen species production across multiple plant species. PcCF16-induced cell death was independent of the co-receptors BAK1 and SOBIR1, while defense gene activation remained SOBIR1-independent but was partially dependent on BAK1. Recombinant PcCF16 pretreatment enhanced resistance to P. capsici, while P. capsici lines constitutively expressing PcCF16 exhibited reduced virulence. Structure-function analysis identified residues 202-291 as the shortest fragment tested that was sufficient for cell death induction, whereas N-glycosylation enhanced PcCF16 accumulation and activity but was not strictly required. Structural analyses revealed similarity between PcCF16 and members of the tubular lipid-binding protein (TULIP) superfamily and predicted internal hydrophobic cavities. Consistent with these features, PcCF16 preferentially associated with phosphatidic acid in vitro. Despite substantial sequence divergence, PcCF16 homologs retained similar predicted protein folds but differed in cell death-inducing activity, with surrounding protein context influencing the activity of the conserved C-terminal region. PcCF16 was preferentially expressed during the necrotrophic phase of infection, suggesting a biological function distinct from that of typical early-stage immune elicitors. Together, these findings identify PcCF16 as a Phytophthora-specific secreted immune elicitor with potential lipid-associated functions and reveal an unusual link between late-stage pathogen biology and plant immune activation.
items.authors: Seo YE, Kim S, Kong J, Jung S, Choi D.

items.title: Halotolerant Brucella intermedia PM63 enhances growth, ion homeostasis, antioxidant defense, and salt stress tolerance in rice.
items.abstract: Soil salinity limits rice growth through osmotic stress, ionic imbalance, and oxidative damage. In this study, halotolerant plant growth-promoting bacteria were isolated from Peganum harmala collected at the Khewra Salt Mine, Pakistan, and one of the best isolates, Brucella intermedia PM63, was evaluated for its ability to improve salt tolerance in rice. Ten bacterial isolates were screened for salt tolerance and plant growth-promoting (PGP) traits, and three selected strains were characterized by phenotypic tests, FTIR, SEM, 16S rRNA sequencing, and PCR detection of functional genes. PM63 tolerated up to 3 M NaCl and, under non-saline conditions, produced indole-3-acetic acid (167.27 µg mL⁻¹) and siderophores (110.72 PSU) and solubilized phosphate (157.72 µg mL⁻¹). PCR detected nifH, acdS, ituC, sfp, and opd in PM63. FTIR and SEM analyses showed changes in cell-surface functional groups and cell morphology under salt stress. In a greenhouse experiment with three rice varieties exposed to 0-300 mM NaCl, PM63 inoculation improved root and shoot growth, biomass, photosynthetic pigment content, and osmolyte accumulation. It also modulated antioxidant responses, increased K⁺ retention, reduced Na⁺ accumulation, and lowered oxidative damage (H₂O₂ and malondialdehyde) and electrolyte leakage. The magnitude of the response differed among varieties, with KSK-434 responding most strongly across several traits. These findings identify PM63 as a halotolerant plant growth-promoting bacterial inoculant with potential for improving rice performance under saline conditions.
items.authors: Sultan MA, Paker NP, Ali J, Din BU, Naz I, Sani A, Hassan D, Munis MFH, Chaudhary HJ.

items.title: Effects of Seedling Grade on Biomass Accumulation and Allometric Growth Across Developmental Stages in Pinus yunnanensis Franch. Seedlings.
items.abstract: Pinus yunnanensis Franch. holds significant ecological value as a native conifer endemic to the southwestern uplands of China. The annual P. yunnanensis seedlings were categorized into three quality classes: Grade I, Grade II, and Grade III in accordance with the national specifications for seedling quality. We measured root, stem, needle, aboveground, and individual biomass at six stages from 240 to 690 days. We used the standardized major axis method to analyze allometric relationships among organs and with total biomass. Our results showed that Grade I seedlings had more stable allometric coordination over time. The lower grades showed more fluctuations and weaker coordination.
