Needles dominated biomass throughout the development period, roots grew faster in later stages, and stems grew slower but increased their share. This showed seedlings invest first in needles for carbon gain and then gradually build support and uptake structures. The biomass allocation and growth modes matured between 510 and 690 days. Biomass differed among seedling grades. Grade I seedlings show better growth stability and resource-use efficiency. They are suitable for nursery cultivation and afforestation. This study lays the groundwork for upgrading quality standards and perfecting silvicultural techniques. It also helps design precise tending measures to raise survival rates and early productivity. This work has practical value for plantation establishment, ecological restoration, and timber development in Southwest China.
items.authors: Wang P, Wang H, Lu Z, Kang X, Xu Y, Cai N, Yang B.

items.title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal community abundance, functions, and symbiotic interactions revealed by root metatranscriptomes.
items.abstract: Arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungal communities are often profiled by metabarcoding, but this approach can bias abundance estimates and provide limited insight into community function and interactions with the host. Here, using weekly, field-based multi-omics, we find metatranscriptomes and metagenomes increase estimates of AM fungal relative abundance 6-15-fold over rDNA metabarcoding and that root AM fungal relative abundance correlates strongly with sorghum forage yield (R > 0.9) and moderately with grain yield/quality. AM fungal relative abundance is impacted directly by sorghum development and indirectly by drought via suppressed sorghum fatty acid gene expression. Gene co-expression network revealed coordinated plant and AM fungal functions in structural reorganization, resource exchange, and signal communication between the symbiotic partners. We found that early-season co-transcriptions of AM fungal and host genes feature cytoskeletal genes essential for arbuscule formation, the fungal-plant organs of nutrient and mineral exchange. Late-season plants downregulate cytoskeletal genes, but AM fungi continue their upregulation, which is associated with fungal sporulation and putative mating. Our study identifies previously ignored massive underestimation of AM fungal relative abundance, highlights the predictive role of AM fungal relative abundance for crop productivity, and uncovers symbiotic life history dynamics underpinned by coupled and decoupled co-expression of plant and AM fungal genes.
items.authors: Chen P, Taylor JW, Gao C.

items.title: The Cytosolic Iron-Sulfur Cluster Assembly Targeting Complex Is Hijacked by Magnaporthe Effector AvrPi9 to Suppress Rice Resistance.
items.abstract: The cytosolic iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster assembly (CIA) targeting complex mediates the maturation of cytosolic and nuclear Fe-S proteins and governs core eukaryotic cellular processes. However, whether this complex contributes to plant disease resistance remains unclear. Here, we show that the Magnaporthe oryzae avirulence effector AvrPi9 targets the host CIA targeting complex to suppress rice blast resistance. AvrPi9 physically interacts with and stabilizes OsAE7, a core subunit of the CIA targeting complex. Using biochemical and genetic approaches, we demonstrate that OsAE7 facilitates Fe-S protein maturation, including the Fe-S protein aconitase OsACO1, and negatively regulates blast resistance in cooperation with another CIA targeting complex subunit, OsCIA1, and the carrier protein OsNAR1 in rice. Furthermore, ectopic expression of AvrPi9 enhances the activity of the CIA complex and the maturation of OsACO1. Knockout of OsACO1 elevates ferrous iron levels, triggers a reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst, and activates pathogenesis-related gene transcription, thereby strengthening rice resistance to blast. Our findings reveal a critical role of the CIA targeting complex in plant disease resistance and uncover a novel virulence strategy whereby AvrPi9 hijacks the host CIA pathway to dampen basal resistance and promote infection.
items.authors: Shi H, Liu Z, Zhang Y, Li R, Fu Z, Chen Y, Wen H, Cai L, Chen Z, Qiu J, Kou Y.

items.title: Integration of consensus WGCNA and differential expression analysis reveals stable heat shock protein networks in soybean adaptation to Western Canada.
items.abstract: The expansion of soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merr.) cultivation into Western Canada is constrained by distinct abiotic stressors, including shorter growing seasons and drought. Heat shock proteins (HSPs) are critical regulators of stress adaptation; however, characterizing their expression in field conditions is often confounded by significant annual environmental variability. In this study, we integrated differential expression analysis, consensus Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA), and rigorous protein-protein interactomic modeling across 4 years of field data (2018-2021) involving 10 genotypes grown in Eastern and Western Canada. By filtering temporal noise, we identified a stable, region-specific module that is computationally predicted to resolve into a highly coordinated physical chaperone complex. Subcellular characterization of this network revealed a robust core of chaperones targeting mitochondria and chloroplasts. Crucially, high-confidence predictions identified a physical interaction between a mitochondrial HSP60 hub and a nuclear domains rearranged methyltransferase, suggesting this chaperone complex potentially bridges localized organelle defense with systemic epigenetic regulation to safeguard metabolic capacity. These findings delineate a computationally modeled, geography-dependent stress response machine and provide ideal genetic targets for breeding programs aiming to improve soybean resilience in northern latitudes.
items.authors: Bruggink J, Wozny J, Golshani A, Cober E, Samanfar B.

items.title: Nitrogen Regulation Under Heavy Metal Stress in Soil-Plant Systems: Implications for Plant Growth and Phytoremediation.
items.abstract: Nitrogen (N) is a vital macronutrient that dictates soil fertility and plant productivity. Heavy metal contamination threatens plant health by disrupting nutrient uptake and photosynthesis. Specifically, heavy metals accumulate in soils and inhibit key N-assimilatory enzymes, such as nitrate reductase. This inhibition restricts N availability, which limits protein synthesis and reduces overall plant biomass. This review synthesizes the recent literature to evaluate the mechanisms of heavy metal-N interactions, highlighting a critical scientific insight: N exerts a dual role in heavy metal stress. Externally, the chemical form of N uptake alters rhizosphere pH, which can either mobilize or precipitate toxic metal cations. Internally, optimal N assimilation fuels the synthesis of metal-chelating proteins (e.g., phytochelatins) required for cellular detoxification. A key conclusion of this review is that isolated agronomic or physiological interventions are insufficient to manage this stress in the field. Effective mitigation requires a coupled "soil-to-gene" approach. By combining macroscopic soil management (e.g., pH buffering and biochar application) to restrict external metal bioavailability with targeted molecular interventions (e.g., regulating root ion transporters and leveraging microbiome-assisted multi-omics) to enhance internal detoxification, researchers can improve phytoremediation efficiency and restore soil health in multi-contaminated environments.
items.authors: Sun R, Farooq A, Chen S, Shahani AAA, Liu T, Jiajin L, Farooq TH, Yan W, Wang J.

items.title: Integrated pangenomics and population genomics reveal climate adaptation and maladaptation in an East Asian tree.
items.abstract: Characterizing genomic variation in keystone forest trees is critical for understanding and predicting the adaptation and maladaptation of terrestrial ecosystems to global climate change. In this study, we integrate five high-quality genomes and high-depth whole-genome resequencing data from 222 individuals across 44 natural populations of Populus davidiana in East Asia. Our findings reveal that genome divergence strongly correlates with epigenetic and regulatory features, with variable genomic regions closely associated with dynamic transposon activity linked to epigenetic modifications. A population-scale genotype-environment association analysis identifies 10,372 adaptive single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and 1322 adaptive structural variations (SVs). Among these, a temperature-associated SV and a precipitation-associated SV undergo functional validation providing evidence of their roles in the expression of PdaMSL10, a mechanosensitive ion channel, and the transcription factor PdaWRKY40, respectively. Overexpression and RNAi experiments demonstrate that differential expression of PdaWRKY40 is strongly associated with drought sensitivity or tolerance, facilitating adaptation to diverse environmental conditions. Additionally, genomic vulnerability forecasts under future climate scenarios highlight the increasingly significant role of SVs in environmental adaptation. These findings advance our understanding of the genetic mechanisms underlying climate adaptation in non-model keystone species and provide invaluable genetic resources for breeding programs aimed at enhancing climate resilience.
items.authors: Chen L, Sang Y, Dan X, Jiang Y, Shi T, Feng J, Zhang X, Long T, Zeng X, Lv J, Long Z, Zhou X, Wu J, Jia C, Liang R, Liu J, Wang J.

items.title: There are cores, indicators, and differences - a high-throughput and quantitative PCR study of the Ambrosia artemisiifolia L. leaf, root, and seed endophytic bacterial microbiomes within the European invasive range
items.abstract: Ambrosia artemisiifolia L. is among the most harmful invasive plants in Europe, a major agricultural weed and a source of severe allergenic pollen. Endophytes may affect invasion, but this species' endophytic bacteria were profiled by high-throughput sequencing only in a single study from China. We aimed to characterize the leaf, root, and seed endobacteriome and test whether tissue type, habitat, or region shape its composition within the European invasive range. Plants were sampled from six sites in Poland and Slovakia across three habitat types. 16S rRNA gene amplicons from surface-sterilized tissues and soil were sequenced and bacterial load quantified by qPCR. Analyses included alpha and beta diversity, core microbiome, indicator analysis, differential abundance, and functional prediction. Tissue type, not region or habitat, structured communities. Gammaproteobacteria exceeded Alphaproteobacteria in most plant tissue samples, but in soil the reverse was true. Mean bacterial load in plant tissues ranged from 1.73-3.49 × 10 8 16S rRNA gene copies g dry weight -1 . The pan-tissue core (80% prevalence) contained 13 genera, 9 of them absent from the soil core. Seeds had significantly lower alpha diversity, the smallest core and no seed-exclusive predicted functional indicators. Leaves and roots differed significantly in taxonomic composition but not in predicted functions. Tissues shared a core that overlapped only partly with the soil core. Seeds carried a reduced subset of the endobacteriome that, in this annual invader, may pass across generations. Further studies should compare these communities with native-range populations and test the enhanced mutualism and pathogen spillback hypotheses.
items.authors: Grzyb, T., Hrabovsky, M., Tokarska-Guzik, B., Szulc, J.

items.title: Functional analysis of SmCSN5 in salt stress tolerance of Salvia miltiorrhiza.
items.abstract: Salt stress limits plant growth, but the contribution of COP9 signalosome subunit 5 (CSN5) to salt tolerance in Salvia miltiorrhiza remains unclear. Here, we combined heterologous overexpression in Arabidopsis thaliana with overexpression and RNA interference in S. miltiorrhiza hairy roots. SmCSN5 transcript abundance increased with NaCl concentration and showed a transient response to 150mM NaCl, peaking at 6h among the sampled times. SmCSN5 overexpression improved germination and growth under salt stress and was associated with higher proline accumulation and antioxidant enzyme activities. Overexpressing Arabidopsis also maintained higher relative water content and chlorophyll content, with lower electrolyte leakage, malondialdehyde content, and ROS-associated staining. Separate ion measurements showed lower Na⁺ content, higher K⁺ content, and lower Na⁺/K⁺ ratios in overexpressing Arabidopsis and hairy roots. SmCSN5 RNA interference produced opposite physiological and ion-accumulation responses in hairy roots. Yeast two-hybrid and luciferase complementation assays identified SmCBL3 as a candidate SmCSN5-interacting protein. Collectively, these findings support a positive role for SmCSN5 in salt tolerance, accompanied by improved antioxidant defense, osmotic adjustment, and ion homeostasis. Whether these responses improve medicinal metabolite production under salinity remains unresolved.
items.authors: Shao S, Wang M, Zhu W, Ma P.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Plant endophytic fungi against plant-parasitic nematodes: from direct antagonism to plant-mediated biocontrol.
items.abstract: Plants have evolved sophisticated and tightly regulated immune systems to defend themselves against pathogen, whereas pathogens have developed diverse strategies to evade or manipulate host defenses. Plant-parasitic nematodes pose a particular challenge because of their intimate and prolonged interactions with host tissues, during which they actively manipulate plant physiology and immune responses. The limitations of conventional nematode control strategies have increased interest in plant-associated microorganisms as sustainable alternatives. Among these, endophytic fungi are emerging as promising allies because they can act through complementary mechanisms, combining direct antagonism of nematodes with the ability to modulate and prime plant immunity. This review integrates current knowledge on plant-nematode interactions with emerging insights into the role of endophytic fungi as modulators of plant defense. We examine how fungal endophytes influence hormone signaling, defense-related pathways, systemic resistance, and other components of plant immunity, while also considering their direct effects on nematode survival, development, and reproduction. We demonstrate that the protective potential of endophytic fungi extends beyond direct biocontrol and involves a broader reprogramming of plant responses that can enhance resistance to nematode attack. Finally, we discuss the factors that determine the consistency of these interactions, including fungal and plant genotype, environmental conditions, and the physiological and ecological context of the plant-fungus-nematode interaction. Understanding these mechanisms will be critical for translating endophyte-mediated plant protection into reliable and sustainable strategies for nematode management.
items.authors: Giachero ML, Marquez N, Declerck S.

items.title: Fluorescence in situ hybridization reveals endophytic and epiphytic root colonization of the novel plant growth-promoting bacterium Citrobacter sedlakii CESi7.
items.abstract: Plant growth-promoting bacteria are gaining significant attention as promising biofertilizers. However, the inconsistency between in vitro plant growth-promoting traits and actual field performance remains a challenge, driven partly by a limited understanding of in situ colonization. This study characterized the colonization patterns of Citrobacter sedlakii CESi7, a novel plant growth-promoting bacterium, isolated from oil palm waste compost, during Brassica rapa cultivation. The in situ behavior of CESi7 was observed in both sterilized medium and non-sterilized soil using fluorescence in situ hybridization with a strain-targeting probe. The results revealed that CESi7 can establish both epiphytic and endophytic populations that transiently colonize roots. In a sterilized medium, CESi7 was widely distributed throughout the root tissues. Conversely, in non-sterilized soil, the bacterium formed dense aggregates specifically at the root tips. This study provides direct microscopic evidence of the colonization strategy of CESi7, offering crucial insights for its development as an effective biofertilizer.
items.authors: Inoue H, Maeda M, Koga T, Salman Z, Chin CFS, Mohd Zainudin MH, Ramli NB, Hassan MA, Tashiro Y, Sakai K.

items.title: The Membrane Continuum Governing Cadmium Uptake, Partitioning, and Detoxification in Plants.
items.abstract: Cadmium (Cd) contamination threatens agro-ecological safety and food security; thus, elucidating mechanisms of Cd uptake and accumulation in plants is key to breeding low-Cd crops. Within the defensive network plants deploy against Cd stress, the plasma membrane and endomembrane system act as physical barriers to metal influx and as the core regulatory hub governing signal perception, transmembrane transport, and vacuolar compartmentalization for detoxification. This review examines the physiological and molecular mechanisms by which the cell membrane system influences Cd transport and accumulation in plants, focusing on five key dimensions: (1) the gating roles of plasma membrane transporters (e.g., ZIP, NRAMP, and HMA families) in root Cd uptake, efflux detoxification, and long-distance translocation to shoots; (2) compensatory mechanisms in intracellular homeostasis remodeling mediated by endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress-induced unfolded protein response (UPR) and Golgi vesicle trafficking; (3) the vacuole as a central detoxification depot, achieving compartmentalized sequestration of free Cd2+ and macromolecular chelates through transmembrane transport networks comprising ABC, MTP, and CAX proteins; (4) profound effects of Cd-triggered dynamic remodeling of membrane lipid composition, lipid peroxidation, and membrane microdomain changes on physicochemical states and spatial distribution of transport channels; (5) membrane-initiated signaling networks (lipid sensors, Ca2+, ROS, NO) and their post-translational fine-tuning of transporter abundance and activity. This review integrates dynamic plant response mechanisms to heavy metal Cd from a multi-dimensional membrane biology perspective, aiming to provide theoretical references and novel insights for the molecular design and safe production of low-Cd crop varieties.
items.authors: Li X, Zhang J, Qin Q, Lijuan S, Yang S, Wang J, Jiang X, Xue Y, Sun Y.

items.title: Integrated transcriptomic and functional trait responses reveal ecological strategy-associated biomass accumulation and allocation under drought in mulberry seedlings.
items.abstract: Drought alters both plant growth and biomass accumulation and allocation, but how molecular responses and functional traits jointly reflect these changes in woody plants remains insufficiently understood. We investigated whether plant ecological strategies, quantified using the competitive-stress tolerant-ruderal (CSR) framework, could provide an integrative description of drought-associated biomass responses in mulberry (Morus atropurpurea) seedlings. In this study, mulberry seedlings were maintained under well-watered, mild-drought, or moderate-drought conditions for 30 days, after which biomass accumulation and allocation, leaf and root functional traits, physiological and biochemical responses, and leaf transcriptomes were assessed. Transcriptomic and functional trait analyses revealed coordinated tradeoffs between growth-related processes and stress-defense responses. Total biomass was positively associated with photosynthetic performance, leaf and root growth traits, and genes related to light harvesting and carbon metabolism, whereas root-to-aboveground biomass ratio was positively associated with osmotic adjustment, antioxidant defense, ABA-related signaling pathways, and conservative root traits. The CSR scores revealed a corresponding shift from a predominantly competitive profile under well-watered conditions toward greater stress tolerance under moderate drought. Competitive scores covaried with resource-acquisitive traits and total biomass, whereas stress-tolerant scores covaried with cellular defense and increased relative belowground allocation. This result indicated that the shift in mulberry ecological strategies under drought stress represents an integrative adaptive syndrome that aligns with coordinated changes in biomass accumulation and allocation. The enhancement of competitive strategy is associated with greater aboveground growth and biomass accumulation, while the enhancement of stress-tolerant strategy corresponds to reduced overall growth and increased underground biomass allocation-patterns that collectively shape the balance between drought resistance and growth productivity in mulberry.
items.authors: Zhang C, Yang S, Cisse EM, Wang J, Xu X.

items.title: Plant Responses to Heavy Metal Stress: Molecular Mechanisms, Transcriptomic Regulation, and Multi-Omics Integration in Crop Improvement.
items.abstract: Heavy-metal contamination poses a serious threat to plant growth, productivity, and resilience, as it causes complex changes in cellular homeostasis, redox balance, element transport, and metabolism. This review summarizes current understanding of the molecular mechanisms by which plants adapt to heavy-metal stress, with a particular focus on transcriptional and omics approaches. The main detoxification and defense mechanisms are discussed, including chelation and vacuolar sequestration, antioxidant regulation, hormonal signaling, and ion transport. Particular attention is paid to the role of MAPK cascades and transcription factors in coordinating the expression of genes involved in metal transport, maintenance of redox homeostasis, and detoxification. Analysis of transcriptomic studies shows that the plant response is characterized by pronounced temporal, tissue-specific, and genotypic specificity and involves the reprogramming of genes involved in transport, antioxidant defense, secondary metabolism, and signaling pathways. At the same time, transcript levels do not always reflect the functional state of proteins and metabolic processes. Therefore, the integration of transcriptomics with genomics, epigenomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and single-cell and spatial approaches combined with functional validation is proposed as a key direction that may facilitate the identification of robust molecular markers and functionally validated genes for improving crop tolerance to heavy-metal contamination.
items.authors: Sapakhova Z, Daurov D, Daurova A, Luo X, Abilda Z, Toishimanov M, Kanat R, Isgandarov I, Zhambakin K, Shamekova M.

items.title: Synthetic activation of gibberellin signalling reveals spatial coordination of root growth.
items.abstract: Gibberellins (GAs) influence cell division and elongation, profoundly shaping plant architecture and yield. GA perception occurs when bioactive GAs bind the receptor GID1, promoting DELLA degradation and activating transcriptional programs. While GA signalling in the root endodermis is essential for promoting root elongation, the contributions of other layers have remained unclear. Here we developed a synthetic GA (sGA) that exhibits little or no binding to endogenous GID1, together with a modified GID1 (mGID1) engineered to selectively recognize sGA, enabling cell-specific activation of GA signalling in vivo. Using this system in Arabidopsis, we demonstrate that coordinated action of GA signalling in the endodermis and epidermis is required for full root elongation. Moreover, the distal spatial distribution of GA signalling and GA biosynthetic enzymes supports a model in which bioactive GAs are transported from GA3ox-expressing tissues to the endodermis and epidermis to coordinate root elongation. The sGA-mGID1 system provides a versatile platform for spatially precise reprogramming of hormone signalling, enabling synthetic control of developmental processes such as root-shoot growth balance, thereby advancing applications in plant synthetic biology and sustainable crop improvement.
items.authors: Yagami Y, Yamada R, Ishikawa Y, Meguro E, Kusano S, Itami K, Frommer WB, Hagihara S, Nakamura M.

items.title: MAKR6 integrates TMK and CAMEL/CANAR signalling for auxin canalization in Arabidopsis.
items.abstract: Adaptive plant development is orchestrated, among other means, by directional, intercellular transport of the phytohormone auxin. Self-organizing phenomena such as flexible vasculature formation depend on auxin canalization, which manifests as the gradual formation of auxin-transporting channels through feedback between auxin signalling and transport. Here we identify MAKR6 as a component of this feedback. MAKR6 transcripts accumulate in vascular cells and are tightly regulated by auxin via the Aux/IAA-ARF-WRKY23 transcriptional cascade. MAKR6 is required for auxin canalization-dependent processes, including leaf venation, vascular regeneration and de novo channel formation from local auxin sources. Mechanistically, MAKR6 interacts with the PIN1 auxin transporter and modulates its trafficking and polarization. MAKR6 also associates with and integrates TMK1/4 and CAMEL-CANAR, two key receptor-like kinase complexes involved in canalization. Together, our study establishes MAKR6 as a multifaceted regulator that couples transcriptional auxin signalling to PIN1 repolarization and coordinates multiple RLK-mediated pathways into a concerted process. This provides mechanistic insight into auxin canalization and exemplifies a framework for exploring similar regulatory nodes in other developmental contexts.
items.authors: Ge Z, Koczka L, Mazur E, Molnar G, Vladimirtsev D, Kassem N, Ikene SA, Fiedler L, Friml J.

items.title: Integrated biochemical, metabolomic, transcriptomic, and phytohormone analyses reveal cultivar- specific metabolic regulation in Chaenomeles speciosa fruit during harvest
items.abstract: Abstract Background Chaenomeles speciosa is a dual-purpose fruit with high value for both medicinal and food applications. Its fruit quality varies substantially among cultivars and harvest stages, yet the molecular basis underlying metabolic divergence between cultivars during the harvest window remains poorly understood. Results Here, we analyzed cultivars ‘P’ and ‘L’ at 105 and 120 days after full bloom in terms of morphology and chemical composition, integrating transcriptomics, metabolomics, and hormone profiling to investigate the quality variation. A total of 896 metabolites were identified, with significant variety among the cultivars in carbohydrates (stachyose, D-glucose), phenolic acids (caffeic acid and chlorogenic acid) and flavonoids. Phytohormone profiling revealed that during harvesting, auxin, salicylic acid (SA), jasmonic acid (JA), ethylene, abscisic acid, and cytokinin declined, whereas gibberellin (GA) exhibited the opposite trend. Through integrated correlation analysis of differentially accumulated metabolites, differentially expressed genes, and phytohormones, we predicted a potential GA- JA- SA crosstalk network that may coordinate the balance between fruit growth and defense during the harvest period. Notably, the persistent-calyx ‘L’ variety exhibited greater metabolic stability and higher accumulation of functional saccharides, while the deciduous-calyx ‘P’ variety showed higher peak phenolic content but rapid decline in the later stage of the harvest window. Conclusions Our study provides the first integrated multi-omics and phytohormone profiling of cultivar-specific metabolism in Ch. speciosa fruit during harvest and establish a regulatory framework linking hormone signaling to variety-specific metabolic divergence. The findings offer new insights into the molecular mechanism of cultivar-specific fruit development in multi-purpose medicinal plants.
items.authors: Fang Q, Fang Y, Fang Y, Zheng L, Wu Y, Xu G, Yao Y, Zha L, Peng D.

items.title: Plant cytokinin ortho-topolin riboside suppresses the proliferation of multiple myeloma cells by promoting β-catenin degradation.
items.abstract: Multiple myeloma involves the aberrant activation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, resulting in β-catenin accumulation. Targeting this pathway presents a promising therapeutic approach for multiple myeloma. A cell-based chemical assay revealed that ortho-topolin riboside (oTR), a cytokinin naturally produced by Populus robusta, effectively suppressed the activation of β-catenin response transcription induced by Wnt3aconditioned medium. The mechanism underlying this suppression involved oTR-triggered phosphorylation of β-catenin at Ser33, Ser37, and Thr41, leading to its proteasomal degradation and a reduction in intracellular β-catenin levels. Furthermore, oTR consistently decreased β-catenin levels and inhibited the expression of Axin2, cyclin D1, and c-Myc-genes regulated by β-catenin/T cell factor signaling in multiple myeloma cells. Additionally, oTR inhibited the proliferation of multiple myeloma cells and promoted apoptosis, as evidenced by an increase in Annexin V-FITC-positive cells and elevated caspase-3/7 activity. These findings suggest that oTR exerts its antiproliferative effects by attenuating the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, indicating its potential as a therapeutic agent for preventing and treating multiple myeloma.
items.authors: Kim M, Kang W, Oh S.

items.title: Molecular Basis of Silicon-Mediated Plant Defense: Transporters, Cell Wall Integrity, Redox-Hormone Crosstalk, and Epigenetic Priming.
items.abstract: Silicon (Si) is emerging as a key modulator, and its molecular mechanism of defense regulation keeps emerging. This review focus on Si-uptake by Lsi-type transporters, deposition in cuticles and cell wall, redox buffering, modify cell wall integrity (CWI) and hormonal signaling to increase resistance against adverse conditions and to reshape plant-microbe-soil interaction in rhizosphere. By highlighting the emerging research on Si-mediated regulations at molecular scale, we proposed two working hypotheses which are 'mechanical buffer model' for soluble-Si and 'dynamic signaling model' for Si-nanomaterials (Si-NPs). Mechanical buffer model states that Si-fortified walls could stabilize the ROS profile and wall mechanics to maintain and primed state for cell while dynamic signaling model states that Si-NPs follow an additional vesicle-mediated uptake forming a corona protein, elicit ROS-bursts, robust activation of FERONIA-like receptors, Ca2+ channels, and JA/SA signaling. Furthermore, association of Si-associated chromatin and siRNAs were summarized and how these Si-mediated alterations in DNA methylation under stress conditions could support the stress memory and defense priming. Overall, this framework could provide a molecular basis for Si-mediated inputs and breeding approaches with the aim of climate-resilient crops.
items.authors: Li JJ, Shabbir R, Huang JH, Sheng YJ, Dang H, Javed T, Chen B, Gao SJ.

items.title: A phosphorylation-gated GAPDH-MAPK6-LBD1 module controls drought-responsive transcription.
items.abstract: Drought adaptation requires rapid spatial reorganization of signaling proteins to reprogram stress-responsive transcription, yet how phosphorylation coordinates this process remains unclear. Here we aimed to define how phosphorylation-gated protein relocalization regulates a BpLBD1-centered drought pathway in Betula platyphylla (birch). Drought activated two kinase branches: BpAGC phosphorylated BpMAPK6 at Ser318 within a cryptic nuclear localization signal, promoting importin α recognition, whereas BpCKII phosphorylated BpGAPDH at Thr109, Thr270, Ser279 and Thr298, promoting importin β recognition. Dual phosphorylation enabled coordinated nuclear accumulation of BpMAPK6 and BpGAPDH. In the nucleus, phosphorylated BpGAPDH acted as a scaffold-like adaptor coupling BpMAPK6 to BpLBD1, enabling BpMAPK6-mediated phosphorylation of BpLBD1 at Ser29. This weakened BpLBD1 binding to the BpMYB123 promoter, reduced expression of the drought-sensitivity regulator BpMYB123, and de-repressed drought-responsive genes such as BpRD29B. Disrupting BpGAPDH or BpLBD1 Ser29 phosphorylation compromised drought tolerance. Thus, a phospho-spatial GAPDH-MAPK6-LBD1 switch couples nuclear protein assembly to drought-responsive transcription.
items.authors: He Z, Wang Z, Gao C, Ji X, Wang Y.

items.title: The ROS wave as a central catalyst of systemic acclimation and stress tolerance in plants.
items.abstract: Plants survive in environments where stress conditions fluctuate rapidly and unpredictably and their survival depends on their ability to transform local stress perception into coordinated whole-plant acclimation. Among the systemic signaling mechanisms studied to date, the 'reactive oxygen species (ROS) wave' has appeared as a fundamental process linking local stress perception to whole-plant acclimation. Initially defined as a self-propagating burst of ROS mediated by the plasma membrane enzyme RESPIRATORY BURST OXIDASE HOMOLOG D, the ROS wave is now recognized as one component of a highly integrated signaling network that dynamically interacts with calcium, electrical, hydraulic, redox, hormonal and other signaling molecules (i.e., gasotransmitters). Recent work has reshaped this view by revealing how different systemic signaling components interact with the ROS wave to mount stress-specific systemic responses and coordinate systemic acquired acclimation. Furthermore, ROS-dependent signals were found to propagate between neighboring plants, contributing to stress resilience at the community level. Here, we discuss recent advances that transformed our understanding of the ROS wave from an isolated signaling mechanism to a central regulator within an interconnected systemic signaling network.
items.authors: Mittler R, Mohanty D, Fichman Y, Zandalinas SI, Lorenzo O, Peláez-Vico MÁ.

items.title: The Ash Dieback Pathogen Resists the Chemical Defences of Its Host Tree, European Ash, by Depleting Them From the Growth Medium.
items.abstract: Plant pathogenic fungi are major drivers of disease in forest trees, often causing substantial ecological and economic damage. Ash dieback, caused by the ascomycete Hymenoscyphus fraxineus, has resulted in the widespread decline of Fraxinus excelsior populations throughout Europe. As infection is initiated in leaves containing diverse plant defensive metabolites, the ability of H. fraxineus to cope with host chemistry may determine successful host colonisation. We therefore investigated the responses of H. fraxineus to crude ash leaf extracts and individual defensive compounds. In contrast to the non-ash associated fungi tested, H. fraxineus was not inhibited by crude methanolic leaf extracts or most plant defence compounds tested. In addition, H. fraxineus depleted ash compounds extensively from the growth medium. Consistent with these findings, untargeted metabolomics revealed extensive alterations of the ash leaf-based medium by H. fraxineus, with 48% of detected chemical features being significantly reduced following fungal growth. Moreover, the growth of H. fraxineus was promoted by nearly all tested ash metabolites in minimal medium, indicating that these compounds can support fungal growth and may serve as carbon sources. Together, these results suggest that successful colonisation of ash tissues by H. fraxineus depends on its resistance to host defences, facilitated by its ability to deplete defensive compounds from colonised tissue.
items.authors: Lichnock B, Gentsch N, Papadopulos A, Rauch N, Reichelt M, Langer G, Jochner-Oette S, Gershenzon J, Lehenberger M.

items.title: Development of Approaches and Identifying Limitations toward Functional Yeast Surface Display of FLS2.
items.abstract: Pattern recognition receptors such as FLAGELLIN SENSING 2 (FLS2) are central to plant immunity and attractive targets for engineering broader detection of bacterial phytopathogens for application in pest management (and diagnostics) in food crops and sustainable agriculture practices. However, evaluating numerous FLS2 variants for altered pathogen sensing specificity directly in plants is slow and has low throughput and has been seldom optimized for heterologous display systems. Here, we established conditions that enabled Arabidopsis thaliana FLS2 ectodomain expression on the surface of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and evaluated binding to its cognate ligand, flg22. We show how yeast high-mannose glycosylation of the FLS2 ectodomain contributes to inefficient folding and loss of detectable flg22 binding in standard yeast surface display conditions. Substitutions at all N-glycosylation motifs compromised surface expression, indicating that some glycosylation is required for trafficking. We tuned the extent of glycosylation using tunicamycin, an N-linked glycosylation inhibitor, in combination with thermal stress to modulate ER quality control. Under these conditions, we observed a reproducible subpopulation of cells with improved flg22 binding despite reduced overall expression, and we confirmed flg22 selectivity against non-FLS2 proteins using both flow cytometry and magnetic bead-based enrichment. Guided by structural modeling of high-mannose glycans on the FLS2 ectodomain, we then substituted asparagines at selected N-glycan sites with serine. We identified a key glycan-site variant, N388S, which lies proximal to the flg22 binding interface and increased the binding population size under stress conditions. Binding assays against FLS2 variants and a reported non-binding variant affirmed that FLS2 selectivity was specific to FLS2 display, showing that all variants maintained a low affinity interaction with flg22. Together, these results point to FLS2 display conditions, not only glycosylation state, as an underlying limitation to detect true flg22 interactions, which will require more sensitive approaches to confidently resolve true binding populations.
items.authors: Dolgikh B, Schulte S, Woldring DR.

items.title: A Mechanochemical Model of Plant Cell Expansion Regulation: Beyond the Acid Growth Hypothesis
items.abstract: The acid growth hypothesis explains the role of apoplastic acidification in auxin-induced plant cell expansion; however, it does not, on its own, explain the conditions under which this process develops into sustained, irreversible growth. Apoplastic acidification, cell-wall loosening, and the presence of turgor pressure do not invariably result in the same growth response. This indicates that cell expansion should be understood as an outcome of interactions among hormonal regulation, cell-wall mechanical properties, water availability, and metabolic status. Here, we propose an integrative mechanistic model of plant cell expansion regulation in which the transition to a growth-permissive functional state is a central component. Within this framework, apoplastic pH is not considered a sufficient determinant of growth in itself, but rather a regulatory factor that influences the capacity of the cell wall to undergo mechanical deformation. The realization of growth depends on the coordination of this process with turgor pressure, water transport, metabolic capacity, and mechanosensory feedback mechanisms. This approach integrates the regulation of plasma membrane H⁺-ATPases, cell-wall remodelling, the TOR–SnRK1 signalling axis, and Ca²⁺- and reactive oxygen species-mediated pathways into a unified conceptual framework. The model describes cell expansion as a sequence of transitions among restricted, growth-permissive, actively expanding, and reinforcing states. Rather than rejecting the acid growth hypothesis, it extends its explanatory scope by linking local changes in apoplastic pH and cell-wall mechanics to the regulation of water relations, metabolism, and sustained growth. The proposed framework provides a basis for experimental investigation of the mechanisms through which plant cells convert regulatory signals into irreversible expansion.
items.authors: Khablak SH, Bondareva LM, Kolomiiets YV, Spychak VM, Abdullaieva YA.

items.title: Edge-deployable greenhouse tomato cluster harvesting robot integrating YOLOv8n-BiFPN-WIoU and ROS-based autonomous control.
items.abstract: ObjectiveTo develop an edge-deployable greenhouse tomato cluster harvesting robot capable of accurate fruit detection, three-dimensional localization, autonomous navigation, and robotic harvesting under complex greenhouse conditions. The objective was to improve detection performance under fruit occlusion and variable illumination while maintaining real-time inference and stable robotic operation on embedded computing hardware.MethodsA lightweight YOLOv8n-based tomato detection model, termed YOLOv8n-BiFPN-WIoU, was developed by incorporating a bidirectional feature pyramid network and Wise-IoU loss to improve multiscale feature fusion and localization accuracy. An RGB-D vision system based on the Intel RealSense D435 was used for three-dimensional fruit localization. The robotic system integrated a rail-guided mobile platform, a six-axis manipulator, a dual-claw harvesting end-effector, and a ROS-based distributed control architecture. The vision model was optimized and deployed on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano using ONNX and TensorRT. Robot kinematics, hand-eye transformation, trajectory planning, and autonomous harvesting procedures were integrated to enable station-to-station operation and fruit harvesting.ResultsThe proposed YOLOv8n-BiFPN-WIoU model achieved a precision of 88.534%, recall of 89.377%, F1-score of 88.954%, mAP@0.5 of 92.338%, and mAP@0.5:0.95 of 71.368%. Compared with the baseline YOLOv8n model, these metrics improved by 2.143, 2.779, 2.460, 4.587, and 5.675 percentage points, respectively. The proposed model increased the parameter count from 3.2 million to 3.6 million and computational complexity from 19.6 to 22.4 GFLOPs. After ONNX and TensorRT optimization, the model achieved an inference speed of 21.1 frames per second at an input resolution of 640 × 640 with batch size 1 on the Jetson Nano. The robotic system achieved a mean positioning error of 3.70 ± 0.32 mm across five representative targets, demonstrating the feasibility of accurate visual localization and robotic positioning for greenhouse tomato harvesting.ConclusionThe proposed edge-deployable greenhouse tomato cluster harvesting robot integrates lightweight deep learning, RGB-D three-dimensional localization, ROS-based autonomous control, rail-guided mobile operation, and robotic harvesting into a unified system. The YOLOv8n-BiFPN-WIoU model improved tomato detection performance while maintaining real-time inference on embedded hardware, and the integrated vision and manipulation system demonstrated accurate positioning suitable for autonomous harvesting. The results indicate that the proposed architecture provides a practical foundation for intelligent greenhouse tomato harvesting under complex visual and operational conditions.
items.authors: Meng F, Wang Z, Wang H, Li X, Xu X, Zeng N, Wang G, Wei D, Li X, Shi Y.

items.title: Integrating cortical microtubules into plant gravity signaling: dynamics, tubulin phosphorylation, and growth regulation.
items.abstract: Plant gravity responses depend on coordinated signaling and growth-control mechanisms that convert directional and mechanical stimuli into differential cell expansion. Cortical microtubules are central to the conversion: they pattern cellulose synthase trajectories, set cell-wall anisotropy, and are remodeled in altered-gravity and tubulin-mutant systems. Yet the cytoskeletal regulatory pathway remains only loosely connected to the canonical, auxin-centered picture of how plants perceive and respond to gravity. Physiological, genetic, and phosphoproteomic evidence linking microtubules to gravitropism and gravity resistance, obtained under gravistimulation by reorientation at 1 g, hypergravity, and real or simulated microgravity, is organized into an explicit, layered framework. Three regulatory layers are proposed to act on cortical microtubule organization on distinct time scales: a slow transcriptional layer that adjusts the tubulin and regulator pool, an intermediate regulator-mediated layer of nucleation and severing, and a fast post-translational layer that modifies tubulin directly. Within the framework, phosphorylation of α-tubulin at threonine 349 (Thr349) by PROPYZAMIDE-HYPERSENSITIVE 1 (PHS1) is the best-characterized candidate for a molecular link between stress signaling and control of microtubule polymerization. Whole-seedling spaceflight phosphoproteomic data show reduced Thr349 phosphorylation across four α-tubulin isoforms (TUA1, TUA3, TUA4, and TUA6) and highlight Thr349 phosphorylation as a candidate post-translational regulator of cortical microtubule responses under spaceflight conditions. Future studies should test whether PHS1 controls Thr349 phosphorylation during gravity responses and identify the activating signal and opposing phosphatase. Resolving links with γ-tubulin-dependent nucleation, katanin-mediated severing, auxin transport, and cell-wall remodeling will explain how cortical microtubules shape gravity-directed growth.
items.authors: Islam MS, Wyatt SE.

items.title: Colonization, growth-promoting effect, control efficacy against tobacco black shank, and mechanism of action of the tobacco endophyte Microbacterium foliorum 5SY32.
items.abstract: Tobacco black shank (TBS) severely restricts sustainable tobacco cultivation. Endophytic bacteria serve as promising biocontrol agents due to strong host colonization ability. Microbacterium foliorum 5SY32, isolated from healthy tobacco, inhibits Phytophthora nicotianae growth by over 60% and synthesizes 15.13 μg/mL indole-3-acetic acid. This study assessed its colonization, growth-promoting capability and disease suppression efficacy via greenhouse and field trials, and explored functional mechanisms through transcriptome sequencing. Re-isolation and molecular verification proved that strain 5SY32 stably colonizes tobacco roots, stems, and leaves, with the highest population detected in roots. The strain significantly optimized root morphology and physiological activity, and improved aboveground agronomic traits, leaf chlorophyll and nitrogen content. Field yield was elevated by more than 20%. It achieved 58.58% protective and 30.31% curative efficacy in the greenhouse, and sustained 48.99%-52.31% control efficacy in the field against TBS. 5SY32 boosted antioxidant and defense enzyme activities, and activated key genes related to jasmonic acid, ethylene and abscisic acid pathways. A total of 12,485 differentially expressed genes participating in cell wall formation, oxidative response and secondary metabolism were modulated, ultimately inducing systemic resistance in tobacco. This study first clarifies the integrated mechanism of colonization, growth promotion and disease resistance induction mediated by M. foliorum 5SY32, offering a valuable microbial resource for green management of TBS.
items.authors: Zheng W, Du H, Wu D, Xu J, Kang Y.

items.title: Culturomics and amplicon-based insights into the endophytic microbiome of Kalmegh (Andrographis paniculata (Burm.f.) Nees) and its implications in plant growth promotion.
items.abstract: Leaf and stem endophytic microorganisms play an important role in plant physiology and secondary metabolite biosynthesis of plants, particularly in medicinal plants. Kalmegh (Andrographis paniculata (Burm.f.) Nees) is an important medicinal plant with liver-protective, anti-inflammatory, ovicidal, larvicidal, and anti-urolithatic properties. The medicinal activities are due to presence of andrographolides. This study investigated the culture-independent diversity of endophytic bacteria associated with Kalmegh at nursery, vegetative, and flowering stages using a metagenomic approach. The results revealed that Sphingomonas was the dominant bacterial genus during nursery and vegetative stages, whereas Halobacterium predominated during the flowering stage. Microbial abundance was highest in the nursery stage, followed by flowering and vegetative stages. Functional analysis showed that flowering stage endophytes were enriched with specialized carbon metabolism and aromatic compound degradation pathways, potentially influencing andrographolide biosynthesis. Chemical analysis supported these findings, showing the highest andrographolide content in leaves during flowering (3.1%). Gene expression analysis further demonstrated that increased andrographolide accumulation was associated with upregulation of methyl erythritol phosphate pathway (MEP) pathway and diterpene biosynthetic genes. Bacterial endophytes isolated from flowering-stage leaves exhibited plant growth-promotion, antifungal, and seed germination-enhancing activities. In vitro assays against Fusarium wilt and Rhizoctonia disease showed that Bacillus cereus strains KL11, KL12, and KL5 inhibited pathogen growth by 60-65%. Biopriming with strains KL3 and KL5 of Bacillus cereus improved seed germination and plant growth. Pot trials with Micrococcus luteus KES1 increased herbage yield, plant height, and andrographolide content by 43%. These findings highlight the potential of leaf and stem endophytes for sustainable improvement of Kalmegh productivity and andrographolide content in the plant.
items.authors: Bagul SY, Sarkar R, Suthar MK, Kumar V, S S, Rana VS, Sircar D, Reddy NRR.

items.title: Stimulation of growth in Piper betle L. via induced systemic resistance (ISR) under combined pathogenic stress through priming of Jasmonic acid.
items.abstract: Plant tolerance to biotic stress is significantly regulated by Jasmonic Acid (JA), which orchestrates induced systemic resistance (ISR) through synergistic signaling pathways. This study evaluates the efficacy of exogenous JA priming in conferring resistance to Piper betle L. against a broad spectrum of pathogens, including Xanthomonas campestris, Colletotrichum piperis, Fusarium semitectum, and Phytophthora parasitica. Experimental groups comprised a uninfected-untreated control (N), a pathogen-infected control (P), and a JA-primed infected group (T3). Our findings demonstrate that JA treatment significantly mitigates pathogenic damage by restoring morphological integrity, including leaf turgidity and stomatal architecture, which were severely compromised in the P group. Quantitatively, T3 plants exhibited superior physiological performance, with significantly higher relative water content (RWC), chlorophyll, and carotenoid levels compared to both N and P groups. Biochemical profiling revealed that JA priming suppressed oxidative stress markers, specifically reducing electrolyte leakage, H2O2 accumulation, and malondialdehyde (MDA) content to near-basal levels. Simultaneously, JA significantly enhanced the antioxidant defense system, as evidenced by elevated levels of proline, glutathione, ascorbic acid, and total protein. Transcriptome analysis further elucidated the molecular basis of this resistance, revealing a robust upregulation of ISR-related, growth-regulating, and metabolic genes in T3 leaves. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) confirmed a strong positive correlation between ISR traits and biomass accumulation. Furthermore, GO and KEGG enrichment analyses highlighted the optimization of defense-priming pathways and the strategic downregulation of redundant metabolic genes in JA-primed plants validated by metabolic profiling using GCMS analysis. Collectively, these results establish JA priming as a potent strategy for enhancing broad-spectrum immunity and growth vigor in P. betle.
items.authors: Chaurasia SK, Acharya C, Pandey JK.
items.journal: Physiology and molecular biology of plants : an international journal of functional plant biology

items.title: Integrative GWAS and Transcriptome Analysis Reveal Genetic Architecture and Candidate Genes for Drought Tolerance During Soybean Germination.
items.abstract: Drought stress severely limits soybean production, and understanding the genetic basis of drought tolerance at the germination stage is important for breeding tolerant varieties. In this study, a panel of 270 soybean accessions was used for phenotypic evaluation and a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of five drought tolerance indices under control and PEG-simulated drought conditions. Using single-locus and multi-locus GWAS models, we detected 109, 115, 121, 86, and 46 significant SNPs, and 14, 7, 9, 10, and 3 QTNs for the five indices, respectively. Combining the results from both models, 97 important QTNs consisting of those controlling multiple traits under the single-locus model and those detected by both models were identified. These QTNs were distributed across 14 genomic intervals, with qDT-4-2 and qDT-9-1 which were associated with all five indices, being the key loci. Transcriptome analysis revealed 2109 genes that were commonly differentially expressed in three tolerant accessions under PEG treatment compared with control conditions. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses showed significant enrichment of pathways related to cell wall metabolism, osmotic adjustment, and antioxidant defense, including amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism, starch and sucrose metabolism, galactose metabolism, and ascorbate and aldarate metabolism. Integration of GWAS and transcriptome data predicted 12 candidate genes within these loci, which may function in drought stress responses through regulating cell wall-modifying enzyme activity, accumulating osmoprotectants, and scavenging reactive oxygen species. Our findings provide useful information for understanding the genetic regulatory network of drought tolerance during soybean germination and offer candidate gene resources for marker-assisted breeding and functional gene discovery.
items.authors: Xia Z, Du S, Zong J, Zhang M, Zhang Q, Song F, Yuan F, Li G, Li S, Cao Y.

items.title: Proline transporters coordinate immune activation and regenerative capacity after injury in plants.
items.abstract: Effective survival after injury requires the precise coordination of immune activation and tissue regeneration, yet the molecular mechanisms balancing these opposing processes remain poorly understood. Here, we identify proline transporters as key regulators of this trade-off in plants. Genetic disruption of two wound-induced proline transporters, ProT2 and ProT3, enhances regenerative capacity and abolishes salicylic acid (SA)-mediated suppression of regeneration while preserving SA-responsive gene expression and SA-mediated antibacterial resistance. Mechanistically, a ProT3-CPK1 complex modulates wound-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS), sustaining a ROS level that restricts de novo root regeneration (DNRR) after wounding. Notably, pharmacological inhibition of proline transport functionally separates immune activation from regenerative suppression and promotes regeneration across multiple plant species. These findings support the role of proline transporters as a regulatory hub integrating stress-induced proline metabolism, SA signaling, and ROS homeostasis to coordinate immunity and regeneration, and highlight chemical inhibition of proline transport as a strategy to improve regeneration without compromising immune defense.
items.authors: Xu D, Belew ZM, Ferreira Dias NC, Wang L, Zhang A, Stephanie Chen YF, Newton CJ, Kong F, Zheng Y, Yao Y, Brewer MT, Pereira Lima Teixeira PJ, Nour Eldin Auis HH, Xu D, Yang L.

items.title: Omics-based characterization of physiological and transcriptomic resilience during cold de-acclimation and re-acclimation in GSK-like kinase mutants.
items.abstract: BackgroundCold acclimation, de-acclimation, and re-acclimation are critical adaptive phases that determine plant survival under fluctuating temperatures. Although the physiological and molecular basis of initial cold acclimation is well studied, the regulatory mechanisms governing the loss and re-acquisition of freezing tolerance remain poorly understood. Brassinosteroid (BR) signalling, mediated by glycogen synthase kinase-like (GSK-like) kinases, modulates both stress tolerance and plant growth; however, its role under fluctuating cold-related temperature conditions has not been explored in detail. This study investigated the physiological and transcriptomic responses of Arabidopsis thaliana wild-type (Col-4) and two BR-signalling mutants carrying T-DNA insertions in GSK-like kinase genes BIL1, (At2g30980); GSK3 (At1g06390) across cold acclimation, de-acclimation and re-acclimation phases.ResultsAll genotypes exhibited reduced leaf water content (~ 55%) and suppressed photosystem II efficiency during cold acclimation, with partial recovery during de-acclimation and re-acclimation. Notably, the genotypes showed divergent roles in re-acclimation responses: Col-4 showed the greatest freezing tolerance (LT₅₀ = -20 °C), whereas BIL1 and GSK3 mutants showed more moderate re-hardening (~-15 °C and - 13 °C, respectively). In contrast, both mutants showed higher post-freeze canopy regrowth (headroom recovery ~ 80%) compared with Col-4 (~ 20%) during de-acclimation, revealing a trade-off between maximal freezing tolerance and vegetative recovery. Chlorophyll fluorescence analysis showed that GSK3 achieved the strongest photosynthetic recovery, while BIL1 displayed persistently impaired electron transport efficiency. Transcriptomic profiling revealed a genotype-specific reprogramming switch: during de-acclimation, GSK3 produced the largest transcriptional response (1,433 differentially expressed genes), whereas during re-acclimation this pattern reversed, with BIL1 exhibiting the most extensive but poorly coordinated reprogramming (1,876 differentially expressed genes). The co-expression network analysis revealed a dense, highly connected re-acclimation module in GSK3, contrasting with a fragmented network architecture in BIL1, which indicates qualitatively different transcriptional coordination capacities between the two mutants.ConclusionsOur findings suggest that GSK-like kinase signalling may contribute to cold resilience, potentially influencing the balance between freezing tolerance, photosynthetic recovery, and transcriptional coordination under fluctuating cold temperature conditions. The BIL1 mutant enhances post-freeze regrowth but compromises re-hardening and coherent transcriptional reprogramming, whereas GSK3 supports stronger photosynthetic and transcriptomic recovery. These findings identify GSK-like kinases as candidate regulators that warrant further functional validation as potential targets for engineering cold resilience in crops exposed to increasingly variable thermal environments.
items.authors: Ahmar S, Rapacz M, Mahmood T, Sadura-Berg I, Maksymowicz A, Pociecha E.

items.title: Apoplast-Confined Nanozyme Catalysis for Selective 1O2 Generation and Host Defense in Plants.
items.abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS)-based antimicrobial strategies in plants are often constrained by limited oxidant selectivity and collateral phytotoxicity. Here, we report an apoplast-confined nanozyme that integrates selective singlet oxygen (1O2) catalysis with host defense activation. The copper-iron Prussian blue analogue nanozyme CuFePBA exhibits oxidase-like activity under physiologically relevant conditions, converting molecular oxygen into 1O2 without detectable generation of superoxide or hydroxyl radicals. Following foliar application, CuFePBA is retained within the apoplast because of exclusion from the symplast by the plant cell wall. In this extracellular compartment, localized 1O2 production damages bacterial membranes, suppresses respiration, and eliminates apoplastic pathogens while minimizing intracellular oxidative stress. The resulting apoplastic redox perturbation also elicits a transient intracellular ROS burst, promotes cell wall reinforcement, activates pattern-triggered immunity, and induces sustained expression of defense-related genes. Through this catalytic-immunological coupling, CuFePBA enhances disease resistance in planta without detectable phytotoxicity. These findings establish spatially confined nanozyme catalysis as an effective strategy for combining antimicrobial activity with host-compatible immune activation and highlight microenvironmental confinement as a general design principle for biologically compatible nanomaterials in plant protection.
items.authors: Yan Y, Huang R, Kang S, Jiang X, Wang F, Ma Z, Zheng X, Gao X, Miao M, Chen K, Wu YE, Wang F.

items.title: RXLR effectors of Phytophthora infestans: delivery, host targets and immune suppression.
items.abstract: Phytophthora infestans, the pathogen responsible for the devastating potato disease known as late blight, poses a significant threat to plant health. A major determinant of its pathogenic success is the deployment of cytoplasmic effector proteins, particularly the RXLR class of effectors, which accumulate within the host cells and manipulate plant immune responses. These effectors function as key virulence factors that interfere with multiple layers of plant defense, including pattern-triggered immunity (PTI) and effector-triggered immunity (ETI). Recent studies have revealed that RXLR effectors target diverse host cellular processes such as transcriptional regulation, post-translational modifications, vesicle trafficking, autophagy, chloroplast-mediated immune signalling, and protein stability. By converging on these critical immune hubs, RXLR effectors reprogram host cellular networks to promote pathogen colonization and disease progression. Advances in genomics, structural biology, and host-interactor screening have significantly expanded our understanding of RXLR effector diversity, their molecular mechanisms, and their interactions with host susceptibility factors. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge on the functional roles of RXLR effectors of P. infestans, highlighting their subcellular localization, host targets, and mechanisms of immune suppression. We also discuss emerging concepts in effector biology and their implications for developing durable resistance strategies against late blight disease.
items.authors: Saini O, Arora A, Kaur A, Saini S.

items.title: Transcriptome and metabolome analyses reveal the molecular mechanisms of Rhododendron pulchrum under cadmium stress.
items.abstract: Soil contamination by cadmium (Cd) poses a persistent threat to plant growth and ecosystem health. To clarify the physiological and molecular basis of Cd tolerance in Rhododendron pulchrum, a woody ornamental species, seedlings were grown for 30 d in soil amended with five Cd levels (nominal 0, 10, 50, 100 and 200 mg·kg⁻¹; measured 0.33, 6.07, 20.27, 64.52 and 126.54 mg·kg⁻¹), and growth, physiological traits, and the leaf transcriptome and metabolome were analyzed. Low Cd did not inhibit growth and was accompanied by increased ground diameter and total biomass, whereas high Cd reduced growth, lowered pigment contents, and increased lipid peroxidation. Cd was retained predominantly in roots. Tissue concentrations followed the order root > stem > leaf, the translocation factor remained below 0.38 in all treatments, and 50.60-71.71% of the Cd accumulated by the plant remained in the roots. Omics analyses showed that Cd-responsive genes and metabolites were enriched in the phenylpropanoid and flavonoid biosynthesis pathways; key genes of these pathways (CCR, CAD, POD and DFR) were upregulated in leaves, together with the accumulation of flavonols and flavan-3-ols, indicating activation of antioxidant metabolism and ROS scavenging in leaf tissues. These results show that R. pulchrum combines high Cd tolerance with root-dominated Cd retention, supporting its use for the phytostabilization of soils with low to moderate Cd contamination.
items.authors: Zhao X, Sun J, Han J, Zhang Y, Fei R, Duan S, Zhang M, Liu L.

items.title: Calcium restricts cadmium accumulation in rice by competing for iron plaque adsorption sites.
items.abstract: Calcium (Ca) amendments are widely used to restrict cadmium (Cd) accumulation in rice; however, the mechanisms governing competitive adsorption between Ca and Cd in iron plaque (IP) of rice roots remain poorly understood. Here, hydroponic and adsorption experiments using detached roots and goethite (Gt), a simulant for IP, were conducted to investigate these interactions. Results showed that exogenous Ca did not affect IP formation but decreased Cd concentrations in IP, roots, and shoots by 21%-28%, 11%-25%, and 17%-27%, respectively. Detached-root adsorption experiments showed that Ca reduced Cd adsorption in IP by 70% when the Ca: Cd ratio reached 20, with root Cd uptake declining by 50% compared with the Ca-free treatment. Gt experiments introduced competitive mechanisms through a dual-pathway model. First, Ca adsorption shifted the point of zero charge of Gt towards higher pH, weakening electrostatic attraction for Cd. Second, spectroscopic evidence supported that Ca bound to surface hydroxyl groups (Fe-OH) through ligand exchange to form inner-sphere complexes (Fe-O-Ca), competitively occupying surface binding sites. This study not only revealed molecular-scale mechanisms of Ca/Cd competition in roots IP, but also provided new insight into quantitatively estimating Ca detoxification when optimizing Ca compound strategies in Cd-contaminated paddy soils beyond pH effects.
items.authors: Feng X, Pang Z, Huang X, Liang Y, Guo B.

items.title: Arabidopsis NLR Immune Receptors: Structural Diversification, Signaling Networks, and Emerging Principles of Immune Activation.
items.abstract: Plant intracellular nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors (NLRs) are central to effector-triggered immunity (ETI), but the rapid expansion of structural data has outpaced an integrated explanation of how receptor architecture, oligomerization, and network context determine immune output. Recent structural and biochemical studies, particularly in Arabidopsis, have revealed that NLRs operate as dynamic signaling assemblies rather than simple pathogen-recognition switches. Here, we synthesize recent evidence across coiled-coil NLRs (CNLs), Toll/interleukin-1 receptor NLRs (TNLs), and RPW8-like helper NLRs (RNLs), with emphasis on mechanisms that are broadly conserved and those that remain receptor- or pathway-specific. ZAR1 (HopZ-Activated Resistance1) and selected helper RNLs form membrane-associated Ca2+-permeable channels, whereas TNLs use Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR)-domain enzymatic activity to generate signaling molecules that are decoded through branch-specific modules formed by ENHANCED DISEASE SUSCEPTIBILITY1 (EDS1)-PHYTOALEXIN DEFICIENT4 (PAD4)-ACTIVATED DISEASE RESISTANCE1 (ADR1) or EDS1-SENESCENCE-ASSOCIATED GENE101 (SAG101)-N REQUIREMENT GENE1 (NRG1). Paired NLRs partition recognition and signaling, while recent work on ADR1-L1 indicates that higher-order spatial organization can further tune immune execution. We also distinguish structurally resolved complexes from inferred higher-order assemblies, examine crosstalk with cell-surface immunity and transcriptional regulation, and assess NLR-engineering strategies according to their experimental validation and potential fitness costs. Together, the evidence supports a modular view in which oligomerization is a recurrent activation principle, but biochemical output, partner dependence, and membrane execution are not interchangeable across NLR classes.
items.authors: Huang J.

items.title: Enhanced auxin and cytokinin signalling gene expression associated with improved organogenesis in platinum nanoparticle-treated Cicer arietinum L.
items.abstract: Platinum nanoparticles (PtNPs) were evaluated for their role in enhancing in vitro regeneration and phytohormone-related gene expression for the first time in Cicer arietinum. PtNPs were synthesised using pectin and characterised by various analytical techniques. Multiple shoot cultures were achieved from half-seed explants cultured on MS medium with 1 mg L-1 zeatin (ZT). Various concentrations of PtNPs (15-60 µg L-1) with 1 mg L-1 ZT were tested to evaluate their effect on C. arietinum shoot multiplication. The maximum regenerative response (96.66 ± 0.57%), shoot proliferation (20.23 ± 0.11), and shoot length (5.42 ± 1.12) were observed from cultures maintained on MS medium with 30 µg L-1 PtNPs. After shoot regeneration, rooting was induced using 1.5 mg L-1 Indole-3-butyric acid (IBA). The highest rooting response (95.00 ± 0.57%), root count (16.53 ± 0.11), and root length (6.14 ± 0.02) were recorded on MS medium amended with 1.5 mg L-1 IBA and 30 µg L-1 PtNPs. Real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) analysis revealed increased expression of cytokinin-related genes, namely LONELY GUY-Like10 (LOGL10;7.32-fold) and LONELY GUY-Like1 (LOGL1; 3.70-fold), along with auxin-related genes, AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR18 (ARF18; 2.37-fold) and SMALL AUXIN-UP RNA32 (SAUR32; 2.58-fold), following treatment with 30 µg L-1 PtNPs. Genetic stability of the regenerated C. arietinum plantlets, assessed using RAPD and ISSR markers, revealed no detectable polymorphism. These findings suggest that biosynthesised PtNPs can enhance regeneration efficiency and are associated with changes in the expression of selected cytokinin and auxin-related genes in C. arietinum, highlighting their promising application in plant tissue culture.
items.authors: Megha D, Rajalakshmi S, Vignesh S, Manickavasagam M.
items.journal: Physiology and molecular biology of plants : an international journal of functional plant biology

items.title: Nuclear NPR1 Modulates Salicylic Acid/Jasmonic Acid Crosstalk via Transcriptional Control of WRKY Transcription Factors
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The plant hormones salicylic acid (SA) and jasmonic acid (JA) are major regulators of plant defense. They can antagonize each other’s activity, enabling an optimized defense response. The SA master regulator NPR1 is a key player in this SA/JA crosstalk, although the mechanisms of NPR1-mediated SA/JA crosstalk remain only partly understood, especially regarding the ethylene-coregulated ERF branch of the JA pathway. Here, we investigated the function of NPR1 in SA/JA crosstalk using several Arabidopsis npr1 mutant variants. Assays using the NPR1-HBD and npr1-nls lines, expressing only cytosolic NPR1, revealed that NPR1 has a nuclear role in SA/JA crosstalk. RNA-seq analysis of lines expressing NPR1 mutated in residues Cys 82 or Cys 216 , in which repression of the JA pathway was impaired while SA pathway induction remained mostly intact, identified 32 SA-responsive genes with reduced expression compared to Col-0, including four WRKY transcription factor genes. Of these, WRKY53 and WRKY70 could suppress expression of the JA marker gene PDF1.2 induced by ORA59, the master regulator of the ERF branch of the JA pathway, in a protoplast system. Additional SA-inducible WRKYs (WRKY50, WRKY54, WRKY63, and WRKY67) similarly suppressed ORA59-induced PDF1.2 expression, implicating WRKY63 and WRKY67 for the first time in SA/JA crosstalk and confirming earlier reports on the role of the other WRKY TFs. WRKY53 and WRKY67 were further shown to reduce accumulation of the ORA59 protein in protoplasts. Thus, our study indicated that NPR1 can regulate SA/JA crosstalk in the nucleus via transcriptional activation of genes encoding specific JA-repressing WRKY transcription factors. MAIN CONCLUSION NPR1 has a nuclear function in regulating salicylic acid/jasmonic acid crosstalk by activating specific WRKY transcription factors that suppress the jasmonic acid pathway, likely in part by reducing ORA59 accumulation.
items.authors: Aerts, N., Caarls, L., Visscher, T. W., Groutars, B., Kapteijn, R., van Verk, M., Pieterse, C. M. J., Van Wees, S. C. M.

items.title: CRK5 preserves antioxidant homeostasis and prevents cell death during dark-induced senescence through inhibiting the salicylic acid signaling pathway.
items.abstract: BackgroundDark-induced senescence (DIS) is a widely used model for dissecting the regulatory mechanisms that manage leaf aging, redox imbalance, and cell death (CD) in plants. Salicylic acid (SA) is a central hormonal regulator of these processes. However, the mechanism involving upstream components, which integrate SA-dependent pathways with antioxidant homeostasis during DIS, remains unresolved. CYSTEINE-RICH RECEPTOR-LIKE KINASE 5 (CRK5) is a membrane-localized protein that plays a role in developmental and stress-responsive pathways. Its promoter contains multiple W-box cis-elements, indicating regulation by WRKY factors in SA-mediated pathways. This study investigates how CRK5 modulates SA-dependent CD and antioxidant dynamics during DIS.ResultsIn this study, SA-accumulating mutant crk5 exhibited accelerated senescence, elevated electrolyte leakage, enhanced micro-lesion formation, and markedly increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation under both control and dark conditions. These phenotypes were accompanied by a substantial reduction in carotenoid and xanthophyll pools, enhanced accumulation of phenolic compounds, and increased free radical scavenging capacity, including ascorbate peroxidase, catalase, and superoxide dismutase activities. Importantly, crk5 phenotype was fully reverted in crk5sid2 and crk5NahG double mutants, confirming that crk5 DIS phenotype is induced by activation of the SA signaling pathway. Transcriptome profiling revealed extensive deregulation of senescence-, CD-, and redox-associated genes in crk5 during darkness, including strong induction of SAGs, metacaspases, autophagy, and antioxidant-related transcripts. The line with constitutively enhanced SA level (cpr1), used as a control, showed similar phenotypes to crk5, although transcriptional reprogramming was largely absent in cpr1 after darkness, highlighting CRK5 as a key upstream negative regulator of SA-mediated CD and positive regulator of antioxidant homeostasis.ConclusionOur work presents CRK5 as a central regulatory hub that inhibits the SA signaling, ROS burst, and CD activation during DIS. Loss of CRK5 function is associated with the activation of SA signaling, altered antioxidant systems, increased ROS burden, and ROS-driven CD acceleration, resulting in accelerated senescence. Conversely, suppression of SA-biosynthesis or catabolism in a crk5 background restores the wild-type phenotype. These findings position this receptor kinase as a key mediator that coordinates hormonal, metabolic, and oxidative pathways to maintain leaf viability, providing mechanistic insight into the control of stress-induced senescence and CD in Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana).
items.authors: Kamran M, Burdiak P, Rusaczonek A, Zarrin Ghalami R, Karpiński SM.

items.title: Calcium application coordinates seedling heat tolerance and yield-quality formation in ginger under summer high-temperature conditions.
items.abstract: Summer heat stress constrains ginger production. Although calcium (Ca) enhances stress tolerance in various crops, its effects on heat tolerance, yield, and quality in ginger remain unclear. A pot experiment was conducted using Zingiber officinale cv. 'Laiwu Big Ginger' to evaluate Ca effects on plant growth and quality under natural summer high-temperature conditions. Six Ca rates (0, 15.2, 30.5, 45.7, 60.9, and 76.2 mmol Ca2+ plant-1) were established using calcium nitrate tetrahydrate [Ca(NO3)2·4H2O]. Seedling-stage physiological and biochemical parameters were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models; harvest-stage growth, biomass, and quality parameters were analyzed with ANOVA or non-parametric tests. PCA, correlation analysis, and membership function analysis were used for multivariate evaluation. At Day 16, the 60.9 mmol Ca2+ plant-1 treatment significantly improved photosynthetic capacity (chlorophyll +23.3%, Pn +13.0%), antioxidant enzyme activities (SOD, POD, CAT), and proline content, while reducing oxidative damage (MDA, REC) and ROS (O2 ·-, H2O2). These adjustments promoted biomass and rhizome quality, with the highest rhizome fresh weight (727.7 vs. 447.3 g plant-1), dry matter (+3.6%), soluble sugars (+28.1%), soluble protein (+36.5%), free amino acids (+19.1%), and vitamin C (+17.5%). Multivariate analyses confirmed positive correlations among photosynthetic traits, antioxidant activity, biomass, and quality parameters, with the 60.9 mmolCa2+ plant-1 treatment ranking highest in comprehensive evaluation by membership function analysis. Calcium application at this optimal rate, as determined under our experimental conditions, was associated with enhanced heat tolerance and subsequent growth and quality formation. These findings provide practical insights for sustaining ginger productivity under heat stress within the scope of our experimental conditions.
items.authors: Wang X, Ni X, Liu X, Li Z, Guo H, Xue Q, Li C.

items.title: The interactome of the receptor kinase THESEUS1 reveals how cell wall integrity is linked to hormone signalling in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: The receptor kinase THESEUS1 (THE1) activates responses to impairment of cell wall integrity (CWI). However, the interaction partners enabling THE1 to mediate the responses remain underexplored, impeding a mechanistic understanding of THE1. We produced a set of THE1 GFP fusion constructs in which THE1 is either wild type, mutated in its kinase domain, has a loss of function mutation in its ectodomain, or lacks the kinase or extracellular domain. We used these constructs to perform localization studies and immunoprecipitation liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry under control and stress conditions (isoxaben induced cell wall damage and sorbitol induced hyperosmotic stress) to identify the THE1 interactome. The interactome of THE1 changed in a context dependent manner, linking THE1 to known signaling components in CWI maintenance and phytohormone response (such as proton pumps, calcium pumps, other receptor kinases or cellulose synthesis regulators). Moreover, we identified novel interactors, associating THE1 with hitherto unexplored signaling pathways in response to CWI impairment. Our results also suggest that the THE1G37D protein (corresponding to the the1 1 allele) is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum, explaining its loss of function phenotype. The THE1 interactome and localization data provide the foundation to build a mechanistic understanding of THE1 mediated CWI maintenance.
items.authors: Zwartkruis, S. T. W., Haeger, W., Ticha, T., Braun, N., Bartosova, Z., Sharma, A., Zeiner, A., Madej, G., Klein, v., Amanda, D., Alonso Baez, L., Barbez, E., Wrzaczek, M., Hagen, L., Hamann, T.

items.title: Multimodal Plant-Animal Communication: Signaling Mechanisms, Coevolution, and Environmental Disruption.
items.abstract: Plant-animal communication involves diverse forms of information transfer that can mediate ecologically important interactions, including pollination, seed dispersal, herbivory, and plant defense. This review synthesizes current knowledge of the chemical, visual, gustatory, electrical, acoustic, and vibrational information involved in these interactions, with particular emphasis on volatile organic compounds, herbivore-derived elicitors and effectors, multimodal signaling, sensory perception, learning, and evolutionary processes, including coevolution where reciprocal evidence is available.
