A central distinction is made between detectable traits or cues and functional biological signals, emphasizing the need for evidence linking signal production or modification to receiver detection, behavioral or physiological responses, and ecologically meaningful outcomes. Acoustic and vibrational phenomena are considered critically because their communicative significance remains less firmly established than that of chemical and visual signaling. The review further examines how climate change and other anthropogenic pressures may alter signal production, transmission, perception, and phenological synchrony, thereby reorganizing plant-animal interactions. Genetic manipulation of hormonal, volatile, and specialized-metabolite pathways is also evaluated as a potential tool for modifying plant signaling, together with its possible unintended ecological consequences. By integrating plant physiology, sensory ecology, animal behavior, evolution, and environmental change, this review identifies major evidence gaps and highlights the importance of plant-animal communication for biodiversity conservation, pollination, biological control, and sustainable agriculture.
items.authors: Jasim HA, Khudair MY, Jasim SA, Abdulateef SM.

items.title: Pseudomonas avellanae: From Specific Pathogens to a Species Complex.
items.abstract: TaxonomyBacteria; Proteobacteria, gamma subdivision; Order Pseudomonadales; Family Pseudomonadaceae; Genus Pseudomonas; Pseudomonas avellanae species complex, which includes different pathogenic lineages previously classified within the P. syringae complex, namely the pathovars avellanae, theae, actinidiae, and morsprunorum race 2.Microbiological propertiesAs a whole, the P. avellanae species complex genome comprises 19.4% conserved genes and 80.6% flexible genome. Mobile genetic elements are present within the complex. Strains associated with bacterial canker of European hazelnut possess two plasmids, whereas multiple plasmids and megaplasmids can occur in the lineages associated with bacterial canker of kiwifruit and cherry. Fourteen type III secretion system effectors are shared by all lineages of the species, and each lineage apparently possesses specific effector proteins. Phytotoxins, such as phaseolotoxin, coronatine, and tabtoxin, can be produced by some lineages of P. avellanae. Siderophores are present in the P. avellanae species complex.Host rangeCorylus avellana, Camellia sinensis var. sinensis, Actinidia chinensis var. chinensis, A. chinensis var. deliciosa, Prunus avium, P. cerasus, P. domestica. A strain of P. avellanae has also been isolated from river epilithon.Disease symptomsPseudomonas avellanae can cause severe symptoms, including bud necrosis (kiwifruit), leaf necrosis and wilting (hazelnut, tea, kiwifruit, cherry/plum), shoot and twig blight (hazelnut, tea, kiwifruit, cherry/plum), flower necrosis (kiwifruit), fruit necrosis (cherry/plum), trunk canker (hazelnut, kiwifruit, cherry/plum), and plant death (hazelnut, tea, kiwifruit).EpidemiologySome P. avellanae lineages are favoured by air temperatures below 0°C. Penetration mainly occurs through stomata, leaf scars, and wounds induced by frost events. P. avellanae species complex exhibits both epiphytic and endophytic phases. During summer, very high temperatures can reduce the multiplication and dispersal of the pathogen. The global circulation of latently infected propagative plant material largely favours the spread of P. avellanae lineages across different cultivation areas.DetectionPathogens belonging to this complex can be detected in both symptomatic and asymptomatic plant tissues (e.g., twigs, buds, and cankers) using various conventional techniques and molecular tools (standard-, duplex-, TaqMan-, real-time PCR, LAMP, MLSA). Depending on the targeted symptoms, pathogenicity tests may be conducted on leaf, leaf scars or woody tissues.Disease controlDisease management is based on spray treatments to the crown using copper compounds applied in spring and autumn, as well as after harvest, during leaf fall, and following hail, frost events, and pruning. Balanced plant nutrition is important to reduce the risk of severe infection. Alternative promising strategies include the application of biocontrol agents, natural products, and bacteriophages.
items.authors: Scortichini M, Popović Milovanović T, Iličić R.

items.title: Immunolocalization of L-DOPA and differential MpPPO1-3 expression in the embryonic axis and cotyledons of germinating Mucuna pruriens var. utilis seeds.
items.abstract: The cell-specific localization of L-DOPA (levodopa) in plant tissues has not been reported previously. Here, we describe the first immunolocalization of L-DOPA in mature seeds of Mucuna pruriens var. utilis at 2-6 days after imbibition (DAI), using silver-enhanced light microscopy immunocytochemistry with a specific polyclonal anti-L-DOPA antibody. Histological sections from the embryonic axis and embryo cotyledons revealed that L-DOPA accumulates predominantly in the cytoplasm of parenchymatous and starch-containing cotyledon cells, as well as in the cells of the fundamental SAM and RAM meristems of the embryonic axis. A strong immunoreactive signal at the plasma membrane and intercellular spaces of root apical meristem cells is consistent with apoplastic L-DOPA accumulation and suggests potential export to extracellular compartments. Complementarily, we analyzed the expression of the three polyphenol oxidase genes (MpPPO1, MpPPO2, and MpPPO3) by semi-quantitative RT-PCR in germinating tissues (shoot apex, primary root, and radicle) grown under light (LG) and dark (DG) conditions, alongside L-DOPA quantification by TLC. MpPPO1 was the only isoform expressed in aerial tissues (shoot apex), whereas all three isoforms were detected in radicle and root tissues, with MpPPO3 showing the highest transcript levels in roots. L-DOPA content, as estimated by TLC densitometry, showed a positive, though not statistically significant, association with MpPPO1 expression across tissues (Spearman ρ = 0.77, p = 0.10, n = 6 tissue-condition pairs). Taken together, these results may support a model in which L-DOPA stored in embryonic tissues serves as a pre-formed deterrent. At the same time, active biosynthesis via MpPPO genes in germinating roots may contribute to allelopathic exudation during early seedling establishment.
items.authors: López-Sánchez L, Camas-Reyes A, Hernández-Orihuela AL, Martínez-Antonio A.

items.title: Calcium-dependent protein kinase signalling in plant immune responses: current status and future prospects.
items.abstract: Main conclusionThis review focuses on the critical role of CDPKs in advancing plant immunity research, highlighting how their functions can uncover key defence mechanisms and bridge critical knowledge gaps in the field. Calcium serves as the cornerstone of immune signalling, propagating pathogen-induced signals through specific sensors and decoders. Among these, calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) stand out as plant-specific signal transducers, directly converting calcium fluxes into defence activation. By modulating key immune components, CDPKs act as key hubs in plant immunity. Deciphering their role and crosstalks with other signalling networks is crucial for understanding the complexities of plant defence mechanisms. Although functional redundancy and extensive crosstalk among CDPK family members have historically hindered precise functional characterization, these features also highlight the robustness and adaptability of plant immune systems. Recent advances including high-throughput transcriptomics, comprehensive CDPK family-wide analyses, and multiplex genome-editing approaches such as CRISPR-Cas-based multi-gene targeting are now enabling finer functional resolution of CDPK members within complex multigene families. This review synthesizes current insights into CDPK-mediated signal transduction, with particular emphasis on their roles in coordinating defence responses and integrating with major signalling pathways, including mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascades, reactive oxygen species (ROS) signalling, and WRKY transcription factor-mediated gene regulation. Importantly, the continued development of integrative and high-resolution approaches is poised to overcome longstanding limitations in the field, facilitating deeper dissection of CDPK-specific functions. Collectively, these advances position CDPK research at the forefront of plant immunity studies, with strong potential to reveal novel regulatory mechanisms.
items.authors: Amrutha K, Resmi MS, Soniya EV, Vivek PJ.

items.title: Uncovering Physiological Responses of Idesia polycarpa 'Yuji' Under Alkali Stress via Transcriptomics
items.abstract: Abstract This study aimed to investigate the growth, physiological, and molecular responses of Idesia polycarpa ‘Yuji’ under different intensities of alkali stress, thereby providing a theoretical basis for its wider cultivation and application in saline-alkali areas. Two-year-old I. polycarpa ‘Yuji’ seedlings were used in a pot experiment. A mixed alkali stress solution of NaHCO₃:Na₂CO₃ = 9:1 molar ratio was applied at three concentration gradients: J1, 60 mmol·L − 1 ; J2, 90 mmol·L − 1 ; and J3, 120 mmol·L − 1 . Deionized water was used as the control treatment (CK). Our integrated analysis revealed that I. polycarpa ‘Yuji’ exhibited heightened sensitivity during the later stages of alkali stress, which progressively inhibited growth, damaged the microstructure of leaves and root tips, and severely impaired photosynthetic function, as evidenced by reduced pigment content and decreased net photosynthetic and transpiration rates. Physiological analysis revealed that as stress intensity and duration increased, soluble sugars (SS), soluble proteins (SP), proline (Pro) accumulated significantly, while malondialdehyde (MDA) content rose continuously, indicating severe oxidative damage to the cell membrane system. Peroxidase (POD) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activities showing distinct activation patterns. Hormonal analysis revealed that under J1 to J2 stress, abscisic acid (ABA) levels fluctuated, while indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), zeatin riboside (ZR), and gibberellic acid-3 (GA₃) levels increased, whereas under J3 stress they were suppressed. A total of 9,995 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified in the transcriptome sequencing of the control group (CK) and the J3 group. KEGG enrichment analysis revealed that DEGs were significantly enriched in pathways such as photosynthesis-antenna proteins. Transcriptome analysis identified 9 995 DEGs. KEGG enrichment analysis indicated that photosynthesis-antenna proteins, photosynthesis, and the plant MAPK signaling pathway played key roles in the response to alkali stress. In addition, hormone signal transduction-related genes, including ARR , ABF , PYR / PYL , and AHP , were significantly DEGs. This study clarified the physiological and molecular mechanisms underlying alkali tolerance in I. polycarpa ‘Yuji’ and identified candidate genes and key metabolic pathways associated with alkali stress resistance. These findings provide a theoretical foundation and genetic resources for stress-resistance improvement, efficient utilization of saline-alkali land, and the large-scale cultivation of this tree species.
items.authors: Chen C, Liu C, Dang Q, Shi Z, Wang Y, Li Z, Cai Q, Geng X, Zhang M, Dai L, Zhen L.

items.title: An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root.
items.abstract: Plant development is highly plastic, with growth and architecture continuously shaped by environmental conditions. Roots, for instance, adjust their development to local water, nutrient and soil conditions. Despite this plasticity, individual root cell types are generally viewed as largely homogeneous populations that progress along a single developmental trajectory1. Here we show that rather than progressing along a single developmental trajectory, most Arabidopsis root cell lineage trajectories exhibit a stereotyped bifid topology, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcript mapping. One branch is characterized by a transcriptional program that is shared across multiple cell types and enriched for genes associated with environmental responses, including abscisic acid (ABA) signalling. This state occurs reproducibly in a subset of cells across multiple cell types, independent of developmental lineage, thereby revealing an additional layer of root cell identity. It is conserved across Arabidopsis ecotypes and persists despite major perturbations in developmental identity. Moreover, it is reduced in ABA-deficient and ABA-insensitive mutants and becomes more prevalent under water-deficit conditions. Together, these findings reveal an additional layer of root cell identity that is superimposed on developmental lineage and its prevalence is modulated by environmental conditions. These results uncover a previously unrecognized source of environment-associated transcriptional heterogeneity shared across root cell types.
items.authors: Oliva M, Stuart T, Tang D, Khan A, Clement O, Makosa D, Poppe D, Pflueger J, Jabbari JS, Gigante S, Dragwidge JM, Petterson M, Whelan J, Lewsey MG, Lister R.

items.title: Carboxymethyl cellulose-ferulic acid nanocomposite enhances salinity tolerance and phytochemical accumulation in Dracocephalum moldavica via coordinated redox and osmotic regulation.
items.abstract: BackgroundSalinity is a significant constraint on medicinal and aromatic plants that limits their growth and photosynthetic activity, increases oxidative stress, and disrupts water balance.ResultsThe present paper prepared a carboxymethyl cellulose-ferulic acid nanocomposite (FA-NC), which is a bio-based nano-formulation to enhance the performance of Dracocephalum moldavica in the presence of salinity stress, and the effect was directly compared to free FA. Carboxymethyl cellulose was successfully used to prepare the FA-NC, which was verified by conventional physicochemical characterization. Salinity stress significantly reduced growth, fresh and dry biomass, stomatal conductance, chlorophyll pigments, and photochemical efficiency, and enhanced membrane damage and oxidative stress indicators. Both FA and FA-NC reduced these negative effects, but FA-NC was always stronger in protection compared to free FA. FA-NC was more effective in enhancing leaf hydration and membrane stability, and more powerful in minimizing oxidative damage (reducing H2O2 and MDA). This increased stress alleviation was accompanied by an improved antioxidant capacity (increased CAT, APX, and GPO activities and low protease activity). FA-NC also enhanced the accumulation of proline, glycine betaine, soluble sugars, and free amino acids that assist in the enhancement of osmotic adjustment in exposure to salt. Notably, FA-NC had a greater effect on the accumulation of major secondary metabolites, such as phenolics, flavonoids, anthocyanins, and tannins, than free FA, which is beneficial in maintaining medicinal quality during stress. PCA combined responses and emphasized the greater change in the FA-NC-treated plants towards desirable associations of traits when compared to free FA.ConclusionIn general, FA-NC nano-formulation is a sustainable and more efficient substitute for free FA to improve salinity tolerance and phytochemical potential in D. moldavica.
items.authors: Sarvi S, Razavi SM, Khalofah A, Zargar M, Ghorbani A.

items.title: Tropical leaf phenology as a thermoregulation trait: how changes in crown structure modulate thermal dynamics for two dominant Hawaiian trees.
items.abstract: Canopy and leaf temperatures often diverge from air temperature, influencing photosynthesis, water loss, and heat stress. While leaf traits are known to affect heat exchange, how changes in crown structure interact with environmental drivers to regulate canopy thermal dynamics is poorly understood, particularly in tropical forests. In a Hawaiian wet tropical montane forest, we used repeated UAV-based (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) thermal and LiDAR (light detection and ranging) measurements of sunlit leaves within and across 397 tree crowns of Acacia koa and Metrosideros polymorpha to investigate (1) seasonal and species-specific variation in crown traits; (2) how crown traits and environmental drivers interact to determine canopy-air temperature differences (Tdiff), within-crown thermal variability (TcanSD), and maximum leaf temperatures (TcanMAX); and (3) whether crowns with greater seasonal structural change exhibit enhanced thermoregulation. All crown traits showed species-specific seasonal dynamics, with trait-trait and trait-environment interactions shaping thermal metrics differently across species. In M. polymorpha, crowns with greater seasonal structural change exhibited lower relative Tdiff, whereas A. koa did not show this buffering effect. These results indicate that canopy thermoregulation emerges from interacting crown traits dynamically reshaped across phenological and seasonal cycles. Seasonal crown dynamics provide partial thermal buffering in some species, highlighting species-specific pathways of thermal acclimation or vulnerability under climate change.
items.authors: Bayliss SLJ, Broadbent EN, Almeyda Zambrano AM, Pau S.

items.title: Unexpected Localization of AGP Epitopes in the Plastids of Aldrovanda vesiculosa: New Questions About the Distribution of These Epitopes in Angiosperms.
items.abstract: Arabinogalactan proteins (AGPs) are the glycoproteins that are characteristic of plant cells (except for some algae) and are essential for cell function (cell-cell communication, cell adhesion, cell expansion, cell-wall organization, and signaling) but also for the development of roots, shoots, leaves, flowers, and reproductive structures. They occur inside and on the surface of plant cells, but mainly at the interface between the plasma membrane and the cell wall. Reports on the occurrence of arabinogalactan proteins in plastids are very rare and unclear. Our goal was to determine whether AGP-reactive carbohydrate epitopes are associated with plastids and starch in turion cells of Aldrovanda vesiculosa L. To do this, the localization of the AGP-reactive carbohydrate epitopes was assessed using immunolabeling and confocal and electron microscopy. Abundant signals for the antibodies LM2 and JIM8 against the AGP epitopes were detected in plastids. The LM2 signals were particularly frequent in starch grains. Also, electron microscopy confirmed the presence of AGP-reactive carbohydrate epitopes in plastids. These findings provide further evidence for the unusual intracellular localization of AGP-reactive carbohydrate epitopes in plastids and highlight starch grains as a target for future studies aimed at determining the molecular identity and biological significance of these epitopes.
items.authors: Płachno BJ, Kapusta M, Feldo M, Stolarczyk P, Świątek P, Leszczuk A.

items.title: Bacterial diversity in gut compartments of Tomicus brevipilosus: from shoot-boring preconditioning of Pinus yunnanensis to trunk-boring reproduction.
items.abstract: BackgroundGut bacteria are critically important to bark beetles, especially under environmental fluctuations. Tomicus brevipilosus undergoes a niche shift from shoot-boring (which weakens Pinus yunnanensis) to trunk-boring for reproduction. The relationship between this transition and the gut microbiota remains to be elucidated.MethodsUsing 16S rRNA sequencing, we characterized gut bacterial communities across adult feeding phase, sexes, and intestinal compartments.ResultsThe alimentary canal was composed of six morphologically distinguishable regions, to which Malpighian tubules were affixed. At the shoot-boring stage, no clear compartmentalization was observed in either sex, and no particular genus emerged as prominently associated. In trunk-boring adults, females undertake oviposition, whereas males evacuate excreta and food residues from the burrow entrance using their abdominal apex and elytral declivity. During the trunk-boring phase, compartment-specific differentiation was evident: the male rectum exhibited the highest bacterial ASV richness and complexity, harboring the greatest number of unique bacterial taxa at all taxonomic levels (phylum to genus), with significant enrichment of two short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing genera (Dietzia and Acinetobacter), suggesting a potential defensive role against gallery pathogens. In contrast, female trunk-boring adults showed no clear gut compartmentalization, although the genera Delftia and Halomonas may contribute to cellulose breakdown and thereby facilitate reproduction. These functional inferences, however, await direct experimental confirmation. Interaction analyses further revealed that gut bacterial communities across intestinal segments varied significantly with both stage and sex.ConclusionThese stage- and sex-specific patterns likely reflect differing physiological and behavioral demands during the niche shift. Our findings demonstrate that this transition drives structural alterations in gut bacterial communities across both compartments and sexes, and provide a basis for future exploration of symbiont-based management strategies for this destructive forest pest.
items.authors: Yang MR, Xie H, Dong SY, Li ZB, Kang WN.

items.title: A HAT7/ATHB13/Brassinosteroid signaling module mediates growth of laticifer cells in Euphorbia lathyris.
items.abstract: Laticifers, the coenocytic cells responsible for latex production, represent one of the most extreme examples of continuous and polarized growth in plants. Their unique architecture, extending over large distances, requires tight coordination between wall extensibility, cytoplasmic organization, and hormonal control. Here, we characterized the poor in latex 13 (pil13) mutant of Euphorbia lathyris which, similar to the previously described pil1 and pil6 mutants, is defective in laticifer expansion during post-embryonic phases of plant growth. Through comparative transcriptomic analyses of these three pil mutants, we identified a core set of 266 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) that define a transcriptomic signature associated with laticifers. We further identified a regulatory network linking two HD-Zip I transcription factors, HAT7 and ATHB13, with brassinosteroid (BR) signaling in the mediation of laticifer growth. This HAT7/ATHB13-BR module regulates the expression of laticifer DEGs involved in cell wall remodeling. Consequently, we found that laticifer cell walls are highly enriched in low-esterified homogalacturonan (HG) and branched rhamnogalacturonan-I (RG-I) pectins. Whole-mount immunolocalization revealed that laticifer cell walls exhibit a peculiar spatial segregation of pectic polysaccharides. These pectins follow a characteristic complementary, non-overlapping deposition pattern along the laticifer longitudinal axis, presumably conferring both elasticity and mechanical integrity. This modular pectin assembly appears compatible with the high flexibility and mechanical sinuosity required for growing of laticifers through host tissues, while accommodating internal turgor pressure changes derived from latex accumulation. Our findings define the laticifer as a cellular model in which wall remodeling, cell growth, turgor pressure, and hormonal signaling are mechanistically coupled.
items.authors: Escaray FJ, Antonelli CJ, Balaguer B, Vera-Antón C, Grau J, Franco-Zorrilla JM, Vera P.

items.title: CaZAT10-CaWRKY11 module positively regulates pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) salt stress response.
items.abstract: Salinity stress markedly impairs plant growth and yield. Pepper (Capsicum annuum L.), a prominent economic horticultural species, demonstrates a pronounced sensitivity to saline conditions. However, the adaptive mechanism of pepper plants under salt stress remains largely unclear. This study explores the physiological function of the transcription factor CaZAT10 in modulating the responses of pepper to salt stress. Our results reveal that CaZAT10 is primarily localized in the nucleus, and its expression is significantly upregulated following salt exposure. The silenced CaZAT10 pepper plants exhibit increased sensitivity to salt stress. Furthermore, the CaZAT10-silenced pepper plants also present heightened reactive oxygen species (ROS) concentrations. We also show that CaWRKY11 acts as an interacting partner of CaZAT10. Silencing of CaWRKY11 also results in a comparable salt-sensitive phenotype and increased ROS levels, mirroring the observations in CaZAT10-silenced pepper plants. Collectively, our findings suggest that the CaZAT10-CaWRKY11 regulatory module plays a crucial role in regulating pepper's resistance to salt stress by maintaining ROS homeostasis.
items.authors: Wang Y, Yu Y, Qiu L, Han H, Zhang L, Hu Y, Li H, Wen Y, Ji C, Liu J.

items.title: Diterpenoid alkaloids as potential insecticidal constituents from Aconitum carmichaelii lateral roots against Acyrthosiphon pisum and their neurotoxicity-associated responses.
items.abstract: Botanical pesticides are increasingly being explored for integrated pest management with environment friendly properties, which attracts our interests on the discovery of insecticidal candidates from Aconitum carmichaelii lateral-root for pest control. Herein, we evaluated the insecticidal activity of A. carmichaelii lateral-root extracts against the pea aphid, Acyrthosiphon pisum. The Total Alkaloids fraction, in which diterpenoid alkaloids represented the largest annotated category (35.07%), showed insecticidal activity after oral exposure (24-h LC₅₀ = 0.82 μg/mL) and contact exposure (24-h LC₅₀ = 16.47 μg/mL). Seven known diterpenoid alkaloids were isolated from this fraction; among them, neoline and isotalatizidine were potential insecticidal constituents, with mortality rates of 63.3% and 60.0%, respectively, against A. pisum at 100 μg/mL. Biochemical assays showed that Total Alkaloids exposure reduced acetylcholinesterase and glutamate decarboxylase activities, induced acetylcholine accumulation, and decreased Ca2+/Mg2+-ATPase activity. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses further indicated that the aphicidal action of the Total Alkaloids fraction was associated with neuroactive ligand-receptor interactions, ion homeostasis disturbance, detoxification responses, and metabolic stress. Molecular docking predicted that isotalatizidine and neoline may interact with neurotoxicity-related protein models, including GAD67, AChBP, AChE, and RDL. The results indicated that diterpenoid alkaloids were representative active constituents of the Total Alkaloids fraction from A. carmichaelii, supporting its potential development as a biopesticide for aphid control, and its potential neurotoxic mechanisms involved changes in cholinergic signaling, GABA metabolism, and calcium-mediated ion homeostasis.
items.authors: Liu B, Ma J, Li Z, Quan Y, Zhao X, Tian X, Gao J.

items.title: Integrated physiological, biochemical, and transcriptomic analyses reveal the mechanisms by which light intensity affects flowering traits and secondary metabolism in Dendrobium denneanum.
items.abstract: Dendrobium denneanum, valued for its ornamental and medicinal properties, exhibits significant regulation of flowering and secondary metabolism by light intensity. This study employed physiological, biochemical, and transcriptomic analyses to compare the regulatory effects of five light intensity gradients (50, 100, 200, 400, and 600 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹) on flowering traits and secondary metabolism in D. denneanum at different developmental stages. Results demonstrated that 400 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ markedly promoted flower organ growth, extending the flowering period, increasing the flowering rate, and enhancing flower color saturation, while simultaneously improving photosynthetic capacity and secondary metabolite accumulation. Notably, the regulatory effects of light intensity on floral morphological traits were most pronounced during the full blooming stage (S2), when flowers exhibited the greatest improvements in organ expansion, pigmentation, and bioactive compound accumulation. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that this light intensity upregulated photosynthetic light-harvesting processes and regulated carbon metabolism, optimizing light energy utilization and carbon flux to support flower development and flavonoid synthesis. Genes in the phenylpropanoid/flavonoid pathway were significantly upregulated, likely serving as key genes of flower coloration and medicinal component accumulation. Additionally, the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway suppressed stress-related genes and upregulated growth-related genes, promoting stomatal development and maintaining reactive oxygen species (ROS) balance to enhance stress tolerance.The transcriptomic results were further validated by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). These findings highlight how 400 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ optimizes photosynthetic efficiency, metabolic redirection, and growth-stress equilibrium, offering novel insights into light-mediated regulatory mechanisms in Orchidaceae plants and a foundation for precision cultivation strategies.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s12298-026-01815-2.
items.authors: Wang H, He S, Fan Y, Li T, Xu L, Ma J, Wu J, Liu H, Liu X, Mou C, Zhao M, Chen L, Zhu L, Zeng L, Luo A.
items.journal: Physiology and molecular biology of plants : an international journal of functional plant biology

items.title: A Review of Nuclear-Organellar Communication in Response to Heat Stress.
items.abstract: Plants coordinate their growth and developmental programs through dynamic communication in the core of the nucleus, enabling them to adapt to persistently high-temperature environments. Upon heat stress, plants primarily perceive and transduce thermal signals between the nucleus and other organelles, a process defined as nuclear-organellar communication. The published research on plants in response to heat environments mainly focuses on sensing heat physical signals from the plasma membrane (PM)/cytosol to the nucleus, eliciting nuclear transcriptional reprogramming and decoding organelle-derived retrograde signals to the nucleus. Consequently, plants have evolved sophisticated systems to decode adverse temperature signals relying on efficient nuclear-organellar coordination. This review summarizes how plants maintain cellular homeostasis via nuclear crosstalk. Heat signals are initially perceived, which triggers the production of secondary messengers including phosphatidic acid (PA), calcium ions (Ca2+) and reactive oxygen species (ROS). In addition, proteins also deliver thermal signals to the nucleus. As the central signaling hub, the nucleus orchestrates global transcriptional reprogramming predominantly through the Heat Shock Transcriptional Factors (HSFs)-heat shock proteins (HSPs) regulatory module, and sends instructions to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), chloroplasts and mitochondria. Conversely, organelle-derived retrograde signals coordinate stress adaptation: the unfolded protein response relieves ER stress, and heat stress activates ROS-mediated chloroplast-to-nucleus and mitochondria-to-nucleus feedback pathways. We further outline candidate thermosensing proteins residing in different organelles, and highlight major unsolved issues. Critical knowledge gaps include the intrinsic thermosensing capacity of chloroplasts and mitochondria, inter-organellar coordination of second-messenger dynamics, specific organelle functions, and the biological roles of membrane contact sites. Further mechanistic insights will facilitate the application of genome editing, synthetic biology and artificial-intelligence-aided design to breed heat-tolerant crops without yield penalties.
items.authors: Zhang L, Li X, Pan A, Su X, Chen L, Chen T, Feng B, Ni S.

items.title: Auxin interacts with kynurenine metabolism during organogenesis in Hypericum perforatum L.
items.abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated the presence of kynurenine (KYN) and kynurenic acid (KYNA) in several plant species, but their function in plant growth and metabolism remains undefined. We hypothesized that KYN and KYNA are metabolites of auxin and play a role in plant morphogenesis. To test our hypothesis, we developed a plant tissue-culture-based bioassay using Hypericum perforatum (St. John's wort; SJW), a model system for auxin and indoleamine metabolism which uses exogenous treatment with IAA, KYN or pharmacological inhibitors of KYN metabolism in humans (PF- 04859989, PF; RO -61-8048, RO or JM6) to investigate both morphogenetic and metabolic responses of kynurenine metabolism in planta. 10μM KYN supplementation increased root number and internodal length relative to control, and increased concentrations of downstream metabolites KYN, KYNA, and 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid (3-HAA) in both roots and shoots. Application of the inhibitors JM6 and PF which targets KYN monooxygenase (KMO) and KYN aminotransferase, respectively, lead to an increase in the pool of KYN present in tissues, but did not significantly reduce KYNA or 3-HAA. To investigate interactions between auxin and KYN, treatment with exogenously applied IAA with or without the inhibitors was also evaluated. IAA alone, significantly increased KYN and 3-HAA in explants. Co-application of JM6 and IAA partially recovered root organogenesis in explants. IAA + JM6 co-treatment also lead to the highest KYN accumulation in tissues, supporting an interaction between the pathways. Together, these data propose a role for KYN in IAA metabolism, shoot and root organogenesis.
items.authors: Gaudet D, Greene A, Murch SJ, Erland LAE.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: CaSNF1 interacts with and phosphorylates CaHD-ZIP to enhance cold tolerance in pepper.
items.abstract: Cold stress severely restricts pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) growth and productivity by disrupting cellular homeostasis and inducing oxidative damage. Although HD-ZIP transcription factors play important roles in plant abiotic stress responses, the molecular mechanisms regulating their function during cold stress remain largely unknown. Here, we characterized the pepper HD-ZIP transcription factor CaHD-ZIP and demonstrated that it is a nuclear-localized, cold-responsive protein that positively contributes to cold stress tolerance. To further investigate the regulatory mechanism underlying CaHD-ZIP function, a yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) screen identified the sucrose non-fermenting 1-related protein kinase CaSNF1 as a previously unrecognized interacting partner of CaHD-ZIP. Their interaction was confirmed by yeast two-hybrid, luciferase complementation imaging, and bimolecular fluorescence complementation assays, with BiFC indicating that the interaction occurs predominantly in the nucleus. In vitro phosphorylation analysis further demonstrated that CaSNF1 directly phosphorylates CaHD-ZIP, providing biochemical evidence for a functional regulatory relationship between these proteins. Complementary loss- and gain-of-function analyses, including virus-induced gene silencing and transient overexpression in pepper together with stable overexpression in Arabidopsis, demonstrated that CaSNF1 positively regulates cold tolerance. Silencing of CaSNF1 increased oxidative damage, impaired antioxidant enzyme activities, and suppressed the expression of antioxidant and cold-responsive genes, whereas overexpression produced the opposite effects and significantly enhanced cold tolerance. Together, these findings identify CaSNF1 as a CaHD-ZIP-interacting kinase and reveal a potential CaSNF1-CaHD-ZIP regulatory module involved in pepper cold stress adaptation. This study advances our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying pepper cold tolerance and provides potential genetic targets for improving cold resilience in pepper and other Solanaceae crops.
items.authors: Ullah I, Pei Y, Wang M, Hussain A, Guo J, Zhang H, Chen R.
items.journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik

items.title: Transforming Cadmium in Paddy Soils into a Catalytic Driver for Chlorantraniliprole Degradation: Implications for an Integrated Strategy for Tackling Heavy Metal-Organic Cocontamination.
items.abstract: Developing remediation strategies for heavy metal-organic cocontamination in paddy soils is imperative to ensure food safety. Current soil remediation strategies typically address these pollutant classes separately, often creating trade-offs in which mitigating one class of contaminants exacerbates the mobility or persistence of the other. Here, we demonstrate an integrated strategy that transforms heavy metal contaminants into a functional driver for organic contaminant degradation. Using cadmium (Cd)-chlorantraniliprole (CAP) cocontaminated paddy soil as a model system, we show that amendment with 0.5 wt % porous calcium-doped iron oxide (P-Ca@Fe2O3) achieves efficient Cd sequestration via Ca-Cd isomorphous substitution. This structural incorporation restructures the mineral electronic environment, generating abundant oxygen vacancies that activate ambient oxygen and water to produce reactive oxygen species, which drive the catalytic degradation of CAP applied during rice cultivation. Accordingly, Cd and CAP concentrations in rice grain are reduced by 77% and 61%, respectively, at the end of the 140-day rice cultivation experiment. By repurposing a soil pollutant into a functional component of the remediation process, our strategy provides a scalable, closed-loop catalytic process that restores contaminated croplands with minimal external inputs while safeguarding food safety.
items.authors: Yang L, Hou S, Zhou D, Cao Z, Alvarez PJJ, Chen W, Zhang T.

items.title: Integrated metabolomic-transcriptomic profiling of dwarf Camellia reticulata 'Hentiangao' reveals key gibberellin metabolism genes and multi-hormone crosstalk under GA3 treatment.
items.abstract: BackgroundCamellia reticulata 'Hentiangao', a dwarf camellia cultivar, possesses distinctive ornamental traits and high value for urban landscaping. Dwarfism is an important agronomic and ornamental trait, and gibberellin (GA) plays a central role in regulating stem elongation and plant height. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying its dwarf phenotype and the interactions between stem development and endogenous hormone networks remain unclear, limiting the promotion and targeted breeding of this cultivar. We analyzed shoot tips of C. reticulata 'Hentiangao' treated with 800 mg·L-1 GA3 at three growth stages (S1, S2, and S3; representing 0 d, 20 d, and 35 d after GA₃ treatment, corresponding to the untreated baseline stage, rapid internode elongation stage, and late developmental stage, respectively) using integrated metabolomic and transcriptomic approaches. Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) was used for metabolite detection, and Illumina HiSeq was used for transcriptome sequencing. Additionally, histological observations, endogenous hormone measurements, and differential gene expression analyses were conducted to characterize stem developmental changes induced by GA3.ResultsLC-MS analysis identified 31, 35, and 22 differentially accumulated metabolites (DAMs) in S1/S2 (S2 vs. S1), S1/S3 (S3 vs. S1), and S2/S3 (S3 vs. S2), respectively, with six DAMs shared among comparisons. Transcriptome sequencing generated 255,131 unigenes, of which 138,761 were annotated. A total of 4,396 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified, including 4,366 stage-specific and 30 common DEGs. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment analysis identified 36 DEGs associated with hormone pathways, particularly auxin, cytokinin, and gibberellin metabolism. Key genes (KAO, GA20ox, GA3ox, and GA2ox) and the DELLA protein were predicted to participate in GA biosynthesis and signaling. Quantitative real-time PCR analysis of six GA pathway genes (DELLA, KO, KAO, GA20ox, GA3ox, and GA2ox) showed expression patterns that were significantly correlated with transcriptome TPM values (P ConclusionsOur findings suggest that stem growth is regulated by a multi-hormonal network, with GA, auxin, and abscisic acid playing major roles during early development, whereas cytokinin, ethylene, and jasmonic acid become more influential at later stages. These results provide a preliminary basis for understanding the hormonal regulation of dwarfing in C. reticulata 'Hentiangao' and offer valuable insights for future fundamental research.
items.authors: Wang J, Tang X, Liu X, Zheng X, Zhu P, Sun M, Wang X, Yun H, Ge J, Li X.

items.title: Transcriptome analysis and hormone metabolic profiling provide molecular insights into flowering process in petunia.
items.abstract: BackgroundThe flowering process is a complex biological event regulated by coordinated transcriptional programs and hormone signaling. Petunia hybrida is an important ornamental plant, yet the integrative regulatory mechanisms between hormones and gene expression during flowering remain poorly understood. In this study, flowers of the petunia cultivar '112' were classified into three developmental stages based on days before anthesis: 7 days before flowering (DBF7), 4 days before flowering (DBF4), and the day of flowering (F). Integrated transcriptomic and hormone profiling analyses were conducted to systematically investigate gene expression dynamics and hormone metabolism during the flowering process.ResultsHigh-quality RNA sequencing generated over 483.36 million clean reads, with mapping rates exceeding 83.9% against the petunia reference genome. Comparative transcriptome analysis identified 7,160, 8,687, and 11,161 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in DBF4 vs. DBF7, F vs. DBF4, and F vs. DBF7, respectively. K-means clustering divided DEGs into four expression modules associated with primary metabolism, secondary metabolite biosynthesis, hormone signal transduction, and floral organ morphogenesis. Transcription factor analysis revealed that bHLH, bZIP, MADS, TCP, and WRKY families exhibited distinct stage-specific expression patterns during the flowering process. Hormone profiling revealed dynamic changes in auxin, gibberellin, jasmonate, salicylic acid, and abscisic acid contents. Integrated transcriptomic and hormone analyses showed that auxin, gibberellin, and jasmonate biosynthesis pathways were predominantly active during early developmental stages, in accordance with the expression dynamics of major biosynthetic genes (PhYUC, PhTAR, PhGA20ox, PhGA3ox, PhLOX, PhAOS, and PhOPR3). Gene-hormone network analysis revealed interconnections among phytohormone signaling pathways, particularly between jasmonate-gibberellin and abscisic acid-cytokinin, which are associated with representative genes involved in jasmonate-related lipid metabolism (PhPLA2A and PhOPR11), phenylpropanoid metabolism (PhPAL1 and PhCAMT3), and cell wall modification (PhPGLR4 and PhGUN25) during the flowering process.ConclusionsThis study provides a comprehensive overview of the transcriptional and hormonal regulatory networks governing the flowering process in petunia. Our results reveal a stage-specific regulatory framework in which coordinated gene expression and phytohormone interactions contribute to flower development and opening, providing potential genetic resources for the improvement of ornamental traits in petunia.
items.authors: Chen Y, Gao X, Chen J, Xu Y, Zhou Y, Yao D, Luo H, Liu J, Pan J, Zhang W.

items.title: Gfa1-dependent hexosamine metabolism maintains cell-wall integrity and developmental fitness required for crop colonization in Aspergillus flavus.
items.abstract: The fungal cell wall is a dynamic structure whose composition and integrity are closely coupled to metabolism, morphogenesis, and environmental fitness. Glutamine fructose-6-phosphate amidotransferase (Gfa1), the committed enzyme of the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway, supplies precursors for UDP-N-acetylglucosamine production and cell-wall chitin synthesis. Although Gfa1 is essential for growth and virulence in Aspergillus fumigatus, its role in the cell-wall biology and developmental program of the aflatoxigenic fungus Aspergillus flavus remains unclear. Here, we characterized a gfa1 deletion mutant and a complemented strain of A. flavus. Loss of gfa1 caused glucosamine/N-acetylglucosamine auxotrophy and markedly impaired vegetative growth and conidiation. Despite amino-sugar supplementation, the mutant exhibited increased sensitivity to cell-wall perturbing agents and significant reductions in cell-wall chitin and glucan, indicating disrupted cell-wall homeostasis. Gfa1 deficiency also severely impaired sclerotial formation and increased sensitivity to several environmental stresses. Importantly, the mutant showed markedly reduced colonization of peanut and maize seeds and no detectable aflatoxin B1 accumulation under the conditions tested. Consistent with its broad fitness defects, Δgfa1 displayed strongly attenuated virulence in Galleria mellonella. These findings establish Gfa1-dependent hexosamine metabolism as an important determinant of cell-wall homeostasis and developmental competence in A. flavus and reveal a link between amino-sugar metabolism, fungal surface integrity, sclerotial differentiation, and crop-associated fitness.
items.authors: Qin Q, Wang B, Fang W.

items.title: CPK10 phosphorylates zinc-sensing transcription factors bZIP19/23 to establish time-delayed negative feedback in plant zinc homeostasis.
items.abstract: Zinc (Zn) homeostasis is essential for plant growth; yet, how zinc-deficiency-triggered calcium (Ca) signals are decoded into homeostatic adjustments remains elusive. Here, we identify the calcium-dependent protein kinase 10 (CPK10) as a key decoder of zinc-deficiency-triggered Ca2+ signals. Under zinc-deficient conditions, both the protein level and the kinase activity of CPK10 increase. Subsequently, CPK10 interacts with and phosphorylates the zinc-sensing transcription factors bZIP19 and bZIP23, thereby repressing their DNA-binding and transcriptional activities. Zrt/Irt-like protein (ZIP) family members are the primary transporters responsible for zinc uptake from the soil, and CPK10-mediated phosphorylation of bZIP19 and bZIP23 reduces the expression of ZIP1, ZIP4, and defensin-like (DEFL) genes such as DEFL208. CPK10 activation is time-delayed, peaking at 72 h after zinc-deficiency treatment, providing a braking mechanism that prevents prolonged high-rate ion flux driven by sustained high-level expression of zinc transporters. The CPK10-targeted phosphorylation site Ser241 of bZIP19 is conserved in dicots but absent in monocots, suggesting evolutionary divergence in this zinc homeostasis-regulatory module. Our work reveals a Ca2+-CPK10-bZIP19/23 module that mediates spatiotemporal control of zinc homeostasis, highlighting a key regulatory layer in plant nutrient signaling.
items.authors: Deng Y, Yang C, Wu Y, Zhou Y, Chen Y, Wang C, Zhang Z, Ju C.

items.title: NIK receptor kinases propagate phytocytokine-triggered immunity by driving early phosphorylation events.
items.abstract: The perception of damage-associated molecular patterns and phytocytokines by pattern recognition receptors activates danger-triggered immunity, thereby amplifying plant immune responses. However, how phytocytokine receptor complexes are assembled, activated and regulated remains poorly understood. Here we show that all six members of the nuclear-shuttle-protein-interacting kinase (NIK) family, a clade within LRRII-RLK subfamily, contribute redundantly but distinctively to immune responses triggered by Peps and SCOOP12 in Arabidopsis. NIKs associate with the phytocytokine receptors PEPR1 and MIK2 and the co-receptor BAK1, and ligand perception transiently enhances these associations. NIK1, NIK3 and NIK6 undergo robust ligand-dependent phosphorylation that requires PEPR signalling, whereas PEPR1 and BAK1 can each phosphorylate NIKs. NIKs are dispensable for Pep2-induced PEPR-SERK association but are required for full phosphorylation output from the receptor complex, for efficient recruitment of BIK1 and PBL1 and for the activation of BIK1. Genetic complementation further identifies Ser615 and Tyr618 as essential for NIK1-mediated immune signalling, with Tyr618 preferentially controlling BIK1 recruitment and phosphorylation. These findings define NIKs as non-canonical, signal-propagating components of multiple phytocytokine receptor complexes and reveal how early phosphorylation events mediate danger-triggered immunity.
items.authors: Zhu W, Huang M, Li X, Lin Y, Xie J, Cheng J, Fu Y, Jiang D, Tsuda K, Yu X, Li B.

items.title: VvGAMYB Orchestrates Multi-Signaling Networks to Modulate GA-Induced Parthenocarpic Seedless Berry Development in Grapes.
items.abstract: Exogenous gibberellin (GA) efficiently induces seeded grape parthenocarpy and improves berry quality, with VvGAMYB serving as a key response factor. However, the VvGAMYB-mediated regulatory networks underlying this process remain unclear. In this study, GA3 treatment induced ovule abortion in 'Wink' grape, leading to the formation of parthenocarpic seedless berries. Exogenous GA drastically repressed VvGAMYB levels, thereby promoting parthenocarpy in grape ovaries. Through protein interaction screening, we identified 181 predicted VvGAMYB-associated proteins, which include differentially expressed genes related to hormone signaling, sugar metabolism, and transcriptional regulation, and further revealed that GA-induced grape parthenocarpy likely operates through a VvGAMYB-mediated network, coordinating key genes such as VvGID1B (GA signaling), VvRAP2-4 (ETH signaling), VvGAPC2 (glycolysis), and VvMETKs (methylation modification). Among these candidates, VvGAMYB repressed VvMETK2 promoter activity, whereas GA3 treatment weakened this repression, as demonstrated by a dual-luciferase assay in tobacco. Collectively, this study established an integrative framework in which VvGAMYB orchestrates phytohormone crosstalk, sugar metabolism, and epigenetic modification during GA-induced parthenocarpy. Our findings provide significant insights into the molecular network of GA-induced grape parthenocarpy and offer key target genes for the molecular breeding of high-quality seedless grapes.
items.authors: Wu Q, Chao R, Luo L, Huang Y, Li J, Liang L, Xuan X, Liu Y, Chen X, Wang X, Wang C.

items.title: Plant-derived extracellular vesicles deliver spermidine to reprogram macrophage metabolism and ameliorate rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is driven by macrophage-mediated synovial inflammation closely linked to metabolic dysfunction, highlighting immunometabolism as a therapeutic target. Here, we engineered spermidine-loaded red cabbage-derived extracellular vesicles (RCEVs@SPD) as a plant-based nanoplatform to reprogram macrophage bioenergetics. In LPS-stimulated macrophages, RCEVs@SPD suppressed pro-inflammatory polarization and enhanced mitochondrial function, as evidenced by increased ATP production and mitochondrial membrane potential. Assay-based measurements further showed reduced extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) and elevated oxygen consumption rate (OCR), indicating a shift from glycolysis toward oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Untargeted LC-MS metabolomics revealed coordinated alterations in pathways supporting mitochondrial cofactor biosynthesis, redox balance, and central carbon metabolism. Transcriptomic analysis confirmed enrichment of OXPHOS and mitochondrial respiration gene signatures with concomitant repression of glycolytic programs and PI3K-AKT signaling. In vivo, RCEVs@SPD significantly alleviated collagen-induced arthritis, improved joint histopathology, and promoted anti‑inflammatory macrophage polarization. Notably, systemic macrophage depletion abolished the additional therapeutic benefit of RCEVs@SPD, demonstrating macrophage dependence. Collectively, these findings establish plant-derived extracellular vesicles as a biocompatible delivery system that potentiates spermidine to restore macrophage metabolic balance and mitigate RA pathology.
items.authors: Wang X, He J, Hong Y, Zeng X, Li M, Cao S, Liang R, Zhou G, Wang Q.

items.title: Molecular mechanisms and application potential of MYC2 transcription factor-mediated plant stress responses.
items.abstract: Plant adaptation to drought, salinity, temperature extremes, pathogens, and herbivorous insects depends on coordinated hormone signalling, transcriptional control, and metabolic reprogramming. The jasmonic acid (JA) pathway is a major regulator of defence and the growth-defence trade-off, and the bHLH transcription factor MYC2 is a central node in JA output. Mechanistically, MYC2 is controlled through demonstrated protein-protein interactions with JAZ repressors, MED25, and selected transcriptional or chromatin regulators; it binds G-box-related cis-elements to regulate specific promoters, whereas many reported links to LOX/AOS, CBF, and antioxidant pathways are transcriptional or pathway-level rather than physical interactions. This integrative narrative review compares MYC2 orthologues across species, distinguishes MYC2-specific functions from those shared with MYC3/MYC4 or other clade IIIe bHLHs, and organises beneficial and detrimental stress phenotypes around pathogen lifestyle, target-gene polarity, tissue and developmental context, paralogue redundancy, and experimental design. We integrate genome-wide DNA-binding, transcriptomic, metabolomic, and protein-level studies, and critically evaluate demonstrated versus prospective applications of CRISPR/Cas genome editing. The synthesis identifies regulatory strategies that may exploit MYC2 networks whilst limiting growth, defence, and quality trade-offs.
items.authors: Yang LQ, Shu SL, Zhang YH, Huang G.

items.title: Plant Stress Signaling in a Cross-Kingdom Context: Metabolic Control of Redox and ROS-Ca2+-Hormone Interactomes.
items.abstract: Biological systems maintain functional integrity under environmental stress through tightly coordinated signaling networks, yet the mechanisms that preserve signal fidelity in the presence of stochastic oxidative and ionic fluctuations across taxa remain incompletely understood. Although redox regulation, coupling between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and Ca2+, and hormone-mediated feedback loops have been extensively characterized within individual kingdoms, a cross-kingdom framework linking these pathways through metabolite-mediated modulation is lacking. Here, a cross-kingdom compilation of evidence from plant, animal, and microbial systems is presented to examine how specific endogenous and microbe-derived metabolites and plant fructans modulate the fidelity of stress signaling networks. We propose a metabolite-guided signal fidelity hypothesis in which certain specialized metabolites act as molecular stabilizers in the response of organisms to stress. They buffer transient ROS bursts, limit variability in calcium signaling, and strengthen hormone-regulated feedback loops. Together, these functions preserve the signal-to-noise ratio of stress responses, independent of overt toxicity. These insights lay the groundwork for testable predictions and the development of translational strategies in agriculture, biotechnology, and medicine aimed at improving stress tolerance by stabilizing the flow of biological information.
items.authors: Warda M, Bolat M, Tekin S, Çinar B, Atasever A, Şengül E, Çelebi F, Cinar A, Taspinar MS, Ahmed BY, de Fátima Â, Ferreira ACS, Souza LFMP, Baek JI, Modolo LV, Bae J, Abd El-Aty AM.

items.title: A Simple and Highly Efficient Regeneration Protocol for Bougainvillea glabra: Achieving Callus Induction, Shoot Organogenesis, and Elongation on a Single Medium
items.abstract: Bougainvillea is among the most economically and horticulturally important flowering shrubs worldwide, yet its genetic improvement is severely constrained by low natural seed-set and frequent embryo abortion. Existing micropropagation protocols rely predominantly on nodal stem segments and thus bypass a totipotent callus phase, limiting their utility for molecular breeding and genetic manipulation. In this study, we systematically evaluated and compared the in vitro morphogenic competence of -young leaf versus seed-derived juvenile hypocotyl explants in B. glabra Choisy 'Light Violet'. Although -young leaf explants readily formed vigorous calli on medium containing 2.0 mg/L 6-benzylaminopurine (6-BA) and 0.2 mg/L 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D), they consistently failed to differentiate into adventitious buds across all tested conditions, indicating an intrinsic morphogenic recalcitrance. In sharp contrast, juvenile hypocotyl explants successfully overcame this developmental block, establishing a complete and highly efficient callus-mediated whole-plant regeneration system. Among six tested combinations of 6-BA, 2,4-D, and kinetin on Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium, the combination of 2.0 mg/L 6-BA and 0.2 mg/L 2,4-D uniquely induced compact, actively dividing callus that spontaneously initiated bud primordia within 25 days, achieving the highest adventitious bud differentiation rate of 90.4 ± 2.5%. Regenerated shoots rooted most effectively on half-strength MS (1/2 MS) medium supplemented with 1.25 mg/L 1-naphthaleneacetic acid (NAA) and 0.75 mg/L indole-3-butyric acid (IBA), reaching a rooting rate of 95.2 ± 0.7%. Crucially, the entire developmental sequence from hypocotyl callus induction and de novo bud organogenesis to shoot elongation was coordinated on a unified single medium (2.0 mg/L 6-BA + 0.2 mg/L 2,4-D), substantially streamlining the operational process and enhancing multiplication efficiency. This robust protocol provides a practical pipeline for high-efficiency mass propagation and establishes an indispensable cellular foundation for future genetic transformation and molecular breeding in Bougainvillea.
items.authors: Abolade O, Sang L, Lin X, Wang J, Huang S, Weng C, Yang J, Ren J, Zhao H, Song J, Wang H, Zhao H.

items.title: Heatwave-Resilient Cuticular Microbiota Protect the Leaf Beetle Plagiodera versicolora From Fungal Infection.
items.abstract: The increasing frequency and intensity of heatwaves-extreme thermal events characterized by prolonged supra-optimal temperatures-exert profound impacts on global ecosystem stability and species interactions. While the disruptive effects of thermal stress on host physiology and gut microbiota are well documented, the role of cuticular microbiota in host defense under heatwaves remains poorly characterized. Here, we show that the cuticular microbiota of the willow leaf beetle Plagiodera versicolora may serve as a thermostable protective barrier against the entomopathogenic fungus Beauveria bassiana. Using microbiota-manipulated larval models, we found that cuticular microbiota significantly bolstered host survival under both control (27°C) and simulated heatwave (32°C) regimes. High-throughput 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a dramatic microbial regime shift: Pantoea dominated at control temperatures, whereas Enterobacter proliferated and became predominant during simulated heatwaves. Both genera exhibited potent antifungal activity that markedly increased with rising temperature, suggesting a potential functional compensation property whereby thermally adaptive taxa may maintain host defensive capacity under climatic perturbations. Recolonization experiments confirmed that cuticle-isolated Enterobacter gergoviae and Pantoea anthophila are sufficient to reduce the increased fungal susceptibility of germ-free larvae. Mechanistically, these symbionts appear to inhibit fungal germination through direct antagonism and modulate host immune responses by upregulating antimicrobial peptide effectors while potentially reducing excessive immune recognition signaling. These findings highlight the resilience of cuticular defensive symbioses in the face of climate change and provide new insights into the adaptive mechanisms that sustain host-microbe-pathogen dynamics in a warming world.
items.authors: Wu J, Tu C, Fan R, Xu L.

items.title: MdMPK6a/b-mediated phosphorylation of MdANN2 restricts cytosolic Ca2+ influx and attenuates cold tolerance in apple.
items.abstract: Annexins (ANNs) are Ca2+-dependent phospholipid-binding proteins that play important roles in plant responses to environmental stress. However, the apple ANN gene family and the regulatory mechanisms by which ANNs participate in cold-stress responses remain poorly understood. In this study, 15 MdANN family members were identified in the apple genome and divided into three subfamilies. Among them, MdANN2 expression was strongly induced by low temperature. Functional analyses showed that MdANN2 overexpression markedly enhanced cold tolerance in apple, whereas virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) of MdANN2 compromised cold tolerance. Subcellular localization assays revealed that MdANN2 localized to the plasma membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus. Non-invasive micro-test technology (NMT) further showed that MdANN2 is associated with Ca2+-permeable channel activity: cold stimulation significantly enhanced cytosolic Ca2+ influx in MdANN2-overexpressing plants, whereas exogenous application of the Ca2+ channel blocker LaCl3 or the Ca2+ chelator EGTA substantially inhibited this influx. The kinases MdMPK6a and MdMPK6b physically interacted with and phosphorylated MdANN2 both in vitro and in vivo. Silencing MdMPK6a/b significantly increased apple cold tolerance, whereas overexpression of MdMPK6a/b reduced apple cold tolerance. Moreover, transient overexpression of MdMPK6a/b in the MdANN2-overexpression background attenuated MdANN2-mediated cold tolerance and Ca2+ influx. In addition, co-localization assays showed that MdMPK6a/b decreased the accumulation of MdANN2 at the plasma membrane. Together, these findings demonstrate that MdANN2 positively regulates apple cold tolerance by promoting cold-induced Ca2+ influx, a process inhibited by MdMPK6a/b-mediated phosphorylation. This study identifies a novel MdMPK6a/b-MdANN2 module that governs Ca2+ signaling in apple under cold stress, thereby providing promising molecular targets for improving cold tolerance in apple and other crop species.
items.authors: Wang J, Yang M, Li Y, Jiang L, Long Y, Zhang Z, Qiu L, Yang J, Ma F, Mao K.
items.journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology

items.title: MycorrhizaFinder: a user-friendly machine-learning tool to quantify endomycorrhizal colonisation of nursery and field roots.
items.abstract: Root colonisation by endomycorrhizal fungi has long been a widely used metric in mycorrhizal studies. However, due to the significant time required to assess colonisation using traditional microscopy techniques, studies of colonisation at large scales are impractical. Machine-learning-based approaches may increase output and facilitate ecosystem assessments. We trained a machine-learning-based tool (MycorrhizaFinder) on 42 field roots (132 unique 1 cm sections, with > 100,000 tiles) and validated on a further 37 sections from grasslands and heathlands hosting common Northern European plants with arbuscular (AM) and ericoid mycorrhizal (ErM) fungal structures, and dark septate endophytes (DSE), also common in field-sourced roots. We incorporated a user-customized confidence threshold to encourage engagement with morphological ambiguities, in e.g. ErM and DSE. A Macro F1 statistic was used to assess the tool's development performance. We provide a sample workflow from root processing and microscope slide scanning to semi-automated model training and performance evaluation. Our model performance combining all classes, the Macro F1, is conservatively 66% for arbuscular and 57% for ericoid mycorrhizal colonisation assessment. MycorrhizaFinder is user-friendly, requires no programming skills and offers flexibility for advanced agronomists or ecologists to train the tool using their own labelled mycorrhizal root datasets, including images acquired from different instruments or staining protocols. This adaptability allows users to customize the model for specific ecosystems or experimental designs. Leveraged with molecular identification and/or functional traits of fungi (e.g. arbuscules), MycorrhizaFinder supports scalable and repeatable nursery experiments and monitoring across ecosystems to assess mycorrhizal status and track land-use changes over time.
items.authors: Kowal J, Buckley S, Upham R, Kiani A, Rickards M, Serpell E, Bidartondo MI, Evangelisti E, Schornack S, Sibbit J, Treder KP, Weidinger S, Suz LM.

items.title: ATM2 promotes phosphoinositide formation to stabilize actin-plasma membrane contacts in pollen tubes.
A multidisciplinary characterization of Apulian chickpea local varieties by integrating SSR markers, drought-related gene expression and biochemical traits
items.abstract: Abstract The ongoing climate changes are increasing the frequency and severity of drought events, thereby threatening the productivity of many crops in the Mediterranean basin. Chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.), a nutritionally valuable grain legume of global importance, is widely cultivated in Southern Italy and exhibits considerable local biodiversity. In this study, nine chickpea landraces were comprehensively characterized by an integrated approach combining microsatellite-based genetic analysis, seed biochemical profiling, and gene expression analysis under simulated water deficit. Genetic variability assessed by SSR markers resolved the landraces into three clusters that largely corresponded to seed coat colour (white, red, black). Seed quality was evaluated by quantifying key biochemical parameters, including protein content, total phenolic compounds and carotenoids; red and black seeds contained significantly higher levels of phenolics and carotenoids than white seeds. Drought tolerance potential was investigated by imposing polyethylene glycol (PEG)-induced osmotic stress and quantifying the transcript abundance of two Kunitz-type trypsin inhibitor genes by quantitative PCR. The CaTPI-1 transcript exhibited a marked up-regulation in roots of red and black landraces under stress, whereas white-coated landraces showed reduced root accumulation of CaTPI-1. Collectively, these results indicate that red and black landraces combine enhanced antioxidant-related seed chemistry with a stress-responsive transcriptional profile potentially associated with improved tolerance to water deficit. These locally adapted chickpea genotypes constitute valuable genetic resources for conservation and breeding programmes aimed at enhancing chickpea resilience and nutritional quality in semi-arid Mediterranean agroecosystems.
items.authors: sialer MMF, Piergiovanni AR, SABETTA W.

items.title: On her cue: Papilla-derived jasmonic acid triggers rapid calcium signaling for pollen germination.
items.authors: Hafidh S, Tichy J.

items.title: α-galactosidase-mediated raffinose turnover regulates carbon allocation and vascular patterning of roots during chickpea germination.
items.abstract: Alpha-galactosidase is a hydrolytic enzyme that catalyzes the breakdown of raffinose family oligosaccharides (RFOs), releasing sucrose and galactose for metabolism during germination, development, and under stress. In chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.), RFOs serve as important carbohydrate reserves that support energy supply, phloem transport, and cell wall biosynthesis. This study investigates the effects of deoxygalactonojirimycin (DGJ), a known inhibitor of α-galactosidase, on root anatomy, sugar dynamics, and gene expression to elucidate its role in root development. DGJ-treated chickpea seeds resulted in reduced germination and root elongation. Anatomical analysis exhibited a decrease in root diameter, root cortex area, and vascular bundle area and a reduced number of metaxylem vessels with a difference in the architecture of the vascular bundle. From the sugar profile it is highlighted that RFO accumulated in the developing root tissues, reducing the sucrose and reducing sugar availability. This substantiated that α-galactosidase plays a crucial role in carbohydrate mobilization, vascular patterning, and root tissue development. Furthermore, DGJ-induced sugar stress triggered tissue-specific upregulation of α-galactosidase isogenes across both vascular and non-vascular root tissues, suggesting a coordinated transcriptional response to help restore sugar homeostasis. Collectively, this study uncovered that α-galactosidase plays a key role in the mobilization of RFOs during germination for the early root development.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s12298-026-01829-w.
items.authors: Jenisha JJ, Samuel M, Arunraj R.
items.journal: Physiology and molecular biology of plants : an international journal of functional plant biology

items.title: ZnO and SiO2 nanopriming enhancing seedling performance and changing volatile profiles of Melissa officinalis under drought and salinity stress.
items.abstract: IntroductionMelissa officinalis L. is an important medicinal and aromatic plant whose germination, seedling establishment, and secondary metabolism can be adversely affected by drought and salinity. This study investigated whether ZnO and SiO2 nanopriming could mitigate these effects and modify the volatile profile of M. officinalis.MethodsTwo independent factorial experiments were conducted under drought and salinity stress. Seeds were hydroprimed as the control or nanoprimed with ZnO or SiO2 at 50 or 100 mg L-1. Drought treatments were 0, -0.2, -0.4, and -0.6 MPa, while salinity treatments were 0, 4, 8, and 12 dS m-1. Germination and early seedling traits were evaluated. Selected 50 mg L-1 treatments under moderate stress conditions were subsequently subjected to volatile profiling by GC/GC-MS.ResultsNanopriming significantly improved several germination and early seedling traits, with the strongest responses generally observed at 50 mg L-1. ZnO at 50 mg L-1 increased germination from 42% in the non-primed control to 56% under -0.4 MPa drought and from 36% to 52% under 8 dS m-1 salinity. Low-dose ZnO and SiO2 also improved radicle and plumule growth and seedling vigour, although their effects declined under severe stress. Eleven volatile compounds were detected in all analyzed samples, with geranial and neral as the predominant constituents. Alloaromadendrene showed the largest descriptive change, increasing from 2.4% in the control to 6.3 -6.8% in selected treatments. Because volatile analysis was performed once per selected treatment (n = 1), these compositional differences were interpreted descriptively.DiscussionLow-dose nanopriming, particularly ZnO at 50 mg L-1, improved early-stage tolerance of M. officinalis to independently imposed drought and salinity stress and was associated with changes in its volatile profile. Replicated chemical analyses and greenhouse and field experiments are required to confirm the observed volatile responses and agronomic applicability.
items.authors: Mokhtarzadeh S.

items.title: Physiological and Antioxidant Responses of Rough Lemon (Citrus jambhiri L.) Rootstocks to Foliar-Applied Green-Synthesized ZnO Nanoparticles Under Drought Stress.
items.abstract: Drought stress affects citrus growth and physiological responses by impairing photosynthesis and antioxidant homeostasis. In this study, we produced green-synthesized zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) using leaves from Calotropis gigantea L. We assessed their effects on drought-stressed rough lemon (Citrus jambhiri L.) seedlings. UV-Visible spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and dynamic light scattering (DLS) confirmed the formation of hexagonal wurtzite ZnO nanoparticles with predominantly spherical morphology and nanoscale particle size. The synthetic material had a particle size of about 10 nm. We conducted a pot experiment under well-watered and drought conditions, withholding irrigation for 15 days and applying foliar ZnO-NP at 0, 50, 100, 150, and 200 ppm. Drought caused decreased plant growth, biomass, gas exchange, PSII performance, and chlorophyll relative content. ZnO application reduced these effects, and 150 ppm produced the strongest responses in plant height, number of leaves, biomass, SPAD, and PSII-related traits. Additionally, under drought conditions, 100-150 ppm ZnO also positively affected photosynthetic performance and antioxidant responses such as SOD, CAT, POD, TPC, and DPPH activity. Overall, green-synthesized ZnO NPs, especially at 100-150 ppm, enhanced the physiological attributes and antioxidant defense of rough lemon rootstocks under water-deficit conditions. These results indicate that they could be a nano-enabled method for citrus drought management.
items.authors: Tehseen M, Hou Y, Khan TA, Munir M, Zang X, Cao Z, Hu L, Zhou C, Wang L.

items.title: Comparative Performance of Biosorption Pretreatments for Vinasse Phytoremediation Using Salvinia minima.
items.abstract: Sugarcane vinasse is a liquid waste generated during bioethanol production. It is characterized by high organic load, acidity, elevated salinity, and recalcitrant compounds, including soluble phenolic compounds and melanoidins, which can hinder its treatment and limit biological processes. This study evaluated batch and fixed-bed column biosorption as pretreatments coupled with phytoremediation using Salvinia minima at laboratory scale. System performance was evaluated based on changes in pH, electrical conductivity (EC), dissolved oxygen (DO), chemical oxygen demand (COD), true color, soluble phenolic compounds (SPCs), and the non-dialyzable melanoidin fraction. Plant physiological responses were evaluated by measuring hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and malondialdehyde (MDA) contents. Following phytoremediation, vinasse pretreated by fixed-bed column biosorption showed greater removal of COD, SPCs, true color, and the non-dialyzable melanoidin fraction. Plants exposed to column-pretreated vinasse also showed lower H2O2 and MDA contents. In contrast, batch-pretreated vinasse adjusted to pH 6 showed an increase in the non-dialyzable melanoidin fraction after phytoremediation, suggesting structural modifications of Maillard reaction-derived compounds rather than their removal. The results indicate that the physicochemical changes occurring during biosorption improved the conditions of sugarcane vinasse for the growth of *S. minima*. Under the conditions evaluated in this study, fixed-bed column biosorption followed by phytoremediation proved to be a more suitable treatment than batch biosorption followed by phytoremediation for the integrated treatment of sugarcane vinasse.
items.authors: Tabernero NR, Chocobar-Ponce S, Gultemirian ML, Suárez F, Bruno C, Rosa M, Prado C.

items.title: Differential physiological responses to sodium and potassium chloride in Salicornia europaea, a model euhalophyte.
items.abstract: Sodium (Na) and potassium (K) have comparable crustal abundances and similar physicochemical properties. However, due to the predominance of NaCl over KCl in natural salinity, most studies on plant salt responses have focused on NaCl, leaving responses to KCl salinity largely unexplored. To compare plant responses to Na and K salts, the euhalophyte Salicornia europaea was grown under equimolar (100 mM) NaCl and KCl treatments. NaCl salinity enhanced plant dry biomass, succulence, water relations, and the accumulation of organic osmolytes, whereas KCl salinity induced defence responses, lignin deposition, and caused complete plant mortality within 7 weeks. The levels of signalling molecules (H2O2, NO, and H2S) showed distinct patterns between NaCl and KCl treatments. Genes involved in ion compartmentation (HKT1, NHX1, SOS1, and VHA-A) were upregulated only under NaCl salinity. Moreover, NaCl reduced cellular ammonium levels, whereas KCl led to its accumulation, accompanied by declines in amino acid and protein contents, suggesting a disruption of ammonium assimilation under KCl stress. Comparative studies involving two glycophytes and four halophytes revealed that whereas glycophytes exhibited similar or less growth inhibition under KCl than NaCl, halophyte growth was severely inhibited by KCl but stimulated by NaCl. Notably, ammonium accumulation patterns differed between the two plant types; being higher under NaCl in glycophytes, but higher under KCl in halophytes. Overall, despite the chemical similarity between Na+ and K+ ions, our findings demonstrate that K fails to activate adaptive signalling pathways to salt stress, highlighting ion-specific mechanisms underlying halophyte tolerance to NaCl salinity.
items.authors: Mohammadzadeh P, Hajiboland R, Haeili M.

items.title: The Fraxinus mandshurica genome reveals a dual adaptive strategy linking rapidly evolving immune receptors and structural fortification.
items.abstract: Fraxinus mandshurica exhibits high tolerance to ash dieback and superior wood mechanical properties, yet the genomic basis of these dual traits remains incompletely understood. Here, we present a chromosome-scale genome assembly of the elite clone 'M8' and integrate comparative genomics with temporal transcriptomics to investigate its adaptive architecture. We show that recent tandem and proximal duplications have contributed to the diversification and candidate positive selection of the NLR immune repertoire. Transcriptomic profiling reveals a stage-associated deployment pattern, in which expressed NLR genes are enriched during the Transition Stage, consistent with reinforced immune surveillance during rapid xylem expansion. As development progresses, the Latewood Stage shifts toward phenylpropanoid metabolism, lignification-related programs, and structural reinforcement. We identify and experimentally validate a latewood-recruited FmNAC104-FmPRX1 candidate regulatory module, in which FmNAC104 binds to and activates the FmPRX1 promoter and promotes endogenous FmPRX1 expression. Formal NAC/PRX gene family analysis further supports an enlarged NAC/PRX repertoire relative to P. trichocarpa and clarifies the orthogroup status of the FmNAC104-FmPRX1 module among related ash species. Collectively, our findings support a 'fortified defense' working model in which F. mandshurica temporally coordinates immune-receptor diversification with latewood-associated structural reinforcement. This study provides a genomic resource and candidate targets for breeding programs aimed at improving wood quality and disease resilience in Fraxinus.
items.authors: Yan J, Yang S, Feng Q, He L, Xin Y, Qi F, Zhan Y, Zeng F.

items.title: Genome-Wide Characterization of Phosphate Transporters Reveals Differential Regulation of Growth and Medicinal Metabolite Accumulation Under Phosphorus Deficiency in Ginkgo biloba.
items.abstract: Ginkgo biloba L. (G. biloba) is an important medicinal tree species rich in bioactive flavonoids and terpene lactones. Phosphate transporters (PHTs) play essential roles in phosphate uptake, transport, and homeostasis; however, their characteristics and functions in G. biloba remain unclear. In this study, 21 non-redundant GbPHT genes were identified from the G. biloba genome and classified into five subfamilies, including PHT1, PHT2, PHT3, PHT4, and PHO, containing five, one, four, six, and five members, respectively.
