items.title: Pantoea ananatis- triggered systemic resistance requires root sensing through the LORE receptor kinase in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: Abstract Systemic immunity induced by beneficial bacteria enhances plant resilience to subsequent pathogen attacks. However, the mechanisms by which plants perceive these bacteria and translate this perception into a systemic response remain poorly understood. The Brassicaceae LIPOOLIGOSACCHARIDE-SPECIFIC REDUCED ELICITATION (LORE) receptor kinase is the direct sensor of bacterial medium-chain-length 3-hydroxy fatty acids (mc-3-OH-FAs) and 3-(3-hydroxyalkanoyloxy)alkanoic acids (HAAs), both of which activate local Brassicaceae immunity. Here, we show that the HAA-producing bacterium Pantoea ananatis BRT175 can colonize Arabidopsis thaliana roots independently of the production of HAAs, but these compounds induce a lore-dependent local immune response in roots. P. ananatis triggers induced systemic resistance (ISR) against the necrotrophic fungus Botrytis cinerea, but not against the hemibiotrophic bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000. This ISR can be mimicked by HAAs or 3-hydroxy-decanoic acid (3-OH-C10), the strongest agonist of LORE. Both bacterium- and 3-hydroxylated fatty acid MAMP-induced ISR against B. cinerea rely on LORE-mediated sensing, involve salicylic acid, jasmonic acid/ethylene signaling pathways, and activate similar defense gene expression profiles in infected leaves. Our results demonstrate that lipidic microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) produced by beneficial microorganisms are necessary and sufficient to trigger rhizobacteria-mediated ISR and could differentially activate systemic resistance against biotrophic and necrotrophic pathogens.
items.authors: Duchateau S, Crouzet J, Cordelier S, Touchard M, Schellenberger R, Borrego C, Villaume S, Guise JF, Esmaeel Q, Groleau MC, Cloutier M, Gauthier C, Dhondt-Cordelier S, Mazeyrat-Gourbeyre F, Baillieul F, Ranf S, Déziel E, Aziz A, Dorey S

items.title: Root rot suppression by synthetic microbiota is associated with rhizosphere bacterial shifts and amino acid metabolism
items.abstract: Abstract Root rot caused by Fusarium oxysporum (F. oxysporum) severely constrains Codonopsis pilosula (C. pilosula) production. Indigenous culturable bacteria associated with C. pilosula were screened for antifungal activity, plant growth-promoting traits, and interstrain compatibility, and two defined three-member synthetic microbial communities, SCI and SCII, were constructed. Both SynComs alleviated root rot, with SCI showing stronger overall performance and a biocontrol efficacy of 57.8%, together with improved root growth and photosynthetic performance. Rhizosphere bacterial profiling was integrated with rhizosphere metabolite profiling and root tissue metabolomics. SynCom treatment was associated with limited changes in overall bacterial diversity but variation in specific rhizosphere taxa. In roots, pathway-enrichment patterns shifted from sulfur metabolism and oxidative stress-related processes under pathogen stress toward amino acid-related metabolism after SynCom treatment, accompanied by treatment-associated variation in medicinally relevant metabolite features. Associations between metabolic changes and potentially beneficial bacteria indicated coordinated variation between host metabolism and rhizosphere bacterial composition. In vitro assays further showed that L-valine elicited chemotactic and growth responses in a representative Sphingomonas isolate. Collectively, SynCom-mediated root rot suppression was associated with constituent-strain antagonism, plant recovery, rhizosphere bacterial shifts, and amino acid-related metabolic variation.
items.authors: Zhu N, Zhao P, Liu X, Leng F, Guo X, Yang Z, Zhou J, Wang X, Luo W, Gao D, Luo M, Wang Y

items.title: MGS-HCT enables resistance gene discovery and functional sequence design in forest trees.
items.abstract: Resistance gene discovery in forest trees remains challenging because of their large, repeat-rich genomes and the sparse distribution of functional elements, which restrict the direct application of deep learning approaches developed for crop species. While genomic language models have shown promise in crop species, their application to forest trees remains limited. Here, we present MGS-HCT (Multi-scale Gated Sparse Encoder-Hybrid Convolutional Transformer), a deep learning framework tailored for forest tree genomic sequences. The model integrates multi-scale gated units with structure-aware sparse attention for efficient sequence compression, and combines convolutional modules with transformer layers to capture both local motifs and long-range regulatory dependencies. We show that MGS-HCT supports two key applications in forest tree biotechnology: (1) the conditional generation and prioritization of putative NLR candidates for Alnus glutinosa (common alder) and (2) the de novo generation of synthetic DNA sequences containing promoter-like and splice-site-like elements. These results provide a computational foundation for accelerating disease-resistance gene discovery and genomic-assisted breeding in forest tree species, expanding the scope of deep learning from crop plants to forest genomics. By prioritizing candidates supported by multiple computational criteria for subsequent experimental validation, the framework is intended to narrow the experimental search space and help shorten the long breeding cycles of forest trees.
items.authors: Guan X, Wei Z, Wang L, Zhi D, Chen W.

items.title: Disruption of OsMAPKKK24 activation by the Xanthomonas oryzae effector XopY leads to compromised disease resistance in rice.
items.abstract: Mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase (MAPK) cascades are highly conserved signaling modules that play crucial roles in plant disease resistance. Emerging evidence shows that MAPK cascades are potential targets of plant pathogen effectors. Bacterial leaf blight (BLB), caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo), is a devastating disease in rice. Xoo secretes multiple effectors into host rice plants to suppress immune activation. XopY is a conserved effector across diverse Xoo strains; however, how XopY manipulates disease resistance and what its host targets are in rice remain largely unknown. Here, we report that XopY from the Xoo strain PXO86 interacts with the MAPK kinase kinase OsMAPKKK24 and RECEPTOR-LIKE CYTOPLASMIC KINASE 55 (OsRLCK55). OsRLCK55 phosphorylates OsMAPKKK24, and both contribute to rice BLB resistance by positively regulating early immune responses. XopY suppresses the activation of OsMAPKKK24 by enhancing its intramolecular interaction between the N- and C-terminal regions. The association of XopY with OsRLCK55 and OsMAPKKK24 also interferes with their interaction and suppresses OsRLCK55-mediated transphosphorylation of OsMAPKKK24, ultimately inhibiting MAPK activation and subsequent disease resistance. Taken together, these findings not only reveal that OsRLCK55 and OsMAPKKK24 are crucial for BLB resistance but also uncover a mechanism by which XopY compromises disease resistance by manipulating OsMAPKKK24 activation in rice.
items.authors: Chen L, Chen Y, Xu W, Wu X, Deng S, Wang Z, Tang D, Wang W.

items.title: MdAGL29 positively regulates MdBRC1/2 and negatively controls shoot branching in apple.
items.abstract: Key messageThe MADS-box transcription factor MdAGL29 serves as a negative regulator of branching in apple by modulating MdBRC1/2 expression. Branch number is one of the major determinants in apple tree architecture. MdAGL29, a member of the MADS-box transcription factor family, is downregulated by 6-benzylaminopurine, a synthetic cytokinin. Heterologous overexpression of MdAGL29 in poplar resulted in fewer branches and lower endogenous cytokinin content compared with the control after decapitation treatment. Yeast one-hybrid and dual-luciferase reporter assays verified that MdAGL29 positively regulates the expression of branch negative regulators MdBRC1/2. Collectively, MdAGL29 acts as a negative regulator governing branch development in apple. These findings provide a promising target for precise regulation of plant branching.
items.authors: Ji M, Li JW, Yang F, Liu JS, Zhang D, Ma JJ.

items.title: An investigation of the dual mechanism of uORF-mediated regulation of GGP1 expression and the effects on drought stress in cotton.
items.abstract: Upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are intrinsic regulatory elements that fine-tune gene expression at the translational level without altering genomic sequences or protein structures. Here, we targeted the conserved uORF that resides in the 5'-untranslated region (5'-UTR) of a GDP-galactose phosphorylase gene (GhGGP1) in cotton (Gossypium hirsutum). Regulation of GGP1 is a key control point of plant L-ascorbic acid biosynthesis. Using a dual-luciferase reporter system, we demonstrate that this uORF represses translation of the downstream GGP1 coding sequence in a feedback manner in response to elevated ascorbate, confirming previous findings in other species. Furthermore, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of the uORFGhGGP1 generated homozygous uorfGhGGP1 mutants with unchanged transcript levels but markedly increased protein abundance and L-ascorbic acid accumulation. Under drought stress, these mutants exhibit reduced malondialdehyde levels, enhanced total antioxidant capacity, and improved drought tolerance. Mechanistically, we further show that under drought conditions, the transcription factor GhBBM directly binds to the uORF-containing cis-regulatory element, enhancing (GhGGP1) transcription and drought resistance. Together, our findings establish the uORFGhGGP1 as a dual-layer regulatory module that integrates transcriptional activation by GhBBM with translational control of the downstream protein encoding open reading frame, thereby fine-tuning drought stress responses in cotton.
items.authors: Liu M, Li C, Zheng J, Cai Y, Wang P, Yuan J, Wang Y, Yan M, Li X, Bulley S, Ge X, Zhan J.

items.title: Identification of a stable major locus and candidate genes for drought tolerance during wheat germination.
items.abstract: We identified QRSH.scwl-4B as a pleiotropic QTL for basal shoot growth and drought-stress response at the wheat germination stage, predicted its putative candidate genes, and confirmed it as a promising locus for drought-tolerance and limited yield loss. Drought stress during germination severely reduces the wheat germination rate and seedling establishment, leading to significant yield losses. Understanding the genetic control of this trait is important for breeding drought-tolerant and high-yielding wheat varieties. Here, we detected 21 quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for maximum root length (MRL), root number (RN) and shoot height (SH) under control (CK) and drought treatment (DT) at the germination stage using a recombinant inbred line (RIL) population. Among them, QSH.scwl-CK-4B, QSH.scwl-DT-4B and QRSH.scwl-4B were co-localized to a common region on chromosome arm 4BS, which exhibited pleiotropic effects on both basal shoot growth and the drought-stress response. QRSH.scwl-4B was also identified by bulked segregant analysis sequencing (BSA-Seq), mapped to a 2.09 Mb interval on 4BS, and explained 24.32%-30.89% of the phenotypic variation (PVE). Through RNA-seq, BSA-Seq and parental genome sequencing, TraesCS4B03G0104700 and TraesCS4B03G0102800 were identified as the putative candidate genes. KEGG enrichment analysis suggested that TraesCS4B03G0104700 may regulate drought tolerance during germination via jasmonic acid (JA) biosynthesis. Moreover, the positive allele of QRSH.scwl-4B increased productive tiller number (PTN) by 13.37%, while showing only limited adverse effects on other yield-related traits. This suggests that QRSH.scwl-4B is a promising locus for improving wheat drought tolerance, with potentially minimal negative impact on yield. Collectively, these findings provide a foundation for cloning QRSH.scwl-4B and for improving drought tolerance in wheat through molecular breeding.
items.authors: Liu J, Wang D, Zhou Q, Qin N, Liu J, Liu X, Li Y, Peng H, Ma J.
items.journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik

items.title: Regulatory architecture tunes gene expression noise in the plant heat shock response
items.abstract: Cells within the same tissue can respond differently to the same stress, yet how gene regulatory networks generate and control this variability remains unclear. Here, we show that cell-to-cell variation in the Arabidopsis heat shock response is coordinated across the heat shock regulon and that the distribution of responses is tuned by the underlying regulatory network. Imaging of an HSP70 promoter reporter revealed basal activity in a subset of root cells and heterogeneous induction after heat shock, with some cells remaining near pre-stress expression levels. Dual reporters showed strong coordination between independently integrated HSP70 reporter loci, consistent with substantial shared upstream regulatory variation. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing confirmed heterogeneous but coordinated activation of heat shock genes across root cell types. Stronger heat shock states at both ambient and heat stress temperatures were associated with a recurrent thermoprotective programme across root cell populations, whereas weak responders after heat shock were associated with distinct cell-type specific transcriptional programmes, including defence- and jasmonate-associated states in some root cell types. Stochastic modelling suggested that HSFA2-dependent amplification could broaden the distribution of HSP70 expression across cells. Consistent with this prediction, experiments showed that loss of HSFA2 reduced HSP70 induction and lowered cell-to-cell variability after controlling for differences in mean expression. Together, these results show that the plant heat shock network controls both the magnitude and distribution of stress-responsive gene expression across cells.
items.authors: Goswami, R., Cano Ramirez, D., Abley, K., Afsharinafar, M., Reynolds, C., Zeng, J., Bhattarai, M. ,, Zhang, F. J., Cortijo, S., Hall, A., Colizzi, E. S., Locke, J. C. W.

items.title: Spent mushroom substrate mediates lead-cadmium immobilization and plant growth in tailings: Enhanced phosphorus availability and rhizosphere microbial modulation.
items.abstract: Mining activities cause severe heavy metal dispersion in tailings, threatening regional water and food security. The global mushroom industry generates enormous spent mushroom substrate (SM), a promising organic material for mine restoration. However, mechanistic comparisons between SM and three specific inorganic amendments (calcium carbide slag, CS; phosphogypsum, PG; coal gangue, CG) remain limited. A 60-day pot experiment on heavily polluted lead-zinc tailings (total lead: 16733 mg/kg; total cadmium: 78.04 mg/kg) compared SM with CS, PG, and CG treatments. SM reduced bioavailable cadmium by 50.46 %, lowered mild acido-soluble cadmium from 81.88 % to 70.15 %, and decreased plant cadmium. Higher bioavailable lead under SM still reduced root lead accumulation by 62.31 %. Microbially, SM enriched key functional microbes: Bacteroidetes rose from 2.66 % to 29.67 %, Leucobacter increased by 30.43 %, and AMF spore density increased tenfold. These shifts were associated with metal transformation and immobilization, reducing root cadmium and lead accumulation. Functional predictions indicated potential enhancement of microbial metal detoxification and organic phosphorus mineralization. Despite higher total phosphorus in PG, SM exhibited superior phosphorus availability. Improved nutrient supply and metal immobilization boosted photosynthetic rate by 230.89 % and lowered malondialdehyde (P < 0.0001). CS suppressed microbial diversity, probably through elevated pH, and CG exerted negligible remediation effects. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) revealed that soil nutrients indirectly lower metal bioavailability, linking soil fertility to plant performance. This study demonstrates that SM remediates tailings via integrated chemical and biological regulation, providing sustainable waste recycling for mine rehabilitation.
items.authors: Zhang Y, Wan M, He X, Li Z, Zhang H, He Y, Zu Y, Zhan F.

items.title: Direction-aware graph attention modeling and co-expression integration reveal novel core regulators of shared drought and salinity stress responses in rice leaves.
items.abstract: Although differential expression analysis has identified numerous drought- and salinity-responsive genes in rice, it cannot resolve the directional, transcription factor (TF)-driven regulatory architecture underlying responses across independent drought and salinity datasets. To address this, we applied TF-Anchored Directed SiGaResNet, a signed, direction-aware graph attention residual network with a TF-anchored edge-retention rule and permutation-based validation, to RNA-seq profiles from 92 rice leaf samples (51 stress, 41 control) derived from independent drought and salinity studies. Unlike conventional correlation- or co-expression-based approaches, the framework constrains regulatory inference around TF nodes while learning directed, signed relationships through supervised graph representation learning. Differential expression analysis identified 719 genes (405 upregulated, 314 downregulated), with induced transcripts enriched in stress-response and hormone-signaling processes and repressed transcripts dominated by photosynthesis- and secondary-metabolism-related processes. The framework showed strong cross-validated classification performance (MCC = 0.78 ± 0.17; AUC = 0.95 ± 0.05). The resulting directed gene regulatory network comprised 137 nodes and 163 edges and exhibited a sparse, modular architecture (modularity = 0.77; 15 communities), with TFs significantly enriched among regulatory source nodes (P < 0.001). Hub regulators were distributed across multiple TF families, predominantly bZIP, MYB-related, and NAC. Eighteen of thirty-two prioritized TF-encoding genes were independently corroborated within stress-associated WGCNA modules, and four comparatively uncharacterized candidates (Os07g0176200, Os05g0569300, Os03g0231000, and Os02g0187700) received convergent computational support from promoter cis-element enrichment, protein functional-association topology, and leave-one-out cross-validation classification. Quantitative real-time PCR further confirmed stress-responsive expression of all four candidates under separate drought and salinity treatments, supporting their prioritization as putative candidate regulators. These findings indicate that direction- and sign-aware graph attention modeling can integrate transcriptomic information from independent drought and salinity studies to identify biologically coherent, TF-centered regulatory patterns and prioritize candidate regulators for further functional investigation, without establishing causal regulatory mechanisms.
items.authors: Safarzadeh M, Tohidfar M.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Generation of lachrymatory factor synthase-suppressed onion (Allium cepa L.) by Agrobacterium-mediated gene transfer for CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing.
items.abstract: IntroductionLachrymatory factor, an irritating volatile compound that induces tearing, is produced when onion bulbs are cut or chopped. Lachrymatory factor synthase (LFS)-specific suppression in onion may reduce the lachrymatory effect and enhance flavor and health-functional properties. Genome editing enables precise modification of target genes in plant genomes. However, no reports targeting genes controlling onion-specific traits have been published. Therefore, we aimed to generate onion plants with reduced LFS activity via clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) genome editing.MethodsCalli induced from primary roots were transformed with Agrobacterium tumefaciens carrying expression cassettes for CRISPR/Cas9, guide RNA, green fluorescent protein (GFP), and hygromycin resistance; callus lines with a high frequency of stable GFP expression were selected as "elite callus lines" suitable for transformation. Cleaved amplified polymorphic sequence (CAPS), heteroduplex mobility assay (HMA), and Sanger sequencing confirmed mutations introduced into the LFS gene, and plants were regenerated from the confirmed LFS-edited callus lines.Results and discussionThe LFS enzyme activity was lower in the leaves and bulbs of the LFS-edited plants than in those of control plants, while the LFS-edited plants exhibited severe growth abnormalities and failed to set seed, possibly due to long-term culturing to maintain the elite callus line. The present study demonstrates the feasibility of onion genome editing to modify a specific onion trait, namely, LFS activity. Our findings provide a basis for further development toward the ultimate goal of producing tear-free onions with enhanced health-functional properties.
items.authors: Tamaru S, Imai S, Watanabe S, Ikegai T, Kondo S, Igawa T, Kamoi T.

items.title: CiSPL31, an SPL transcription factor, promotes fruit enlargement by upregulating SEPALLATA2 and LONGIFOLIA3 in pecan (Carya illinoinensis).
items.abstract: The SQUAMOSA PROMOTER BINDING PROTEIN-LIKE (SPL) family has been implicated in various plant growth and developmental processes; however, its role in flowering and fruit development remains poorly characterized in pecan (Carya illinoinensis). In this study, we identified 32 SPL genes in the pecan genome and divided them into six groups which displayed structurally conserved within groups but show structural divergence between groups. they Furthermore, transcriptome and RT-qPCR analysis indicated that CiSPL31 was highly expressed in flower buds and early developing fruits. Subcellular localization and transcriptional activation activity assay demonstrated that CiSPL31 is a nuclear-localized transcription factor with transcriptional activity. Overexpression of CiSPL31 in Arabidopsis promoted primary root elongation, flowering, and increased seed size and 1000-seed weight. And the expression of several seed size positive regulators, such as SEP2, FUL, LNG3, SHB1 and so on, were upregulated in CiSPL31 overexpression lines. Yeast one-hybrid and luciferase assays confirmed that CiSPL31 positively regulates CiSEP2 and CiLNG3 transcription by directly binds to the GTAC motif in the CiSEP2 and CiLNG3 promoter regions. Overall, our results provide a comprehensive understanding of the potential functions of the SPL family genes and a novel regulatory network of fruit size in pecan.
items.authors: Jin H, Feng X, Li C, Lim KJ, Wang Z, Yang Z.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Defining membrane-bound transcription factors in plant stress responses.
items.abstract: Biotic and abiotic stresses rapidly alter water and H2O2 fluxes, membrane fluidity, organelle redox state, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) proteostasis, affecting nuclear gene expression. Membrane-bound transcription factors (MTFs) and related membrane-associated pathways regulate the generation, localization, and activity of nuclear-competent forms of transcription factors through proteolysis, unconventional mRNA splicing, and post-translational regulation. This mini review examines ER-to-Golgi trafficking and proteolytic activation of bZIP17/28, IRE1-dependent splicing of bZIP60/OsbZIP50, the varied activation mechanisms of NAC/NTLs, and PIP-associated MYBs. PIP-MYB studies support transporter participation in MTF activation, although the contributions of transport activity and physical interaction remain difficult to separate. Most bZIP and NAC/NTL pathways respond to changes in ER, membrane, or organelle status. We discuss their roles in proteostasis, growth restraint, and immunity, and how pathogens exploit them. We also assess the evidence for direct transporter-MTF coupling and indirect regulation by membrane state. Their use in crops will depend on establishing how endogenous MTFs are activated and switched off, and whether the resulting responses improve yield across environments.
items.authors: Zhu Z, Yi D, Peng J, He Y, Wang C, Li J, Hu Q, Zou J, Wu J, Zhang S.

items.title: Genome-wide identification and expression profiling of IQM family genes in Chrysanthemum nankingense in response to abiotic stresses.
items.abstract: IQM proteins are plant-specific central modulators of calcium signaling, coordinating plant growth, development, and stress adaptation via calmodulin binding, yet no systematic characterization of the IQM family has been reported in Chrysanthemum nankingense. Here, we performed a genome-wide identification of the CnIQM gene family and conducted systematic bioinformatic analyses of their physicochemical traits, chromosomal distribution and phylogenetic relationships. RT-qPCR was used to detect transcriptional responses of CnIQM genes to exogenous phytohormones and major abiotic stresses, and yeast heterologous expression assays validated the stress tolerance of key CnIQM candidates. A total of nine CnIQM genes were identified. Most encode alkaline proteins predominantly localized to the nucleus or cytoplasm. Tandem duplication appears to be a major contributor to CnIQM family expansion, and all duplicated gene pairs are under strong purifying selection; high syntenic conservation of IQM loci is observed between C. nankingense and its congener Chrysanthemum lavandulifolium. All CnIQM proteins contain the canonical conserved IQ motif, whereas several paralogs exhibit structural variation with truncated UTR regions. Transcriptional profiling revealed differential induction under phytohormone, salt, drought, and cold treatments, with most genes rapidly upregulated by salinity and drought stress. Yeast heterologous expression assays showed that CnIQM5, CnIQM6, and CnIQM9 significantly improve salt and drought tolerance in yeast, while none enhances cold resistance in this heterologous system. This study clarifies the evolutionary and functional features of the CnIQM family and provides theoretical references and promising candidate genes for future functional research and stress-resistant molecular breeding of chrysanthemum.
items.authors: Wang T, Xie Z, Li S, Liu L, Lu N, Li C, Fan X, Han Q, Wang W, Pu S.

items.title: Nanobody-fluorescent protein fusions for erasable immunostaining.
items.abstract: Immunofluorescence (IF) staining is widely used to visualize biomolecules in cells and tissues. Conventional IF typically relies on fluorophore-conjugated antibodies, whose preparation requires chemical modification procedures that can compromise antibody performance and incur product loss during subsequent purification. In addition, iterative immunostaining depends on harsh stripping or fluorescence-quenching treatments that may damage sample architecture and epitope integrity. Here, we present protease-cleavable nanobody-fluorescent protein fusions (NFPFs) for reversible IF staining. Unlike fluorophore-labeled antibodies, NFPFs are genetically encoded and can be produced without post-synthetic chemical modification. By incorporating a tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease cleavage site between the nanobody and fluorescent protein, we engineered HER2- and EGFR-targeting NFPFs that retained high target specificity and enabled robust, concentration-dependent immunostaining of Capan-1 cells. TEV-mediated cleavage efficiently removed the fluorescent reporter while preserving cellular morphology and antigen accessibility, allowing subsequent staining of targets. Sequential labeling of distinct receptors demonstrated the feasibility of iterative immunostaining within the same specimen. Collectively, NFPFs provide a simple, scalable, and versatile approach for molecular imaging, enabling repeated rounds of immunostaining.
items.authors: Xu X, Kong Z, Su Z, Cheng C, Wan Y.

items.title: Jasmonate-Induced Metabolic Reprogramming Enhances Fruit Quality, Bioactive Compounds, and Stress Tolerance.
items.abstract: Jasmonates (JAs), including jasmonic acid (JA), methyl jasmonate (MeJA), jasmonoyl-isoleucine (JA-Ile), and cis-jasmone, have emerged as central integrators of plant stress adaptation, developmental regulation, and fruit quality formation in horticultural crops. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in JA biosynthesis, metabolic conversion, signal perception, and downstream regulatory networks governing abiotic stress resilience and quality-associated traits. We highlight the coordinated chloroplast-peroxisome biosynthetic pathway leading to the formation of bioactive jasmonates and discuss the molecular basis of JA signaling mediated through the SCF^COI1-JAZ co-receptor complex and key transcriptional regulators, including MYC, MYB, NAC, ERF, WRKY, and bHLH families. Emerging evidence demonstrates that JA signaling orchestrates reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis, antioxidant defense, osmotic adjustment, secondary metabolism, hormonal crosstalk, and stress-responsive gene expression in response to drought, salinity, temperature extremes, and heavy metal toxicity. Beyond stress adaptation, jasmonates play pivotal roles in regulating fruit ripening, anthocyanin biosynthesis, phenolic accumulation, aroma volatile production, cell wall remodeling, vitamin C metabolism, and postharvest quality maintenance. We also discuss recent progress in multi-omics integration, epigenetic regulation, CRISPR/Cas-based genome editing, systems biology, and precision agriculture approaches that are accelerating understanding and manipulation of JA-mediated pathways in horticultural species. This review provides a mechanistic framework linking JA signaling with metabolic plasticity, stress adaptation, and fruit quality. However, major knowledge gaps remain regarding context-dependent JA responses, hormone crosstalk, metabolic trade-offs, and field-scale validation. Future research should integrate multi-omics, spatial analyses, and standardized field trials to develop precise strategies for improving fruit quality and stress tolerance.
items.authors: Iqbal S, Tariq K, Elatafi E, Elhendawy B, Yu H, Liu W, Ali S, Aziz RB, Nadeem MY, Fang J.

items.title: Laccase-Based Biosensors for Functional Screening of Transcription Factors in Trichoderma reesei.
items.abstract: Efficient transcription factor (TF) screening is essential for the rational optimization of industrial microbial strains. Here, we present an absorbance-activated laccase-based biosensor (AALB) platform designed for rapid functional screening of TFs in Trichoderma reesei. By using laccase as a reporter, the AALB platform offers a robust and cost-effective screening system for TF functional evaluation. The secreted heterologous laccase also complements T. reesei's native cellulolytic machinery, expanding its enzymatic repertoire for lignocellulosic biomass deconstruction. The core of the AALB platform is a Pcbh1-regulated laccase expression cassette, enabling sensitive and efficient selection of TF variants based on absorbance readouts. To further improve sensitivity, we introduced a quadruple repeat of the cis-element-dense segment in the cbh1 promoter and integrated a high-activity heterologous laccase at the SLP1 site of the T. reesei genome. Following a miniaturized 2 day pre-culture in 24-well plates, the AALB platform enables TF variant ranking within 30 min of absorbance readout in 200 μL 96-well reactions, reducing the need for extended shake-flask fermentation and separate downstream enzymatic or molecular assays during the initial screen. Using AALB, we successfully identified TF variants with robust transcriptional regulation. The screening results were validated through transcript quantification of laccase and XYR1 and extracellular laccase activity assays. Notably, the XYR1 mutation XYR1_V821F, selected via AALB, significantly increased laccase transcript levels compared to PoLAC-SLP1 chassis control, with laccase activity reaching 17.74 ± 0.76 IU/mLa 2.7-fold improvement. Further characterization of the AALB-selected XYR1_V821F strain showed increased extracellular laccase activity together with increased xylanase and filter paper activities, with extracellular xylanase and filter paper activities increased by 2.7- and 1.9-fold, respectively, and enhanced rice straw hydrolysis under the tested fermentation and hydrolysis conditions. The AALB platform provides valuable insights into the synthetic biology and metabolic engineering of T. reesei, facilitating the development of industrial strains for lignocellulosic biomass processing and enzyme production.
items.authors: Xia Y, Yu J, Wang X, Feng Y, Lin Y, Lin X.

items.title: Genomic Signatures of Endemic Pathogen Exposure in a Declining Amphibian.
items.abstract: Endemic wildlife diseases can impose strong selection on threatened populations, yet whether persistence is associated with adaptive genomic responses remains poorly understood. We tested whether long-term exposure to Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) following population declines has left detectable selection signatures in the genome of the alpine tree frog, Litoria verreauxii alpina. Because prior work suggests limited immunity to Bd within the species, we did not expect persistence to be explained primarily by repeated shifts at canonical immune genes. Instead, we expected pathogen-associated differentiation, if present, to be diffuse and weakly shared across contrasts, potentially involving regulatory, signalling or reproduction pathways consistent with tolerance, compensatory recruitment or demographic turnover. Using genome-wide SNP data, we compared Bd-naïve and Bd-endemic populations and two 11-year temporal resampling contrasts. Candidate SNPs were annotated to identify genomic context, nearby genes, putative functions and overlap with previously reported Bd-associated transcriptomic responses. Using an empirical 99th-percentile XtX threshold, scans identified high-differentiation candidate SNPs in all contrasts. Most occurred in noncoding and putatively regulatory regions, with relatively few canonical immune genes. Candidate-associated genes were more often linked to signalling, transcriptional regulation and cell-cycle processes. A descriptive comparison with previous work in the species identified 64 candidate-associated genes matching Bd-associated transcriptomic annotations, supporting several immune-adjacent, regulatory, cellular and reproduction candidates. Persistence under endemic Bd might reflect pathogen-associated selection, compensatory recruitment and demographic change following recurrent adult mortality rather than uniform adaptive rescue through immune resistance.
items.authors: Wendt AS, Berger L, Skerratt LF, Brannelly LA.

items.title: Metabolically robust ratiometric autoluminescent reporters
items.abstract: Abstract Self-sustained luminescence enables non-invasive monitoring of molecular events at the whole-organism level, but its intensity depends on both gene expression and cellular metabolism, limiting quantitative interpretation. Here we present an approach that disentangles the contributions of gene expression and metabolism. By co-expressing an engineered reference luciferase variant that uses the same substrate but emits light at a different wavelength and monitoring the colour ratio, we substantially reduced signal variability, enabling quantitative physiological imaging despite changes in metabolic activity.
items.authors: Morozov VV, Balakireva AV, Gao F, Fleiss A, Mishina NM, Perfilov MM, Mitiouchkina TY, Palkina KA, Gorbachev DA, Gavrikov AS, Kotik AA, Mislavskiy SM, Wood KV, Yampolsky IV, Sarkisyan KS, Mishin AS

items.title: Genetic canalization of nutrient resorption in the widespread grass Phragmites australis under salt stress
items.abstract: Nutrient resorption is a key plant strategy for nutrient conservation, yet whether it responds plastically to non-nutrient stressors such as salinity remains unresolved. Using a common garden experiment with 110 genotypes of the cosmopolitan grass Phragmites australis , we first established that the imposed salinity treatment induced strong multilevel stress responses: above-ground biomass declined by >60%, sodium accumulated three- to fivefold across all leaf stages, and 484 metabolites showed significant differential accumulation, including canonical markers of osmotic and oxidative stress. Against this backdrop of confirmed stress, we found that nutrient resorption efficiency (NuRE) remained largely unaffected by salinity. Instead, NuRE was strongly correlated with phylogeographic lineage, ecotype, and latitude of origin, demonstrating evolutionary canalization rather than short-term acclimation. Element-specific regulatory patterns were also evident: while phosphorus resorption followed concentration-dependent control regardless of stress, nitrogen control was disrupted under salinity, and potassium resorption showed no such dependence. Our findings reveal that intraspecific variation in nutrient resorption is predominantly shaped by historical adaptation and geographic context, not by plasticity to salinity. This genetic canalization of a key functional trait implies that predictions of nutrient cycling under global change must account for the phylogeographic composition of plant populations.
items.authors: Liu L, Sheng W, Song H, Wang C, Li N, Lin L, Guo Y, Du N, Guo W
